exp.3:13:
Here is the explanation of 1 Samuel 4:14 in plain, modern English. It says that Eli, when he heard the loud noise of the people crying out, asked what the uproar meant. A loud roar is a very loud noise, and a great crowd crying out all together makes a din. The man came running quickly and told Eli what had happened.

Eli was a priest at Shiloh, and he was now very old and nearly blind. Israel had fought against the Philistines, and the ark of God was on the battlefield. Eli waited beside the road with a trembling heart, worried about the ark. The city had already cried out on hearing the news, and Eli, unable to see, could only ask.

When we fear bad news, we can see ourselves in Eli: his heart was anxious about what mattered to God. Today we can bring our worries to God honestly, and ask Him to help us put first what matters to Him.
exp.1:8:
He will watch over the steps of those who belong to him, whom the verse calls his holy ones because they are set apart for him. The wicked, those who live without God, fall into darkness, that is, into ruin and confusion. It ends with a clear truth: no one truly succeeds by their own strength alone.

The one speaking is Hannah, in a prayer of thanksgiving. She had been barren and humiliated, but God gave her a son, Samuel, and she dedicated him to serve in the sanctuary. Her song celebrates that God changes circumstances: he lifts up the humble and brings down the proud. That is why this verse speaks of trusting in God and not in oneself.

For today: when you feel weak or insecure, do not depend only on your own abilities. Pray and entrust your steps to God, trusting that he sustains and guides you.
exp.7:0:
And it came to pass, when Samuel was old, that he appointed his sons as judges over Israel. Judges were leaders who settled disputes and governed the people with justice.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not Samuel. Samuel had been a faithful prophet and judge for many years. This verse opens the account of how Israel ended up asking for a king. The verses that follow explain that the sons, Joel and Abijah, did not follow their father's example: they pursued gain and twisted justice. The Bible does not say why Samuel gave them that role, so it is better not to guess his reasons.

For today: faith and good character are not inherited automatically. If we have children, students, or people under our care, let us teach them by example and pray for them. And when choosing leaders, let us look more at their integrity than at their family name or their closeness to us.
exp.24:41:
Abigail did not waste any time. She got up right away, mounted a donkey, and went off with David's messengers, accompanied by five young women who served her. When she arrived, she married David and became his wife.

The narrator is telling the end of a story that began when Nabal, Abigail's foolish husband, insulted David and died shortly afterward. Abigail had acted with wisdom and humility to prevent a tragedy. Now David takes her as his wife. In that time it was common for a man to have more than one wife, and the Bible reports this here without approving or explaining it. The passage then mentions Ahinoam and Michal, which shows that David's life was complicated.

For today: Abigail responded promptly and humbly when a new chapter opened. When God opens a door, we can act with simplicity and without delay, trusting Him even when the future is not entirely clear.
exp.25:13:
Here David shouts from a distance, from the top of a hill, to all of Saul's army and especially to Abner, their commander. He challenges him: "Answerest thou not, Abner?" Abner replies with another question: "Who art thou that criest to the king?"

David has just entered the camp at night and taken Saul's spear and water jug while Saul was sleeping. Everyone was in a deep sleep sent by God. David stands at a safe distance and calls out to Abner to show that he could have killed the king but did not. He wants to prove his innocence and rebuke Abner for neglecting his duty.

For today: when someone accuses us or pursues us, we can respond with respect and truth, without seeking revenge. David had the chance to do harm and chose to trust God. Today too we can let God do justice.
exp.7:19:
Here the people of Israel insist on having a king. They say they want to be "like all the nations," that is, like the other peoples around them. They expect the king to govern them, go out before them, and fight their battles. The phrase "all the nations" here refers to the peoples or nations around them.

The people speak, represented by their leaders, before the prophet Samuel. He had just warned them what it would cost to have a king: he would take their sons, their lands, and their goods. Even so, they would not listen. God had already shown them that he himself was their King and their defender, so asking for a king like the other peoples showed a lack of trust. Even so, God grants them what they ask.

For today: it is easy to want to live like everyone else and to seek security in something visible. Before deciding, ask yourself whether you are trusting in God or merely copying others.
exp.17:26:
The explanation says that David went out with his men, defeated two hundred Philistines, and brought the king proof of his victory: the foreskins, that is, the skin cut away in circumcision. These were the bride price that Saul had asked for. He handed over the full count, even double what had been asked, and so Saul gave him his daughter Michal as wife.

Saul had asked for a hundred foreskins, but his real plan was for the Philistines to kill David. He wanted to be rid of him without getting his own hands dirty. David, unaware of that trap, gladly accepted the chance to become the king's son-in-law. The text that follows shows that the plan failed: God was with David, and Saul feared him all the more.

For today: faithfully do what is your responsibility, even when others have evil intentions against you. Do your part with integrity and trust that God can care for you and turn into good what others planned for harm.
exp.22:19:
The people of Ziph tell Saul to come down as soon as possible, to do everything his heart desires. They promise that they themselves will hand David over into the king's hands. The word for "come down" refers to going down from Gibeah toward the region of Ziph, which was higher and more desert-like terrain.

The speakers are some men of Ziph, from the tribe of Judah, who had already revealed David's hiding place. David, unjustly pursued, had just made a covenant with Jonathan before God. The men of Ziph seek to win Saul's favor, and he blesses them without seeing that he is pursuing an innocent man. The Bible does not fully explain why they acted this way.

For today: before joining in with what a powerful person wants, let us ask whether it is just. Pleasing others is worth no more than obeying God and protecting the innocent.
exp.5:13:
The cart carrying the ark came to the field of a man named Joshua, from Beth-shemesh, and stopped beside a large stone. The people split the wood of the cart for fuel and offered the cows that had pulled it as a burnt offering, meaning a sacrifice burned completely for God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark and suffered plagues, so they decided to send it back on a cart pulled by cows. The cows went straight toward Israel, and this was understood as a sign that God was directing everything. The people of Beth-shemesh, upon seeing it, rejoiced and worshiped.

For today: when God gives us back something or brings us out of a trouble, let us respond with gratitude and devotion. We can offer to Him from the heart what we have, holding nothing back.
exp.28:4:
The Philistine lords remind their king Achish of a famous song among the Israelites. The women sang it while dancing in rounds, which were groups or circle dances. The song said that Saul had defeated his thousands, but David his ten thousands. The lords use it as proof that David is a warrior greatly feared.

The Philistine princes speak, distrustful. Achish trusted David, but they thought that, in the middle of a battle against Israel, David could win Saul's favor by handing over Philistine heads. For this reason they demand that he leave. Without knowing it, they spare David from having to fight against his own people.

For today: sometimes God closes a door for us through people who reject us, and later we see that it was a protection. We can trust that He watches over our path, even when we do not understand it.
exp.3:21:
She says that the glory has departed from Israel, because the Philistines had taken away the ark of God. The word rendered here as "departed" does not mean wounded but carried away or sent into exile, like someone going into exile.

She is the wife of Phinehas, who is dying in childbirth. That same day Israel lost the battle, her father-in-law Eli and her husband died, and the ark was captured. She does not find comfort even in the birth of her son, and she names him Ichabod, a name usually understood as "no glory" or "where is the glory?". Scholars debate its exact meaning.

For today: God's presence does not depend on objects, buildings, or traditions. These may help us, but they do not replace God. Place your trust in God himself, and seek a living faith, not merely a religious one.
exp.24:36:
It says that the next morning, when Nabal was already sober (the wine had gone out of him), his wife Abigail told him what had happened. Then his heart died within him, meaning he was struck down and lost his strength, and he became as a stone. Many think it may have been a stroke or a heart attack, though the text gives no further details.

Context: the narrator explains that Abigail had saved her household from David's anger, since David was coming to take revenge because Nabal had insulted him. She waited until Nabal was sober before speaking to him. Ten days later, the text says the LORD struck Nabal and he died.

For today: there are right moments and right ways to speak hard truths. Abigail acted with prudence, and her hope was in God, not in revenge. Before we react with anger, let us ask for wisdom to act with calm and to trust in the justice of God.
exp.14:32:
Samuel tells Agag, king of the Amalekites, that just as his sword left many mothers without their children, so his own mother will be left without her son. Then Samuel executes him in Gilgal, before the Lord. "Hewed in pieces" is a strong expression; the wording is rarely used, and some understand it as a violent execution.

God had commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites, but Saul spared Agag and kept the best of the spoil. Samuel, as a prophet, carries out what Saul failed to complete. The Amalekites had attacked Israel cruelly in the wilderness. It is a hard passage, and Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: half-hearted obedience is not obedience. We can ask God to help us fully carry out what He asks of us with sincerity, without keeping only what suits us. And let us remember that Christ taught us to love even our enemies.
exp.14:33:
It says that Samuel went to his town, Ramah, and that King Saul returned to his house in Gibeah, his city. The words "went up" indicate that Saul went back to a higher place, as Gibeah was. The two men part ways after a very tense day.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul had disobeyed God by not completely destroying the Amalekites, nor their king Agag, as he had been commanded. Samuel put Agag to death and broke with Saul. The verses that follow say that Samuel never saw Saul again and that he mourned for him, while God regretted having made him king.

For today: obedience to God is not replaced by excuses or good intentions. And when someone strays from the path, we can grieve for that person and pray for them, without excusing the wrong.
exp.8:12:
They say that Saul and his servant will find Samuel as soon as they enter the city, before he goes up to the high place to eat. The people would not begin eating until he arrived, because he was to bless the sacrifice. Afterwards the guests would eat. The words "high place" refer to a raised place of worship, and "seer" refers to a prophet, and the guests are the invited ones. They are told to hurry, because it is the right moment.

Some young women who were going out to draw water are speaking. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys and wanted to consult the prophet. They give him precise and urgent information. The text that follows shows that God had already spoken to Samuel a day earlier, so this meeting was not chance.

God can guide our steps even in small and everyday matters. Today we can be attentive, act with diligence, and trust that God works behind circumstances, even when we do not notice it right away.
exp.24:13:
Here a servant of Nabal tells Abigail, the wife of his master, that David sent messengers from the wilderness to greet Nabal, and that Nabal treated them with contempt. The word "railed" in the verse means to insult or speak harshly to someone with words.

The one speaking is a young servant of Nabal. We already know that David asked for provisions respectfully, because his men had protected Nabal's flocks. Nabal answered with scorn, and David armed himself with four hundred men. The servant knows there is danger and goes to Abigail, because she has good sense, and Nabal listens to no one.

For today: when you see that a situation may end badly because of someone's pride, do not stay silent. Speak in time and with respect to the wise person who can help calm things down.
exp.21:21:
Here David tells Abiathar that he knew, on that day, that Doeg the Edomite was present and would surely tell Saul. The reference to Edom is clear in the verse itself, so no separate comment is needed. David acknowledges that he was the occasion, that is, the cause or reason, for the death of all the people of his father's house, the priests of Nob.

David is speaking while fleeing from Saul. He had passed through Nob and received help from the priest Ahimelech, and Doeg saw him. Saul ordered the priests killed, and only Abiathar escaped. David, on hearing of it, feels grief and takes his share of responsibility, although Saul and Doeg were the ones who carried out the slaughter.

For today: when our decisions, even without bad intent, have contributed to harm, we can acknowledge it with humility, without excuses. Then, like David, let us care for those who were wounded, offering them companionship and protection, and trust God with what we cannot repair.
exp.19:20:
Jonathan explains to David a secret signal. He will send a young servant to fetch the arrows. If he says to the boy, "The arrows are on this side of you, take them," David will be able to come out of his hiding place, because he is safe and there is no danger. The boy is a young servant, and the phrase "as the Lord liveth" is a solemn oath.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, speaks. David suspects that Saul wants to kill him, and Jonathan prepares a safe way to find out the truth and warn him without anyone else noticing. Their friendship is bound by a covenant made before God.

For today: true friendship shows itself in loyalty and care, even when it costs something. Think about who needs your discreet and faithful support this week, and help them sincerely, placing everything before God.
exp.12:8:
Saul orders that the complete offering be brought to him, called a "burnt offering" (an animal burned entirely for God), along with the "peace offerings" (offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving). Then he himself offers the burnt offering.

Saul is the first king of Israel. He was at Gilgal, with the Philistines preparing to attack and his people fleeing in fear. Samuel, the prophet, had told him to wait seven days, but he was taking a long time. Saul grew impatient and offered the sacrifice himself, something that was Samuel's task to do as priest and prophet. The verses that follow show that this was a serious mistake.

For today: when the pressure rises and God seems slow, it is tempting to act on our own. Let us learn to wait and obey, trusting that God knows the right time.
exp.28:2:
The chiefs of the Philistines see David and his men among the army and ask with irritation: "What are these Hebrews doing here?" Here "princes" refers to the rulers or leaders of the Philistine cities. Achish, the king of Gath, defends David: he says David has been with him for some time and that he has found no fault in him since David came over to his side.

The Philistines were getting ready to fight against Israel. David had taken refuge with Achish while fleeing from Saul, and Achish trusted him. The other chiefs distrusted him, fearing that David might turn against them in the middle of the battle. The Bible does not say that Achish knew of David's deceptions; it only shows what he believed.

For today: the way we live speaks about us. Even when others distrust us, honest and steady conduct can bear witness. But we must also take care that our alliances do not put us in difficult situations, and we should ask God for wisdom and direction.
exp.27:4:
This verse tells us that Saul looked at the camp of the Philistines and was very afraid. The word "trembled" in the verse above conveys that he was shaken, filled with anxiety and restlessness. The phrase "greatly" means exceedingly much. His heart, that is, his whole inner self, was shaken by fear.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel had already died, and Saul, king of Israel, faced an enemy army at Shunem. He had turned away from God through his disobedience, and that is why his fear was so great. Because God was not answering him, Saul ended up seeking a medium, something God's law forbade.

For today: when fear overwhelms you, do not rush to forbidden or doubtful sources looking for security. Come to God sincerely, acknowledge your failures, and trust that he listens to those who approach him with humility.
exp.10:12:
Saul says that no one is going to be put to death that day. The reason he gives is that the Lord has brought salvation to Israel. Saul does not take credit for the victory himself but gives the glory to God.

Saul is speaking just after being proclaimed king, following his defeat of the Ammonites who were threatening Jabesh Gilead. Some of the people had doubted that he could reign, and now they wanted to put them to death. Saul stops that revenge. Then Samuel leads the people to Gilgal to renew the kingdom and to offer sacrifices of thanksgiving to God.

For today: when God gives us a victory, we can respond with humility and mercy, not with pride or revenge. Giving thanks to God and forgiving those who doubted us shows a heart that has received grace.
exp.8:7:
Here the servant of Saul answers that he has in his hand a fourth part of a shekel of silver. The word "answered" carries the sense of replying again, and "man of God" means a man of God, a prophet. The servant offers that money to the prophet so that he may tell them which way to take.

Saul and his servant were looking for the donkeys of Saul's father that had been lost. They had no more bread, and they thought they could not appear empty-handed before the man of God. It was customary to bring a gift to the one being consulted. The servant, practical and attentive, solves the problem.

For today: when we seek direction from God, let us do it with humility and generosity. Also, God can use ordinary people, like this servant, to guide others toward his will.
exp.8:20:
Saul answers Samuel with amazement and humility. He says that he is from Benjamin, one of the smallest tribes of Israel, and that his family is the least important of that tribe. That is why he does not understand why Samuel speaks to him about something so great. The phrase "such a thing" refers to Samuel's statement that all of Israel's desire is set on him.

Here Saul speaks, a young man who was looking for his father's lost donkeys. Samuel, the prophet, already knew that God had chosen him as the future king. That Benjamin was "small" probably alludes to its size or little influence, and the Bible suggests something of this in Judges 20–21. Saul sees himself as unimportant.

For today: God does not look at what we appear to be, small or unimportant. We can accept his calling with humility, without boasting and without making excuses out of fear, trusting that He equips us.
exp.17:15:
It says that all the people, both Israel (the northern tribes) and Judah (David's own tribe), loved David. The reason was that he "went out and came in before them," an old expression that speaks of leading the people in their day-to-day life, especially guiding them in battles and returning with them. "Loved" is simply the ordinary word for love.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier it was said that God was with David and that Saul, the king, feared him. This verse shows the contrast: while Saul felt fear and envy, the people held David in high regard. Afterward Saul will try to use the Philistines to get rid of him.

For today: true leadership is earned through constant service and faithfulness, not through appearances. If you have some responsibility, make it a point to be present, to fulfill your duties, and to care for others, trusting that God sees and sustains your effort.
exp.16:17:
Jesse asks David to take ten cheeses of milk to the captain, that is, to the commander of the thousand soldiers where his brothers were. He also asks him to find out how they are doing. The word "well" means that they are in good health. "Take their pledge" means to bring back some sign or proof that they are alive and well; some think of a personal object, others of a reliable piece of news.

Jesse, David's father, is the speaker. His three oldest sons were in Saul's army, and Goliath had been challenging Israel for forty days. Jesse did not know how things were going, so he sends his youngest son with food and the task of bringing back news. Without knowing it, that simple errand would put David face to face with Goliath.

For today: God often uses small, everyday assignments to prepare us for great things. Do faithfully and lovingly what is asked of you today in your family.
exp.9:15:
Saul tells his uncle what happened with the donkeys: that Samuel had assured them the animals had already been found. The quoted phrase in the source wording, which is not in the verse your reader sees, has no equivalent to explain here, so that sentence is removed. Saul did not tell him anything about the kingdom, that is, that Samuel had anointed him as the future king.

Saul had gone out to look for his father's lost donkeys and ended up with the prophet Samuel. There he received an enormous piece of news: God had chosen him to rule Israel. His uncle asks him with curiosity, and Saul answers only part of it. The Bible does not explain why he kept quiet; it could have been humility, prudence, or fear, and this cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: not everything God entrusts to us must be shared right away. Asking God for wisdom helps us know when to speak and when to wait, with humility and without boasting.
exp.0:23:
This verse tells us that Hannah, once her son Samuel had been weaned, brought him up to the house of the Lord in Shiloh. She also brought three young bulls, an ephah of flour (a large measure of ground grain), and a bottle of wine, to offer as a sacrifice. Being weaned means he no longer nursed. The verse also makes clear that the child was young.

This is the narrator's account. Hannah had promised God that, if he gave her a son, she would give him back to serve him. Now she keeps her promise. The exact age of Samuel is not known; in that time weaning could happen at two or three years old, though this is not certain.

When we make a promise to God, Hannah encourages us to keep it faithfully and gratefully, even when it costs us. She also reminds us that what God gives us, we can return to him with trust.
exp.15:3:
Samuel obeys what God commanded him and goes to Bethlehem. When he arrives, the elders of the town come out to meet him trembling with fear and ask him: "Comest thou peaceably?" The word "peaceably" here means whether his visit is for good or for something bad.

God had rejected Saul as king, and he sent Samuel to anoint another man in secret. Samuel feared that Saul would kill him. The elders probably knew that Samuel was a prophet of great weight and that he sometimes arrived with messages of judgment. That is why they were frightened.

For today: obeying God does not always remove fear or tension, but He gives the next step. Do what God shows you, even when you feel afraid, and trust that He will guide you.
exp.15:9:
Here the account tells how Jesse brought seven of his sons before Samuel, one by one. After looking at them, Samuel told him that the Lord had not chosen any of them. The old wording is easy to follow: "made to pass" means he had them stand in line before the prophet, and "chosen" means picked out for a task.

Samuel had gone to Bethlehem on God's command to anoint a new king over Israel, because Saul had been rejected. Jesse was the head of the family, and Samuel was looking for the man whom God would point out. The older sons seemed like good candidates, but God was looking at something different. David, the youngest, was still missing; he was out caring for the sheep.

For today: let us not judge people, or ourselves, only by appearance or by the place they hold. God sees the heart and can call the one no one expected.
exp.1:33:
This verse says that God would give Eli a sign: his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, would die on the same day. A "sign" is a proof that what was announced would come to pass. In this way Eli would know that the rest of the message was also true.

A man of God, sent to Eli, speaks on God's behalf. Eli was a priest, but he did not correct his sons firmly, though they abused their office and despised the offerings. God announces judgment on that household. The fulfillment appears afterward, in 1 Samuel 4, when both of them die in battle.

For today: God takes sacred service and the responsibility of those who lead seriously, whether in the church or in the family. If we guide others, let us ask God for the courage to correct with love and to live with integrity, because our example matters greatly.
exp.9:7:
Here Samuel tells Saul to go down ahead of him to Gilgal. Samuel would come afterward to offer sacrifices: the burnt offerings, which were wholly burned up for God, and the peace offerings, which were offerings of fellowship and thanksgiving. Saul was to wait seven days, until Samuel came to tell him what to do.

Samuel, the prophet, has just anointed Saul as future king and has given him signs to confirm that God was with him. This command was a test of obedience at the beginning of his reign. Later, in 1 Samuel 13, Saul did not wait for the appointed time, although interpreters debate exactly how that scene relates to this command.

For today: God calls us to obey, and also to wait. Even when we have a good opportunity or a lot of pressure, trusting his timing protects our hearts from hasty decisions.
exp.12:1:
Saul chose three thousand men of Israel to form a small army. Two thousand stayed with him at Michmash and in the hill country of Bethel, and a thousand were with his son Jonathan in Gibeah of Benjamin. He sent the rest of the people home, each man to his own house.

The narrator of the book speaks here, describing how Saul organized his army at the beginning of his reign. Israel lived under pressure from the Philistines, their enemies. This step prepares for Jonathan's attack that comes later and for the whole conflict that follows. The figures for Saul's reign in the previous verse are difficult, and scholars explain them in different ways.

For today: great challenges are met with concrete, orderly steps, but without forgetting that victory depends on God, not only on our preparation. Let us plan wisely and trust in Him.
exp.16:51:
Here the explanation says that, on seeing Goliath fallen, the soldiers of Israel and of Judah rose up with a war cry and pursued the Philistines. They followed them to the valley and to the gates of Ekron. Many Philistines fell wounded along the road to Shaaraim, as far as Gath and Ekron. "Shouted" means crying out loudly, and "wounded" here refers to men who were killed or severely struck down.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. For forty days Israel had been paralyzed with fear before Goliath. When David defeated him by trusting in God, the army regained its courage and advanced. Israel and Judah are mentioned separately, perhaps because the kingdom was already distinguished into two groups, though scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: the courage of one person can encourage many. When you face your fear by trusting in God, your faith can give strength to others. And when God gives you a victory, do not stand still: move forward with gratitude and courage.
exp.19:7:
Here David asks Jonathan to deal faithfully with him. He calls for kindness and loyalty, and he reminds Jonathan that the two of them have made a covenant before the Lord. If there is any wrongdoing in him, he asks Jonathan to kill him himself, and not to hand him over to Jonathan's father, King Saul.

David speaks with Jonathan, the son of King Saul. David suspects that Saul wants to kill him, but Jonathan does not yet believe it. David proposes a test during the New Moon feast: if Saul becomes angry because of David's absence, they will know Saul's true intentions. David shows himself to be sincere and is willing to be judged if he is guilty.

For today: when a friendship or a commitment is based on truth and on God, we can speak with sincerity, even in difficult moments. Let us strive to be honest people, faithful to what we have promised.
exp.24:11:
After being turned away by Nabal, David's young men turned around and went back the same way they had come. When they arrived, they repeated to David everything Nabal had said. The note that "turned" means "turned around" and that the "young men" were the servants who attended David has been removed here, since those words are not part of this verse in your translation.

David and his men lived in the wilderness and had looked after Nabal's flocks without charging anything. David asked for some food during a feast day, but Nabal answered with scorn and mockery. The servants simply carry out their task: they bring back the full message. What follows shows that David reacted with great anger.

For today: when someone offends us, we can pause before acting. David let anger take hold of him after hearing those words. Let us ask God for calm so that we may respond with wisdom and not with revenge.
exp.16:21:
He says that David set down the baggage he had brought and left it with the keeper of the supplies at the camp. Then he ran toward the battle line. When he arrived, he greeted his brothers and asked how they were. The word "baggage" here is rendered in the verse above as "carriage," and "squadron" is a group of soldiers formed to fight, so the two are not mentioned further.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, and he does so with simple detail. Jesse, David's father, had sent him with food for his older brothers, who were in Saul's army. David carries out the errand with care and haste, just before Goliath appears. The text does not say that he knew what was about to happen.

For today: God often prepares important moments in the middle of small tasks. David was only carrying out a family errand, and there he met his great opportunity. Be faithful in doing what is at hand today.
exp.24:37:
This verse says that ten days after that night, God struck Nabal and he died. "Struck" here means that God hit him or punished him. The Bible does not explain how it happened; it only states that God was the one who acted.

The narrator tells of the end of Nabal, a rich and foolish man who scorned David and his men when they asked for help. David was going to take revenge with violence, but Abigail, Nabal's wife, stopped him with wisdom. Then, when he learned what had happened, Nabal's heart failed within him. Some think it may have been a stroke or a heart attack, but the text does not specify.

For today: we do not need to take revenge on someone who wrongs us. David recognized that God brought about justice without him having to stain his hands. We can entrust our hurts to God, do what is right, and trust that He judges with justice.
exp.8:25:
They got up very early the next day. When the first light of dawn was just beginning, Samuel called Saul, who had slept on the roof (the flat roof of the house). He said to him, "Get up, so that I may send you on your way." Here "send you on your way" means letting him leave or sending him back on his path. Saul got up at once, and the two of them went out into the street.

Samuel is the prophet and judge of Israel. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys, and God had already told Samuel that this young man would be the first king. Samuel had hosted him, given him a place of honor at the meal, and talked with him. Now he wakes him early to take him aside and give him a message from God, as the next verse shows.

God often speaks to those who rise ready to listen. If we give the first hours of the day to prayer and to the Word, our hearts will be more attentive to hear his direction.
exp.4:11:
It says that in Ekron the plague kept striking the people. Those who did not die were left sick with "emerods," a word that in the Hebrew can indicate painful tumors or sores; the exact illness is not known. Also, the city's cry "went up to heaven," that is, it was a very great cry of anguish.

The one who narrates is the author of Samuel. The Philistines had captured the ark of God and carried it from city to city. Wherever it arrived, punishment came with it. The people of Ekron became frightened and asked that it be returned to Israel. They understood that they could not treat God as an object of war.

For today: God is not a piece we use for our own convenience. We can draw near to Him with respect and humility, without wanting to manage Him or ignore Him. If today we feel anguish, rather than hardening ourselves, let us cry out to Him with sincerity.
exp.13:15:
The watchmen of Saul, who were in Gibeah of Benjamin, saw something strange in the Philistine camp: the crowd was confused, it moved back and forth, and it was falling apart. The watchmen are the lookouts who keep guard from a high place. The word translated as "troubled" means disturbed and frightened. The phrase "melted away" means that it was coming undone and falling to pieces.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan and his armor-bearer had attacked a Philistine outpost alone, and God sent a great trembling over the enemy camp. Saul's watchmen could only see the result, without yet knowing the cause. Soon afterward Saul discovered that Jonathan was missing.

For today: sometimes God works in ways we do not understand right away. A small act of faith can have great effects. Trust, and take a brave step, even when no one sees you.
exp.27:23:
The woman of Endor had a fattened calf at home, and she killed it right away. She also took flour, kneaded the dough, and baked unleavened bread, that is, bread that is prepared quickly because it does not need to wait for the dough to rise.

The narrator tells what happened after Samuel, who had been called by the woman, announced to Saul his defeat and his death. Saul was left without strength, for he had not eaten all day or the night before. The woman, who had seen his distress, urged him to eat, and his servants encouraged him too. She took a great risk in helping Saul.

For today: the woman generously cared for someone weak, expecting nothing in return. We can imitate that gesture by serving someone who is suffering with something concrete, such as a meal.
exp.17:1:
Saul took David that same day to keep him with him, and did not let him return to his father's house, Jesse's. The words used in the original are "took him" (which means "took him into his service") and "would not let him return" (which means "did not allow him to go back").

The narrator tells what happened after David defeated Goliath and spoke with Saul. Until then David went back and forth between the palace and his home to tend the sheep. Now Saul brings him into his court on a permanent basis. The text does not say what exact position he gave him here; later on he puts him in charge of men of war. All of this happens while the friendship with Jonathan is taking root.

God sometimes takes us out of our daily routine and leads us to a new place of service. If you face a change like this, trust that God is with you. And while it comes, be faithful in small things, as David was with his sheep.
exp.28:10:
This verse tells us that David got up early, together with his men, to return to the land of the Philistines, that is, to Ziklag, the city that Achish had given him. Meanwhile, the Philistines went up to Jezreel to prepare for war against Israel. "Early in the morning" means very early, and "his men" are David's men.

King Achish explained to David that the Philistine lords did not trust him and did not want him to fight at their side. Achish respected him, but he had to send him away. So David was spared from fighting against his own people, although the text does not say what David was thinking at that moment. Many see in this the care of God, who protected him without his planning it.

For today: sometimes a door closes and it hurts us, like a rejection or a plan that falls through. We can obey calmly, without fighting, and trust that God may be caring for us in something we cannot yet see.
exp.11:21:
The explanation says that God will not abandon his people. The reason is not that the people deserve it, but for the sake of his "great name" and because he himself chose to make them his own. "Will not forsake" means to leave or abandon someone alone. "Because it hath pleased" means that he chose them of his own will.

Samuel, the prophet and judge, speaks here in his old age. Israel had just asked for a king, showing little trust in God. The people were frightened and recognized their mistake. Samuel reassures them: they sinned, but God does not reject them. He asks them to keep serving him wholeheartedly and not to chase after empty idols.

For today: when you fail, do not pull away from God out of shame. His faithfulness does not depend on your perfection, but on his character and his love. Return to him sincerely, trusting that he has not let go of you.
exp.16:22:
This verse tells us that while David was talking with his brothers, Goliath came up, the Philistine champion from Gath, who stood between the two camps. He came out from the Philistine ranks and repeated the same challenge as always, and David heard it.

The narrator sets the scene. David, a young shepherd, had come to the battlefield to bring supplies to his brothers and see how they were doing. Goliath had been issuing his challenge for days, and the people of Israel lived full of fear. This is the first time David hears the challenge in person, and that prepares what he will do next.

For today: when everyone freezes before a giant problem, we can stop and listen carefully and ask ourselves what God thinks about it. Other people's fear does not have to decide how we respond.
exp.23:1:
This verse tells that Saul had just returned from fighting the Philistines. As soon as he came back, someone told him that David was in the wilderness of En-gedi. The phrase about being told is simply the news being given to him. En-gedi was a desert area near the Dead Sea, with caves and rocky cliffs.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Saul, the king, was pursuing David because he felt jealousy and fear of losing the throne. David kept hiding in strong places, that is, places that were hard to reach. As soon as Saul finished a war against an enemy of the people, he spent his strength again against David, whom God had chosen.

For today: Saul had a real enemy outside, but his greatest problem was inside, in his heart full of envy. Let us ask God to help us recognize these feelings and surrender them to him before they take control of us and harm others.
exp.6:2:
Samuel tells all the people of Israel that if they truly want to return to God with all their hearts, they must put away the foreign gods, including Ashtaroth, a goddess worshiped by the neighboring peoples. They must give their hearts fully to the Lord and serve him alone. Then God would deliver them from the power of the Philistines.

Samuel, prophet and judge of Israel, speaks here. About twenty years had passed since the ark arrived at Kiriath-jearim, and the people felt sorrow and longing for God. The Philistines held them in subjection. Samuel shows them that repentance is not only feeling sorry but also changing how one lives. Afterward, the people removed their idols.

For today: returning to God truly means letting go of whatever has taken his place in our hearts, such as money, pride, or an addiction. Ask God to show you what you should let go of today.
exp.19:33:
This verse says that Jonathan got up from the table in great anger and ate no food on the second day of the new moon feast. He was grieved for David and hurt because his father had shamed him.

Here the narrator is speaking, not a character. Jonathan had just defended David before his father Saul, and Saul responded by hurling a spear at him. So Jonathan understood that Saul was determined to kill David. His anger comes from the injustice, and his grief from his friendship with David.

For today: when you see injustice done to someone innocent, do not ignore it. Let it hurt you, but seek to act with wisdom and loyalty, as Jonathan did, and not with revenge.
exp.6:10:
This verse tells how the men of Israel went out from Mizpah, which were already disordered and defeated. They pursued the Philistines and struck them down along the way as far as a place called Beth-car. The words "pursued" and "smote" here mean that they chased them and kept defeating them.

The writer of the book relates what happened when Israel gathered at Mizpah to repent and return to God. The Philistines wanted to attack them, but God intervened with a great thunder that confused them. Then Israel went out to pursue them. It is not known for certain where Beth-car was; scholars have not reached an agreement.

For today: God acts when his people return to him with humility. Even so, we must take the step that we are able to take. Israel did not win alone, but neither did it stay still. Trust in God and act with courage.
exp.30:5:
It says that Saul, the first king of Israel, died that same day in the battle against the Philistines. With him died his three sons, his armourbearer (the young man who carried his weapons) and his men. It was the end of his reign and of his family's place on the throne.

The narrator tells how the battle of Mount Gilboa ended. Saul, wounded and fearing that the Philistines, the uncircumcised, would mock him, took his own life. His armourbearer followed his example. Years before, Saul had disobeyed God, and his story ended in tragedy. Some scholars debate how to understand his death, and the Bible only records it without approving it.

For today: a life can end badly when it drifts away from God, but today we can return to Him with humility. Our decisions also affect those who follow us, so it is wise to walk in obedience and ask for His guidance.
exp.9:20:
Here Samuel narrows down the selection of Israel's first king. First the tribe of Benjamin was singled out, then the family of Matri, and finally Saul, son of Kish. "Was taken" means that he was singled out, probably by casting lots. But when they searched for him, they could not find him.

Samuel speaks before the whole people gathered at Mizpah. Israel had asked for a king like the other nations, and Samuel reminds them that by this they were rejecting God as their protector. God grants them a king, but He is the one who makes the choice. According to the next verse, Saul was hidden among the baggage. The Bible does not explain why; many think it was out of fear or humility, though this is an interpretation.

For today: when God calls you to a responsibility, do not run away out of fear. Pray, ask for strength, and trust that He sustains the one He calls.
exp.8:2:
This verse tells us that the donkeys belonging to Kish, Saul's father, had been lost. Kish then told his son to take one of the servants and go out to look for them. The female donkeys are the she-asses in the verse, animals very valuable for work and transport.

Kish speaks here. He is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, described as a man of substance, that is, of good standing and respect. Before this moment, Israel had asked for a king, and the text presents Saul, a tall and handsome young man. This ordinary task, searching for lost animals, becomes the way by which Saul will come to meet Samuel. The Bible does not explain this here, but the account shows how God can work through everyday events.

For today: do not despise small tasks or setbacks. Do them with responsibility and trust in God, because he can use the ordinary to guide your life.
exp.17:4:
This verse tells us that David carried out every assignment Saul gave him, and he did it with wisdom and good judgment. Saul's appointment of David as commander over the men of war came because David conducted himself with intelligence and care. The people and Saul's servants approved of him and received him well.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. It comes after David defeated Goliath and became a close friend of Jonathan. The text shows that David's success came not only from his courage but also from his conduct. What follows, the song of the women, will stir up Saul's jealousy.

For today: do well whatever you are given to do, even when it is small, and do it with wisdom and honesty. That builds a good reputation. And if others praise you, keep a humble heart.
exp.2:5:
God calls Samuel a second time. The boy gets up, goes to Eli, and says, "Here am I; for thou didst call me." Eli answers that he did not call him and tells him to lie down again.

Samuel was a young man who served Eli, the priest, at the sanctuary in Shiloh. Eli was already old. Samuel thought the voice was Eli's, because, as the text says, he did not yet know the Lord personally or had not yet received his word. So he runs to obey his teacher.

For today: Samuel responded quickly and willingly, even though he did not understand what was happening. Sometimes God speaks to us in ways we do not recognize right away. We can cultivate an attentive and willing heart, and ask for help from people with more experience in the faith, as Samuel did with Eli.
exp.9:19:
He says that Samuel had all the tribes of Israel come near, and that the tribe of Benjamin was the one chosen. "Caused to come near" is an older way of saying bring close or gather together. "Was taken" means it was singled out, probably by a lot cast before God. The Bible does not describe the exact method here.

Samuel speaks at Mizpah before all the people. First he reminds them that God had brought them out of Egypt and that, even so, they asked for a human king. Now Samuel begins the process of presenting the first king. God guides the choice step by step: first the tribe, then the family, and then the person, Saul.

For today: God can guide our decisions, but first He wants us to examine our hearts. Before we ask Him for something, let us ask ourselves whether we trust that He cares for us and that He is enough.
exp.3:6:
The Philistines were frightened when they heard the shouting of the Israelites. They thought, "God has come into the camp," and they cried out, "Woe to us! Nothing like this has ever happened before." The word "camp" here means the military camp, and "woe to us" is a cry of distress.

The speakers are the Philistines, enemies of Israel. Israel had lost a battle and brought the ark of the covenant into the camp, as if its presence would guarantee victory. The Philistines believed in many gods, which is why they later speak of "mighty gods." They knew, though in a vague way, the stories of the Exodus. Their fear was real, but the account will show that Israel trusted in an object rather than in a sincere relationship with God.

Today we can learn that God is not a charm we control. Having religious symbols or shouting with enthusiasm is not enough. What matters is drawing near to Him with obedience and a sincere heart, not using Him for our own purposes.
exp.25:4:
David got up and went to the place where Saul had camped. From there he looked at where Saul and Abner, son of Ner, the commander of the army, were lying. Saul was sleeping inside the camp's defensive ring, which was probably the circle of wagons or baggage that surrounded the camp. The army's people were sleeping all around him.

Here the narrator is speaking. Saul was pursuing David in the wilderness, and David, who was fleeing for his life, learned from his spies where Saul was. This is the second time David has the chance to harm Saul.

When someone has treated us unjustly, we may have the chance to get even. Before acting, it is wise to stop, observe calmly, and ask God to guide us, so that we respond with justice and respect rather than revenge.
exp.28:8:
Here Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, tells David that he regards him as a good and trustworthy man, as an angel of God. But he explains that the Philistine lords do not want David to go with them to the battle. "Lords" here means leaders or rulers.

Achish speaks because David and his men were living among the Philistines, fleeing from King Saul. The Philistines were preparing to fight against Israel, and the other leaders distrusted David. Achish defends him, although in the end he sends him away. David says he wants to fight, but the Bible does not fully clarify his true intentions.

For today: sometimes others reject us or misunderstand us, even when our conduct has been good. We can keep a life of integrity and trust that God uses even closed doors to keep us from difficult situations.
exp.7:12:
This verse says the king would take the daughters of the Israelites to put them to his service. The ones who prepared perfumes and ointments, the cooks who prepared the food, and the bakers who made the bread were all tasks for the king's household and court.

The prophet Samuel is speaking. The people had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. God told him to warn them how a king would act. Samuel lists what the king would demand: sons, daughters, lands, and a share of the harvests. It is a warning, not a command from God for kings.

For today: before we insist on getting something, let us think about what it will cost us. And let us remember that no human leader can take the place of God in our lives.
exp.21:17:
This verse tells that King Saul ordered Doeg, a man from Edom, to attack the priests. Doeg obeyed and that same day killed eighty-five men who wore a linen ephod, a simple garment that priests used in their service. The word "fall upon" means to rush forcefully against someone.

Saul speaks out of jealousy and fear toward David. He had accused the priests of helping his enemy, although Ahimelech had helped David without knowing there was any treachery. Saul's own guards refused to kill the priests of the Lord, but Doeg, a foreigner, did it.

For today: when fear and pride rule the heart, they can lead a person to commit terrible injustices. Let us ask God for a humble heart, and have the courage to refuse to obey an unjust order, as those guards did.
exp.5:10:
This verse tells how the Philistines placed the ark of the Lord on the cart. They also put a chest with golden mice and golden figures in the shape of the tumors that had afflicted them. The "emerods" here refers to those painful tumors or sores, and the "coffer" is a small chest.

The Philistines had captured the ark, but a plague fell upon them. Their priests and diviners advised them to return it with an offering. To test whether the suffering came from God or was mere chance, they let two milk cows that had calves pull the cart. If the cows went toward Beth-shemesh, that would be a sign that God was acting.

When we face difficult situations, it is wise to recognize God rather than look for explanations that let us carry on as if nothing had happened. Humbling ourselves before Him opens the way to restoration.
exp.26:8:
He says that David attacked the region and left no man or woman alive. He would take sheep, cattle, donkeys, camels and clothing, and then return to Achish, the Philistine king. "Smote" means attacked; "asses" are donkeys; "apparel" can refer to clothing or spoils.

The narrator tells how David was living in Ziklag, fleeing from Saul. He attacked ancient enemies of Israel, such as the Amalekites, but led Achish to believe he was attacking Judah. To hide this, he eliminated the witnesses. The text describes these events without approving them; the Bible does not say here that God commanded them.

For today: even a man chosen by God can take paths of fear and deception. When we are under pressure, let us not justify lying or violence. Let us seek God and his guidance before we act.
exp.16:26:
The people of Israel repeated to David what had already been said before: whoever defeated the Philistine would receive a reward.

David had just arrived at the camp to visit his brothers. He asked what would be given to the one who struck down Goliath, and the soldiers answered him with the reward King Saul had promised. David was not asking only about the prize. It grieved him that this man was mocking the armies of the living God. His brother Eliab became angry when he heard it, but David kept asking.

For today: when something stirs you because it dishonors God, do not let criticism or fear silence you. Ask questions, look for what you can do, and act with humility, trusting that God works through ordinary people.
exp.14:4:
He says that Saul came to the city of Amalek and set an ambush in the valley. An ambush is a hiding place used to attack by surprise. The text does not explain more details of the plan.

God, through the prophet Samuel, had commanded Saul to punish Amalek, a people who had attacked Israel when Israel came out of Egypt. Here the narrator tells how Saul began the campaign. It is a difficult passage, and many understand it within the ancient context of God's judgment on a nation. Later, Saul obeys only in part.

For today: obedience to God is tested in the details, and it must be complete, not half-done. We can ask ourselves whether we are sincerely carrying out what God asks of us, or only what is convenient for us.
exp.24:33:
In this passage David swears by the name of God that, if Abigail had not hurried to come out and meet him, he would have killed every male in Nabal's household before morning light. Since the verse does not appear in the reader's wording in those terms, the explanation of the old phrasing is simply rendered as plain speech: David says that no one in Nabal's house who urinates against a wall would have been left alive by morning. He acknowledges that God held him back from doing harm.

David goes out with his men, angry, because Nabal, a rich man, rudely refused to give them food even though they had protected his flocks. Abigail, Nabal's wife, acted quickly and wisely, and brought provisions to David. Here David speaks with gratitude and recognizes that she stopped him.

Today we can learn to pause before acting in anger. If someone offends us, it is wise to listen to a wise voice and leave revenge in God's hands. Giving thanks for those who correct us in time spares us from mistakes we would later regret.
exp.16:10:
The explanation says that when Saul and all the people of Israel heard the challenge of the Philistine, they were dismayed and felt great fear. "Dismayed" means being very disturbed and left without courage. "Philistine" refers to Goliath, the warrior of the enemy army.

Goliath has been challenging Israel for days. He proposes that one man fight him alone, and that the losing side serve the winner. Saul was the king and was supposed to lead the army, but he and everyone else were paralyzed. The text does not say that they prayed or sought God at that moment; it only shows the fear. This sets the scene for David's arrival.

For today: when a great problem speaks loudly to us and fills us with fear, it is easy to look only at its size. We can stop, pray, and remember who God is before deciding how to respond. Fear is human, but it does not have to rule over us.
exp.13:24:
All the people of the land came to a forest, and there was honey on the ground, right where everyone could see it. The phrase about the ground refers to the honey lying on the earth, within easy reach of the hand. In this passage, the people of the land are the Israelite soldiers who were pursuing the Philistines.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had just come out of a victory that God had given them, but they were tired and hungry. Saul, their king, had made a hasty oath: no one was to eat until evening, or they would be cursed. So, although the honey was there, the people did not touch it.

For today: before making promises or giving orders, it is wise to think carefully. A decision made in haste, even when it seems zealous, can burden others with needless weight. Let us ask God for wisdom and calm.
exp.7:21:
God tells Samuel to listen to the people and give them a king. "Listen to their voice" means "do what they ask." Then Samuel sends the men of Israel away and tells each one to go back to his own city.

The elders of Israel had asked for a king so that they could be "like all the nations," that is, like the neighboring peoples. Samuel was troubled, but God explained to him that the people were rejecting Him as their King. God allows their request, although Samuel had earlier warned them what a human king would be like. Some see here a divine concession, not God's ideal plan.

Today, we sometimes want to copy what most people do instead of trusting God. Before asking for something, let us ask ourselves whether we really need it or only want to be like everyone else. God may allow what we ask for, but He also lets us live with its consequences.
exp.27:12:
The woman of Endor is frightened here because she sees something she did not expect. She realizes that her client is King Saul, and she protests to him. Saul calms her and asks what she sees. She says that she saw gods ascending out of the earth. The Hebrew word behind "gods" can mean a spiritual being or someone of great importance. "Deceived" here means "disguised."

Saul had gone in disguise at night, since he himself had forbidden consulting the dead. He was desperate: the Philistines were attacking him, and God no longer answered him. Scholars disagree about whether Samuel truly appeared or something else took place, but the text says that Samuel spoke.

Today, when we feel that God is silent, let us not look for answers in forbidden places. Instead, let us return to Him with humility and sincerity, and wait with patience.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that the sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were wicked men. The word "wicked" means that they lived without any respect for God. And the phrase "they knew not the Lord" does not mean they had never heard of Him, but that they did not truly know Him, with reverence and obedience.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. It comes right after Hannah's prayer, and the author sets Samuel, who serves the Lord, against these corrupt priests. The verses that follow show how they abused their office and took for themselves the meat of the people's sacrifices.

For today: we can know a great deal about religion and even serve in the church, but that is not the same as knowing God. Let us ask Him for a sincere heart that respects Him, and that our service never becomes an excuse for taking advantage of others.
exp.28:5:
Here Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, calls David and speaks to him honestly. He swears by the Lord that David has been upright, that he is pleased with David's conduct in coming and going, and that he has found no wrong in him. But he adds that the rulers, the leaders of the Philistines, do not approve of him.

The Philistines are preparing to fight against Israel. Their leaders distrust David and fear that in the middle of the battle he will turn against them. Achish, who did trust him, explains that David must go back. We do not know for certain what David would have done in the battle; the text does not make it clear. What we see is that God delivers him from a very difficult situation.

For today: sometimes someone recognizes our good conduct and yet others reject us. Let us not depend on everyone's approval; let us live with integrity and trust that God cares for our way.
exp.12:2:
It says that Jonathan, Saul's son, attacked and defeated the Philistine garrison, that is, the group of enemy soldiers who guarded the place. The word for hill in the verse is "Geba." Hmm, that's a place name, so I'll leave it. The Philistines heard about it, and Saul had trumpets blown throughout the land to call the Hebrews, that is, the Israelites.

The narrator tells how a war against the Philistines began, the people who dominated Israel. Saul was the first king, and here he calls the people together. The following verses show that Saul received the credit, though Jonathan was the one who struck the blow. Afterward the Philistines gathered a huge army, and the people were filled with fear.

For today: taking a brave step can bring a bigger reaction than expected. Before acting, let us pray, ask God for direction, and trust that He sustains the one who obeys Him, even when the path becomes hard.
exp.13:17:
Saul orders the priest to bring the ark of God. The text adds that at that time the ark was with the Israelites. Old or unusual words: the ark is the sacred chest that represented God's presence.

Saul and his people notice great confusion in the Philistine camp and discover that Jonathan and his armor-bearer are missing. Saul wants to consult God through the priest. But the commotion grows so much that Saul says, "Withdraw your hand," and goes out to battle without waiting for an answer. Some scholars point out that, according to the Hebrew text, it could be the ephod and not the ark; this is debated.

Seeking God is good, but doing it halfway, in a hurry, or without waiting for his answer leaves us acting on our own. Before deciding, take the time to pray and listen, and do not leave it unfinished when the pressure comes.
exp.24:32:
Here David tells Abigail that her advice is good and that she is blessed, because she kept him from killing someone and from taking vengeance with his own hand. "Good judgment" means sound thinking, the wise way of reasoning. "Held back" means hindered or stopped.

David speaks after Nabal, a rich and foolish man, treated him with contempt and refused food to his men. David, angry, set out with armed men to kill the males of Nabal's household. Abigail, Nabal's wife, went out to meet him with provisions and spoke to him humbly, reminding him not to burden his conscience with a vengeance. David acknowledges that God sent her.

When we are angry, it is wise to listen to someone who speaks to us with wisdom. Before we take revenge, let us pause and allow God to guide the situation.
exp.22:1:
This verse tells how David asked God whether he should go to fight the Philistines who were attacking Keilah. God told him plainly that he should: go, strike them down, and save that town.

The phrase "asked God" in this verse means David sought direction from the Lord, and "strike" here means attack or defeat. The threshing floors mentioned in the wider passage were the places where grain was separated from the straw.

David was running from King Saul, and yet he learned that Keilah, a town in Judah, was being plundered. Before acting, he did not rely only on his own courage; he asked God. Later, when his men became afraid, he asked again and received the same answer along with a promise of victory.

For today: before making important decisions, even good ones, pray and seek God's guidance. When doubts or fears arise, ask him again for direction with humility, and look for confirmation in his Word and in wise counsel.
exp.1:25:
This verse says that Samuel, while still a child or young man, grew in stature and also in character. The phrase "grew on" means that he kept advancing, improving, and making progress. He did so in a way that pleased both God and the people around him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He sets Samuel in contrast with the sons of the priest Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, who abused their position and led the people into sin. Eli rebuked them, but they did not listen. Afterward, a messenger of God arrives with a judgment against Eli's house.

For today: growing is not only a matter of getting older. We can ask God to help us advance in honesty, humility, and service, so that our lives are good before Him and also before others.
exp.2:2:
This verse tells us that Samuel was sleeping in the temple of the Lord, near the ark of God. The lamp of God had not yet gone out, meaning it was still before dawn. "Temple" here refers to the sanctuary at Shiloh, which was a tent with structures built around it.

The writer describes a difficult time: the word of the Lord was rare and visions were not frequent. Eli, the priest, was already old and nearly blind. The young Samuel served him. The lamp was probably the lampstand of the holy place, which burned through the night. Some think the mention marks the hour, just before dawn, and others that it emphasizes the faint light in dark times. The text does not fully make this clear.

God often speaks when we are available and in stillness. Set aside a quiet moment each day, perhaps at dawn, to read the Bible and listen with humility.
exp.1:13:
The verse tells how the priest's servant would thrust a three-pronged fork into the pot where the meat of the sacrifice was cooking. Whatever the fork brought up, the priest kept for himself. This was not a one-time event: it was done to every Israelite who came to Shiloh.

Here the narrator of the book describes the conduct of Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas. The text says they were wicked and did not know the LORD. Shiloh was the place where the sanctuary stood, and the people went there to offer sacrifices. They took by force what did not belong to them and treated what was holy as if it were their own.

For today: when we serve in the church or in any position of responsibility, let us not use that position for our own benefit. Serving God means giving with honesty and respect, not taking advantage of others.
exp.21:14:
Ahimelec, the priest, defends himself before Saul. With the question "Did I then begin to enquire of God for him?" he means that this was not the first time he had helped David, and that he did it as something ordinary, with no conspiracy behind it. "Be it far from me" means "I would never think of it." "Impute" means "accuse." He declares that he knew nothing of the matter, less or more.

Ahimelec speaks before a jealous and furious king. Earlier, David had come to Nob saying he was on a mission for the king, and the priest believed him. So Ahimelec acted in good faith, but Saul did not believe him and sentenced him to death.

For today: you can act with honesty and still be misunderstood or unjustly accused. Even so, tell the truth calmly and trust God, who sees the heart.
exp.29:9:
This verse tells us that David kept pursuing the Amalekites with four hundred men. Another two hundred stayed behind, because they were so worn out that they could not cross the brook Besor. The phrase that says David "kept up the pursuit" means he continued the chase. A brook like this one carries a great deal of water at certain seasons.

It is part of the account in chapter 30. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the families of David and his men as captives. David asked God whether he should pursue them, and God promised that he would overtake them and recover everything. The narrator only reports that two hundred men could go no further. He does not say they were cowards, but that they were exhausted.

For today: God calls us to keep moving forward, but he also recognizes our limits. We can advance with confidence in his promise, and we can treat those who are tired with compassion, without looking down on them.
exp.24:8:
This verse says that the young men sent by David came to where Nabal was and repeated, word for word, the whole message from David. After they spoke, they stopped and waited for his answer. The "servants" are David's attendants or young men, and "ceased" means they stopped speaking.

David was hiding from Saul in the wilderness, and his men had looked after Nabal's flocks without harming them. It was sheep-shearing time, a season of feasting and plenty. That is why David respectfully asked for some help. The messengers spoke "in David's name," that is, as his representatives. Nabal's reply, which comes next, was harsh and scornful.

For today: when you have to ask for something or speak with someone difficult, do it with clarity and respect, and then know how to wait without pressing. We cannot control how others will respond, but we can control how we speak.
exp.16:30:
This verse says that David's words were passed along among the soldiers, and someone told them to King Saul. Then Saul sent for David. The words "rehearsed them" in the King James Version mean that they were repeated and reported, and "he sent for him" means that Saul called for David to be brought to him.

David had come to the camp to bring food to his brothers. There he heard how the giant Goliath was challenging the army of Israel, and he boldly asked what would be done for the man who defeated him. His brother Eliab became angry with him, but David kept speaking. His words reached the king, who needed someone with faith to face the fear of everyone.

For today: do not keep quiet about your faith even when others mock you or correct you harshly. God can use simple, brave words to open doors you never imagined.
exp.6:8:
Samuel took a young lamb that was still nursing, meaning a very small one, and offered it to God whole as a burnt offering, a sacrifice that was burned completely. While he offers it, he prays earnestly for Israel, and God hears him.

The people had gathered at Mizpah to return to the Lord, and the Philistines, powerful enemies, came up to attack them. The Israelites were afraid and asked Samuel not to stop praying for them. So Samuel presents the sacrifice and cries out. Shortly afterward, God answers with a great thunder that throws the Philistines into confusion.

When you are afraid, come to God with humility and sincerity, and also ask for the prayers of other believers. We do not always know how he will respond, but he listens to those who trust in him.
exp.5:3:
Here the Philistines ask what offering they should send along with the ark to make amends for their wrong. A "trespass offering" means an offering of repair. The priests and diviners answer that they should send five golden tumors and five golden mice, one for each Philistine lord. The tumors here refer to the growths or sores of the plague; the Hebrew is not entirely clear about their exact nature. They say the same plague struck everyone, rulers included.

The speakers are the Philistine priests and diviners. The ark of God had been in their territory, and plagues had come upon them. They wanted to return it to Israel without further offending the God of Israel. Their gold figures represented what was afflicting them, and it was a way of acknowledging his power.

For today: when we recognize that we have failed before God, it is not enough to feel fear or to look only for relief. We can humble ourselves, acknowledge his authority, and come to him sincerely, trusting in the grace he offers us in Christ.
exp.27:22:
It says that Saul at first refused to eat. But his servants, together with the woman, urged him until they persuaded him. "Compelled" here means they pressed him with gentle force to accept.

Saul had just visited the medium of Endor and had received from Samuel a terrible message: he would lose the battle and die. He had fallen to the ground, drained of strength, and had gone a full day without eating. The woman, grateful that he had not punished her, offers him food. Saul is broken and desperate.

When we are exhausted or discouraged, we sometimes turn away help. God often uses ordinary people to care for us. Let us learn to accept the support of others humbly, and also to offer it with tenderness.
exp.24:31:
In this verse, David praises God after listening to Abigail. He says, "Blessed be the Lord God of Israel," because God sent her to meet him that very day. The word "blessed" here means praised or thankful. David recognizes that God was behind that meeting.

David was coming with his men, armed to kill Nabal and his household, because Nabal had insulted them and refused to help them. Abigail, Nabal's wife, went out with food and wise words, and asked him not to stain his conscience with blood shed without cause. David listens to her and sees the hand of God in her.

For today: when you are about to react in anger, stop. God sometimes uses a wise person and a timely word to hold you back. Listen to the advice and give thanks.
exp.1:15:
When someone answered the priest's servant, "Let them burn the fat first, as the law commands, and then take whatever you want," the servant responded roughly: "No, give it to me now; if not, I will take it by force." The fat is the fat of the animal, and "by force" means by force.

This happens at Shiloh, where the sons of the priest Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing their position. The servant and the worshiper are the ones speaking. The law required that the fat be burned for God before the meat was shared out. The servants demanded their share first and by force, and in this way they despised the offering to the Lord, as the text says afterward.

For today: God should hold first place, not our own interests. Anyone who has authority in the church, at work, or at home should serve with humility, without taking advantage of others.
exp.17:19:
This verse says that Michal, Saul's other daughter, loved David, and that someone told Saul. The news pleased the king. The phrase "pleased him" is an older way of saying "it seemed good to him" or "he liked it."

Here the narrator tells us what was happening in the palace. Saul had already promised Merab, but she was given to another man. The verses that follow show that Saul was not happy about Michal's love for David out of affection for him, but because he planned to use it as a trap so that the Philistines would kill him. It is noteworthy that the Bible says Michal loved David, but it does not say that Saul acted with good intentions.

For today: not everything that looks like good news is good for everyone. Before we rejoice or make a decision, let us ask God for discernment to see the true motives, including our own.
exp.30:0:
This verse tells that the Philistines attacked Israel. The Israelites fled, and many died on Mount Gilboa. "Fought against Israel" means they fought against them. "Fell down slain" means they were killed in combat.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book, who recounts the last battle of Saul's reign. It comes after Saul had turned away from God and God had stopped answering him (1 Samuel 28). The verses that follow show that Saul and his sons also died. It is a sad ending, and the Bible tells it without embellishment.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and listening to God in time matters. If today you have drifted away from Him, you can return and ask for His help with humility, before things get worse.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that God lifts the poor and the needy out of their humiliation and seats them among princes, giving them a place of honor. Needy is the word for those in want, and the lowest place is a heap of rubbish or the ground in the dust. An inheritance is a possession that is received. At the end it states that the earth belongs to God, who holds it up as though on pillars.

The one speaking is Hannah, in a prayer of thanksgiving. She had been barren and humbled, and God gave her Samuel. She sees in her own case an example of how God works in the world. Her song also points toward a king, the anointed one, although Israel still had no king.

Today we can trust that God sees the humble and the forgotten. If you are going through a time of discouragement, pray sincerely and wait on Him. And if you are in a high position, do not forget that everything belongs to God.
exp.0:8:
This verse tells that Hannah got up after they had eaten and drunk in Shiloh. Meanwhile, the priest Eli was sitting on a seat beside a post (a pillar or doorpost of the entrance) of the Lord's temple. Here "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "temple" refers to the sanctuary where worship took place in Shiloh.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book, who recounts what happened. Hannah came from a family that went up to worship every year. Her rival wounded her with words, and she wept and would not eat. Although her husband comforted her, her pain continued. So, when she got up, she went to pray. The verse sets the scene for her sincere prayer.

For today: when your sorrow weighs on you, do not keep it silent. Hannah brought her sadness to God with honesty. You can do the same, even if you do not have beautiful words, and trust that he listens.
exp.1:30:
God says that days are coming when he will "cut off the arm" of Eli and his family. The arm represents strength, power and protection. Cutting it off means taking away their strength and influence. The phrase "that there shall not be an old man in thine house" means that no one in his family would reach old age; many would die young.

A prophet, called a "man of God," speaks on behalf of the LORD to the priest Eli. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, abused the offerings, and Eli did not correct them firmly. God had promised that his family would serve as priests, but that promise depended on their truly honoring him.

For today: God looks at the heart, not just the office or the tradition. Honoring him means obeying him, even when it costs us to correct those we love.
exp.15:11:
What it says: David, the youngest son of Jesse, was called in from the field and brought before Samuel. He is described as ruddy, and also as having a beautiful countenance and being goodly to look at. Then God told Samuel to anoint him, because this was the chosen one. To anoint is to pour oil on someone to set them apart for a task.

Context: Samuel was looking for Israel's new king, because God had rejected Saul. Samuel had examined seven sons of Jesse, and God had chosen none of them. David was tending the sheep, and no one had considered him. A few verses earlier, God had told Samuel that He does not look at the outward appearance but at the heart.

For today: God sees and calls people whom others overlook. If you feel unimportant, remember that God knows you. And when you judge others, try to look more deeply than appearances.
