exp.13:44:
Here the people speak up for Jonathan in front of Saul. They ask whether Jonathan, the one who brought such a great victory to Israel, should really be put to death. They swear by the name of the Lord that not one hair of his head will fall to the ground, because that day he acted with God's help. The word for "rescued" here means saved or set free. So the people rescued Jonathan from death.

The speaker is the people of Israel, Saul's army. Saul had made a hasty vow that no one should eat during the battle. Jonathan did not know about it and tasted a little honey. Saul wanted to keep his word at any cost, but the people saw that God was with Jonathan.

For today: it is not enough to be firm in what we say; we also need wisdom and mercy. Before promising something with great force, it is wise to think carefully. And if we realize that a decision is unjust, we should have the courage to speak up with respect.
exp.11:15:
The explanation says that Samuel invites the people to stand still and carefully watch something great that God is about to do before their own eyes.

Samuel, the prophet and judge who is now an old man, is speaking. Israel had asked for a king, and Samuel reminds them that what matters is obeying God, both the people and the king. Since it was the season of the wheat harvest, normally a dry time, God sent thunder and rain. That sign showed them that asking for a king, for the reasons they had, had been a mistake before God.

Today, God remains the one who deserves our trust more than any human leader or plan. Before we seek security in other things, we can stop, listen to his voice, and obey him with humility.
exp.18:19:
Saul sent messengers to capture David. They arrive and see a group of prophets prophesying, with Samuel standing at the front as their leader. Then the Spirit of God came upon the messengers, and they also prophesied. "Standing at the front" means that he was leading or heading the group. "Prophesying" here refers to speaking or praising under the influence of God, although the text does not describe in detail how this happened.

This is a narrative. David fled from Saul, who wanted to kill him, and took refuge with Samuel in Naioth, near Ramah. Saul insists on capturing him, but God protects David in an unexpected way: the soldiers cannot carry out the king's order. The text does not explain everything, but it shows that God is acting upon them.

When someone seems to have all the power to do harm, God remains greater. We can seek refuge in Him and in people of faith, and trust that He cares for his own, even when we do not see how.
exp.4:6:
What it says: The people of Ashdod see what is happening and conclude that they cannot keep the ark of God. They say that "his hand is sore" upon them, meaning that God's power weighs heavily on them and on Dagon, their idol. The painful disease is described in the verse only as a sore upon them; some think it may have been a plague or tumors, but the text does not specify.

Context: The speakers are the Philistines of Ashdod. They had captured the ark of Israel and placed it in the temple of Dagon. Then came the fall of their idol and the disease. They acknowledge the power of the God of Israel, but they do not repent; they only want to get the ark away, and they send it to another city.

For today: We can recognize that God is powerful and still resist surrendering our lives to him. Today, instead of pushing away God from what troubles us, we can draw near with humility and let him correct our hearts.
exp.13:5:
Jonathan says to the young man who carried his armor, "Come, let us go over to the outpost of these uncircumcised men." By "uncircumcised" he means the Philistines, who did not have the sign of God's covenant.

He adds, "It may be that the Lord will work for us, for it is no hard thing for Him to save by many or by few."

Jonathan speaks in the middle of the war against the Philistines. Israel was at a disadvantage and had few people. Jonathan does not take the outcome for granted: he says "it may be," acknowledging that God acts as He chooses. But he trusts that God does not depend on the size of the army.

For today: when you feel small or short on resources, take the step you can with faith and humility. Trust God, without demanding results, because He can work even with very little.
exp.22:15:
This verse tells that Jonathan, the son of King Saul, got up and went to find David in the woods. There he "strengthened his hand in God," an old-fashioned expression meaning that he encouraged and strengthened him, helping him to trust in God. The woods here is a secluded, hidden place in the wilderness of Ziph.

David was fleeing because Saul was looking for him to kill him. He was tired and lived in fear. Jonathan, his faithful friend, risked his own safety to visit him. He reminded him that God had a plan for David and that Saul would not reach him. Afterward, the two of them made a covenant before the Lord.

Today we can be like Jonathan: seek out someone who is discouraged and encourage them, not only with kind words but by pointing them to God and his promises. And if you are exhausted, let a believing friend strengthen you.
exp.9:17:
Samuel speaks to the Israelites on behalf of God. He reminds them that God brought them up out of Egypt and delivered them from the power of the Egyptians and from all the kingdoms that oppressed them. "Afflicted" means that they mistreated them or made them suffer.

Samuel, the prophet and judge, gathers the people at Mizpah. They want a king like the other nations, and Samuel first reminds them of what God had already done for them. Afterward he will tell them that, in asking for a king, they are rejecting God as their protector. Meanwhile, Saul has not yet told anyone what Samuel said to him about the kingdom.

For today: before looking for human solutions to our fears or problems, it is good to remember how God has cared for us in the past. That remembrance strengthens trust. You can write down three moments when God helped you and give thanks for them.
exp.25:1:
This verse says that King Saul rose up and went to the wilderness of Ziph. He took three thousand of the best soldiers of Israel with one purpose: to seek David. The verse says Saul went down from Gibeah toward that desert region.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The Ziphites, who lived in that area, had just told Saul where David was. Saul had pursued David before, and this shows that his jealousy was still alive. Meanwhile, David trusted that God was watching over him, even though he was living as a fugitive.

For today: when someone pursues us or treats us unjustly, we can respond with calm and trust in God, without letting resentment carry us away. And we ourselves should examine our hearts, so that envy does not lead us to harm others.
exp.24:40:
Abigail receives David's marriage proposal. She rises, bows down to the ground, and offers herself with humility. She says she is willing to be a servant who washes the feet of David's servants.

After Nabal died, David praised God and sent messengers to Abigail. She had acted with wisdom and courage to prevent bloodshed. Her response shows respect and humility before David. The text tells us that she then married him, although it does not explain her innermost feelings.

For today: true greatness is shown in humble service. We can serve others without seeking applause, with a willing and grateful heart before God.
exp.24:9:
Nabal answers David's messengers with contempt. He pretends not to know who David is and calls him "the son of Jesse," as if he were a man of no importance. Then he hints that David is a rebellious servant who runs away from his master. Here "servants" refers to the men who serve a master, and "break away" means to run off and escape.

Nabal was a rich man, the owner of many sheep, and he was at the time of the sheep-shearing, a season of feasting and plenty. David, who was fleeing from Saul, had protected Nabal's shepherds, and now he respectfully asked for some food. Nabal, whose name means "fool," answered with pride and stinginess. The Bible does not say that David was a runaway servant of Nabal; it is a mockery.

Today we can learn to respond with gratitude and humility to those who have done us good. Pride and contempt, even in words, can bring serious consequences.
exp.27:5:
It says that Saul, very frightened, asked God what to do before the Philistine army, but God did not answer him. The three ways God used to answer were: dreams, the Urim (a sacred object that the priests used to learn God's will; it is not known exactly how it worked), and prophets. None of them worked.

The narrator tells that Saul, the first king of Israel, faced an enormous battle and was afraid. He had earlier disobeyed God repeatedly, and God's silence appears in the story as part of that distance. In despair, he sought out a medium, something God's law forbade.

When we feel afraid, it is good to draw near to God with sincerity and repentance before the crisis arrives, and not to look for forbidden shortcuts when we feel that He is silent.
exp.6:15:
It says that Samuel went around each year to three places: Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah. In each one he took care of the people's cases and gave them justice. The word "went around" here means that he made a circuit, and "judged" means that he governed and settled disputes, not only that he handed down verdicts.

The one telling this is the narrator of the book, not Samuel. After the victory over the Philistines and a time of peace, it shows how Samuel led the people. The three places were in the part of Israel where he could reach many people. Then he would return to Ramah, his home, where he also judged and built an altar to the LORD.

For today: good leadership draws near to people. Samuel went to where the people were, with steadiness and service. We can ask ourselves whom we need to draw near to in order to help, listen, or act justly, and do it with faithfulness and humility.
exp.22:4:
He says that David went with his men to Keilah and fought against the Philistines. "Brought away their cattle" means that he took the Philistines' livestock, and "smote them with a great slaughter" means that he defeated them with a great slaughter. So David saved the inhabitants of Keilah.

The narrator tells what happened after God gave David his command. David's men were afraid, but he asked God again, and God promised him the victory. Keilah was being attacked by the Philistines, who were stealing its grain. David obeyed, though he was in danger, since Saul was pursuing him.

When God shows us clearly what to do, we can obey even when we feel afraid. It is good to seek his direction more than once, as David did, and then to act with courage to help someone in need.
exp.9:13:
It says that Saul's uncle asked him and his servant where they had gone. Saul answered that they went out to look for the lost donkeys, and that when they saw the donkeys were nowhere to be found, they went to Samuel. The word "were" appears in the verse itself, so no note is needed on it.

Saul had just been anointed in secret by Samuel as the future king, and he had experienced signs that confirmed it, including prophesying with a group of prophets. His uncle, curious, asks him about the trip. Saul answers, but according to the verses that follow, he keeps silent about the matter of the kingdom. The Bible does not explain why; some think it was humility or prudence, others that it was fear or insecurity.

For today: not everything God entrusts to us must be told right away. Ask him for wisdom to know when to speak and when to keep silent, and treat with respect what God is only beginning to do in your life.
exp.27:21:
In this verse the woman asks Saul to listen to her, just as he listened to her. She offers him a little bread to eat, so that he may regain his strength and be able to continue on his way.

The speaker is the woman of Endor, to whom Saul had gone to consult Samuel. Saul had just received a dreadful message of judgment, and he was so distressed that he fell to the ground. Moreover, he had not eaten all day or all night. She, who had risked her life in helping him, now shows compassion and care for him. At first he refused, but then he accepted.

For today: when someone is exhausted or downcast, a simple gesture of care, such as sharing a meal, can be a real act of kindness. God calls us to notice the practical needs of others.
exp.23:2:
This verse tells us that Saul gathered three thousand chosen soldiers from all over Israel and set out to look for David and his men. He went through the high rocky places where wild goats lived, that is, rugged, elevated terrain. "Chosen" here means selected for their strength.

The narrator of the book is speaking. Saul, Israel's first king, had just returned from fighting the Philistines, and he learned that David was in the wilderness of Engedi. Although David had done him no harm, Saul saw him as a threat to his throne and pursued him with a huge army.

When someone pursues us or treats us unjustly, we can remember that God sees everything. David was at a disadvantage, but he did not lose his composure. Trusting God helps us avoid responding with revenge.
exp.8:23:
The cook lifted up the shoulder, meaning the front leg of the animal, along with what was on it, and placed it before Saul. Samuel told him that this portion had been kept for him. The phrase "on purpose" in the source was used to explain that Saul was deliberately given this place of honor. So Saul ate with Samuel that day.

Samuel was speaking at a sacrifice meal with about thirty guests. Saul had gone out to look for his father's lost donkeys and arrived where Samuel was. God had already told Samuel that he would send him the man who would be prince over Israel. This set-aside portion showed special honor, though Saul did not yet understand everything God would do through him.

For today: God may be preparing things for us long before we notice. We can trust that he guides our steps, even on ordinary days, and receive with humility and gratitude what he gives us.
exp.24:34:
In this verse David accepts the gifts Abigail brought him. He tells her to go home in peace, because he listened to her and showed her respect. The phrase that means "I have accepted your request" or "I have shown you consideration" is the one that appears here in the verse as "have hearkened to thy voice, and have accepted thy person."

David speaks with Abigail, the wife of Nabal. Nabal had insulted David and refused to help him and his men. David, angry, was going out with armed men to kill the males of that household. Abigail went out to meet him with food and with humble and wise words. David acknowledges that she kept him from shedding blood and from avenging himself with his own hand.

For today: when we are very angry, we can stop and listen to someone prudent. A wise word at the right time can keep us from doing something we will regret for the rest of our lives.
exp.24:28:
It says that even though someone has risen to pursue David and take his life, God will keep him safe. The phrase "bound in the bundle of the living" is an image of a bundle or small pouch where something precious is kept carefully. By contrast, God will fling the lives of the enemies away, like a stone slung from a sling, that is, far off and out of control.

Abigail is the one speaking, the wife of Nabal. David was coming in anger to kill everyone in Nabal's household because of an insult. She goes out to meet him with provisions and begs him not to take revenge with his own hands. She reminds him that God defends David, and that he should not stain his conscience with needless bloodshed. She is referring to Saul, who was pursuing him.

For today: when someone wrongs you or pursues you, do not take revenge. Entrust your life and your cause to God, who knows how to care for you and to do justice in his time.
exp.30:1:
The verse tells that the Philistines pursued Saul and his sons closely. They overtook and killed three of them: Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchi-shua. The word "followed" here means "going after them, pursuing them."

The one who narrates is the author of the book, who recounts the end of the battle of Mount Gilboa. Israel had already fled and many had fallen. This is the last day of Saul's reign. With the death of his sons, including Jonathan, the faithful friend of David, a painful chapter in the history of Israel comes to an end.

For today: our decisions can affect those we love. Saul turned away from God through his disobedience, and his family suffered the consequences as well. This invites us to live with humility and faithfulness, remembering that what we do influences others. And if you suffer a loss today, God remains faithful.
exp.9:21:
The Israelites inquired of God again to find out whether Saul, the chosen man, had yet arrived. God answered that Saul was hidden among the baggage, that is, among the luggage and supplies of the people gathered there.

Samuel had called the people together at Mizpah to present the first king of Israel. The choice was made by lot, tribe by tribe, until it came to Saul, but they could not find him. Then the people asked the Lord, and He Himself showed where he was. The text does not say why he hid himself; many think it was out of fear or humility, but the passage does not make this clear.

For today: sometimes we feel small or afraid in the face of what God calls us to do. We can come to Him with sincerity, and remember that He knows where we are and can encourage us to move forward.
exp.20:13:
Here Achish, king of Gath, speaks to his servants and tells them that they are looking at a man who is mad. He asks them why they have brought him to him. "Mad" means that he is not in his right mind, that he is out of his senses.

David was fleeing from King Saul and came to Gath, a Philistine city, looking for refuge. His servants recognized him, and Achish had him in his hands. David felt great fear and pretended to be insane: he scribbled on the doors and let saliva run down his beard. So Achish, the one speaking here, dismissed him as harmless and let him go. Some think this episode inspired Psalm 34, although that is interpreted in different ways.

For today: David was afraid and did not hide it. When you are afraid, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Be honest with God, ask him for wisdom, and trust that he can take care of you even in difficult situations.
exp.9:18:
Samuel tells them that by asking for a king they have rejected God himself. God had looked after them through all their troubles and distress, but they answered, "Nay, but set a king over us." Rejected means refused or looked down upon. The thousands are the large groups or clans into which each tribe was divided. Now Samuel orders them to present themselves before the Lord, tribe by tribe.

Samuel speaks at Mizpah, where he had gathered all Israel. He reminds them that God brought them out of Egypt and delivered them from other oppressing kingdoms. The people had already asked for a king (1 Samuel 8), and now the king is chosen by lot, beginning with the tribe of Benjamin. Saul is singled out, though he does not appear right away.

For today: when we feel we need something more secure than God, let us remember how he has cared for us before. Trusting in him, even when we have human plans, protects us from placing our hope in the wrong place.
exp.20:5:
It says that the priest Ahimelech gave David the holy bread, because he had no other. It was the bread set out before God in the sanctuary. That day the old bread had been taken away to make room for hot bread, that is, freshly baked bread.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. David was fleeing from King Saul, he was hungry, and he came to Nob, where the priest was. David said he was on a mission from the king, and that was not entirely true. The priest set one condition: that the young men be ceremonially clean. Jesus mentioned this episode in Matthew 12, to teach that mercy weighs more than ritual.

For today: God's law seeks the good of people. When someone is hungry or in need, help them generously, without hiding behind rules.
exp.14:21:
Samuel asks whether the Lord takes as much pleasure in burnt offerings and sacrifices as in obeying his voice. He answers that obeying is better than sacrifice, and paying attention is better than offering the fat of rams.

Samuel speaks to Saul, the first king of Israel. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites, but Saul spared King Agag, and the people kept the best of the livestock. Saul justifies himself by saying it was to sacrifice them to God. Samuel shows him that religion without obedience is worth nothing.

For today: it is not enough to sing, attend church, or give offerings if we ignore what God has already asked of us. Ask yourself: is there something God has shown you that you keep postponing or changing for some excuse that sounds pious? Obeying him simply pleases him more.
exp.4:2:
The explanation says that the next day, the people of Ashdod got up early and found their god Dagon fallen, face down on the ground, in front of the ark of the Lord. Lying face down means lying flat on the ground. They lifted the statue and set it back in its place.

The book of Samuel tells what happened without any character speaking. The Philistines had defeated Israel and taken the ark, believing that their god was stronger. Dagon was a deity greatly honored by them. Here the account shows that the Lord does not depend on a temple or an army to show who He is.

Today we can remember that nothing can take the place of God. If something, such as money, success, or the approval of others, tries to sit on the throne of our heart, it is good to put it in its place and let God be God.
exp.11:7:
When Jacob and his family arrived in Egypt, their descendants suffered and asked God for help. Then God sent Moses and Aaron, who brought them out of Egypt and settled them in the promised land (the phrase "this place" in the original). Some old words: "cried out" means they asked for help at the top of their voices; the small word "to" is just a plain connecting word.

The prophet Samuel speaks at an assembly in Gilgal, after Saul had already been confirmed as king. Samuel reminds the people of the story of God's faithfulness. He wants to show them that God always rescued them when they cried out, and that their true king and savior is the LORD. Then he mentions how the people forgot God again and again.

Today, this verse invites us to remember how God has helped us in the past. Take a few minutes this week to recall the times He sustained you, thank Him, and trust that He will also hear you when you cry out to Him today.
exp.29:13:
Here the young Egyptian tells David what his band of Amalekites did. "We made a raid" means they attacked by surprise and plundered. They struck the southern area of the Cherethites (who were Philistines of the coast), also the territory of Judah and the south of Caleb. At the end he says they burned Ziklag, the town where David lived with his people.

It is an Egyptian slave speaking, sick and abandoned by his master three days earlier. David finds him in the field, feeds him, and asks him questions. In this way David learns who carried off his families and that Ziklag was destroyed. This detail, given almost without intending to, leads him straight to the enemy camp.

God can use the smallest and most forgotten people to show us the way. David was kind to a weak stranger, and that opened the door to the answer he needed. Today, treating with kindness someone no one attends to can bring blessings we do not expect.
exp.7:7:
God tells Samuel that the people have always acted this way: from the day He brought them out of Egypt until today, they have abandoned Him and served other gods. Now they are doing the same thing to Samuel by rejecting him. "According to all the works" means "just like", and "other gods" are the gods of other peoples.

The Lord speaks to Samuel, who is now old. The Israelites ask for a king like the other nations, and it grieves Samuel. God makes clear that the rejection is not so much against the prophet as against Him as their true King. Even so, He will allow them to have a king, but Samuel must warn them what it will cost them.

For today: sometimes we want something or someone else to give us security, instead of trusting God. Ask yourself where you are placing your trust. If this is hard for you, tell God honestly and ask Him to be first in your heart again.
exp.8:4:
It says that Saul and his servant reached the land of Zuph, and that Saul wanted to turn back. He thought that his father, Kish, would no longer be worried about the lost donkeys but would be anxious about them instead. Saul is speaking, a young man whom his father sent to look for some lost donkeys. After searching several regions without success, he grows tired of looking and thinks about his family. What follows shows that the servant suggests consulting a man of God, and so the meeting with Samuel begins. We do not know for certain the exact location of Zuph.

Saul was concerned about how his father was feeling. Sometimes, when things do not turn out as we hope, it is good to think also of those who love us and are waiting for us. And, as happened here, sometimes a simple piece of advice from someone else leads us to seek God.
exp.8:13:
Saul and his servant went up into the city. As they were entering, right in the middle of it, they came upon Samuel, who was coming toward them to go up to the high place. The high place was an elevated site where sacrifices were offered and religious ceremonies were held.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys, and he went to ask about the seer. Some young women told him that Samuel was about to arrive. The meeting seems accidental, but the text that follows shows that God had already announced it to Samuel.

God can guide our steps even in ordinary things, such as searching for something lost. We do not always notice it at the time, but we can trust that he is at work. Live each day with attention and with faith.
exp.3:10:
This verse records two terrible blows to Israel on the same day: the Philistines took the ark of God, and Hophni and Phinehas, the two sons of the priest Eli, were killed. "Was taken" means that the enemy captured it. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among his people.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts the events without embellishment. Earlier, the Philistines gathered courage to fight hard and defeated Israel. The Israelites had brought the ark into battle as if it were a charm for victory, but they had not turned back to God. Eli's sons, moreover, were corrupt priests.

For today: we cannot treat sacred things as if they were a talisman to obtain what we want. God asks for a sincere heart, one that repents and obeys him, rather than symbols or rituals.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that Elkanah gave Hannah a special portion of the offering, because he loved her. But Hannah could not have children: the text states that the Lord had shut up her womb. The phrase "worthy portion" is hard to translate, and some understand it as a double portion or a portion of honor.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who presents a family that goes up every year to Shiloh to worship. He wants to show Elkanah's affection and, at the same time, Hannah's deep pain, which sets up what follows in the story.

For today: a gift or a kind gesture helps, but it does not take away the pain of the one who is suffering. Accompany others with patience and listen to someone who is going through grief. And if the pain is yours, bring it to God honestly, as Hannah will do.
exp.12:16:
The verse tells that the Philistines sent three groups of soldiers from their camp at Michmash to raid the territory of Israel. "Spoilers" means a quick attack to steal and cause harm. A "company" is a group of soldiers. The first group went along the road toward Ophrah, in the land of Shual. The other two are mentioned in the next verse.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel was weak: Saul had only about six hundred men, and the Philistines dominated the area, even controlling the weapons. No one knows exactly where each place was, but the account shows that the people lived under constant threat.

For today: when you feel surrounded by pressure and short on resources, do not just stare at your weakness. Bring your situation to God in prayer, ask for his guidance, and take the next step with faith and patience, trusting that he works even when everything seems to be against you.
exp.23:7:
The explanation says that David calmed his men with firm words and did not let them attack Saul. Here, the idea is that he held them back and stopped them, like someone who grips another person firmly. Afterward, Saul left the cave and went on his way, without knowing what had happened.

Saul was chasing David to kill him. Without knowing it, he entered a cave where David and his men were hiding. His men saw there an opportunity to finish off their enemy. David only cut off a piece of Saul's robe, and even that weighed on his conscience. He respected Saul as the anointed of God, that is, the king chosen by Him.

When we have the chance to take revenge, we can choose the opposite: let God be the judge. And if others urge us to do wrong, we need courage to tell them no.
exp.8:14:
This verse says that God had told Samuel, one day before Saul arrived, what was going to happen. The phrase "revealed in the ear" means that God spoke to him clearly and directly, like someone whispering a secret. After this, God explains his plan to him.

The narrator tells a detail that Saul did not know. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys, and without knowing it he was being led toward Samuel. God had already prepared the meeting. He wanted to raise up a leader to deliver Israel from the Philistines, because he had heard the cry of his people.

For today: God may be at work in your life even when you do not notice it. What seems like coincidence or an ordinary problem, God can use to guide you. Trust that he hears your cry and move forward faithfully, one step at a time.
exp.18:17:
This verse tells us that David managed to flee from Saul and came to Samuel at Ramah. There he told him everything Saul had done to him. Afterward, David and Samuel went to stay in Naioth.

The narrator describes what happened after Michal, David's wife, helped him get away and tricked Saul's messengers with a statue in the bed. David sought out Samuel, the prophet who had anointed him as the future king. Naioth was probably a place where prophets gathered, though it is not known exactly what it was like.

When everything becomes unjust or dangerous, it is wise to seek out someone of mature faith to share what we are going through. David did not carry his pain alone. Talking with a wise counselor and praying together gives us clarity and protection.
exp.21:5:
When Saul learned that David had been seen, along with the men who were with him, Saul was sitting under a tree in Ramah with his spear in his hand, and all his servants were standing around him. The narrator describes what happens right after the prophet Gad advised David to return to Judah. Saul hears about it and gathers his men. The spear shows his power, but also his suspicion. In the verses that follow, he accuses his servants of conspiring against him, even though he has no proof.

For today: when fear and jealousy take hold of us, we begin to see enemies where there are none. Instead of clinging to control, we can pray, trust God, and listen to sincere advice.
exp.0:0:
This verse introduces a man named Elkanah, who lived in Ramathaim-zophim, in the hill country of Ephraim. His family line is named: he was the son of Jeroham, and before him come Elihu, Tohu and Zuph.

The word "man" here simply means a man, and "Ephrathite" indicates that his family came from the tribe of Ephraim (there is debate about whether it refers to this or to Bethlehem).

Here the narrator of the book speaks, beginning the story of Samuel. We do not know for certain who wrote the book. First he introduces Elkanah's family, because Samuel, an important prophet for Israel, will be born from it. The verses that follow speak of Hannah, her sorrow and her faith.

For today: God begins great works with ordinary people and simple families. Your daily life, though it may seem small, can be the place where God does something important.
exp.24:17:
Abigail acts quickly and gathers a generous gift of food: two hundred loaves of bread, two skins of wine, five sheep already prepared, five measures of roasted grain, one hundred clusters of raisins, and two hundred cakes of figs. She loads everything onto donkeys. "Ready dressed" means prepared and cooked, ready to eat. The raisins are given as clusters of raisins.

This is the narrator's account. A servant had warned Abigail that Nabal, her husband, had insulted David's men, and that David was coming with his men to harm him. She acts at once to calm the situation and provide what her husband had refused, without telling him.

When we see a problem that could grow, it is wise to act early, with humility and with concrete deeds. A generous and wise gesture at the right time can prevent much pain and open the way to peace.
exp.23:16:
This verse tells that David finished speaking to Saul. Then Saul asked him, "Is this your voice, my son David?" and he began to weep aloud. The word "happened" in the verse means "came about," and "lifted up his voice" means that he wept openly.

David had Saul in his power inside a cave and did him no harm; he only cut off a piece of his robe. Then he went out and spoke to him from a distance, showing him that he was not his enemy. Saul had been pursuing him out of jealousy. Here Saul calls him "my son," and his weeping shows that, at least for a moment, he recognized his wrong. The Bible does not say whether that change lasted.

For today: when someone treats you badly, responding with kindness and truth can touch a hardened heart. You will not always succeed in changing them, but you will keep your conscience clear before God.
exp.16:42:
Goliath asks David if he is a dog, that he comes to fight him with sticks. Goliath then curses David by calling on his gods, that is, the Philistine gods.

Goliath, the Philistine champion, speaks here. He feels insulted because he sees David as a young man without weapons of war. The "sticks" most likely refer to the shepherd's staff David was carrying, and he also had his sling. Goliath trusts in his strength and in his gods, but David will answer by trusting in the God of Israel.

Today, others sometimes mock our faith or our strength. We do not have to defend ourselves with pride or respond in kind. We can face our problems with humility, trusting that God is the one who gives the victory, even when we feel small.
exp.24:42:
It says that David also married Ahinoam, a woman from Jezreel. "Took" means that he received her as a wife, and "both of them" means "the two of them." So Abigail and Ahinoam became David's wives.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. David was fleeing from Saul, who was pursuing him, and he had just married Abigail. The next verse tells that Saul had given Michal, David's wife, to another man. Although the Bible reports that David had several wives, that does not mean it approves of that practice. Several passages show the problems it brought.

For today: it is not enough for something to be common in our culture. It is wise to measure our decisions by what God teaches throughout the whole Bible, and to trust Him, especially in uncertain times.
exp.9:26:
These verses tell of certain wicked men, described as "the children of Belial" (meaning people with no worth and no reverence for God), who despised Saul. They doubted that he could deliver the people. Their scorn meant they held him in low regard. They did not bring him the gift that was customarily carried to a king as a sign of honor. Saul kept silent and did not answer them.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul had just been presented as king before Israel. While many followed him, with hearts that God had moved, others rejected him. Some understand his silence as a sign of wisdom or humility; others think he did not yet have firm authority.

For today: not every criticism deserves an immediate reply. When someone despises us, we can remain calm, trust God, and act wisely, without letting the offense carry us away.
exp.13:31:
This verse tells that the people, very tired and hungry after the battle, rushed upon the spoil. They took sheep, oxen and calves, killed them right there on the ground, and ate the meat with the blood.

The narrator is the author of the book. Saul had made the people swear that they would not eat all day, and they were left worn out. As evening came, hunger pushed them to eat carelessly. The law of Moses forbade eating blood (Leviticus 17:10-14), since life was in it. That is why they reported to Saul that the people were sinning.

Today, pressure and exhaustion can lead us to disobey God. Orders given without wisdom can also push others to fail. Let us seek to decide calmly and lead with prudence, without burdening anyone with unnecessary demands.
exp.3:2:
What it says: After losing a battle against the Philistines, the people returned to the camp. The elders, who were Israel's leaders, asked why God had let them lose. Then they proposed bringing the ark of the covenant from Shiloh, hoping that God, being among them, would deliver them from their enemies. "Defeated" here means beaten.

Context: The elders of Israel speak, discouraged after about four thousand men had died. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence. They ask why, but they do not examine themselves or seek God with repentance. The text does not say they consulted the Lord. Later, the story shows that treating the ark as a good luck charm did not bring them victory.

For today: When something goes wrong for us, it is not enough to ask for a quick fix or to rely on religious symbols. First let us seek God with humility, examine our hearts, and trust Him Himself, not objects or customs.
exp.24:20:
This verse shows David's anger. He says it was in vain that he guarded Nabal's possessions in the wilderness, since nothing of his was lost. And in return, Nabal repaid him evil for the good he had received. The phrase "repaid him evil for good" means that Nabal answered a kindness with an insult.

Here the narrator tells us what David had said before he met Abigail. David and his men had protected Nabal's flocks, and Nabal refused them help with contempt. For that reason David was on his way to take revenge with violence, and Abigail goes out to meet him without her husband knowing.

For today: when someone repays us evil for a good we have done, the hurt is real, but we should not decide in the heat of anger. It is wise to stop, listen to wise counsel, and leave justice to God.
exp.16:39:
He took his staff, the shepherd's rod, and chose five smooth stones from the brook. He put them in his shepherd's bag, the pouch he carried for his things. With the sling in his hand, which is a strip for hurling stones, he drew near to the Philistine, Goliath.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul, the king, had lent David his armor, but David was not used to it, so he took it off. The soldiers of Israel were afraid of the giant, and David, a young shepherd, offered to fight. Why he chose five stones, the Bible does not explain, and several ideas have been suggested.

Today we can learn to serve God with what we already have and know how to do, without copying others. God can use your simple tools when you trust Him.
exp.13:33:
Saul tells the people to scatter and bring each man his ox or his sheep to be killed right there. In this way they can eat without sinning against the Lord, that is, without eating meat with the blood still in it. Words that need explaining: the old word for "turned" means "went back," "scatter" means "spread out," and "slew them" means "cut their throats and kill them." That night everyone brought his animal and killed it there.

Saul, king of Israel, speaks after a battle against the Philistines. The people were worn out and hungry, and they killed animals on the ground and ate the meat with the blood. The law of Moses forbade eating blood (Leviticus 17:10-14). Saul uses a large stone to kill the animals in the proper way, and then he builds an altar.

God cares about how we obey, even in simple things, and not only about what we do. When we notice that we have gone astray, let us correct ourselves with humility and not ignore the mistake.
exp.3:16:
Here the messenger gives Eli four pieces of news in a row: Israel fled before the Philistines, many of the people died, his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, also died, and the ark of God was captured. The word for the great loss of life means a great slaughter. The phrase that says the ark "was taken" simply means it was captured.

The speaker is a man who escaped from the battle and arrives at Shiloh with terrible news. Eli, an old man who is nearly blind, is waiting to learn what happened. The messenger saves the most painful news for last: the ark, the symbol of God's presence. For Eli, that was the gravest loss. His sons had acted wickedly as priests, and the people had treated the ark almost like a good-luck charm.

For today: let us not use what is sacred as a talisman, and let us not allow religion to become only a custom. God cannot be manipulated. Let us seek him with a sincere and obedient heart, and not merely with symbols or rituals.
exp.25:7:
Abishai tells David that God has handed his enemy over to him. For that reason he offers to kill Saul with one blow of the spear, pinning him to the ground.

Abishai, David's nephew and a loyal soldier, speaks in the middle of the night. Saul had been pursuing David to kill him for a long time, and now he is sleeping in his camp, with no one keeping proper watch. Abishai reads the opportunity as a sign from God. David, in the next verse, will reject that plan.

For today: a favorable opportunity is not always a sign from God to do what we want. Before acting, it is wise to ask ourselves whether what we are about to do honors God and respects his principles, even when someone has wronged us.
exp.25:3:
This verse tells how David sent out men to watch Saul's movements in secret. The "spies" are scouts sent out to gather information. They came back with the news, and David knew for certain that Saul had really arrived with his army.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not David speaking. Saul had brought three thousand men to capture David, who was hiding in the wilderness of Ziph. David had already heard rumors that Saul was following him, but he was not satisfied with that. He wanted to confirm it before acting, and what he did afterward, sparing Saul's life, grew out of that preparation.

For today: before making an important decision, look for clear information and confirm the facts. Trusting God does not remove the duty to be wise. We can pray and, at the same time, investigate calmly so that we act with understanding.
exp.10:9:
The men of Jabesh tell their enemies, the Ammonites, that they will come out to them the next day. They offer to let the Ammonites do with them whatever seems good to them. The phrase about what seems good to them is simply that: whatever seems good to you.

The people of Jabesh of Gilead were surrounded by the Ammonites. They had already sent word asking for help from Saul and from Israel, and news had reached them that they would be delivered. Many understand that their words sounded like surrender, but they concealed their hope of rescue. The text does not explain this, so it is one possible interpretation.

For today: when you find yourself surrounded by a problem, do not lose hope. If God has already given you a promise or help is on its way, wait with confidence, and be wise in what you say and do.
exp.18:8:
It says that an evil spirit, sent or allowed by God, came upon Saul. He was sitting in his house with a spear in his hand, while David was playing the harp.

Here it is not a character speaking, but the narrator of the book. Saul had already disobeyed God and had lost his favor. Now he was dominated by jealousy toward David, who had just defeated the Philistines. Interpreters explain in different ways how God allowed that spirit, but the text shows that God still rules even in dark times.

Unchecked jealousy can turn into violence. If you feel envy at another person's success, bring it to God in prayer soon and ask for a humble heart, before it grows and takes control of you.
exp.29:20:
David came back to the brook Besor, where two hundred men had been left behind, too exhausted to continue the pursuit. They went out to meet David and the people who were with him. David drew near and greeted them with peace; that is, he asked how they were and treated them with kindness.

The narrator tells what happened after David recovered everything the Amalekites had taken at Ziklag. The two hundred had stayed behind to guard the baggage (v. 24). This kind greeting sets up the scene that follows, where some selfish men want to keep the two hundred out of the spoils, and David stops them.

For today: let us not measure people's worth only by what they manage to accomplish. Whoever is tired or limited also deserves respect and care. Let us receive the weak with peace and generosity.
exp.17:3:
Jonathan took off his robe and gave it to David. He also gave him other pieces of his clothing and his equipment: his sword, his bow, and his belt.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had just defeated Goliath, and Saul had taken him to live with him. Jonathan, the king's son and the natural heir to the throne, made a covenant with David because he loved him very much. Giving him his clothing and his weapons was a sign of friendship and loyalty. Some think he also recognized David as someone chosen by God, but the text does not state this clearly.

Today we can learn to give generously and without envy. Jonathan had much to lose, but he valued friendship and what God was doing in another person more highly. Ask yourself whom you can truly encourage and support.
exp.19:16:
The explanation says that Jonathan made a vow to David again, and that he did it out of love. "He made a vow again" means that he swore once more. "As he loved his own soul" means that he loved David as he loved his own life, with a deep and sincere affection.

David was fleeing from King Saul, Jonathan's father, who wanted to kill him. Jonathan, although he was the king's son, recognized that God was with David. For that reason he made a covenant with him, asking for kindness toward his family in the future. The narrator makes clear that the oath arose from love, not from self-interest. It is a faithful friendship in the midst of danger.

For today: true friendship is shown through loyalty and sacrifice, above all when it is costly. Ask yourself whom you can accompany or protect this week, even if it costs you something, and do it with a sincere love.
exp.16:19:
He says that David got up early in the morning, left the sheep in the care of a keeper, and set out carrying the food that his father Jesse had asked him to take. He arrived at the camp just as the army was going out in formation and giving the war cry. The fortified camp is the place where the army was gathered; the battle line is the formation for fighting; the keeper is the one who looked after the sheep; and what David carried was the supplies he had brought.

The narrator is the author of the book, and he tells us that Jesse sent David to visit his older brothers, who were soldiers in Saul's army. David was to take them provisions, greet the commander, and come back with news of them. David was not going to fight; he was obeying a simple errand from his father.

For today: God often uses the person who is faithful in small things. David cared for the flock responsibly and carried out his father's errand without complaint. Let us do our daily tasks with care, because in them God may be preparing us for greater things.
exp.16:29:
This verse says that David stopped speaking with his brother Eliab, turned toward other people, and asked them the same question as before. The soldiers answered him the same way they had the first time. The phrase "turned from him" means he turned away from Eliab, and "after the former manner" is rendered here simply as "the same way as before."

Eliab had just accused David of pride and of being nosy. David did not get caught up in an argument. His question was about what reward would go to the man who defeated Goliath and took away the disgrace from Israel. Those words reached the ears of Saul, and that opened the way for David to present himself before the king.

For today: when someone criticizes you unfairly, you do not have to defend yourself until you win the argument. Answer with calm, keep going with what God has placed in your heart, and keep doing what is right with patience.
exp.21:3:
This verse tells that David brought his parents before the king of Moab, and they stayed there with him while David remained in the stronghold. The word "brought" here is the same as in the verse above. The stronghold was a protected place, probably a refuge in the mountains.

David was fleeing King Saul, who wanted to kill him. With four hundred distressed men around him, he sought a safe place for his parents. Moab had some connection to his family, since Ruth, his great-grandmother, came from there. Soon after, the prophet Gad told him to return to Judah, and David obeyed.

For today: when hard times come, care for your family and seek counsel, but stay attentive to God's guidance. David said he hoped to know what God would do with him. A temporary refuge should not become a place where we stay if God tells us to move forward.
exp.14:5:
Saul speaks to the Kenites, a people who lived among the Amalekites. He tells them to go away and separate themselves from them, so that they will not be destroyed along with Amalek. He gives them this chance because they had shown kindness to the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt. The Kenites heeded the warning and departed.

God had commanded Saul to judge Amalek for its attack against Israel in the wilderness. Before the battle, Saul gathers the army and prepares an ambush. Then he warns the Kenites in order to protect them. The Bible does not say in detail how that kindness had been shown, but it is remembered that it was not forgotten.

For today: God remembers and honors the good we do, even when it seems small. And if we find ourselves in a place that pulls us away from God, it is worth heeding the warning and leaving in time.
exp.15:14:
What it says: King Saul's servants notice that something is wrong with him. They say that an "evil spirit from God" troubles him. "Servants" are the attendants or staff of the king's household, and "troubles" means it causes him anguish and disturbance.

Context: Shortly before this, God had rejected Saul as king because of his disobedience, and the Spirit of the LORD had departed from him. Samuel had just anointed David. The servants speak out of concern and suggest that Saul seek a musician who plays the harp to bring him relief. Interpreters explain in different ways how God allowed or sent that spirit, and the text does not spell it out.

For today: When someone close to us suffers in their spirit, we should not ignore it. Like those servants, we can speak with respect, notice their pain, and offer concrete help, such as companionship, music, or pointing them toward appropriate support.
exp.21:16:
Here King Saul gives a terrible order to his guard: "Surround and kill the priests of the Lord." He accuses them of being on David's side, because they knew he was fleeing and did not tell him. But the king's servants refused to raise their hand against the priests of the Lord.

Saul speaks full of jealousy and fear, convinced that everyone is plotting against him. Ahimelech had just defended himself by saying he knew nothing of the conflict. Saul did not listen to him and pronounced an unjust sentence.

For today: when fear and pride govern, we can harm the innocent. Let us learn from those servants: obeying an authority does not oblige us to do wrong. Let us obey God first.
exp.22:11:
Here David asks God whether the people of Keilah would hand him over, along with his men, to King Saul. God answers plainly: they will hand you over. The explanation's note about the divine name and the word for neighbors is not needed here, since those terms do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

David speaks in prayer, using the guidance God provided through the priest and the ephod. He had rescued Keilah from the Philistines, but Saul was pursuing him and planned to attack the city. David wanted to know whether the people of Keilah, whom he had helped, would be loyal to him. God warns him that they would not, and so David leaves with his six hundred men. The Bible does not say why the people of Keilah would act this way; it could have been fear of Saul.

For today: God can give us wisdom when we ask him sincerely. Sometimes his answer is not what we expect, but it protects us. Before deciding something important, pray, seek wise counsel, and do not trust only that others will repay your kindness.
exp.1:2:
This verse asks us to stop speaking with pride and boasting. "Arrogancy" refers to words full of arrogance. The reason is that the Lord is a God who knows all things, and it is he who weighs our actions, that is, who evaluates and judges what we do and why we do it.

Speaking is Hannah, who prays with thanksgiving after giving her son Samuel to serve God. Before this, she had suffered because she had no children and because of the mockery of her rival. Now she praises God and warns the proud, because he changes the fortune of the strong and the weak, as seen in the verses that follow.

Today we can guard our words: avoid bragging about our achievements or looking down on others. If we remember that God knows the heart, we will speak with more humility and gratitude.
exp.25:15:
David rebukes Abner, the commander of Saul's army, for failing to guard the king. He tells him that what they did is not good, and that they "deserve to die," meaning they merit death for that failure. To "guard" means to protect, and a "jar" is a vessel for water. David shows them the proof: the king's spear and water jar, which he took while everyone slept.

David speaks from a distant hill, after entering Saul's camp at night. Saul was pursuing him to kill him. David could have killed him, but he did not want to harm the Lord's anointed, the king chosen by God. He uses these proofs to show that he is not a traitor.

For today: trusting God frees us from taking revenge. When someone treats us unjustly, we can act with integrity and respect, leaving God to be the judge.
exp.23:11:
The explanation says David shows Saul a piece of his robe, the "edge," meaning the border or hem of the cloth. David cut it off when he could have killed Saul, but he did not do it. "You are hunting my life" means that Saul is chasing David like an animal in order to kill him. David asks Saul to recognize that there is no evil or treachery in him.

David speaks with Saul, the king of Israel, who was pursuing him out of jealousy. David had hidden in a cave, and Saul went in without knowing he was there. His men kept telling him to kill Saul, but David respected Saul as the one anointed by the Lord, that is, chosen by God to be king.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not answer with revenge. Do what is right, speak the truth with respect, and let God be the judge.
exp.23:4:
David's men tell him that this is the day God had promised: Saul, his enemy, is in his hands, and he can do to him whatever he wishes. David gets up and, without making a sound, cuts off the edge of Saul's robe. The word for "quietly" means in silence. The edge is the hem or lower border of the garment.

Saul was pursuing David with three thousand soldiers in order to kill him. He entered a cave alone to relieve himself, and David and his men were hidden at the back. His men read the situation as an opportunity given by God. The Bible does not record that God said those exact words; they apply them in their own way.

A favorable opportunity is not always a sign that God wants us to act. Before taking advantage of it, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it is right before God. David, even under pressure from his own men, stopped and sought to act with respect and a clear conscience.
exp.20:0:
David came to Nob, where the priest Ahimelech was. The priest was surprised and alarmed to see him, and asked him why he was alone, with no one to accompany him. "Was surprised" means that he was disturbed or puzzled.

David was fleeing from King Saul, who wanted to kill him. Nob was a place where the sanctuary stood, and Ahimelech served as priest there. Ahimelech speaks because a man as important as David, the king's son-in-law and military commander, would normally travel with an escort. Later David tells him he is on a mission for the king, but that was not true. The Bible reports the event without approving his deception, and the consequences were painful.

When we are in trouble, it is tempting to bend the truth to get out of a difficulty. This passage invites us to seek God sincerely, trusting that his care is better than any lie that might seem useful to us.
exp.26:6:
This verse says that David lived in Philistine territory for four months and some days. It is a brief note about time. The word "dwelt" means that he lived there, and I will not explain the older forms of the verse.

The narrator is the one speaking, not David. He tells how long that period lasted. David was fleeing from King Saul, who wanted to kill him, and he took refuge with Achish, a Philistine king of Gath. Achish gave him Ziklag, a small town where he could live apart with his people. The texts that follow show that David carried out raids and deceived Achish about them. The Bible only reports these events here and does not approve or condemn them.

For today: difficult times have a limit, even though we sometimes cannot see it. If you are in an uncomfortable season, ask God for wisdom so that you do not take doubtful shortcuts. Trust that He sustains you and knows when it will end.
exp.24:43:
This verse tells how Saul gave his daughter Michal, David's wife, to another man named Phalti, son of Laish, who was from a place called Gallim. The word "wife" in the verse is the one that reflects David's wife, so the reader can see her as David's wife directly.

The author of the book is the one telling this, not a character in the story. He makes this point right after mentioning David's other marriages. Saul, angry and jealous of David, had taken Michal away from him. Later, in 2 Samuel 3, David gets her back. So we see how the king's decisions affected the lives of others.

For today: when someone with power acts out of jealousy or resentment, others end up suffering. Let us ask God for a humble heart, so that we do not use our influence to harm others, and so that we care with respect for the people He places in our charge.
exp.1:4:
It says that things are turned around. Those who were "full," that is, well fed, now have to work for wages to get bread. In contrast, those who were hungry no longer go without. The woman who was barren, who could not have children, ends up having seven, and the one who had many children is left weak or sorrowful. The number seven speaks of completeness.

It is part of Hannah's prayer, who could not have children before and now has Samuel. She gives thanks to God and praises how he changes circumstances, bringing down the proud and lifting up the humble. She speaks with gratitude, but also with a warning to the arrogant.

For today: if you are going through a difficult season, do not lose hope, because God can change your situation. And if things are going well for you, do not boast, but be humble and thankful, for everything comes from him.
exp.0:22:
Elkanah tells Anna to do what seems best to her and to stay at home until she has weaned the child. He adds: "only the Lord establish his word." To wean means to stop nursing the baby. Anna stays and raises her son Samuel until that time.

Elkanah, Anna's husband, is the one speaking. She had promised to dedicate to God the son she was given, and he respects that decision. It is not certain which word is meant here; it could be God's promise or Anna's vow. In that time weaning usually took place around two or three years of age, although the Bible does not give the exact age here.

Today we can respectfully support the promises others make to God, and keep our own promises with patience. Waiting for the right moment is also a form of faithfulness.
exp.16:6:
The shaft of Goliath's spear is described. The "staff of a loom" was the thick beam of a weaver's loom, so the shaft was very thick. The iron head weighed six hundred shekels, about 7 kilograms according to common calculations. His "shield-bearer" was the assistant who carried his shield and weapons.

The narrator of the book details the armor of the Philistine giant. He wants the reader to see how imposing he was, and why all Israel felt fear. Right after, Goliath challenges Israel's army to send one man to fight on behalf of them all.

Today, we sometimes face problems that seem enormous and well armed. This scene reminds us not to measure everything by its appearance. Before letting fear paralyze us, we can place the problem in God's hands and ask him for courage to act with faith.
exp.24:4:
Here David sends ten of his young men up to Carmel, a region in the south of Judah, to go to where Nabal is. He asks them to greet him on David's behalf. The word "young men" refers to servants or young men in his service, and the phrase "greet him" means "give him greeting."

David is in the wilderness, fleeing from King Saul, with a group of men who need food. He learns that Nabal is shearing his sheep, a time of festivity and plenty. David and his men had looked after Nabal's shepherds, and now he approaches with respect to ask for help. The text presents Nabal as a harsh man, and Abigail as a wise woman.

For today: when you need to ask for something, begin with respect and good treatment. A kind greeting does not guarantee that you will be answered well, but it shows your character and opens the way to peace.
exp.24:26:
Abigail tells David that she brings him a gift, a "blessing," and asks that it be shared among his men, whom she calls "servants." The word "handmaid" refers to herself, speaking with humility. "My lord" is David, whom she addresses with respect.

Abigail speaks with David when he is coming out armed to kill Nabal and his household, because Nabal had insulted him and refused him food. She goes out to meet him with bread, wine, and other provisions to calm David's anger and prevent bloodshed. Her gift comes with wise and humble words.

For today: when there is tension or anger, a generous and humble gesture can disarm a conflict. Before reacting with vengeance, we can look for ways to bring peace, and ask God to guide our hearts.
exp.16:11:
This verse introduces David and his family. It says that David was the son of Jesse, a man from Ephrath in Bethlehem of Judah, who had eight sons. "Ephrathite" means from the region or clan of Ephrath, which is connected with Bethlehem. Jesse was already an old man in the time of King Saul, very advanced in years for his generation.

The narrator interrupts the scene of the Philistine giant to introduce David and his origins once again. Israel is paralyzed by fear before Goliath's challenge. At that moment, a young man from an ordinary family, from a small town, appears. Some scholars think this repetition is due to how the ancient accounts were joined together, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God often works through ordinary people and in places that go unnoticed. Do not be discouraged if you feel small; trust that God can use your life right where you are.
exp.28:6:
Here Achish tells David to turn back and go away at peace. "Turn back" means to return, and "at peace" means without trouble or dispute. He asks David not to do anything wrong before the Philistine lords, that is, not to cause displeasure or conflict with them.

Achish speaks as the Philistine king of Gath. David lived under his protection and accompanied him with his men, but the Philistine commanders distrusted David, remembering that he was Israel's hero. Achish personally trusted David, although he gave in to the pressure of the lords. Some understand that God used this situation to keep David from fighting against his own people, though the text does not say this in so many words.

For today: sometimes a door is closed to us even though we have done nothing wrong. We can respond with calm, without fighting, and trust that God can take care of us even when doors are shut.
exp.13:4:
This verse describes the location of two rocky cliffs or crags in the pass where Jonathan wanted to cross. One stood to the north, facing Michmash, where the Philistine garrison was. The other stood to the south, facing Gibeah, where the Israelite side was.

Here the book's narrator speaks. He wants the reader to picture the difficult terrain over which Jonathan and his armor-bearer took their risk. Israel was at a disadvantage against the Philistines. Jonathan acts without telling the people, trusting that God could work. The names Bozez and Seneh appear in the context, but their exact meaning is not certain.

For today: sometimes the path God sets before us is narrow and difficult. Even so, we can take a step of faith, with prudence and prayer, trusting that it is no trouble for God to help, whether we have much or little.
exp.27:13:
Saul asks the woman what form the figure has that she is seeing. She describes an old man coming up, covered with a robe. Saul concludes that it is Samuel and bows down with his face to the ground.

Saul speaks with a medium at Endor. He is desperate because the Philistines are attacking him and God no longer answers him. He had banned divination, but now he seeks it out. Notice that Saul works out who it is from the description, since he himself sees nothing. Some believe it was truly Samuel; others, that it was a deception. The text does not fully settle the question.

When we are distressed, it is easy to look for answers in places God does not approve. It is better to return to him with humility and sincerity, and not look for shortcuts.
exp.18:0:
Saul told his son Jonathan and all his servants that they should kill David. Jonathan, although he was Saul's son, loved David very much.

The narrator tells us that Saul's jealousy of David had grown, because David was successful and the people admired him. Now Saul stops hiding it and gives an open order to kill him. Jonathan is caught in the middle: he is the king's son, but he is also David's faithful friend. So he warns David of the danger and promises to speak with his father.

When a friendship or a loyalty places us between two people in conflict, we can choose what is right, even when it costs us. Jonathan did not keep silent or go along with the crowd. He protected an innocent man with courage, and he also tried to speak respectfully to his father. Let us ask God for wisdom to defend what is just without losing humility.
exp.10:2:
The elders of Jabesh ask Nahash, king of the Ammonites, for seven days. During that time they want to send messengers throughout Israel. If no one comes to defend them, they will surrender to him. The word "coasts" in the verse means territories or regions.

The leadership of Jabesh in Gilead is speaking, a city under siege. Nahash had set a cruel condition: to gouge out the right eye of all of them to humiliate Israel. The elders ask for time, perhaps to seek help from their brothers. We do not know for certain whether Nahash accepted out of confidence or out of pride, but the text shows that he granted them the time.

For today: when you face a situation that overwhelms you, do not remain silent or alone. Ask for help in time from your family, your church, or trusted people, and at the same time trust that God can use others to come to your aid.
exp.23:12:
David tells Saul that God should be the judge between the two of them. He asks God to judge his case and to decide between them. David will not take revenge on his own: he places his cause in God's hands and declares that his hand will not be raised against the king.

David is speaking from the mouth of a cave, where Saul had gone in without knowing that David was inside. His men urged him to kill Saul, but David only cut off a corner of Saul's robe. Now he shows it to Saul as proof that he could have killed him and did not, even though Saul was pursuing him unjustly.

For today: when someone treats you unfairly, do not repay evil with evil. Place your cause in God's hands, do what is right, and trust that He is a just judge. Waiting on Him requires patience, but it protects your heart from bitterness.
exp.11:24:
It says that if the people keep on doing wrong, both they and their king will face ruin. The word "still" in the verse shows that this is about continuing in wrongdoing. This is a serious warning, given plainly.

The prophet Samuel speaks in his farewell address as judge of Israel. The people had asked for a king, though God was already their King, and Samuel reminds them that God had cared for them. He shows them that, with a king or without one, what matters most is obeying God. This follows the line of the blessings and warnings of the law of Moses.

For today: no one is so high up or so secure that they can ignore God. Today you can examine whether there is something wrong that you keep repeating, and ask God for help to change and to serve him wholeheartedly.
exp.25:18:
Here David asks Saul to listen. He sets out two possibilities: if the Lord himself has stirred Saul up against him, then let Saul offer a sacrifice to seek peace with God. But if it is men who have provoked him, then let them be cursed, because they have driven David out from living in the Lord's inheritance, that is, the land of Israel. "Other gods" are foreign, false gods.

David speaks from the wilderness, after sparing Saul's life while Saul was sleeping. Saul was pursuing him unjustly, perhaps influenced by accusations from others. David suffers from being far from the land and from worshiping God. Interpreters debate how to understand "if the Lord has stirred you up"; David seems to leave the possibility open without affirming it.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, speak with respect and truth, without seeking revenge. Leave your cause in God's hands, and value being close to him more than any advantage.
exp.10:14:
The verse says that all the people went to Gilgal and there made Saul king before the Lord in Gilgal. "Made king" here means that they formally established or confirmed him in his position. Then they offered peace offerings before the Lord, which were sacrifices of fellowship and thanksgiving to God, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced greatly.

The narrator tells what happened after Saul rescued the city of Jabesh-gilead. Saul credited the victory to God, not to himself, and he showed mercy to those who had earlier doubted him. Samuel, the prophet, invited the people to renew the kingdom at Gilgal, that is, to publicly confirm Saul as king. Scholars debate whether this was a first coronation or a ratification, but the text emphasizes that everything was done before the Lord.

When God gives us a victory, it is fitting to pause, give thanks, and celebrate with others. We can also recognize those who lead with humility, setting pride and the desire for revenge aside.
exp.4:0:
This verse tells that the Philistines, after capturing the ark of God, carried it from Eben-ezer to Ashdod, one of their main cities. The ark was the sacred chest that represented God's presence among Israel.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had defeated Israel in battle and took the ark as a war trophy. They thought their god was stronger. The verses that follow show that this was not so: the image of Dagon fell face down before the ark. God did not need an army to defend his honor.

For today: sometimes it seems that circumstances or people defeat what belongs to God. But He remains sovereign even when everything seems lost. Trust that God works with power, even in silence, and do not be carried away only by appearances.
exp.12:3:
What it says: All Israel heard that Saul had defeated the Philistine outpost. They also learned that the Philistines now despised them. Then the people gathered to Saul at Gilgal.

Context: This is the narrator's account. Although the text says that Saul struck the garrison, the previous verse says it was Jonathan. Some think Saul received the credit as king, and others think he blew the trumpets and claimed the victory. It is not certain. The attack provoked Philistine fury and put Israel in danger.

For today: A brave action can bring harsh and unexpected consequences. Before acting, let us seek God's guidance and not only the applause of people. And when pressure comes, let us trust in Him, not in our pride.
exp.26:3:
It was reported to Saul that David had fled to Gath, and so he stopped searching for him. The phrase "the news" means "the report," and "had fled" means David had gone away to escape.

The narrator describes what happened after David, with his six hundred men and their families, went to live with Achish, a Philistine king of Gath. David had already had to flee from Saul many times. Earlier, he had said that one day he might die at the hands of Saul. The Bible does not say that going to Gath was a command from God, so some see it as a fearful human decision and others as a wise way out. What we do see is that Saul gave up the search.

For today: when you feel great pressure, ask God for wisdom before you decide. He can take care of you even when your decisions are not perfect.
exp.14:14:
Saul explains to Samuel why animals can be heard. He says they were brought from the Amalekites, and that the people kept the best of the sheep and the cattle to offer as a sacrifice to the Lord. According to him, everything else was destroyed.

The Lord had commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites completely. Samuel, the prophet, discovers that Saul did not obey fully, since Saul had just said he had carried out the word of the Lord. Notice that Saul says "the people" and "your God," as if he were stepping away from responsibility. His excuse sounds religious, but it does not change the fact that he disobeyed.

For today: do not use good religious intentions to justify what God has already asked of you clearly. Obeying from the heart is worth more than any offering. And when you fail, admit it without blaming others.
exp.13:39:
Saul divides the people into two groups: all Israel on one side, and he with his son Jonathan on the other. The people answer him, "Do what seemeth good unto thee," that is, "Do whatever seems best to you."

Saul speaks as king in the middle of the war against the Philistines. God had not answered his inquiry, and Saul thought someone had committed a sin. He had made a rash oath, and Jonathan, without knowing it, had broken it. Saul is about to find the guilty person by lot, and he includes himself and his son. Commentators see this as a gesture of justice, though also of a reckless oath.

Today we can learn to be honest when examining our faults, without protecting our loved ones or ourselves. We should also think carefully before making solemn promises.
exp.1:22:
Eli asks his sons why they act this way. He tells them that he has heard, from the mouth of all the people, the wicked things they are doing.

Eli speaks as the priest, now very old. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were also priests, but they abused their office and sinned at the entrance of the tabernacle. Eli rebukes them because their bad example was leading the people away from God. The following verses show that they would not listen. Some scholars point out that his correction was weak for the seriousness of the case.

Those who hold some responsibility over others, such as parents, leaders, or teachers, must correct wrongdoing firmly and lovingly, and in time. And all of us should listen to correction before our hearts become hardened.
exp.18:14:
When Saul learned that David was "sick," he sent the messengers again, but this time with a harsher command: to bring David to him "in the bed," that is, carried on his couch, so that he could kill him. "Turned" means "returned." "Bring him to me" means "bring him to me." Saul no longer cared about David's condition; his desire to kill him was stronger than any excuse.

The speaker is King Saul, full of jealousy and resentment toward David. Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, had put an idol in the bed to give David time to escape. Saul insists, not knowing he has been deceived.

For today: jealousy and resentment, if not surrendered to God, grow and make us hard and blind. Ask God to heal your heart before envy decides for you.
exp.5:2:
The Philistine priests and diviners advise that, if they send back the ark of the God of Israel, they must not send it away empty. They should accompany it with a guilt offering. Here "guilt offering" means a payment for the wrong done, and "being healed" refers to being freed from the plague. In this way they would know why the hand of God was still upon them.

The ark had been among the Philistines for seven months, and with it came plagues and suffering. Their own religious leaders speak, without knowing the God of Israel well, but they recognize that the punishment could come from Him. Their advice resembles the customs of their culture, and the Bible records only what they said.

For today: when we recognize that we have done wrong, lamenting is not enough. It is good to humble ourselves before God and make amends for the harm with sincerity. Today we know that Christ paid for our sin, so we come to Him with confidence.
exp.0:5:
This verse tells us that Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, treated Hannah cruelly. It says her rival "provoked her sore," and this means she kept provoking and annoying her without stopping. She did it to make Hannah miserable, and she used the fact that Hannah could not have children as her reason. The Bible says "the Lord had shut up her womb," meaning that God had not allowed her to become pregnant.

Here the narrator of the book explains Hannah's pain. Elkanah had two wives, something the Bible shows happening in that time, although it is not presented as God's ideal. Peninnah had children and Hannah did not, and Elkanah loved Hannah and gave her a special portion. Peninnah, perhaps out of jealousy, took advantage of every trip to the house of the Lord to wound her.

Today we can learn not to mock anyone's pain. If you suffer from a wound like this, do as Hannah did: bring your sorrow to God with honesty.
exp.29:5:
