It says that David was greatly distressed. His men, full of grief and anger over their sons and daughters who had been taken captive, spoke of stoning him. The phrase "was greatly distressed" means he was in great difficulty. A "bitter spirit" is a heart full of sorrow and anger. The phrase "encouraged himself in the Lord" means that he found strength in God.

The passage is narrative; there is no speaker, only the account. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the families while David and his men were away. David also lost his two wives, and now his people, in despair, were looking for someone to blame, namely their leader.

For today: when everything falls apart and even those close to us blame us, we can do what David did: stop and seek God before we react. Praying, asking for direction, and remembering who God is give us strength we cannot find in ourselves.
exp.23:21:
Saul asks David to swear to him by God that he will not destroy his descendants or wipe out his name from the family. David promises that he will do so. Then Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to a stronghold.

Saul speaks after David spared his life in the cave of En-gedi, although he could have killed him. Saul acknowledges that David will be king. In those times, a new king sometimes wiped out the family of the previous one, and that is why Saul asks for protection. David keeps his word, and later he cares for Mephibosheth, Saul's grandson (2 Samuel 9). That David stays in the stronghold shows that he does not fully trust Saul, and the Bible does not explain his reasons.

For today: keep what you promise, even to someone who has wronged you. But also be wise: forgiving and acting with wisdom can go together.
exp.8:5:
The servant of Saul answers that there is a man of God in that city who is held in high regard. He says that everything this man declares comes true, so he proposes that they go to see him. Perhaps he will show them the way they should go.

The servant of Saul is speaking. They have searched through several regions for the lost donkeys of Kish, the father of Saul, and have not found them. Saul wants to turn back so as not to worry his father. The servant proposes that they seek out this man of God, who, according to the text, is Samuel. His name is not yet mentioned here, but the account confirms it later on.

When we do not know which path to take, it is wise to seek counsel from people who live close to God and know his Word. It is also good to listen to someone who speaks to us with humility, like this servant. And while we ask for counsel, let us pray that God himself will guide us.
exp.10:11:
It says that, after the victory, the people spoke with Samuel. They recalled those who had earlier doubted Saul, when they asked, "Shall Saul reign over us?" Now they were asking that these men be brought out to be put to death.

The speakers are the Israelites, excited because Saul had just rescued Jabesh from the Ammonites. Earlier, some had looked down on Saul (1 Samuel 10:27). The people wanted to punish those critics, but Saul stopped them and said that day belonged to the salvation that God had given.

For today: when God gives us a victory, the temptation can be to settle accounts with those who doubted us. Saul shows us another way: give God the glory, forgive, and seek peace instead of revenge.
exp.25:2:
This verse says that Saul set up his camp on the hill of Hachilah, facing the wilderness, beside the road. Meanwhile, David was in the wilderness and realized that Saul was coming after him.

The narrator tells us that the Ziphites, people who lived in the area, informed Saul where David was hiding. Saul went out with three thousand chosen men to search for him. David had been running from Saul for some time, since Saul was pursuing him out of jealousy. This moment sets up a scene in which David will have the chance to harm Saul, but he will not take it.

For today: when someone pursues us or treats us unjustly, we should first be alert and trust God, rather than acting in haste or seeking revenge. We can ask him for wisdom to respond with integrity, as David did.
exp.0:2:
This verse tells how Elkanah went up year by year from his city to Shiloh. There he worshiped God and offered sacrifices. The phrase "the Lord of hosts" speaks of God as the Lord of all power. The Hebrew-era term for the place is simply rendered here as "Shiloh," the same name used in the verse. Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, are also mentioned, since they served as priests in that place.

Here the narrator of the book introduces Elkanah's family. Shiloh was then a center of worship for Israel. The sons of Eli are named because the story will later show that their conduct was wrong. For now, the text only sets the scene, and it shows that Elkanah was steady in his faith.

For today: Elkanah worshiped God regularly, even in a setting where the religious leadership was not an example. We can follow his example by being faithful in prayer and worship, without depending on how well or how poorly others do theirs.
exp.12:17:
The text tells us that the Philistines sent out three companies of soldiers to make a "raid," that is, a sudden attack for plunder. This company went toward Beth-horon, and the third toward the border that looks down on the valley of Zeboim, near the wilderness.

The narrator describes how the Philistines were surrounding Israel. Saul and Jonathan were at Gibeah with only a few men, and the people were afraid. The Philistines were going out in several directions to take control of the land. It is not known with certainty where that valley of Zeboim was.

For today: sometimes problems seem to come from every direction. Instead of despairing, we can bring each worry before God honestly and ask him for wisdom to take the next step.
exp.0:3:
This verse tells us that when the day of the yearly sacrifice came in Shiloh, Elkanah offered the sacrifice and gave out portions of the meat to his wife Peninnah and to all her sons and daughters. The word "offered" means that he presented the offering to God, and the "portion" each person received was the share of the sacrificial meal that belonged to them.

Here the narrator of the book describes the customs of Elkanah's family. Notice that Hannah does not appear in this list, and the next verse explains why: she received a special portion, because Elkanah loved her. This sets the scene for Hannah's sorrow, since she had no children and was mistreated by Peninnah.

For today: in family gatherings and at church, there are people who carry quiet sorrows. Let us think of someone who sits beside us with sadness, and offer them attention and sincere comfort.
exp.11:16:
Samuel reminds them that it is wheat harvest time, when normally it does not rain. He tells them that he will pray to God and that God will send thunder and rain. This will serve as a sign so that they understand that their wickedness was great in asking for a king.

Samuel speaks in his farewell as judge of Israel. The people already have Saul as king, but Samuel wants them to understand that, in asking for one, they distrusted that God was their true king. The storm out of season confirmed his word, and the people acknowledged their sin.

Today, this passage invites us to humbly recognize when we have placed our trust in something other than God. He does not reject us for it; He calls us to return to Him and to follow Him with all our heart.
exp.14:10:
God says that it grieves him that he made Saul king. The word "repenteth" in the verse means "regrets" or "is grieved." The reason is that Saul turned back from following him and did not carry out his commandments. Samuel was deeply troubled, and he cried out to the Lord all night.

God speaks, and he speaks to Samuel. God had commanded that the Amalekites be completely destroyed, but Saul and the people kept the best of the livestock and their king, Agag. When the Bible says that God "repents," it does not mean that he made a mistake. It expresses his deep grief at the disobedience. Christians understand this in different ways.

Obeying God halfway is disobeying him. Today we can ask him to help us obey him sincerely, even in what costs us. And like Samuel, we can bring to him in prayer what grieves us.
exp.22:16:
Jonathan speaks to David and says: "Do not be afraid, Saul will not catch you. You will be king of Israel, and I will be at your side as next in line. Even my father Saul knows this." The phrase "the hand of Saul" means that Saul will not be able to reach him.

The one speaking is Jonathan, Saul's son. David was hiding in the wilderness of Ziph because Saul was pursuing him to kill him. Jonathan went to find him to encourage him and strengthen his trust in God. Although he was the natural heir to the throne, he accepted that God had chosen David. We do not know in detail how Saul "knew" this, but the text suggests that he sensed it.

For today: we can be like Jonathan, encouraging others in their fear, reminding them that God carries out his plans, and setting aside pride and rivalry.
exp.10:13:
Samuel invites all the people to go to Gilgal. There he wants them to renew the kingdom, that is, to publicly confirm or re-establish Saul as king. "Come" is the word the verse uses, and it means the same as "let us go," the invitation in the verse itself.

Samuel speaks after Saul defeated the Ammonites and rescued the city of Jabesh-gilead. Some had looked down on Saul earlier, and the people wanted to punish them. Saul pardoned them and gave the glory to God. Samuel uses that moment to unite the nation. Scholars debate whether this "renewal" was a second ceremony or a confirmation of the first, since the text does not make this clear.

For today: when God gives us a victory, it is a good time to let go of grudges, forgive, and come together with gratitude. Giving thanks together strengthens unity.
exp.10:4:
This verse tells how Saul was coming back from the field, following his oxen, when he noticed that the people were weeping. He asked what was wrong, and they told him the news from the men of Jabesh. "Following his oxen" means that he had been working with his animals.

The men of Jabesh in Gilead were threatened by Nahash, king of the Ammonites, and they asked for seven days to seek help in Israel. The messengers arrived at Gibeah, where Saul lived, and the people wept. Saul did not yet act as king in any visible way; he was still going about his daily work. What follows shows that the Spirit of God moved him to act.

For today: God can call us to act in the midst of everyday life. It is good to listen to the pain of others, to ask, and not to ignore it. When someone suffers, we can offer concrete help, with humility and depending on God.
exp.16:18:
This verse tells us where Israel's army was. Saul, his soldiers, and all the Israelite people were in the valley of the oak tree (other versions call it the valley of Elah), facing the Philistines. The word "fighting" here describes more the fact that they were at war and in battle position, as the following verses show.

It is the narrator's explanation. Jesse has just sent David with food for his brothers, and this verse makes clear where he would go: to the front line of battle. This sets up the scene where David will arrive and meet Goliath.

For today: while others live through moments of tension or struggle, God often uses small, everyday tasks, like carrying food or asking how others are doing. Serve faithfully in simple things; that is where something great can begin.
exp.25:22:
Here David says that God is the one who rewards each person according to their righteousness (doing what is right) and their faithfulness (being loyal). He explains that God put Saul into his hands that day, but he did not want to harm him. "The anointed of the LORD" is the king, whom God himself had set apart for that office with oil.

David speaks to Saul after entering his camp at night and taking his spear while everyone was sleeping. Saul was pursuing him to kill him. David could have taken revenge, but he preferred to respect the king and leave God to be the judge. Saul, for his part, acknowledges his wrong.

For today: when someone has treated us unjustly and we have the chance to get even, we can choose to trust that God will do justice. Acting with integrity, even when no one sees us, is a way of honoring God.
exp.13:2:
Here is the verse: Ahiah, the son of Ahitub, the brother of Ichabod, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eli, the Lord's priest in Shiloh, wearing an ephod. And the people knew not that Jonathan was gone.

This passage introduces Ahiah, the priest who was with Saul and wore the ephod, a priestly garment used to seek guidance from God. It explains that he was the son of Ahitub and a descendant of Eli, the priest of Shiloh. It also says that the people did not know Jonathan had left.

The narrator tells this as Jonathan secretly heads out toward the Philistine camp. Israel was weak, and Saul had about six hundred men. The mention of Eli's family recalls a priestly line under judgment, and the name Ichabod evokes the loss of God's glory. Some think Ahiah is the same person as Ahimelech, but this is not certain.

For today: God can work even when the outlook seems bleak and no one notices. Before taking a step of faith, let us seek his direction with humility, and act with courage and wisdom.
exp.18:4:
He says David risked his life (the phrase "put his life in his hand" means staking his life on something) when he defeated the Philistine, that is, Goliath. God used that to bring a great victory to all Israel. "Thou sawest it, and didst rejoice" means that Saul was glad. Jonathan asks him why he now wants to sin by killing an innocent man.

Jonathan, the son of Saul and friend of David, is the speaker. Saul had said he wanted to kill David out of jealousy. Jonathan defends him calmly, reminds Saul of the good David had done, and asks him not to act unjustly. His plan worked, and Saul swore that David would not die, at least for the time being.

For today: when someone is treated unjustly, we can speak up for them with truth and gentleness. Remembering the good we have received helps us overcome jealousy and resentment.
exp.15:12:
Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed David in the midst of his brothers. "Anointing" means pouring oil over someone to set them apart for a task. From that day on, the Spirit of the Lord (Jehovah) came upon David and stayed with him. Then Samuel rose up and went back to his home in Ramah.

God had rejected Saul as king, and he sent Samuel to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, to choose another. David, the youngest, was tending the sheep, and no one took him into account. The text presents this as a contrast with Saul, from whom the Spirit had departed. How that departure happened, the text does not explain further.

God often calls people whom others overlook, and he shapes their character over time. If today you feel small or ignored, remember that God looks at the heart. Be faithful in the simple things, as David was with the sheep.
exp.0:10:
Hannah makes a promise to God. She asks him to look upon her suffering, not to forget her, and to give her a male child. If God does this, she will give him back to the Lord for his whole life.

Ana habla con el corazón roto is rendered as: Hannah speaks with a broken heart. She was barren and suffered mockery, and she went to Shiloh, where the sanctuary was. Her promise resembles the Nazirite vow (Numbers 6), which included not cutting the hair, although the text of this verse does not use that word. She prayed silently, with tears, and Eli, the priest, mistook her for a drunken woman.

For today: bring your pain to God honestly, without pretending to be strong. And if you make him a promise, think carefully about what you say and be faithful to it. Hannah not only asked; she was also willing to give up what she wanted most.
exp.19:35:
He tells his young attendant (servant boy, helper) to run and find the arrows (darts) that he is about to shoot. While the boy runs, Jonathan shoots an arrow that falls farther than the boy, that is, it goes past him.

Jonathan speaks with his helper. He has just confirmed that his father, King Saul, intends to kill David. Jonathan and David had agreed on a signal: the words Jonathan called out to the boy would be the secret message for David, who was hiding nearby. The young man did not understand anything; he was only gathering arrows.

For today: sometimes we have to deliver bad news or make painful decisions. Jonathan loved his friend and was loyal to him even when it cost him his relationship with his father. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to be faithful to what is right, caring for the people we love.
exp.13:49:
This verse says that the wife of King Saul was named Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz. It also says that the commander of his army was Abner, son of Ner, who was Saul's uncle. "Commander of his army" means the chief commander of the soldiers.

Here the narrator is not speaking through a character; the author of the book gives a brief summary of Saul's family and closest helpers. It comes after the account of his military victories and before a reminder that the war against the Philistines was still fierce. With these details, the story shows who surrounded the king. Abner will appear later as an important figure in the kingdom.

God uses people with names and family ties, not only famous leaders. Today we can value our families and those who walk with us at work or in service, praying for them and thanking them for their support.
exp.29:6:
Here David asks the priest Abiathar to bring him the ephod. The phrase "Yo te ruego," an old way of saying "please," is not in the verse; the verse simply has David asking. The ephod was a sacred garment of the priest, and it was used to seek God's answer. Abiathar brought it to him.

David is speaking in a very hard moment. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the women and children of the families. His own men, full of grief, were talking about stoning him. But David strengthened himself in the Lord and, before acting, wanted to ask him what to do. Scholars believe the ephod was used to receive God's answer, though it is not known with certainty how it worked.

When you are under pressure or afraid, do not act first on impulse. Seek God in prayer and in his Word, and ask him for direction before taking the next step.
exp.18:1:
Jonathan warns David that his father, King Saul, is looking for a way to kill him. He advises David to take heed to himself until the morning, that is, to stay alert until the next day, and to hide in a remote place.

Jonathan speaks, the son of Saul and a very close friend of David. Saul had just ordered that David be killed, because he was jealous of him. Jonathan finds himself between loyalty to his father and love for his friend, and he decides to protect David's life. Soon afterward he promises to speak well of David before Saul.

For today: true friendship acts with courage on behalf of the other, even when it costs. Ask yourself whom you can care for, defend, or warn of danger, and do it with wisdom and love, without ceasing to seek peace.
exp.21:2:
David left the cave of Adullam and went to Mizpeh of Moab. There he asked the king of Moab to let his father and mother come forth and be with them, that is, under his care, until he knew what God would do for him.

David spoke because he was fleeing from King Saul, who wanted to kill him. He already had about four hundred men with him, and his family was in danger. Moab may have seemed like a safe place to him, and the Bible also connects David to Moab through his great-grandmother Ruth, although the text does not say that this was the reason. Later, the prophet Gad tells him to return to Judah.

For today: when you do not know what is coming, care lovingly for your family and take the wise steps within your reach. Then say to God, with humility: "I will wait on you and see what you will do."
exp.16:44:
Here David answers Goliath. He tells him that Goliath comes with a sword, a spear, and a shield, that is, with human weapons. David, on the other hand, comes "in the name of the Lord of hosts," meaning he trusts in the authority and power of God, who commands the armies of Israel. He says that Goliath has defied him, that is, he has challenged and insulted him.

David speaks in the valley of Elah, in front of the Philistine army. Goliath had just mocked him, cursed him, and threatened to leave his body for the birds. David does not see this battle as a personal matter, but as an offense against God and his people.

Today, when problems seem enormous, we can do what David did: not rely only on our own strength or resources, but pray and act trusting in God, doing what is right with humility.
exp.3:18:
This verse tells of the wife of Phinehas, daughter-in-law of Eli, who was about to give birth. When she heard that the ark of God had been taken and that her father-in-law and her husband were dead, she bowed herself down and went into labor, for her pains came upon her suddenly.

The speaker is the narrator of the book. Israel had lost the battle against the Philistines, and the ark, the sign of God's presence among the people, had been taken. She died shortly afterward. Her son was named Ichabod, a name usually understood to mean "the glory has departed," because she felt that Israel's glory had gone.

For today: when you feel that everything is falling apart, remember that God does not depend on objects or places. Seek him sincerely, with humility and repentance, and trust that he is still at work even in dark times.
exp.25:20:
Saul admits: "I have sinned." He asks David to return and promises not to harm him anymore, because David spared his life that day. He recognizes that he acted "foolishly," that is, like a fool, without wisdom, and that he "erred exceedingly," meaning he was very wrong. "My soul was precious in your eyes" means that David valued him and cared for him.

Here Saul, the king, speaks after David, while he was in the cave of the camp, could have killed him as he slept, but chose not to lay a hand on the anointed of the LORD. David has just challenged him over his unjust pursuit. Saul had said similar things before (24:17; 15:24), and his later conduct shows that his repentance did not last. The Bible does not detail how sincere he was at that moment.

For today: saying "I was wrong" is a good start, but true repentance is proven by constant change. Let us ask God to give us a humble heart that corrects its course and does not only speak.
exp.13:48:
This verse gives the names of Saul's sons: Jonathan, Ishui and Melchi-shua. It also names his two daughters: the older was called Merab, and the younger, Michal. The spellings "Jonathan" and "Michal" are simply older forms of these names. Some scholars note that other passages in the Bible mention slightly different names for Saul's sons, and it is not entirely clear why.

The narrator of the book makes a brief summary of Saul's reign here. After recounting his military victories, he presents his family: his sons, his wife, and his commander Abner. This works like a snapshot of the kingdom. Later on, Jonathan and Michal will play an important role in the story of David.

For today: God pays attention to families and to people's names, not only to great achievements. Care for your family with as much dedication as you give to your work, because that is also where your faith is lived out and where you leave your mark.
exp.0:18:
This verse tells us that Elkanah and Hannah got up early and worshiped God. There, Elkanah "knew" his wife, which is an old way of saying that they were intimate as husband and wife. It also says that the Lord "remembered her," meaning that he answered her prayer and acted on her behalf.

The narrator of the book recounts what happened after Hannah, deeply troubled, prayed at the sanctuary and the priest Eli blessed her. Hannah left in peace and went back to eating. Here we see that she placed her burden in God's hands, and that he responded in his own time.

For today: after praying, we can rest in God and carry on with our lives, worshiping him with confidence. He does not forget the one who cries out to him, even when the answer is delayed or comes in his own way.
exp.7:5:
The explanation says that the request for a king displeased Samuel, or sat badly with him, because the people asked for a king to govern and judge them. The verse says the thing displeased Samuel, so the word used there is the one that matters here. Faced with that displeasure, Samuel did not argue or become angry with the people; instead he prayed to the Lord, that is, to God.

The elders of Israel speak with Samuel, who is now old, in Ramah. His sons were not following his example, and that is why they ask for a king like those of the other nations. Samuel felt rejected, but God explains to him that the one truly rejected is Him.

When something hurts us or offends us, the first thing we can do is bring it to God in prayer. In this way we avoid reacting in anger, and we give God room to clarify our hearts and guide us.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that Elkanah had two wives: Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah had children, but Hannah could not have any. The names are spelled as "Hannah" and "Peninnah" here.

Context: the one telling the story is the narrator of the book, not a character. He introduces Elkanah's family, a man from the region of Ephraim who went every year to worship at Shiloh. The Bible only describes that he had two wives; it does not say that God approved of it. This painful situation prepares the story of Hannah and her prayer, which will lead to the birth of Samuel.

For today: if you live with a lack or a comparison that hurts, remember that God sees what others overlook. Bring your pain to Him in prayer with sincerity, as Hannah will do, and seek the support of people who listen to you with respect.
exp.13:23:
This verse tells that the soldiers of Israel were worn out and distressed that day. Saul had made the people swear under a curse: whoever ate anything before evening, before he had taken revenge on his enemies, would be cursed. The word "adjured" here means making people swear under threat, and the phrase about not tasting food means not eating even a bite. No one ate anything.

Here the narrator is speaking, and he reports Saul's order in the middle of the pursuit of the Philistines. God had just given Israel the victory. Saul probably wanted speed and wanted to waste no time, but his order left the people weak. Some think it was sincere zeal, others that it was pride or rashness. The text does not fully make this clear, though it shows that it was an unnecessary burden.

For today: before demanding something with great force, it is wise to think about whether it truly helps others. Religious zeal without wisdom can do harm. Let us ask God for prudence and compassion.
exp.22:8:
This verse says that David realized Saul was planning to harm him. So he asked the priest Abiathar to bring the ephod. The ephod was a sacred garment of the priest, and it was used to seek God's guidance and receive his answer.

David had rescued the city of Keilah from the Philistines. Saul, believing that God had handed David over to him, gathered the army to surround the city. David, who was being pursued without cause, did not act on impulse. Before deciding, he wanted to ask God what he should do, and in the verses that follow God answers him.

For today: when we feel threatened or under pressure, the best thing is to stop and seek God before acting. We can pray, open his Word, and ask for wise counsel, instead of being carried along by fear or haste.
exp.14:6:
This verse tells that Saul defeated the Amalekites over a very wide area. The word "smote" means that he beat them in battle. The campaign went from Havilah to Shur, near the border of Egypt. Scholars are not sure exactly where Havilah was, but the text marks out a large territory.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not a character. God, through the prophet Samuel, had commanded Saul to destroy the Amalekites for attacking Israel when they came out of Egypt. Saul warned the Kenites to move away, since they had shown kindness to Israel. This victory seems complete, but the verses that follow show that Saul obeyed only in part.

For today: a good start is not enough if we do not finish by obeying fully. We can ask ourselves whether we are doing what God asks with a whole heart, or only what suits us.
exp.13:29:
Jonathan says that if the people had eaten today of the spoil they found among their enemies, the defeat of the Philistines would have been even greater.

Jonathan speaks after his father, King Saul, had made the people swear that no one would eat anything during the battle. Jonathan had not heard that oath and ate a little honey, and his eyes brightened, that is, he regained his strength. He sees that his father's command left the army weak and tired, and for that reason he criticizes the decision.

For today: The decisions of a leader, even when well intended, can harm others if they are made in haste or without wisdom. Before imposing rules or vows, think about how they will affect those who depend on you, and ask God for prudence.
exp.0:25:
Anna approaches the priest Eli and reminds him who she is. The phrase "as your soul lives" was an older way of swearing or of speaking with respect, something like "I assure you by your life." She says that she is the woman who years earlier stood there beside him, praying to the Lord. The words "my lord" are a courteous form of address.

It is Anna speaking, who for a long time was unable to have children. At Shiloh she had prayed with great sorrow and promised to dedicate to God the son she was given. Now Samuel has already been weaned, and she comes to fulfill her promise. Eli had seen her pray, but he probably did not remember her well, so she introduces herself.

For today: God hears our prayers, and it is good to remember and give thanks for what he has given us. If we have promised something to God, let us seek to keep it with sincerity and gratitude.
exp.6:5:
This verse tells that the people of Israel gathered at Mizpah. They drew water and poured it out before the Lord, fasted the whole day, and confessed, "We have sinned against the Lord." Also, Samuel judged them, that is, he led them and settled their affairs as their leader. Pouring out water probably expressed repentance and surrender, although scholars explain it in several ways.

This is an account from the time of Samuel. Israel had worshiped the Baals and Ashtaroth, false gods, and now was turning back to the Lord. Samuel called them together to pray for them. Afterward, the Philistines threatened the people, and they asked Samuel to keep crying out to God.

For today: returning to God begins with sincerely acknowledging our sin. It is not enough to feel sorry; we must say it before God, leave behind whatever draws us away from Him, and trust in His forgiveness.
exp.15:7:
This verse tells how Jesse, David's father, made his son Abinadab pass before the prophet Samuel. Samuel understood that God had not chosen this young man either.

Samuel had been sent by God to Bethlehem to anoint a new king over Israel, because Saul had been rejected. Jesse presented his sons one by one. Earlier, Samuel had been impressed by Eliab because of his appearance, but God reminded him that He looks at the heart.

For today: let us not judge people, or ourselves, only by what is seen on the outside. Let us ask God to teach us to value character, faith, and humility, which is what He looks at.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that God spoke to Samuel. Your verse reads "Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel," which is the same idea: the Lord gave Samuel a message. It is a short phrase, but it introduces a very serious message.

God speaks just after Saul and the people did not fully obey. They had been told to destroy the Amalekites and all that belonged to them, but they spared King Agag and the best of the livestock. Samuel was the prophet, and God shares with him what he thinks of Saul. What follows shows that God grieves over Saul's disobedience, and Samuel is deeply saddened.

For today: God speaks to us, above all through his Word, and he expects us to obey completely, not only in what is convenient for us. We might ask ourselves: is there something God has asked of me that I am only doing halfway?
exp.25:17:
David asks King Saul why he keeps chasing him. He calls Saul "my lord" and calls himself "his servant," showing respect. His questions, "What have I done? What evil is in my hand?" mean: "What is my fault? What wrong did I commit?"

David speaks from a hill, at night, after entering Saul's camp while everyone was sleeping. He could have killed the king, but he took only his spear and his water jug as proof. Saul, jealous, was looking for him in order to kill him. David defends his innocence with humility and respect.

For today: when someone treats us unjustly, we can ask for explanations calmly and respectfully, without seeking revenge. We can leave our case in God's hands, for he sees everything and is just.
exp.12:19:
This verse says that all the Israelites had to go down to the land of the Philistines to sharpen their tools for work. Sharpening means putting an edge on a blade. The iron point of a plow, the "coulter," is the blade that cuts the soil ahead of the plowshare, the "axe" is a tool for chopping, and the "mattock" is a kind of small hoe used for digging up the ground.

It is the narrator of the book who describes Israel's situation under Saul. The Philistines dominated the country and did not allow there to be blacksmiths among the Hebrews. According to the text, they did this so that the Hebrews would not make swords or spears. In this way Israel depended on its enemies even for the most basic things, and it went into battle almost without weapons.

For today: when we depend entirely on what others control, we feel weak. This passage invites us to remember that our strength does not lie in having the best resources, but in trusting God, who would later give victory to Israel.
exp.25:14:
Here David speaks to Abner, the commander of Saul's army, with irony. He asks whether Abner is not a brave man, the best in Israel, and then why he did not protect the king. To "keep" means to protect, and "one of the people" refers to an ordinary person who got into the camp.

David and Abishai had entered Saul's camp by night, while everyone was sleeping, and had taken the king's spear and water jar. David could have killed him, but he did not want to harm the anointed of God. Now, from a distance, he exposes Abner's carelessness.

For today: when God entrusts us with a responsibility, we should take care of it seriously and not neglect it. We also learn from David to correct others without taking revenge, respecting people even when we have the opportunity to harm them.
exp.17:11:
Saul was afraid of David. The reason given is that the Lord was with David and had departed from Saul. "Was afraid" means "felt fear." "Was with him" means "was with him" (the same wording as the verse). This was not a fear of respect but of threat: Saul saw that David had something he no longer had.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Just before this, Saul tried to pin David to the wall with a spear while David was playing music. The text says that an "evil spirit from God" troubled him, something scholars explain in several ways. What is clear is that Saul's fear led him to violence, and David escaped by dodging the spear.

For today: when we see that others are doing well, let us not let envy or fear take control of us. Instead, let us seek God with humility and deal with whatever is in our hearts.
exp.2:15:
Samuel had just received a very hard message from God: Eli's house would be judged. Samuel was young and afraid to tell his teacher. Eli, already old and a priest, calls him kindly, though afterward he will firmly ask him to tell him everything. His gentle manner opens the way for Samuel to speak with confidence.

Today, when you have to say a difficult truth, do it with respect and without hiding what is essential. And if someone corrects you or listens to you, answer with the same readiness as Samuel: "I am here."
exp.15:20:
David came to where King Saul was and presented himself before him, that is, he put himself at the king's service. Saul came to love him very much and made him his armourbearer. "Armourbearer" is the attendant who carried the weapons and shield of the king or of a soldier. "Loved him" means that Saul grew very fond of him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul was tormented by an evil spirit, and his servants suggested that he seek someone who could play the harp. David, a young shepherd from Bethlehem, was recommended. God had already chosen him in secret as the future king, but he began by serving with humility.

For today: serve faithfully in small things and in unseen places, without rushing your future. God can use your simple gifts to open doors for you and to help others.
exp.10:5:
He says that when Saul heard the threat against the people of Jabesh, the Spirit of God came upon him with force, and he was filled with a very great anger. The word "seized" here means that the Spirit took hold of him and drove him forward with power. The phrase "when he heard" simply means "upon hearing."

The narrator tells what happened when Saul was returning from the field with his oxen. The people of Jabesh Gilead were threatened by Nahash, king of the Ammonites, and they were asking for help. The people were only weeping, but Saul, already chosen as king, responded. His anger does not seem selfish, but rather an indignation over God's people in danger. Some readers see here the Spirit equipping a leader for a specific moment.

Today, indignation can be good when it moves us to defend the weak and act with justice. Let us ask God to guide our anger, so that it does not destroy, but serves and protects.
exp.27:18:
This verse announces that Israel will lose the battle against the Philistines. Saul and his sons will die, and tomorrow they will be in the realm of the dead, which the text describes as being "with me," that is, in death. The verse says that the Lord will "deliver" Israel into the hand of the Philistines, meaning he will give them over to the enemy. Saying that they will be "with me" is a way of saying that they will die.

The speaker is the figure who appears as Samuel, already dead, and Saul hears him in a consultation with a medium. Saul was afraid of the Philistines, and God was not answering him. Some believe it was truly Samuel, and others that it was an apparition. The text stresses that Saul disobeyed God and lost the kingdom.

For today: disobeying God has consequences, yet He remains just. When you are afraid, do not seek answers in forbidden places. Come to God with sincerity, and obey Him today.
exp.1:21:
Eli was very old at this point, and this verse says that he heard about everything his sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were doing to all of Israel. He also learned that they lay with the women who assembled at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation, that is, the women who gathered at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

The narrator tells us this to show the corruption of Eli's sons, who were priests. They abused their office and the people, while the young Samuel grew faithfully before God. Eli is the one who hears the complaints, and in the verses that follow he rebukes them, though with gentle words. Scholars agree that the sin was serious, though they do not all explain in the same way who those women were or what their service involved.

For today: whoever has authority, in the family, the church, or the workplace, must not ignore the wrong he sees. Correcting it in time and with firmness, but with love, protects others and honors God.
exp.9:1:
Here Samuel tells Saul that on that same day, as he leaves Samuel's side, he will meet two men near Rachel's grave, in the territory of Benjamin. They will bring him news: the lost female donkeys have been found, and his father has stopped worrying about them, but now he is distressed about him and asks what he will do for his son.

Samuel has just anointed Saul as leader of Israel. To confirm that all of this comes from God, he gives him concrete signs that will come true along the way. The exact location of Zelzah is not known with certainty.

God can show us that He knows our small worries and our great ones. While we go around and around a problem, He is already at work somewhere else. We can trust that He cares for us and for those we love, even when we cannot see how.
exp.24:19:
Abigail rode on a donkey and came down along a hidden side of the mountain. Suddenly she saw David and his men coming toward her, and she went out to meet them. "A hidden side" means a path covered or sheltered by the hill. "Went out to meet them" means she went out to receive them.

The narrator describes this moment. Nabal, Abigail's husband, had scorned David and his men, even though they had protected his flocks. David, angered, was coming with armed men to take revenge. Abigail, without telling her husband, brought food to calm the situation and prevent a tragedy.

For today: when you see that a conflict could end in harm, do not wait for others to fix it. Act with wisdom, humility, and courage, seeking peace. Sometimes a generous gesture, offered at the right time, prevents a greater evil.
exp.17:7:
This verse says that Saul became very angry. The women's song bothered him, and he said, "They have credited David with ten thousands, and to me they have credited only thousands; what more can he have but the kingdom?" The phrase about the saying displeasing him means that it upset him deeply.

Saul, the king of Israel, is the one speaking. David had just defeated the Philistine Goliath, and the women came out to celebrate with songs and music. Saul felt that he was being compared with David and that David was outshining him. His anger came from pride and from fear of losing the throne. According to the text that follows, from that day on he looked at David with suspicion.

For today: when we see that someone receives praise or success, we can choose to rejoice instead of comparing ourselves. If we feel envy, it is wise to bring it to God in prayer soon, before it grows and leads us to do harm.
exp.16:54:
Verse 55 says that Saul saw David go out to face the Philistine, that is, Goliath. Then he asked Abner, the commander of his army, "Whose son is this young man?" The reader's verse uses "youth" for this word, which means a young person or a boy. The spelling changes in the original wording do not affect the meaning, so no further comment is needed here.

Saul is the one speaking, and Abner is the one who answers. This is curious, because David had already played the harp for Saul before (1 Samuel 16). Scholars explain this in several ways: perhaps Saul did not remember him well, perhaps he was very troubled, or perhaps he was asking about David's family, since he had promised a reward to whoever won. The Bible does not make it clear.

God can use people whom others do not notice or know. David was a little-known young man, but he trusted God and was faithful in whatever was placed before him. Today, you do not need fame or recognition to be useful. Do with faith what God places in your hands, and let Him take care of the rest.
exp.2:8:
Este versículo cuenta que Eli le da a Samuel una instrucción sencilla: que se vaya a acostar, y que si Dios lo llama otra vez, responda: "Habla, Señor, porque tu siervo escucha". Samuel obedece y vuelve a su lugar.

Samuel era un muchacho que servía en el santuario junto al anciano sacerdote Eli. Dios lo había llamado tres veces, y Samuel pensaba que era Eli quien lo llamaba. Por fin Eli entendió que era Dios quien hablaba y le enseñó cómo responder. Samuel aún no conocía a Dios por experiencia propia.

Para hoy: Dios habla a quien se dispone a escuchar. Antes de pedir o hablar en la oración, podemos dedicar un momento en silencio y decir con sinceridad: "Habla, Señor, porque tu siervo escucha". También conviene aprender de personas con más experiencia en la fe, como hizo Samuel con Eli.
exp.1:18:
This verse tells us that Hannah, Samuel's mother, made him a small robe every year. She would bring it to him when she went up with her husband Elkanah to the sanctuary to offer the yearly sacrifice. The verse's wording refers to making the robe and bringing it, so the sentences about the old phrasing are removed. The robe was an everyday garment, different from the linen ephod that Samuel wore while serving.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, without attributing the words to any character. Hannah had dedicated Samuel to the Lord while he was a child, and he lived with the priest Eli. While the sons of Eli despised the offerings, the account shows Samuel serving faithfully and his mother caring for him with constant love.

For today: love is shown through simple, sustained acts. Although Hannah could not have her son near her, she cared for him with thoughtful details year after year. We can do the same for the people God has entrusted to us, giving them attention, prayer, and practical help faithfully.
exp.16:36:
What it says: David affirms that the Lord, who earlier rescued him from the claws of the lion and the bear that attacked his sheep, will also deliver him from this Philistine. Saul accepts and tells him: "Go, and the Lord be with you." The "claws" are the paws of the wild beasts, and "the hand" here means the power of the Philistine.

Context: David is a young shepherd who offers to fight Goliath, when the whole army of Israel was afraid. He speaks to King Saul, who doubted that a boy could defeat a warrior. David does not trust in his own strength, but in what God had already done for him in private, while caring for the flock.

For today: When you face a big problem, remember how God helped you in earlier ones. That grateful memory strengthens your faith and gives you courage to take the next step, trusting that God remains faithful.
exp.18:23:
The verse tells that Saul took off his clothes, prophesied in front of Samuel, and lay down without clothing all that day and all that night. "Prophesy" here means speaking or acting under a strong spiritual influence, not necessarily foretelling the future. That is why people repeated the saying: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" The phrase "stripped off his clothes" probably indicates that he removed his royal robes, or part of them.

Saul was pursuing David to kill him. David had taken refuge with Samuel in Naioth. Three groups of Saul's messengers arrived and prophesied; then Saul himself went. God stopped his plan to kill David and humbled him.

For today: no one can stop what God decides to protect. When you feel that someone or something rises against your good plans, trust that God cares for his own and knows how to set limits on evil.
exp.1:31:
God announces to Eli that days of distress will come upon his family. "Adversary" means rival or opponent, and some translators understand that it refers to a trouble or affliction in the house of God, because the Hebrew is difficult. Even when God blesses Israel, Eli's house will not share in that blessing. Nobody in his family will reach old age.

A man of God speaks to Eli, the priest. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing their office, and Eli did not correct them firmly. God had promised that this family would serve before him, but the promise did not spare them from the consequences of despising him. He honors those who honor him.

For today: serving God is not a title, but an obedient life. If you have authority in your home, your work, or your church, correct with love and with truth, without looking the other way.
exp.13:34:
The explanation says that Saul built an altar to the Lord, and that it was the first altar he built. The word "built" is the ordinary sense of the verb here, and "altar" refers to the place where sacrifices were offered to God.

The narrator tells this after the people, hungry following the battle against the Philistines, slaughtered animals and ate the meat with the blood still in it, something the law of Moses forbade. Saul ordered them to slaughter the animals over a large stone. Then he built the altar. Some think it was a sincere act of devotion; others, a hasty act. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when we fail, it is not enough to fix the outward situation quickly. It is wise to return to God with humility and listen to his voice before deciding what to do next.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that the Philistines were brought low, that is, defeated and overcome. For that reason they stopped invading the territory of Israel. The word "coast" in the King James wording means the border or territory of a land. "The hand of the Lord" speaks of God's power acting against them while Samuel lived and led the people.

It is the narrator of the book who sums up what happened. Israel had returned to the Lord at Mizpah, with repentance and prayer, and God helped them to win. Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer as a memorial that the Lord had helped them. This verse shows the result: a time of protection and relief.

For today: when God helps us, it is good to return to Him wholeheartedly and to remember His faithfulness. We can keep memorial stones of our own, such as a prayer journal, to give thanks and to trust Him when new difficulties come.
exp.0:24:
It says they killed the bullock, that is, a young bull, to offer it as a sacrifice. Then they brought the boy Samuel before the priest Eli. Some scholars note that the older text varies at this point (three bullocks or a three-year-old bull), but the central idea is the same.

The narrator tells that Hannah, after weaning her son, went with her husband Elkanah to Shiloh. Years earlier she had promised God to give him the son he granted her. Now she keeps her word: she offers the sacrifice and presents the child to the priest, and right away she will remind Eli who she is.

For today: if you promised something to God in a difficult moment, do not forget it when the answer comes. A simple way to keep it is to thank him, and to give back with joy the time, gifts, or goods he has entrusted to you.
exp.12:7:
Verse 8 tells us that Saul waited seven days in Gilgal, as Samuel had instructed him. But Samuel did not come, and the people were scattered from him, that is, they left him, abandoning him little by little.

The narrator describes the pressure Saul was under. The Philistines threatened Israel, the people hid in caves, and others fled across the Jordan. Those who stayed with Saul trembled with fear. Saul had been commanded to wait for Samuel, who would offer the sacrifice. Seeing the army fall apart, Saul grew desperate and offered the burnt offering himself. The following passage recounts this.

When God asks us to wait and everything seems to be falling apart, it is tempting to take shortcuts. Obedience includes trusting God's timing, even when pressure is screaming at us to act now.
exp.18:22:
This verse says that Saul arrived at Naioth in Ramah, looking for David. But before he got there, the Spirit of God came upon him, and he began to prophesy along the way. The words "went thither" and "came" that appear in the source wording are old-fashioned ways of saying "went" and "came"; "prophesying" here is understood as speaking or praising under the impulse of God.

The account tells how Saul pursued David, and David had taken refuge with Samuel. Saul sent messengers three times, and every one of them ended up prophesying. Then he went himself. God protected David and stopped Saul's plans. Scholars understand in different ways what kind of prophecy this was, but the text shows that God acted on Saul without his choosing.

For today: no one can hinder God's purposes. If you are in the middle of an injustice, trust that God can care for you and work in unexpected ways.
exp.15:16:
Saul accepts the suggestion of his servants and asks them to find someone who can play an instrument well. The word "play" here is the verb used for playing a stringed instrument, and the verse asks for someone who can do it skillfully.

The king himself is speaking. His attendants had seen that an evil spirit, allowed by God, was tormenting him, and they proposed that music might bring him relief. Interpreters explain that spirit in different ways, but the text says it truly troubled him. Saul asks for someone skilled, and in this way the path opens for David to arrive.

Today we can learn to listen to the good advice of those around us when we are distressed. Accepting help, whether music, companionship, or counsel, is not weakness. And God can use simple things, such as a song, to bring rest to a weary heart.
exp.20:4:
David tells the priest Ahimelech that his men have kept away from women for about three days ("the day before yesterday" in the old wording has been rendered here as "about these three days," matching the verse). The bodies or belongings of the young men are probably what is meant by the vessels, and they are considered holy even though the journey is common, that is, not set apart for worship. He adds that the sacred bread will be replaced today by other bread.

David speaks while fleeing from King Saul, who wants to kill him. He arrives at Nob hungry and asks the priest for bread, but the priest has only the bread of the Presence, which is reserved for the sanctuary. David does not tell him the whole truth about his mission, and some interpreters see deception here. Jesus later mentioned this episode (Matthew 12:3-4).

Today we learn that God values mercy and human need above the cold letter of the rules. Even so, we should live with integrity and without deceit, because God cares for those who are hungry.
exp.29:24:
This verse says that what David decided that day became a permanent rule in Israel. The text uses a phrase meaning an official norm that had to be followed, and it also shows that the writer saw this practice still in force in his own time.

David had just rescued the families and possessions that the Amalekites had taken from Ziklag. Two hundred of his men, who were very tired, had stayed behind to guard the baggage. Some of the men who had fought wanted to deny them a share of the spoils. David answered that the victory came from the LORD, and that those who guarded the supplies should receive the same share as those who went into battle.

Today we can remember that everything we have is a gift from God. That leads us to value and acknowledge the work of those who serve quietly, without being noticed, in the church, in the family, or at work.
exp.13:28:
Jonathan replies that his father, King Saul, has troubled the land, meaning he has brought serious trouble upon the whole nation. He says that his eyes have been enlightened, that is, he regained strength and spirit after tasting a little honey.

Jonathan speaks with a soldier who told him about Saul's oath, which he had not heard. Israel was pursuing the Philistines, and the people were exhausted and hungry. Jonathan thinks the order was unwise, since it weakened the army just when it most needed strength. The Bible does not say here that God had asked for that fast.

For today: before imposing harsh rules, let us consider whether they truly help or whether they burden others needlessly. Religious zeal needs wisdom and compassion.
exp.19:36:
This verse tells that the young servant arrived at the spot where the arrow Jonathan shot had fallen. Then Jonathan called out to him from behind: "Is not the arrow beyond you?" The older words are understood this way: the arrow is what Jonathan shot, the young man is the servant who ran to fetch it, and "cried after" means that he called out to him.

Jonathan speaks to his servant, but in reality he is sending a coded message to David, who was hiding nearby. Saul, Jonathan's father, was seeking to kill David. Jonathan and David had agreed on this signal: if the arrow fell far away, David must flee because he was in danger. The servant understood nothing.

For today: loyal love sometimes calls for prudence and courage. Jonathan risked his own position to protect his friend. Ask yourself whom you can care for faithfully, even when it costs you something, and act with wisdom.
exp.11:14:
It says that if the people do not obey God and rebel against his commands, God will act against them, just as he did with their ancestors. The old forms of "to hear" and "to be" are rendered as the plain phrases "if you will not obey" and "if you are" in the verse you have. The phrase "hand of the Lord" means his power and his judgment.

Samuel speaks in his farewell address as judge. Israel had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations, and Samuel saw this as a rejection of God's guidance over them. Even so, Samuel shows them that the king does not change what is essential: both the people and the king must continue to obey God. Then comes the sign of the storm during the wheat harvest.

For today: it is not enough to have good leaders, good structures, or good plans. What matters most is listening to God and obeying him sincerely. Today you can choose one word from the Bible and put it into practice.
exp.8:18:
Samuel tells Saul that he is the seer, that is, the prophet Saul had been looking for. He invites him to go up to the high place, where there would be a feast, and to eat with him. The words "I will let thee go" and "tell thee all that is in thine heart" are rendered in the verse above as what Samuel will do the next day: send Saul on his way and make known to him everything that is on his mind.

Saul was looking for his father's donkeys that had gone missing, and he asked about the seer to seek guidance. Without Saul knowing it, God had already told Samuel that this young man would be the ruler of Israel. That is why Samuel receives him with confidence and promises him answers.

God often works behind the scenes, even in small and everyday matters. We can trust that he guides our steps, and seek his direction with humility, even when we are only busy with simple tasks.
exp.3:9:
The explanation says that the Philistines fought against Israel and defeated them. The Israelites fled, each man to his own home. The verse's word "tents" meant their homes or camps. There was a very great slaughter: thirty thousand soldiers on foot fell, that is, footmen. Some scholars believe that this figure could be understood in another way, but the text presents it as a great loss.

The words quoted above were spoken by the Philistines, who were afraid because the ark had come into the Israelite camp. They encouraged one another to fight like men. Israel had carried the ark as if it were a charm, without turning to God with their whole heart. That is why the ark did not secure them the victory.

For today: it is not enough to use religious symbols or customs to have God on our side. What matters is a sincere relationship with Him, marked by obedience and humility.
exp.17:24:
Saul instructs his servants to tell David that the king does not want money as a bride price for marrying his daughter. Instead, he asks for a hundred foreskins of the Philistines, as proof that David has avenged the king of his enemies. The bride price was the payment given for a bride, and the foreskins were the flesh removed in circumcision. The text makes the real plan clear: Saul hoped the Philistines would kill David.

Saul, the king, speaks through his servants. He feels envy and fear toward David, because the people admire him for his victories. He appears to honor David with an offer of marriage, but he is hiding a trap. The Philistines were enemies of Israel, and this mission was very dangerous.

For today: let us be wary of kind appearances when bad intentions lie behind them, and let us not act that way toward others. We can trust that God cares for those who are faithful to him, even when someone plans to harm them.
exp.16:46:
What it says: David declares that all the people gathered there will see that God does not need swords or spears to give the victory. "Congregation" refers to the assembled people, and "haste" (in the next part of the verse) means speed. David says the battle belongs to the Lord, meaning the outcome depends on God, not on weapons.

Context: David, a young shepherd, speaks in front of Goliath, the Philistine giant who had for weeks been challenging the army of Israel. The Israelite soldiers were afraid. David does not trust in armor or military experience but in God, and he wants everyone, Israelites and Philistines alike, to recognize that God acts on behalf of his people.

For today: When a problem seems bigger than you are, do what is within your reach with honesty, but do not place your final trust in your own resources. Pray, ask for direction, and rest in the fact that God remains the one who sustains your life.
exp.11:17:
Samuel prayed to God, and that same day God sent thunder and rain. When the people saw it, they felt a great fear of God and also of Samuel. The phrase about their fear, meaning that they felt a deep reverence and dread, is the point of the verse.

Samuel is speaking to the Israelites, who had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. He sees that request as a rejection of God being their King. It was the time of the wheat harvest, when it normally did not rain, so the storm was a clear sign that God was speaking.

For today: when you recognize a mistake, do not stay with only fear or guilt. As the context shows, return to God with sincerity and keep serving him with all your heart, because his forgiveness and his guidance are still available.
exp.17:22:
Saul's servants repeated to David what the king had ordered them to say. David answered with a question: did they think it a small thing to become the king's son-in-law, when he was a poor man and of no importance? A son-in-law is the husband of one's daughter, and being "of no importance" means that no one held him in high regard.

Saul was speaking in secret through his servants. He pretended to show affection, but his plan was for the Philistines to kill David. David, not knowing this, answered with humility: he did not consider himself worthy to become related to the royal family.

Today we can learn from David's humility. When we receive honor or an opportunity, we need not boast or demand. It is also wise to ask God for wisdom, because not every compliment comes from good intentions.
exp.13:46:
This verse sums up Saul's military campaigns once his kingdom was secure. It says he fought against the enemies surrounding Israel: Moab, Ammon, Edom, the kings of Zobah, and the Philistines. The phrase "whithersoever he turned himself" means "wherever he went," and "he vexed them" indicates that he was successful and overcame them. Some translations say that "he punished them," so the exact sense of that last phrase is debated.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After the episode in which the people rescued Jonathan, the text offers a summary of Saul's reign. It shows that Israel was surrounded by hostile peoples and that Saul had real achievements, before his fall is narrated.

For today: good results do not guarantee a faithful heart. Let us give thanks for successes, but let us guard our obedience to God each day.
exp.19:15:
Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David. He asked that God himself would hold David's enemies to account if they failed to keep it. The phrase "Let the Lord require it" points to the idea that God would call them to answer for it and judge them.

Jonathan is the son of King Saul, who wants to kill David out of jealousy. Even so, Jonathan protects his friend. Since he knows David will be the future king, he asks for kindness toward his own family in case he dies. It is a solemn promise made in the presence of God. Some understand that Jonathan is speaking of the consequences that would fall on anyone who broke the covenant, including himself.

For today: when you pledge loyalty to someone, do it with seriousness and before God. Keep your word, especially when it costs you or when it would be convenient to stay silent. True friendship also thinks about the good of others.
exp.18:18:
This verse says that someone told Saul where David was: at Naioth, a place in Ramah. "It was told" means that he was informed or given the news. Naioth seems to have been a site or group of dwellings near Ramah where Samuel was, though it is not known exactly what it was like.

Here the narrator of the story speaks. Saul, jealous, wanted to kill David. Michal, David's wife, had helped him escape, and David sought refuge with the prophet Samuel. But Saul found out and sent messengers to capture him. What follows shows that God protected David in a surprising way.

For today: even when it seems that troubles find us and surround us, God can care for us in unexpected ways. Let us seek refuge in Him and in wise people of faith, as David did with Samuel.
exp.2:20:
It says that God again revealed himself at Shiloh. "Again" means "once more," and "revealed himself" refers to making himself known. He did so by speaking to Samuel, and that word was a direct message from God. Earlier, in those days, the word of the Lord was rare (3:1), so this marks an important change.

The narrator of the book closes chapter 3 here. Samuel was young and served alongside the priest Eli at Shiloh, where the tabernacle was. God called him, and from then on Samuel was recognized by all Israel as a faithful prophet. The text does not say exactly how God made himself known; only that he did so by his word.

God still seeks to communicate with those who listen to him with humility. We can set aside a moment each day to read the Bible and say, as Samuel did: "Speak, for your servant is listening." Listening willingly and being ready to obey opens the way for God to guide us.
exp.16:28:
Here David answers his brother's harsh accusations with a simple question: "What have I now done?" It is like saying, "What wrong did I do just now?" Then he adds, "Is there not a cause?", meaning, "Was it not only a question?" or "Was I not just speaking about what was being said?"

David had just asked the soldiers about the reward for defeating Goliath. His oldest brother, Eliab, became angry and accused him of pride and bad intentions. David had been sent by his father Isaac to bring food to his brothers. Some understand Eliab's reaction as jealousy or shame.

When someone attacks us without reason, we can respond with calm, without fighting. David did not defend himself with anger and went on with what God had placed in his heart.
exp.11:5:
Samuel reminds the people that the Lord is the one who raised up Moses and Aaron, that is, who appointed them as leaders, and that He brought their ancestors out of Egypt. The word "advanced" here means that God chose them and used them. The forms "unto" and "your" are old-fashioned English for "to" and "of you."

Samuel speaks at a national gathering, when Israel was asking for a king. He had just shown that he had been an honest leader. Now he wants to turn the people's attention from human leaders to God. He is going to review how God has rescued and guided them throughout their history.

For today: before seeking security in leaders, money, or plans, let us remember the times God has sustained us. Remembering His faithfulness strengthens trust and helps us put God first.
exp.27:8:
Here the woman of Endor speaks to the man in disguise, who is Saul, though she does not yet know it. She reminds him that the king has cut off from the land those who have familiar spirits, that is, people who claimed to have a spirit through which they could communicate with the dead, and the wizards. She is afraid and asks why he is laying a trap for her that could cost her her life.

Saul had forbidden these practices, which the law of God condemned (Leviticus 19:31). Now, with no answer from God and filled with fear before the Philistines, he himself breaks his own law. The woman is suspicious because she believes it is a trap. Saul swears to her by the LORD that no harm will come to her, which is a sad irony.

For today: when we feel afraid and God seems silent, it is tempting to look for answers in forbidden places. It is better to wait on God, to be consistent with what we say we believe, and to seek his Word with humility.
exp.11:18:
Here the people of Israel address Samuel in fear and ask him to pray for them so that they will not die. They recognize that, in addition to their earlier sins, they have committed another wrong: asking for a king.

The explanation comments on old word forms in the source wording. Since your verse uses plain modern forms, that comment is removed. The phrase "Llaman a Jehová tu Dios" corresponds to the verse's "the Lord thy God," and it suggests that they felt a certain distance from Him.

Samuel had warned them, and as a sign, God sent thunder and rain during the wheat harvest, which was unusual. Seeing this, the people were frightened and understood that their request for a king showed distrust in God, who was their true King. Samuel, as prophet and judge, interceded for them.

For today: when you recognize a mistake, do not stay only in fear. Confess honestly, turn to God, and keep serving Him wholeheartedly. He receives those who return to Him with humility.
exp.29:30:
This verse finishes a list of places. After defeating the Amalekites, David sent part of the plunder to those who were in Hebron and in all the places where he and his men had been wont to go. The word "a" in this sentence is the older form of "to," and "his own" refers to his companions.

The narrator of the book speaks here. David had returned to Ziklag and found it burned, but God gave him the victory and he recovered everything that had been lost. Then he distributed gifts to the elders of Judah, who had surely helped him or welcomed him while he was fleeing from Saul. The text does not detail how each town helped, so it is not wise to invent that.

For today: do not forget those who have supported you in difficult times. When God gives you a blessing, share it with gratitude. A phone call, a visit, or a concrete act of help can be your way of saying thank you.
exp.18:11:
It says that Michal, David's wife, let him down through a window with a rope. In this way David was able to leave, run away, and get away from those who were chasing him. "Let down" means she lowered him from up high. "Escaped" means he managed to save himself.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Saul, the king, was jealous of David and wanted to kill him. He had sent messengers to watch the house so they could seize him in the morning. Michal, who was Saul's daughter, warned David of the danger and helped him get away, putting herself at risk in the process. Many believe this episode is connected to Psalm 59, although that is interpreted in different ways.

For today: God often looks after us through people who act with courage and love at the right time. We can thank those who have helped us in this way, and be willing to help others when they are in danger, trusting that God guides the way.
exp.17:23:
This verse says that Saul's servants went back to the king and told him what David had answered. The servants are the attendants or helpers of the king. The words "On this manner spake David" mean that they faithfully repeated David's reply, in which he said he was a poor man of little importance to be the king's son-in-law.

Saul was jealous of David and afraid of him. So he sent his servants to speak with David privately, as if they were doing it out of affection. In reality, Saul was looking for a plan that would lead the Philistines to kill David. The servants only carry the message back and forth.

For today: let us be careful with the words we carry from one person to another. We can be honest messengers and yet, without realizing it, help the plans of someone who wants to do harm. Before we repeat something, let us ask God for wisdom.
exp.18:20:
This verse tells that Saul learned what had happened to his first messengers and sent others, and they also prophesied. Then he sent a third group, and the same thing happened to them. The phrase "when it was told" is the wording of the verse above, and "prophesied" here means praising or speaking under the influence of God's Spirit.

This is part of the story of when Saul pursued David out of jealousy. David had taken refuge with Samuel in Naioth, in Ramah. Saul wanted to capture him, but God acted upon his men and prevented it. Scholars understand this episode as God's protection over David.

For today: human plans against God's purpose do not always prevail. If you are in the middle of an injustice, trust that God can care for you in unexpected ways. And examine your own heart: do not keep insisting on something that God is clearly closing to you.
exp.14:25:
Samuel tells Saul that he will not go back with him. The reason is clear: Saul rejected the word of God, that is, he set it aside and did not take it seriously. For that reason God also rejected him from being king.

Samuel, the prophet, speaks with Saul after Saul disobeyed a command from God. Saul had already admitted his sin and asked for forgiveness, but he explained that he acted out of fear of the people. Samuel answers firmly, and many understand that the passage is speaking of the loss of the kingdom, not necessarily of the loss of personal forgiveness. The Bible does not fully spell this out.

For today: obeying God matters more than pleasing people. If fear of others takes control of us, let us ask God for the courage to do what is right and to obey him from the heart.
exp.9:8:
It says that, as soon as Saul turned his back to leave Samuel, God changed his heart. The phrase "turned his shoulder" means he turned around to head off on his way. In addition, all the signs that Samuel had told him about came to pass that same day.

Samuel had just anointed Saul as the first king of Israel, and he had given him several signs to confirm that God was with him. Saul doubted himself, so God was preparing him for his new task. This change of heart can be understood as a new readiness to lead, though the Bible does not spell out exactly what it consisted of.

For today: when God calls you to something that seems bigger than you, you do not depend on your own strength alone. Ask Him to give you the courage, wisdom and attitude you need, and trust that He keeps what He promises.
exp.23:19:
Saul asks who, upon finding his enemy, would let him go unharmed. It is a question that shows his amazement. Saul then asks that the LORD reward David with good for having spared his life.

The king Saul, who was pursuing David in order to kill him, is speaking. David had the chance to finish him off in a cave, but he only cut off a piece of his robe and spared his life. Saul acknowledges his wrong, although the Bible shows that this repentance did not last forever.

For today: when someone has wronged us and we have the opportunity to take revenge, we can choose to do good and leave the matter in God's hands. Responding with kindness can show others our faith.
exp.14:8:
This verse says that Saul and the people did not destroy Agag, the king of the Amalekites, nor the best of the livestock: the sheep, the cattle, the fattened animals and the lambs. They wanted to keep everything that was good. They destroyed only what they considered worthless ("vile") and weak. The phrase "spared" here means they let them live.

The text is narrated; no character is speaking. Earlier, God had commanded through Samuel that the Amalekites be destroyed (1 Samuel 15:3). Saul won, but he obeyed only in part. Afterward, God says that he regrets having made Saul king, because he did not keep his word. Some readers see here a problem of greed; others, of pride. The text clearly shows selective disobedience.

For today: it is easy to obey God only in what suits us and to keep "the best" for ourselves. Today you can ask yourself in what area you are obeying halfway, and ask God for help in surrendering it completely.
exp.22:3:
David did not settle for just one answer. He asked God again whether he should go to Keilah, and God confirmed that he should. He was told to go down there, because God was going to hand the Philistines over into his hands. "Consult" means asking God for direction, seeking his guidance.

David was being pursued by Saul and was living with about six hundred men. Keilah was being attacked by the Philistines, who were stealing its grain. David's men were afraid, so he asked God again to give them assurance. God answered with a clear promise of victory.

When we face difficult decisions or fears, we can pray with humility and seek confirmation in the Word, in the counsel of wise people, and in the peace God gives. Obeying, even with fear, is taking a step of faith.
exp.29:22:
Here David corrects his men. He tells them they must not act that way with what God has given them. He acknowledges that it was the Lord who protected them and delivered into their hands the band that had attacked their camp at Ziklag, a group of raiders.

David speaks after recovering everything the Amalekites had taken. Two hundred men stayed behind because they were exhausted. Some of those who did fight, described as wicked and worthless men, wanted to deny them their share of the spoil. David prevents this and establishes that the division be equal, both for the one who fights and for the one who guards the baggage.

For today: what we have is a gift from God, not only the result of our own merit. This invites us to share generously and to value those who serve quietly, even when they are not at the front.
exp.2:14:
Samuel spent the rest of the night lying down, without sleeping, as it is understood. In the morning he did what he always did: he opened the doors of the house of the Lord, that is, of the sanctuary at Shiloh. He was afraid to tell Eli the vision, meaning what God had shown him and said to him. The word "shew" here means to tell or reveal.

The narrator tells us that Samuel was a young man who served alongside Eli. God had just spoken to him about a harsh judgment against Eli's house, because his sons were doing wrong and he did not restrain them. Samuel feared the message and the respect he owed to his teacher.

Today, telling the truth can sometimes frighten us, especially when it is said to people we love or respect. This verse encourages us to keep carrying out our tasks faithfully, to ask God for courage, and to speak with humility, without harshness, but without hiding what is true.
exp.19:40:
When the lad had gone, David came out of his hiding place on the south side of the stone where he had been concealed. He bowed three times to the ground, as a sign of respect and gratitude. Then the two friends embraced and kissed each other, and wept together, though David wept more.

The phrase "toward the south" here means the south side, and kissing was a common greeting of affection in that culture.
