This is part of the account in 1 Samuel. Jonathan, son of King Saul, had just confirmed with a signal of arrows that his father meant to kill David. The lad understood nothing, since it was a secret message. Now the friends say goodbye, knowing that David will have to flee and live far away.

For today: do not hide your pain in the face of a farewell or a loss. Weeping with a faithful friend is a way of caring for the friendship. If someone is suffering, stay with them without rushing; your presence can comfort more than many words.
exp.10:10:
It says that Saul organized Israel's army into three groups. The next day, during the last part of the night (the watch just before dawn, near sunrise), they entered the Ammonite camp by surprise. They attacked them until the sun grew hot, that is, until close to midday. The Ammonites who survived were so scattered that not even two of them were left together.

Here the narrator tells how Saul rescued Jabesh-gilead. The Ammonites had laid siege to it and had threatened its people with great shame. Saul had gathered Israel, and the messengers had already promised deliverance for tomorrow, by the time the sun grew hot. The plan was carried out, and then Saul gives the victory to the LORD.

For today: God often works where there is courage, order, and unity. Do diligently what is yours to do, and then acknowledge that the victory comes from God, without boasting.
exp.6:3:
This verse tells that the people of Israel put away the Baals and the Ashtoreths, which were false gods of the neighboring peoples, and served the Lord only, the true God. "Put away" means they removed them from among themselves, and "served" means they worshiped and obeyed him.

The writer then describes what happened after Samuel's appeal. For twenty years the people had been sorrowful and seeking God, while the Philistines held power over them. Samuel told them that if they truly returned to God with all their heart, they must put away those idols. The verse shows that they listened to him. Afterward they gathered at Mizpah to pray and to acknowledge their sin.

For today: returning to God is not only feeling sorrow, but also removing from our lives whatever takes his place. Today we can ask ourselves what we are putting above God, and with his help, let it go.
exp.19:12:
Jonathan makes a solemn vow before God. He says that if his father intends to harm David, he will let him know and send him away so he can go in peace. The old formula that opens his oath is a way of saying: "may God punish me if I do not keep my word." Here "reveal" means to warn or to make known. Jonathan also asks that the Lord be with David as the Lord was with his father.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, speaks with his friend David in the field. Saul was jealous of David and perhaps wanted to kill him. Jonathan, although he was the rightful heir, respects what God is planning and protects David with loyalty.

For today: true friendship shows itself in loyalty when there is risk. Seek to be someone who keeps your word, protects others, and trusts God's plans, even when that costs you something personally.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that one day Eli was lying down in his room. His eyes were already growing weak, and he could hardly see. The word "room" is used here for the place where he rested, and "growing dim" means losing sight little by little.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier it was said that the word of the LORD was rare and that visions were not frequent. Eli was the aging priest, and the young Samuel served him. His growing blindness may also reflect the spiritual dimness of those times, though the text does not state this directly. In this way the scene is set for God's call to Samuel.

For today: when everything seems dim or confused, God can still speak and act. Stay attentive to his voice, especially in his Word, and serve him faithfully even when others seem not to see.
exp.1:3:
The explanation says that the mighty warriors lose their strength: their bows, which were their main weapon, are broken. In contrast, the weak receive power. The phrase that the weak are "girded with strength" means that they are clothed with or surrounded by power, like someone who fastens a belt before going into action.

The one speaking is Hannah, in a prayer of thanksgiving. She had been barren and suffered mockery, but God gave her Samuel. She sees in her own case an example of how God works: he humbles the proud and lifts up the one who depends on him.

For today: if you feel weak or without resources, do not lose heart. Bring your need to God with humility. And if you feel strong, remember that your strength is not your own. Trusting in God, and not in our own weapons, is the safest course.
exp.2:10:
The explanation says that God tells Samuel he is about to do something in Israel so shocking that anyone who hears it will have their ears tingle. To tingle means to ring or sound sharply, the way news can leave us stunned. It is a way of saying that this will be something that shakes everyone.

The Lord speaks, having just called Samuel, a young man serving in the sanctuary alongside the priest Eli. Samuel answers with readiness: "Speak, for your servant is listening." What God tells him next is a judgment on Eli's house, because his sons were sinning gravely and he did not correct them.

For today: God speaks clearly, and sometimes his message is uncomfortable. Let us ask for a heart willing to listen to him, even when he confronts us, and act in time on what we need to correct, especially in our own family.
exp.16:8:
Goliath proposes a duel between two men. If Israel's champion defeats him, the Philistines will be servants to Israel. But if Goliath wins, the Israelites will be servants to the Philistines. The word "pudiere," meaning "could" or "were able," and the phrase "be stronger than he," mean that the other man is able to overcome him, so the wording here follows the verse's "if he be able to fight with me, and to kill me." Servants are people who serve another, like slaves or subjects.

Goliath, the Philistine champion, speaks before the army of Israel. It was an old custom for a single warrior to represent a whole people in order to avoid a large battle. Goliath uses this challenge to humiliate Israel, and the text that follows says that Saul and all the Israelites were filled with fear.

For today: our fears often speak with a loud voice and make us feel that losing is unavoidable. Before you let yourself be paralyzed, remember that God can work in ways we do not expect. Place your trust in Him and take the next step with faith.
exp.6:9:
This verse tells how, while Samuel was offering the burnt offering (a sacrifice that was burned whole in honor of God), the Philistines came near to attack Israel. Then the Lord thundered with a great thunder against them. The word "discomfited" in the verse means that He threw them into confusion and disorder, so that they were struck down before Israel.

The narrator describes what happened at Mizpah, where Israel had gathered to turn back to God and put away their idols. The Philistines saw that gathering and went out to attack. The Israelites were afraid and asked Samuel to keep crying out to God for them. The victory came in answer to that prayer, and not through Israel's military strength.

For today: when you feel afraid or find yourself in trouble you cannot solve, return to God with humility and cry out to Him. He will not always answer with thunder, but the Bible teaches that He hears and helps His people.
exp.29:23:
Here David says that no one will agree with those who want to take the spoils away from the tired soldiers. He says the share should be the same for the one who fought and for the one who stayed behind guarding the baggage and supplies. And he gives the order: "they shall part alike," meaning that everything is to be divided equally.

David speaks after recovering what the Amalekites had taken from Ziklag. Two hundred men, very exhausted, had stayed behind to guard the provisions. Some of those who did fight, described as wicked and worthless, did not want to share with them. David reminds them that the victory was a gift from the LORD, not their own achievement. Later this became a rule in Israel.

For today: value those who serve in places that go unseen. If God has given you success, remember that it is a gift, and share it with generosity and justice.
exp.7:20:
Samuel heard all the words of the people and repeated them before the Lord, that is, in prayer, directly to Him. Here the phrase is "in the ears of the Lord," and it means that Samuel brought their words to God himself.

Before this moment, Samuel had warned the people how a king would act, but they would not listen. They wanted a king so that they could be like all the nations around them. Samuel was hurt, for he felt that they were rejecting him, but he did not argue any further; he brought the matter to God. Afterward, God gave him an answer.

For today: when something hurts you or worries you, especially if others do not listen to you, tell it first to God with complete sincerity. He listens, and praying before you react helps you act with more calm and wisdom.
exp.13:38:
Saúl makes a solemn oath in God's name. The phrase "as the Lord liveth" is an oath, meaning "as surely as God lives." He promises that whoever has sinned will die, even if it is his own son, Jonathan. "He shall surely die" means "he will certainly die, without fail." No one among the people said anything, because they all knew what had happened, or at least they feared to speak.

King Saúl is speaking. God had not answered him when he asked whether he should pursue the Philistines, and Saúl concluded that someone had sinned. He did not know that Jonathan, without knowing the order, had tasted honey. Earlier, Saúl had forbidden anyone to eat that day. Many see in this a hasty oath, although the text does not fully explain it.

Before demanding justice from others, it is wise to think carefully about what we promise and to listen to God with humility. Let us be just, but also prudent and merciful, beginning with our own household.
exp.17:2:
It says that Jonathan and David made a covenant, that is, a serious promise of loyalty between the two of them. The reason is that Jonathan loved him as his own soul, that is, as his own life. In today's language this would be: he cared for him as much as he cared for himself.

It does not speak of one particular person; it is the narrator of the book. David had just spoken with King Saul after defeating Goliath. Jonathan, Saul's son, felt joined to him from the heart. The following verses show that he gave him his robe, his sword, and his bow, a gesture that expresses respect and devotion. Scholars discuss the exact scope of that gesture, but it clearly shows a deep friendship.

For today: value and care for loyal friendships. Be a friend who gives, protects, and keeps his word, without envy or rivalry, even when the other person seems to stand out more than you do.
exp.17:18:
This verse tells us that when the time came to give Merab, Saul's eldest daughter, to David, the king did not keep his word. Instead, he gave her as a wife to Adriel, from the town of Mehola. The sentences that explained the old wording have been removed, since the phrases they discussed do not appear in the verse you are reading.

The narrator is describing what happened after Saul's promise. The text suggests that Saul offered his daughter with a hidden purpose: he hoped the Philistines would kill David in battle. When that did not happen, Saul broke his word. The passage does not explain all his motives in detail, but it shows his jealousy and his duplicity.

Today it reminds us that not everyone keeps what they promise, and that David did not need to manipulate anything to move forward. We can trust that God watches over our path even when someone fails or deceives us. It also invites us to be people of our word, without hidden intentions.
exp.12:6:
The explanation says that, facing the threat of the Philistines, some Hebrews fled across the Jordan River to the lands of Gad and Gilead. Saul stayed in Gilgal, but the people who were still with him were trembling, that is, filled with great fear.

This is a moment of crisis early in Saul's reign. The narrator is the author of the book, who describes how the Israelite army was falling apart out of fear. Samuel had told Saul to wait in Gilgal, and the next verse shows the pressure he was under: the people were scattering, and Saul ended up offering the sacrifice without waiting for Samuel.

For today: when fear presses in, it is tempting to act quickly and in our own way. Before deciding, stop, pray, and ask whether you are obeying God or only reacting to pressure.
exp.0:17:
Hannah answers the priest Eli respectfully: "Let your servant find favor in your eyes" means "I hope you will look on me kindly and be pleased with me." Then she went her way, ate, and "her face was no longer sad." The word "went" simply means "she went away."

Hannah had prayed in the sanctuary with great grief because she had no children. Eli had mistaken her for a drunken woman, but she explained her distress to him. He sent her off with a blessing: that God would grant what she had asked. Here Hannah responds to that blessing.

For today: after prayer, we can leave our burden in God's hands. The Bible does not say that her situation changed at that moment, but her spirit did. Praying sincerely can bring us rest, even before we see the answer.
exp.19:29:
Saul was filled with rage against his son Jonathan. The phrase "was kindled" means that his anger flared up. He insulted him with a very harsh expression, "son of the perverse rebellious woman," which also reflected badly on his wife. He told him that by siding with David, he was bringing shame on himself and on his mother. Here "confusion" means shame or dishonor.

Saul spoke at the new moon feast. David had not come to the king's table, and Jonathan had excused him with an explanation. Saul, driven by jealousy and fear of losing the throne, already saw David as an enemy. That is why he erupts against his son.

For today: sometimes the pressure comes from someone in authority, even from within your own family. Jonathan did not answer with insults but kept defending what was right. Ask God for calm and courage to remain loyal to what is right.
exp.9:4:
He says that Saul would come to "the hill of God," a high place where there was a Philistine garrison, that is, an enemy military post. When he entered the town he would meet a group of prophets coming down from the high place, with a psaltery (a stringed instrument), a tabret (a hand drum), a pipe, and a harp before them, and they would prophesy, that is, speak and praise under the influence of God.

Samuel speaks to Saul after anointing him as the first king of Israel. He gives him concrete signs, one after another, to confirm that God had really chosen him. This is the third sign. Scholars do not agree on every detail of how that group prophesying worked, but here it is shown as something connected with music and worship.

God knows that we doubt, and sometimes he gives us confirmations so that we can move forward with confidence. If he has called you to something, walk step by step, attentive to his guidance, and do not expect to have everything clear from the beginning.
exp.16:9:
This verse says that the Philistine Goliath adds another provocation: he declares that today he has defied the whole army of Israel and asks that someone come out to fight him, man against man. "Defied" means that he challenged them publicly, like someone hurling a taunt to provoke a fight.

The one speaking is Goliath, the Philistine champion. The two armies were facing each other, and he proposes to settle the war with a single combat. His challenge does not only threaten the soldiers; it attacks the confidence of the whole people. That is why, in the next verse, Saul and all the Israelites are filled with fear.

For today: when a big problem shouts at us every day, it can paralyze us. We should remember that fear often grows when we look only at the giant. Today we can pause, pray, and ask God to help us see our situation with faith.
exp.17:16:
It says that Saul offers David the chance to marry Merab, his elder daughter, on the condition that he be valiant and fight the Lord's battles ("Jehovah"). But Saul secretly intends something else: he does not want to kill David with his own hand, but to have him killed by the Philistines.

Here the king Saul speaks. David had become very popular and successful, and Saul felt fear and jealousy. His offer seems like an honor, but it is a trap to get rid of him by using the enemy. Afterward, Merab was given to another man, and the Bible does not explain in detail why.

For today: be wary of praise or favors that hide wrong intentions, and do not act out of envy. Like David, serve with humility and trust that God cares for you, even when others want to harm you.
exp.17:6:
The verse tells that the women of Israel sang and danced, taking turns in the song: "Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands." The word "played" refers to their festive dancing, and "thousands" and "ten thousands" are a way of exalting the victories.

The women came out from all the towns to receive the army after David had defeated the Philistine. Their song was a popular celebration, and it probably used poetic parallelism, without intending to offend Saul. But Saul took it as a comparison that left him in second place. The text shows that from that day he began to look at David with suspicion.

For today: when someone beside us receives recognition, we can choose between rejoicing or letting envy grow. Ask God for a grateful heart, one that celebrates the gifts of others without feeling diminished.
exp.7:1:
This verse says that Samuel's two sons were named Joel, the firstborn, and Abiah, the second. Both of them served as judges in Beersheba, a city in the south of Israel. The word "firstborn" means the eldest son.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel was already old, and he appointed his sons as judges to help him. But the text that follows makes clear that they did not follow their father's good example: they sought unjust gain and perverted justice. This led the leaders of the people to ask for a king.

For today: having a godly family or a godly father does not guarantee that children will share the same faith. Each person must seek God for themselves, and those who serve in positions of responsibility must guard their integrity.
exp.16:14:
This verse says that David went back and forth from Saul's camp to look after his father's sheep in Bethlehem. The words "But" and "to tend" are used in the old wording, and "to tend" means to lead the sheep to eat and to take care of them.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. He has just said that David's three older brothers went off to the war with Saul. Now he makes clear that David was not always at the front, but went back and forth between serving Saul and caring for the flock. This detail prepares the next scene, when his father will send him to bring food to his brothers and David will come to see the giant Goliath.

For today: David was faithful in the small and everyday things, caring for sheep, before he faced something great. Do your daily work with care, even when it seems unimportant; God often shapes our character right there.
exp.13:6:
Here the young man who carried Jonathan's weapons responds with complete loyalty. He tells him to do what his heart has already decided, to go forward, and that he will be at his side. "Armour-bearer" is the assistant who carried the warrior's weapons. "According to your heart" means he is willing to follow him in whatever he decides, as if his heart were one with Jonathan's.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, proposes to attack alone with his assistant a garrison of the Philistines, whom he calls "uncircumcised", that is, outsiders to God's covenant. Israel was at a disadvantage, and Jonathan trusts that for the LORD to save does not depend on whether there are many or few. The assistant supports his faith with courage.

Today we can learn the value of faithfully accompanying someone who walks with sincere faith in God. We can also be that kind of support: someone who encourages, without leaving alone the one who takes a brave and good step.
exp.5:16:
This verse lists the gold offerings that the Philistines sent to the Lord as a repayment. There was one gold figure for each of the five main cities: Ashdod, Gaza, Askelon, Gath and Ekron.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark of God, and they suffered a plague. Their priests advised returning it with gifts of gold to acknowledge the Lord. The people of Beth-shemesh received it and offered sacrifices. The five Philistine rulers saw all this and went back to their land.

For today: when we recognize that we have failed, fear alone is not enough; God looks for a humble heart that honors him. Let us ask forgiveness sincerely and treat what belongs to God with reverence.
exp.18:15:
It says that when Saul's messengers entered the house to take David, they found an image in the bed. It had a pillow of goats' hair at the head, so that it looked like a person lying down. The word "image" refers to a household idol (in Hebrew, "teraphim"); scholars are not sure of its exact form, but it was large enough to appear to be a body.

Saul wanted to kill David out of jealousy. Michal, Saul's daughter and David's wife, helped him escape through a window and set up this deception to buy him time. The narrator tells what the messengers saw.

For today: when we face a threat, God often works through wisdom and the help of people close to us. We can act wisely and ask for help, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.13:26:
He says that Jonathan did not know about the oath that his father, King Saul, had imposed on the army. So he dipped the tip of his staff into a piece of honeycomb, brought it to his mouth, and his eyes were "brightened," that is, he regained strength and his tiredness left him. The word "but" in the verse, and the word "charged," mean that he made them swear under a curse.

This is the account of a battle against the Philistines. Saul, without thinking it through carefully, forbade eating until evening, and the people were exhausted. Jonathan, who was not present when the order was given, ate without knowing it. Afterward he himself judges that his father's order was harmful.

For today: before imposing strict rules or vows, let us consider how they will affect other people. Religious zeal without wisdom can wear people out instead of helping them.
exp.8:9:
Saul tells his servant that his idea is good and that they should go. The quoted phrases from the source wording are not in the reader's verse, so I will simply state the meaning: Saul agrees that the servant is right, and then the two of them set out toward the city where the man of God lived.

Saul is looking for his father Kish's donkeys, which have gone missing, and he no longer knows what to do. The servant suggests consulting the seer, as the prophet was called in earlier times, and offers to give a small amount of silver as a gift. Saul accepts the advice. Here the seer is Samuel, although the text does not yet name him.

For today: Saul was the leader, yet he was willing to listen to good advice from someone under his authority. When we are lost or have no answers, it is wise to listen to those who counsel us with good sense and to seek God's guidance, without letting pride get in the way.
exp.9:25:
Samuel sent the people away, and each one went back to his home. Saul also went home to Gibeah, his town. A band of men went with him, men of courage and loyalty, since the word "host" here most likely does not mean a formal army but people who were strong and faithful. God had touched their hearts to follow him.

The narrator tells what happened after Samuel presented Saul as king at Mizpah and explained the rules of the kingdom. God moves some to support him, but soon others look down on him. So we see that Saul's authority began with both support and opposition.

For today: if God gives you a task, do not depend only on everyone's approval. Thank those whom God moves to help you, serve with humility, and do not despair over criticism. Ask God to touch your heart and the hearts of others to do his will.
exp.12:18:
It says that throughout all of Israel there was no smith, that is, no one who worked iron. The Philistines had arranged it this way, thinking: "Let the Hebrews not make themselves swords or spears."

The explanation of the next passage concerns the word "mattock" or "goad point," which is the sharpened tip of the rod used to guide oxen. [Note: this sentence is removed because it explains a word not in the verse.]

It is the narrator of the book who explains the situation. Israel lived under Philistine rule, and Saul was king. The Philistines controlled the iron to keep the people weak and to prevent rebellions. For this reason the Israelites depended on them even to sharpen their farming tools. The verses that follow show how humiliating and costly this was.

For today: when you feel without resources or at a disadvantage, remember that God does not depend on the weapons of the world. In chapter 14, He gave the victory with very little. Do with faith what you have at hand, and trust Him.
exp.6:1:
It says the ark of the Lord stayed in Kirjath-jearim for a long time, about twenty years. During that time, all Israel "lamented after the Lord," that is, they felt sorrow and longing for God, seeking him with grief. "Lamented after" here means they mourned over the Lord's absence.

The narrator tells what happened after the Philistines returned the ark. It was kept in the house of Abinadab, and Israel remained far from God, though with pain. The text does not say exactly what they were doing during those years. Then Samuel calls them to turn to the Lord with all their heart and to put away their idols.

When we feel emptiness or sorrow over being far from God, that pain can be a first step toward him. But lamenting is not enough: we must act, remove whatever has taken his place in our heart, and serve him again with sincerity.
exp.3:7:
The Philistines are frightened when they learn that the ark of Israel has come into the camp. They think the God of the Hebrews is there, and they ask who will rescue them from these mighty gods. They say that it was these gods who struck Egypt with every kind of plague in the wilderness. "Struck" means hit or punished; a "plague" is a terrible punishment or blow.

The speakers are Philistine soldiers, enemies of Israel. They speak out of fear, because the Israelites shouted with joy when the ark arrived. The Philistines speak of "gods" in the plural, which shows that they did not know the God of Israel well. They also mix in some details from the story of the exodus. Even so, they knew the reputation of what God did in Egypt. Afterward they take courage and defeat Israel, which reminds us that God is not bound to act because of a sacred object.

For today: let us not trust in symbols, customs, or rituals as if they were a charm. Let us trust in God himself and seek to live in obedience and sincerity before him.
exp.8:1:
This verse introduces Saul, the son of Kish. He is described as a young man, and as very handsome and good-looking. It is said that no one in Israel surpassed him in attractiveness, and that he stood taller than all the others, head and shoulders above them. Saying he surpassed the others means that he stood out above them.

The narrator introduces Saul just as Israel is asking for a king. His family has been mentioned before, and later we will see him set out to look for some lost donkeys. The description highlights his outward appearance, something the people valued in a leader. Later the story will show that appearance is not what matters most.

Today we can remember that beauty, talent, or height are not enough to form character. Let us ask God for a humble and obedient heart, rather than seeking only what is seen on the outside.
exp.23:10:
Here David tells Saul that today God put him into David's hands inside the cave. Some of David's men told him to kill him, but David decided to spare him. The word "anointed" refers to someone chosen and set apart by God to be king. David respected that position and did not want to raise his hand against him.

It is David speaking, who was fleeing from Saul because the king wanted to kill him. Saul had gone into the cave without knowing that David and his men were inside. David only cut off the edge of Saul's robe, and afterward came out to show him that he was not his enemy and did not seek his harm.

When someone treats us unjustly, we may have the chance to take revenge, but David teaches us not to do so. We can speak the truth with respect, act with integrity, and let God be the judge.
exp.11:11:
It says that when the people saw that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, was coming to attack them, they asked Samuel for a human king. They said, "Nay; but a king shall reign over us." Yet their true king was already the Lord, their God. The phrase "came against you" means that he was threatening them.

Samuel, now old, speaks in his farewell address as judge. He reminds them that God had rescued them many times, even when they had turned away from Him. Samuel shows them that asking for a king out of fear was doubting God's care. Even so, he makes it clear that God could still guide them if they obeyed.

Today, when something frightens us, it is easy to look for security in people, money or plans, and to forget God. Before deciding, we can pray and ask ourselves: am I trusting God, or only reacting to fear?
exp.25:11:
This verse tells that David took the spear and the jug of water that were beside Saul's head, and went away with Abishai. No one saw them or noticed, and no one woke up, because they were all asleep. The text says that God himself sent a very deep sleep upon them.

Saul was pursuing David in order to kill him. That night David entered the camp and found Saul asleep. Abishai wanted to kill him, but David refused, because Saul was the anointed one of the Lord, the king chosen by God. David took the spear and the jug as proof that he could have killed him and did not.

For today: when you have the chance to take revenge or gain at someone else's expense, remember that justice belongs to God. You can act with respect and leave the outcome in his hands, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.12:12:
Samuel tells Saul that he acted foolishly. The phrase about acting foolishly means that he did not act with wisdom. To be commanded means to have been given an order or charge. Saul did not obey God's command, and because of this he lost the chance for his kingdom to be secure over Israel forever.

Samuel, a prophet and judge, speaks to Saul, the first king. Saul had waited for Samuel in Gilgal, but when he saw the people scattering and the Philistines gathering, he offered the burnt offering himself. That was something that was not his to do. Saul justified it by fear and pressure, but Samuel calls it disobedience.

Today, when pressure builds, it is tempting to take shortcuts and give reasons that sound good. But trusting God includes waiting and obeying, even when we do not see results. Before deciding under pressure, ask yourself: does this honor what God has already told me?
exp.13:35:
Saul proposes to attack the Philistines during the night, plunder them until morning, and leave not one of them alive. The people answer, "Do whatsoever seemeth good unto thee," meaning, do whatever seems best to you. Then the priest says, "Let us draw near hither unto God," which means: let us come near to God to seek his counsel before acting.

Saul speaks after a great day of battle. The people are exhausted, and they had eaten meat with the blood still in it, which the law forbade. Saul had the animals slaughtered properly and built an altar. The priest halts the plan and suggests seeking God's guidance. Then God does not answer that day, and Saul looks for the cause of the silence.

For today: before making important decisions, even when we are in a hurry or have the support of others, it is wise to stop and pray and seek God's direction.
exp.0:27:
Here, Hannah says she is giving her son Samuel to God for the whole of his life. The explanation notes that in other versions the verb used for "giving" is translated differently, but since those wordings do not appear in the verse your reader sees, that comment is omitted. The phrase about the worship that took place "there" describes someone bowing down and praising God in that place.

The speaker is Hannah, who could not have children before and asked God for a son at Shiloh, at the sanctuary. God gave her Samuel, and now she fulfills her promise by bringing him to the priest Eli. Some think the one who worshipped was Eli, others that it was Hannah or her family; the Hebrew text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: think about something valuable that God has given you, such as your family, your time, or your gifts. Present it to God with gratitude and ask him how to use it to serve him. Giving thanks and offering what we have is one way of worshipping.
exp.24:12:
David said to his men, "Each of you strap on your sword." So every man strapped on his sword, and David strapped on his sword too. About four hundred men went up with David, while two hundred stayed behind to guard the supplies. The supplies are the provisions and belongings of the group.

David, who was hiding from Saul in the wilderness, spoke these words. His men had protected Nabal's flocks, and David had politely asked for some food. Nabal insulted him and treated him with contempt. David responded in anger and decided to take revenge through violence. The account does not approve of that decision; Abigail soon appears and will intervene to stop him.

For today: when someone offends us, let us not act in the heat of the moment. Before we respond, let us stop, pray, and listen to wise counsel. A hasty reaction can cause harm that we cannot later repair.
exp.15:0:
God speaks to Samuel and asks him how long he will keep mourning for Saul, since God has already rejected him as king over Israel. He tells Samuel to fill his horn with oil and go to Bethlehem, to the house of Jesse, because among Jesse's sons God has already chosen the new king.

The Lord speaks with the prophet Samuel. Saul had disobeyed God, and Samuel was very sad about it. The oil in the horn was used for anointing, that is, setting someone apart for a special task. Samuel is afraid, but God gives him a simple plan so that he can go safely.

For today: it is good to grieve our losses, but God does not want us to stay stuck. When one door closes, he already has a next step prepared. We can obey even when we feel afraid, trusting that he guides us step by step.
exp.14:18:
Samuel asks King Saul a pointed question: why did you not obey the Lord? Instead of carrying out the command, Saul rushed upon the plunder (the goods taken from the enemy) and did what God considered wrong.

Samuel speaks as God's prophet. God had commanded that Amalek be completely destroyed, but Saul spared King Agag and kept the best of the livestock. Earlier, Samuel reminds him that God had raised him up as king when he felt small. It is a rebuke for his ingratitude and disobedience. This passage is harsh, and many read it carefully because of the war it describes.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I obey God completely, or only in the things that suit me? Partial obedience is often a way of justifying what we want. Let us ask for humility to listen and to do his will.
exp.20:3:
Here the priest Ahimelech tells David that he has no ordinary bread, only holy bread, the bread set apart for God in the sanctuary. He could give it to him, but with one condition: that the young men who are with him have kept themselves away from relations with women.

"Servants" are David's young men or attendants, and "common bread" is everyday bread.

David flees from Saul and arrives at Nob, where the tabernacle is. He is hungry and asks for food, although he does not tell the whole truth about his situation. Ahimelech protects the holiness of the bread, but he sees human need. Scholars explain in various ways how this condition of purity is to be understood; what is clear is that the aim was respect for what is dedicated to God.

For today: God deserves our respect, but he also cares about people's needs. We can honor what is holy with reverence and, at the same time, help with compassion anyone who is hungry or in trouble.
exp.26:11:
This verse says that Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, trusted David. He thought David had become hateful to his own people, Israel, and so David would serve him forever. "Believed" here means "trusted" or "took as true." "Hateful" means despised, detested.

The narrator tells how David deceived Achish. David was fleeing from Saul and living in Philistine territory. He told Achish that he was raiding towns of Judah, when in fact he was attacking other enemies of Israel. So that no one would report him, he left no survivors. The text does not approve of everything David did; it only describes what happened.

For today: a lie may bring security for a while, but it is not a healthy path. When you are in trouble, seek God and act with truth, because trust gained through deception is fragile.
exp.29:12:
Here David asks the young Egyptian he and his men found nearly dead from hunger two questions: whose are you, and where are you from? The young man explains that he is a servant of an Amalekite, and that his master left him behind because he became sick three days ago.

David and his men return to Ziklag and find it burned, with their families taken captive by the Amalekites. They pursue the raiders, and along the way they find this abandoned servant. David first takes care of him and then asks him questions. This young man will be the one who leads them to the enemy camp.

For today: God can use people who have been forgotten and discarded to open a way forward. If we treat someone who is suffering with kindness, no matter who they are, we may discover that God is also helping us through that person.
exp.27:1:
Here David answers Achish, the Philistine king, with ambiguous words: "Thou shalt know what thy servant can do." Achish understands that David will fight on his side, and he promises to make him his personal guard, that is, the one who keeps watch over his head, for ever.

David was living among the Philistines because he was fleeing from King Saul. Achish trusted him, and now the Philistines were preparing to attack Israel, David's own people. David does not say clearly whether he will fight against Israel. His answer is shrewd, and the Bible does not explain what he actually intended to do.

For today: when we find ourselves in a difficult situation because of past decisions, we should seek God honestly. Doubtful answers can confuse others and ourselves as well. It is better to ask God for wisdom so that we act with integrity.
exp.21:9:
This verse is part of Doeg the Edomite's report to Saul. It says that Ahimelech "enquired of the Lord" for David, gave him food, and gave him the sword of Goliath the Philistine. The word "victuals" means food for the journey. "Enquired" means that he asked God.

Doeg speaks as Saul's chief servant. Saul was full of suspicion and believed that everyone was plotting against him. Doeg took the chance to accuse the priest. His account leaves out details found in chapter 21, where Ahimelech helped David without knowing that he was fleeing from the king. That is why his report is partial and malicious.

Today we can learn not to repeat half-told reports, especially when they can harm others. It is also good to help someone in need in good faith, even when others misunderstand him. Before we speak, let us ask whether what we are saying is complete, true, and necessary.
exp.9:16:
This verse says that Samuel called all the people of Israel to gather before God in a place called Mizpah. "Called together" means that he summoned them or invited them to an assembly. "Before the Lord" shows that this was not an ordinary gathering, but a meeting in the presence of the Lord.

Samuel was a prophet and judge of Israel. He had already anointed Saul in private, but had not yet presented him to the people. Now he gathers them to announce God's message: the people had asked for a king and, in doing so, had stopped trusting God as their protector. Mizpah had already been a place of assembly and prayer for Israel before.

For today: before making important decisions, it is good to pause and come before God with sincerity. Let us ask ourselves whether we are trusting in Him or seeking security in other things.
exp.13:20:
This verse tells how some Hebrews who had been on the side of the Philistines, and who had gone up with them into the camp, changed sides. They joined the Israelites who were with Saul and Jonathan. The phrase "before that time" means they had already been with the Philistines for a good while.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, not one of the characters. Jonathan had attacked a Philistine outpost, and God sent confusion into the enemy camp. When Saul arrived, the Philistines were fighting among themselves. These Hebrews, perhaps forced to serve the enemy (this is not stated with certainty), saw that the situation was turning and returned to their own people.

For today: when God is at work, He often encourages others to come back. We can pray and remain faithful even when we seem to be in the minority, because our steadfastness can help others return.
exp.15:5:
Samuel arrives in Bethlehem, sees Eliab, the oldest son of Jesse, and thinks he is the chosen one. He says, "Surely the Lord's anointed is before him," meaning "surely this is the one God has chosen."

The speaker is the prophet Samuel. God sent him to the house of Jesse to anoint a new king, because Saul had already been rejected. Samuel looks at what can be seen on the outside, and that is why he is mistaken. In the verses that follow, God corrects him: He does not look at appearance or height, but at the heart.

For today: before judging a person by their appearance, their success, or the way they speak, let us ask God to help us see with more care. And let us cultivate a sincere heart before Him.
exp.22:7:
This verse tells that Saul called all the people together to war. His plan was to go down to Keilah and surround David and his men in order to trap them. The words "to besiege" mean surrounding a city with soldiers so that no one can get out or come in. "Called together" means that he gathered or summoned the people.

Here the narrator speaks. David was in Keilah, a city he had just rescued from the Philistines. Saul, who was pursuing him out of jealousy, thought that God had delivered David into his hand because the city had gates and bars. But Saul did not consult God; he simply drew a conclusion that suited him.

For today: be careful about saying "God has put him in my hands" when we only want to justify what we already desire to do. Before acting, it is wise to seek God with humility, as David did afterward, and to examine whether our heart is free of envy or resentment.
exp.30:4:
This verse tells how Saul's armourbearer, the soldier who carried his weapons, saw that the king was already dead. Then he too threw himself on his own sword and died beside Saul.

The armourbearer was the warrior's helper, the one who carried his weapons.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel was losing the battle against the Philistines on Mount Gilboa. Saul, wounded and afraid of being abused by the enemy, took his own life. The text only tells what happened; it does not approve or recommend these deaths.

For today: in the middle of fear and defeat, it is easy to lose hope. If you are weighed down, do not carry that burden alone. Talk with someone you trust, with a pastor or a professional, and seek help. God cares for you and receives you in your distress.
exp.21:0:
David left Gath, where he had sought refuge, and hid in the cave of Adullam. The verse says he "escaped," meaning he fled to save his life. When his family heard about it, they went to be with him, meaning they went to meet him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David was fleeing from King Saul, who was pursuing him out of jealousy and wanted to kill him. Although he had been anointed as the future king, he was living as a fugitive. His family was also in danger because of their relation to him, though the text does not explain this in detail. Adullam was in the lowland area of Judah, and caves were known to be found there.

For today: in our darkest moments, God often uses family and friends as support. We can seek trustworthy companionship, and we can also be a refuge for others who are suffering.
exp.16:41:
When the Philistine Goliath looked closely at David, he looked down on him. He saw him as someone of no importance.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. Goliath was an experienced warrior and expected a rival who was armed and strong. Instead, he saw a young shepherd with a staff, a sling, and some stones. So he judged him only by what he saw on the outside.

For today: do not let yourself be measured by appearances, and do not measure others by them either. God often works through people whom the world underestimates. If you feel small or unprepared, trust that God can use you when you are faithful to him.
exp.27:3:
The Philistines gathered together and camped at Shunem. Saul also gathered all Israel and camped at Gilboa. The phrases "pitched camp" and "gathered" mean that they set up their military camp, and that he assembled his army.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel is about to enter a serious war. Samuel had already died, and Saul had driven out the mediums and fortune-tellers. Even so, in the next verse Saul feels an enormous fear, seeks God, and receives no answer. The text does not explain here all the reasons for God's silence, but the earlier story shows Saul's disobedience.

When pressure comes, what is in our heart becomes visible. Do not wait until you are afraid to seek God. Draw near to Him every day with sincerity and obedience, so that in times of crisis your trust is already firm.
exp.11:9:
This verse recalls what the people of Israel did when they were oppressed: they cried out to God, acknowledged their sin, and promised to serve him again. The gods Baalim and Ashtaroth were false gods of the neighboring peoples.

Samuel, now an old man, speaks at the close of his leadership. He reviews their history to show them that God always responded when they repented. Through this he wants them to see that asking for a human king revealed little trust in God, their true King.

For today: when you realize you have drifted away from God, do not wait until you are in a bigger crisis. Return to him with sincerity, name what you did wrong, and ask him for help. His mercy remains open to anyone who comes back with a sincere heart.
exp.24:14:
This verse says that David's men treated Nabal's shepherds very well. They did them no harm and did not mistreat them, and nothing was lacking to them while they stayed near them in the field. The word here translated as "conversant" means "living among" or "going about together".

The one speaking is a servant of Nabal, one of his shepherds. He tells this to Abigail, Nabal's wife, because Nabal had insulted David's messengers, and David was coming with four hundred armed men. The servant wants her to act before a tragedy happens. His testimony shows that David's complaint had a real basis: David's men had looked after them.

For today: when someone has done us good, let us not forget it or repay it with contempt. And if we see a conflict approaching, let us speak truthfully and in time, as this servant did, to seek peace.
exp.4:4:
It says that, after what happened to the statue of Dagon, the priests and everyone who entered his temple in Ashdod stopped stepping on the threshold, that is, the lower part of the entrance. Even in the writer's time they still kept this custom. The words "until this day" mean that the custom was still being followed when the book was written.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who explains the origin of a custom. The Philistines had placed the ark of God beside their idol. Dagon fell twice before the ark, and the second time he was left with his head and hands cut off on the threshold. Scholars do not agree on whether that custom was a sign of respect or of fear.

For today: idols, whether things or people, cannot stand before God. It is worth asking ourselves what has taken their place in our hearts, and placing it in the Lord's hands.
exp.9:22:
They ran and brought him out from where he was hiding, and set him in front of everyone. He looked very tall: he stood head and shoulders above anyone else.

Samuel gathered Israel at Mizpah to present the first king. By casting lots, God pointed out the tribe, then the family, and finally Saul. The account does not explain why he hid; many think he felt fear or humility before such a responsibility. His height caught the people's attention, though it was God who chose him.

For today: not everything that impresses the eye is the most important. God calls people who feel small or unsure, and invites us not to hide from what He asks of us, but to trust Him.
exp.30:10:
This verse says that the people of Jabesh-gilead heard about what the Philistines had done to Saul: they cut off his head, put his armor in the temple of Ashtaroth, and hung his body on the wall of Beth-shan. The sentence is left open, and the next verse shows what they did.

Context: the one telling the story is the author of the book, who recounts the tragic end of Saul on Mount Gilboa. Jabesh-gilead was a city that Saul had rescued at the beginning of his reign (1 Samuel 11). For this reason, many understand that their brave response was a gesture of gratitude and loyalty.

For today: gratitude and loyalty do not stay in words alone. Think of someone who helped you in a difficult moment, and look for a concrete way today to honor them, even if it is with a phone call, a visit, or an act of service.
exp.7:10:
Samuel tells them what a king will do with them. He will take their sons to serve in the army: some will go with his war chariots, others will form his cavalry, and others will run ahead of his chariot as guards. "Manner" here means the customs or the way the king will act, not something that is fair. The "horsemen" are the mounted riders.

Samuel speaks on God's command. The people of Israel asked for a king so they could be like the nations around them, and Samuel felt rejected. God told him to listen to them, but to warn them clearly. It was a warning, not an approval, of what that decision would cost.

Today we can learn to think about the price of what we desire. Before asking for something simply because others have it, it is wise to pray and ask what it will require of us, and what place we are giving God in that decision.
exp.19:38:
He says that the young man who was helping Jonathan did not understand anything of what was happening. Only Jonathan and David knew the true meaning of what was done. The young servant is simply the boy, and the arrow is the arrow the boy was sent to find, and the matter means the business or the situation at hand.

Jonathan had agreed with David on a secret signal: he would shoot arrows, and by what he called out to the boy, David would know whether Saul meant to kill him or not. Jonathan's words seemed like an ordinary instruction, but they were a message of danger for David, who was hiding nearby. In this way Jonathan protected his friend without betraying him.

There are truths and difficult decisions that sometimes only those who live through them understand. Let us ask for wisdom to care for those we love, being prudent and loyal, while still acting with honesty before God.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that Samuel spoke to all the Israelites, and that in those days Israel went out to fight against the Philistines. The Israelites camped near Ebenezer, and the Philistines set up their camp at Aphek. The phrase about setting up camp means putting the military camp in place.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Samuel was already recognized as a prophet in Israel. The verse does not say what message he gave, nor whether Israel sought God's guidance before the battle. What follows shows a defeat and an attempt to use the ark as if it were a charm. Some understand that there is a lack of true trust in God in this.

For today: before facing a struggle, it is not enough to have religious symbols or customs. Let us seek God sincerely, listen to his Word, and ask for his direction, instead of trusting in formulas or outward appearances.
exp.11:12:
Here Samuel says to the people: "Look, this is the king you chose and asked for." But he adds that the Lord is the one who set him over them. That is, the people asked for him, and God allowed it.

Samuel speaks at an assembly in Gilgal, when Saul had already been confirmed as king. Samuel is about to step down from leadership. He reminds them that, facing the threat of Nahash the Ammonite, they asked for a human king, even though God was already their King. Right after this he calls them to obey God, both the people and the king.

For today: our decisions have consequences, even when God permits them. Before asking for something out of anxiety or fear, it is good to pray and ask ourselves whether we trust God. And after deciding, the best course is to keep obeying him with humility.
exp.23:15:
David says that God will be the judge between him and Saul. He asks God to look at the case, defend his cause, and free him from Saul's power.

David is speaking, after having been hunted by King Saul. In the cave he could have killed him, but he only cut off a piece of Saul's robe and did him no harm. Now, from a distance, he tells Saul that he will not take revenge with his own hand and leaves the matter in God's hands. In many Bibles this passage appears as verse 15.

When people treat you unjustly, you do not have to repay evil with evil. You can bring your case before God, act with uprightness, and trust that he judges with justice.
exp.16:57:
Saul asks David: "Whose son are you, young man?" And David answers respectfully: "I am the son of your servant Jesse, from Bethlehem."

David has just defeated Goliath and is still holding the Philistine's head in his hand. Abner, the commander of the army, brings him before Saul. It is striking that Saul asks this question, since David had earlier played the harp for him (1 Samuel 16). Some think Saul did not remember David well, or wanted to know about his family because of the promised reward. The Bible does not explain this with certainty.

After a great victory, David does not boast. He answers simply and mentions his humble origin. Today we can learn to receive success with humility, remembering who we are and where God has brought us from.
exp.9:9:
It says that Saul came to the hill, that is, to a height or hill. There he met a group of prophets coming toward him. Then the Spirit of God came upon him with power, and Saul prophesied among them. Here "prophesied" means speaking or praising under the influence of God.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, and he relates what Samuel had announced to Saul after anointing him as future king. Samuel gave him several signs to confirm that God was with him. This was the last one. The text says that God changed his heart, preparing him for his new task. The verses that follow show that the people were amazed.

For today: God is the one who equips those he calls. If you feel that a task is too big for you, ask him for his Spirit and trust that he sustains you. But remember that a powerful experience does not replace a life of continual obedience.
exp.3:11:
This verse tells that a man of the tribe of Benjamin ran away from the battlefield and arrived at Shiloh that same day. He had torn clothes and dirt on his head. In that time these were well-known signs of mourning, deep sorrow, or tragedy. Shiloh was the place where the sanctuary stood and where the priest Eli lived.

It is the narrator who speaks, and he introduces us to the messenger who will bring the news of Israel's defeat. The ark of God had been captured and Eli's sons had died. Before the man says a word, his appearance already announces the disaster. The text does not give his name, so we know nothing more about him.

For today: when hard news arrives, we should not hide it behind false calm. It is healthy to weep sincerely and to bring our pain before God, who listens even when everything seems lost.
exp.19:25:
This verse says that Saul said nothing on the first day of the feast, when he saw that David's place was empty. He thought something had happened to David and that he was not "clean," meaning that David was ceremonially unclean and for that reason could not take part in the meal. The phrase "something hath befallen him" in the King James wording expresses the same idea: "something had happened to him."

Here the narrator tells us what Saul was thinking. David and Jonathan had planned this new moon feast to see whether Saul wanted to kill David. Saul kept silent that day because he believed there was a religious reason for the absence. The law mentioned impurities that kept a person from taking part in certain sacred meals (Leviticus 7:20-21). His reaction would change the next day.

For today: we often explain the behavior of others according to what we believe, and we get it wrong. Before drawing conclusions, it is wise to ask, to listen, and to wait. And when tension lives in the heart, let us ask God to free us from suspicion and resentment.
exp.24:3:
This verse says that David, while he was in the wilderness, learned that Nabal was shearing his sheep. "Shear" means cutting the wool off the sheep. It was important work and, in that time, also a season of feasting and abundance.

The narrator tells this after introducing Nabal, a very wealthy man, but harsh and wicked in his deeds. David was living on the run from Saul, and his band stayed in those lands. Upon learning that it was shearing time, he sends messengers to ask for help respectfully. The text does not explain all his reasons, but that season was usually one of generosity.

For today: before asking for something or making a decision, pay attention to the moment and to the person. Ask with respect and humility, and do not assume that others owe you something. Even so, be ready to respond calmly if they treat you badly.
exp.28:7:
David asks Achish what he has done wrong. He says that since he has been with him, they have found no fault in him. So why won't they let him go to fight against the enemies of my lord the king? Here the word "found" is the one meaning "discovered," and "servant" refers to someone who serves.

David was living among the Philistines, fleeing from King Saul. The Philistine leaders distrusted him, and Achish sent him back. Some think David was speaking sincerely; others think he used ambiguous words, since "my lord the king" could be understood in more than one way. The text does not make this clear.

When someone distrusts you without reason, you can answer with calm and with a clear conscience. And if a door closes, trust that God may be guiding your steps.
exp.19:26:
It says that on the second day of the new moon feast, David's place at the table was still empty. Saul asks his son Jonathan why "the son of Jesse" has not come to eat, neither yesterday nor today. The word "came to pass" in the verse means "happened," and "unclean" refers to a ritual impurity that would have kept him from taking part.

Here Saul, the king, speaks with Jonathan. David had fled because Saul wanted to kill him, and Jonathan and David had agreed on this test to learn the king's intentions. Notice that Saul says "the son of Jesse" and not "David," a disdainful tone that shows his contempt and anger.

Today we can pay attention to how we speak about people. When resentment grows in the heart, even another person's name becomes uncomfortable to say. Let us ask God to heal what hardens us, so that we can speak with respect even about those who make us uneasy.
exp.1:5:
The explanation says that God has control over life and death. "The Lord killeth" and "maketh alive" show that everything depends on Him. "The grave" is the tomb, or the place of the dead. "Bringeth up" means that He can raise up, deliver, or give new life. Some understand it as rescue from deadly dangers, and others also see a foreshadowing of the hope of resurrection.

The one speaking is Hannah, in her prayer of thanksgiving. She was barren and humiliated, and God gave her a son, Samuel, whom she dedicated to the service of God. Her song celebrates that God changes situations: He brings down the proud and lifts up the humble.

For today: when you feel that your situation has no way out, remember that God still rules. Trust in Him with humility, pray with thankfulness, and wait for Him to be able to lift up what seems lost.
exp.18:12:
Michal took an image, laid it in the bed, put something made of goats' hair at the head of it, and then covered it with a cloth. In this way it appeared that David was sleeping. The Hebrew word is usually "teraphim," household figures; it is not clear how large they were or how they were used. It is also not certain exactly what the goats' hair was.

Michal is the daughter of Saul and the wife of David. Saul, jealous, had sent men to kill David early in the morning. Michal warned him and helped him escape through the window. She arranged this deception to give him time to flee.

For today: when we love someone, we sometimes have to act with courage and quickness to protect them. However, this passage tells what Michal did; it does not say that everything she did is an example to imitate. Let us ask for wisdom to help others with honesty and courage.
exp.20:11:
It says that David kept in his mind what Achish's servants had said about him, and he was greatly afraid of the king of Gath. The phrase about keeping these words in his heart means that he took them seriously and thought them over.

Here the book's narrator is speaking. David was fleeing from Saul and came to Gath, a Philistine city, perhaps thinking he would go unnoticed there. But the servants recognized him as the hero who had defeated the Philistines, and David found himself in danger. That is why, in the verses that follow, he pretended to be insane in order to save himself.

For today: sometimes fear leads us to look for ways out on our own. David was afraid, and this reminds us that feeling fear is not sin. What matters is what we do with it. We can bring it to God in prayer, as David later wrote in Psalm 34, which tradition connects with this episode.
exp.15:17:
A servant of Saul recommends a young man, the son of Jesse, from Bethlehem. He says that he knows how to play the harp, that he is brave and strong, that he serves as a warrior, that he speaks with wisdom, that he has a good appearance, and that "the Lord is with him," meaning God accompanies him.

Saul suffers from an evil spirit sent from God, a phrase that has been understood in several ways and that the Bible does not fully explain. His servants look for music that will bring him relief. One of them speaks of David without yet naming him. Shortly after, Saul sends for him, and David arrives with a gift from his father.

For today: God often forms his people in simple places, such as caring for the sheep. Be faithful and honest in small things, and develop your character along with your skills. Others may notice when the opportunity comes.
exp.14:7:
It says that Saul captured Agag, the king of the Amalekites, alive, but killed all the people with the sword. "Took alive" means that he did not kill him. "With the edge of the sword" is the sharp edge, that is, a slaughter by sword.

The narrator tells of the war against Amalek. God, through Samuel, had commanded Saul to destroy this people completely (1 Samuel 15:1-3). Earlier, Saul had spared the Kenites, who had been kind to Israel. But here the disobedience begins: Saul lets the king live. The verses that follow show that the best of the livestock was also kept. This command of total destruction is hard, and Christians understand it in various ways.

Obeying God halfway is a form of disobedience. We can ask ourselves: in what area am I leaving alive something that God has asked me to let go of? Let us ask him for help to obey him sincerely and completely.
exp.0:12:
Hannah was praying silently. Her lips were moving, but no word could be heard, because she was speaking from the deepest part of her heart. Eli, the priest, saw her and thought she was drunk.

Hannah had no children and suffered greatly. She was at the sanctuary in Shiloh, and she had just made a vow: if God gave her a son, she would dedicate him to the Lord for his whole life. Eli watched her and misunderstood the way she was praying, since perhaps he was not used to seeing a prayer so quiet and so intense.

For today: God hears the prayers that no one else understands. When pain keeps you from finding words, you can pour out your heart before Him. And if someone misreads your faith, remember that God knows what is within you.
exp.12:11:
Saul explains why he offered the sacrifice. He thought the Philistines would attack him at Gilgal before he had sought the Lord's favor. Seeking the Lord's favor means asking God for help through prayer. A burnt offering was an offering burned up completely. "I forced myself" means he made himself do it, as someone who compels himself to act.

He is speaking to Samuel, the first king of Israel. Samuel had told him to wait seven days, and Saul, afraid and seeing the people scattering, offered the sacrifice himself, something that was not his place to do. His excuse sounds pious, but Samuel calls it foolishness.

For today: pressure can lead us to justify disobedience with religious words. When you feel you must act right now, stop and ask yourself whether you are trusting God or only calming your fear. Waiting on God is also obeying him.
exp.19:24:
This verse describes how the king's table was arranged at the feast of the new moon. Saul sits in his usual place, next to the wall. Jonathan gets up, Abner sits at Saul's side, and David's place is left empty. The words for the places at the table here refer only to their seats at the table.

Here the narrator speaks. David had hidden himself, in line with the plan he made with Jonathan to find out whether Saul wanted to kill him. David's absence from the table is the proof. Saul says nothing that day, since he assumes David is ceremonially unclean. But his reaction the next day will show his true intentions.

For today: absences and silences say a great deal. Let us learn to notice who is missing from our table, whether at home, in our family, or in our church, and to approach them with love, without resentment or suspicion.
exp.3:1:
This verse tells that the Philistines attacked Israel. The battle broke out and the Israelites lost. About four thousand men died on the battlefield. The phrase about the Philistines starting the battle means they began the attack, and the phrase about Israel being struck down means they were defeated.

The one telling the story is the writer of the book, who does not identify himself. He recounts the start of a war between Israel and the Philistines, a neighboring people and an enemy. What follows shows that the leaders asked why God had let them lose. But instead of examining their hearts, they decided to bring the ark of the covenant, as if it were a charm. This sets up an even greater defeat.

When something goes wrong for us, it is good to stop and humbly ask God what He wants to teach us. Let us not use symbols, customs, or religious formulas as a shortcut. What God seeks is a sincere heart that trusts in Him.
exp.16:38:
David fastened Saul's sword over the clothes the king had lent him and tried to walk, but he could not, because he had never worn armour like that. He told Saul honestly and took everything off. The phrase "he assayed to go" means that he tried to walk in that gear, and "for he had not proved it" means that he was not used to it.

David speaks with King Saul. Israel was facing the Philistine giant Goliath, and Saul, with good intentions, wanted to protect David by dressing him like a soldier. But David trusted that God, who had delivered him from the lion and the bear, would deliver him now as well.

For today: God uses us with the gifts and experience He has already given us. We do not need to imitate others in order to serve with faith. Trust God and be yourself, with humility.
exp.21:10:
This verse tells that King Saul sent for the priest Ahimelech, son of Ahitub, and all his father's household, who were also priests at Nob. All of them obeyed and came before the king. The phrase "sent for" in the explanation is rendered as the verse says: "the king sent to call."

After Doeg the Edomite accused Ahimelech, Saul acted. Doeg reported that Ahimelech had helped David with bread, with the sword of Goliath, and by inquiring of God on his behalf. Saul, filled with suspicion, believed that David and the priests were conspiring against him. The priests came without suspecting the danger, probably because they did not know what they were being accused of.

For today: before reacting to a rumor or an accusation, it is wise to listen calmly and seek the truth. Jealousy and fear cloud judgment and can lead us to harm innocent people.
exp.3:12:
This verse shows Eli, the aged priest, sitting in a seat by the road, watching in the distance. He was keeping watch, alert to see who was coming. His heart was trembling with fear for the ark of God, which had gone out to battle. When the messenger entered Shiloh and gave the news, the whole city cried out in grief.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel lost to the Philistines. The ark was captured, and Hophni and Phinehas, Eli's sons, died. Eli did not yet know anything, but his unease showed that the ark mattered to him more than anything else. The Bible does not explain all his thoughts, so it is not wise to assume too much.

For today: when we feel fear for something we love, we can bring it to God in prayer before the news arrives. And if bad news has already come, we are not alone in facing it.
exp.8:15:
God tells Samuel that the next day, at this same time, he will send him a man from the land of Benjamin. Samuel was to anoint him (pour oil on him as a sign that God had chosen him) as ruler, that is, leader of Israel. This man would deliver the people from the Philistines. God says he has looked upon his people because their cry has come up to him.

This speaks on the day before Saul arrived. Israel was suffering under Philistine oppression and had asked for a king. Saul was searching for his father's lost donkeys, without knowing that God was guiding him toward Samuel. God already had a plan in place.

For today: God hears the cry of those who suffer and acts in his own time, often in ways we do not see. You can pray with confidence, knowing that he sees you and cares for you.
exp.21:20:
Here the text says that Abiathar, the only son of the priest Ahimelech who survived, told David that Saul had killed the Lord's priests.

The account is told by the narrator of Samuel. Saul, full of suspicion and jealousy, believed that the priests of Nob were helping David. Doeg the Edomite accused them, and Saul ordered the slaughter. Abiathar fled to David, who was hiding, and brought him the terrible news. David acknowledged that he bore part of the blame for having been there that day.

For today: when our actions, even without bad intent, bring pain to others, the best thing is to acknowledge it honestly and care for the one who suffered. David did not justify himself, but protected Abiathar and gave him a safe place at his side.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that when the ark of the covenant came into the camp, the people of Israel shouted with such joy that the ground shook. The phrase "gave a shout" means they raised a loud cry. "Joy" refers to a very strong gladness. "Shook" is a way of saying the noise was enormous.

Israel had just lost a battle against the Philistines. The elders thought that if they brought the ark from Shiloh, God would save them. But they did not ask God what to do. The text also notes that Hophni and Phinehas, the sons of Eli, were coming with the ark. Later in the chapter, Israel loses again, so their trust was placed in an object rather than in a relationship with God.

Today we can ask ourselves what we truly trust in. Religious things, such as a cross, a song, or a custom, can help us, but they do not replace obeying God and seeking him sincerely. Before celebrating, it is wise to pray and to listen.
exp.24:25:
Here Abigail tells David that God himself has kept him from shedding blood and from avenging himself with his own hand. She swears by the living Lord and by David's own life. And she wishes that David's enemies end up like Nabal, that is, under the judgment of God. "Withholden" means held back, and "seek evil to my lord" means try to do harm to him.

Abigail is the wife of Nabal, a foolish man who insulted David and refused him food. David was going out with his armed men to kill Nabal's household. Abigail goes out to meet them with provisions, humbles herself, and tries to prevent a tragedy. She sees the hand of God in that meeting.

When someone wrongs us, it is better not to take revenge with our own hands. We can stop, listen to wise counsel, and let God bring justice in his own time.
exp.14:34:
This verse says that Samuel never saw Saul again for the rest of Saul's life. Even so, Samuel grieved over him and mourned for him. God, for his part, is described as having regretted making Saul king. That wording does not mean God made a mistake, but that he was grieved by the direction Saul had taken and changed how he dealt with him.

This is the close of chapter 15. Saul had disobeyed God's command concerning the Amalekites, and Samuel, the prophet, told him that God was rejecting him as king. Afterward Samuel went to Ramah and Saul went home to Gibeah. The relationship between them was broken.

For today: disobedience has painful consequences, even for those who love us. Still, we can follow Samuel's example: to mourn for someone who has gone wrong, rather than to rejoice in their fall.
exp.19:4:
It says that the next day was the start of the new moon, a festival at which David would usually sit down to eat with King Saul. David asks Jonathan to let him hide in the field until the evening of the third day.

David speaks with his friend Jonathan, Saul's son. David knows that Saul wants to kill him and is in danger. Jonathan offers to help him, and David proposes a test: his absence from the king's table will show how Saul reacts. In this way they will know for certain whether there is real danger.

For today: when you face a difficult situation, seek the help of faithful friends and act with prudence. Trusting God does not mean acting without thinking, but asking for wisdom and relying on people you can trust.
exp.15:8:
Jesse brings his son Shammah before Samuel, and Samuel says that the Lord has not chosen him either. The accent marks on "á" in the source are only a feature of older spelling; today we would simply write "a." The phrase "made... to pass by" means that he presented him before the prophet.

Samuel had been sent by God to the house of Jesse in Bethlehem to anoint a new king, since Saul had been rejected. Jesse presents his sons one by one. Earlier, God had told Samuel not to look at appearance or height, because He looks at the heart. Shammah is the third son whom God does not choose.

Often we judge people, and even ourselves, by what can be seen on the outside. Today we can ask God to help us value sincerity, humility, and love, and to trust that He sees what no one else sees.
exp.27:15:
Here Samuel answers Saul with a hard question: if the Lord has already departed from you and become your enemy, why do you come to me?

Saul is desperate because the Philistines are attacking and God is not answering him. For this reason he turns to a medium at Endor, something the law forbade. The text says that Samuel appears, though commentators explain this in different ways. What is clear is that the message agrees with what God had already said: Saul lost the kingdom because of his disobedience.

For today: let us not seek answers in ways God forbids when we are in distress. If we feel that God is far away, let us return to Him with humility and repentance, before fear pushes us into wrong decisions.
exp.27:7:
Saul takes off his royal clothes and puts on other clothes so that no one will recognize him. He goes at night, with two companions, to the house of a woman in Endor. He asks her to use a "spirit of Python," that is, a spirit of divination, to bring up a dead man he wants to speak with.

The narrator tells us that Saul is desperate. The Philistines are approaching, and God no longer answers him. Ironically, Saul himself had driven the mediums out of the land, because God's law forbade such practices. Now he breaks his own command.

For today: when we feel that God is silent, it is tempting to seek answers by paths that He has forbidden. It is better to keep seeking Him with humility and repentance, and to trust what He has already told us in His Word.
exp.16:48:
This verse describes the exact moment of the blow. David put his hand into his shepherd's bag, took out a stone, and slung it with the sling. The stone struck the Philistine on the forehead and sank into it, and the giant fell face down to the ground. The word "slang" in the verse is an old form of "slung," meaning "threw," and "smote" means "struck."

The narrator then tells what happens after David said that the LORD does not save with sword or spear, because the battle belongs to the Lord. Goliath advanced toward him, and David ran to meet him. David wanted everyone to see that the victory came from God and not from weapons. The text does not explain how the stone penetrated so deeply; it simply narrates it as a fact.

For today: God can use what little you have, like a simple stone, when you trust in Him. Do not wait until you have the best resources; act with courage and entrust the outcome to the Lord.
exp.7:13:
It says that the king the people ask for will take their fields, their vineyards, and their best olive groves, and give them to his servants, that is, to his attendants and officials. The olive groves are orchards of olive trees, an important source of food and wealth.

The speaker is the prophet Samuel. Israel asked for a king so as to be like the other nations, and this grieved Samuel. God told him to warn them how a king would act. This list of abuses shows the cost of placing trust in a human ruler instead of in God. Some scholars see here a general warning about human power; others see a description of what later happened in the monarchy.
