For today: before we place all our hope in a person, a leader, or a system, let us remember that none of them can take the place of God. Let us pray for those who govern, and trust Him first.
exp.16:35:
David says that he had already killed both lions and bears while he was looking after his father's sheep. According to him, the Philistine will be just like those animals, because this uncircumcised man, meaning someone outside God's covenant with Israel, has defied and insulted the armies of the living God, that is, the real and active God, not an idol.

David speaks to King Saul. Everyone in the army feared Goliath, and Saul doubted that a young man could fight. David does not boast of his strength; he offers his experience as proof. Then he says that the LORD, who delivered him from the lion and the bear, will also deliver him from this Philistine.

For today: God often prepares us in small and hidden places, such as daily work or caring for others. When a great challenge comes, remember how God helped you before, and trust that he will remain with you.
exp.25:16:
Saul recognizes David's voice in the darkness and asks him, "Is this thy voice, my son David?" David answers with respect: "It is my voice, my lord, O king."

David has just entered Saul's camp at night, while everyone was sleeping, and he could have killed him, but he did not. He took the spear and the water jug as proof and, from a distance, rebuked Abner for failing to guard the king. Saul was pursuing him unjustly, and yet David still calls him "my lord, O king." Saul calls him "my son," though it is not certain how sincere he was.

Today, even when someone treats us badly, we can speak with respect and without revenge, leaving justice in God's hands. A calm answer can open doors to reconciliation.
exp.27:6:
Saul, desperate, orders his servants to find him a woman who has a "familiar spirit". This was a way of speaking about a medium or fortune-teller, someone who claimed to communicate with the dead. His servants tell him that there is such a woman at En-dor. The word "familiar spirit" refers to a kind of spirit that predicts the future and speaks on behalf of the dead.

Saul speaks this way because he is very afraid of the Philistine army. God had not answered him by dreams, by the Urim (a sacred means of learning God's will), or through prophets. Moreover, Saul himself had driven the fortune-tellers out of the land, because God's law forbade them. Now he breaks what he himself had commanded.

When we feel that God is silent, it is tempting to look for answers in forbidden places. It is better to examine our hearts, return to God with sincerity, and wait on Him, even when the answer is slow in coming.
exp.12:10:
Samuel asks Saul, "What have you done?" Saul defends himself with three reasons: the people were scattering from him, Samuel did not arrive within the appointed time, and the Philistines were already gathering at Michmash. The phrase "were scattering from him" means that the people were deserting him. The phrase "within the days appointed" refers to the seven days that had been agreed upon.

Samuel had told Saul to wait seven days at Gilgal so that Samuel himself could offer the sacrifices (1 Samuel 10:8). Saul, pressed by fear, offered the burnt offering without waiting. Samuel arrived just afterward and confronted him. Saul does not confess his mistake; he makes excuses.

For today: when waiting becomes hard and the pressure grows, it is tempting to act on our own. Obeying God, even when it seems that everything is falling apart, is worth more than any quick solution. And when we fail, it is better to admit it sincerely than to justify ourselves.
exp.21:22:
Here David tells Abiathar to stay with him and not to be afraid. The old words are easy: the first phrase means "stay," and the protection he offers is the same safety the verse promises. David explains that the same enemy who wants to kill him also wants to kill Abiathar, so together they will be safer.

David is speaking while he flees from King Saul. He has just learned that Saul ordered the priests of Nob to be killed, and only Abiathar escaped. David feels guilty, because he knew that Doeg the Edomite could report to Saul. With these words he offers shelter and company to a man who has lost everything.

For today: when someone is hurt or frightened, you do not need great answers. Sometimes it is enough to open the door, stay with them, and say, "You are not alone." Think about who needs your company and sincere support today.
exp.29:26:
This verse is part of a list of places to which David sent gifts. It names the people who lived in Beth-el, in Ramoth of the South (called "Ramoth in the south," since "south" is what the name means here), and in Jattir. These were towns in the territory of Judah.

The narrator tells that David, after defeating the Amalekites who had raided Ziklag, shared part of the spoil among the elders of Judah, who were his friends. He called them a gift from the enemies of the Lord. He probably wanted to thank those who had supported him while he was fleeing from Saul, though the text does not give the details. It is not certain that this Beth-el in the south is the same famous one in Benjamin.

For today: David did not keep everything for himself, but recognized those who had helped him. Think about who has supported you and express your gratitude with a concrete gesture, acknowledging that what you have comes from God.
exp.11:13:
He says that if the people and their king fear the Lord, serve him, listen to his voice, and do not rebel against his word, things will go well for them as they follow God. "Fear" here means to respect and honor God with reverence. "Rebels" are those who resist obeying. The final phrase can be understood as "they will follow God" or as "things will go well with him"; the text is brief and can be read both ways.

Samuel speaks, now an old man, at an assembly in Gilgal, when Saul has just been confirmed as king. Israel had asked for a king, partly out of fear of Nahash the Ammonite. Samuel reminds them that their true King is still God and that the new king must also obey him.

For today: it does not matter who leads us or how secure we feel; what is essential is to keep a heart attentive to God. Today you can read his Word and ask him for help to obey it in a concrete decision.
exp.13:14:
This verse tells us that a great trembling and panic filled the whole Philistine camp: the military camp, the open countryside, the garrison (the group of soldiers who guarded the post), and even the raiding parties (quick attacks to plunder). The phrase "the earth quaked" means that the ground seemed to shake, or that everything fell into confusion. The "trembling" was a very great fear.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan and his armor-bearer had just attacked a Philistine outpost alone and killed about twenty men. Then the fear spread. The text presents this as something God allowed, and some understand the trembling as literal while others understand it as only panic.

For today: God can use a small and courageous act of faith to open the way to something much greater. Take the faithful step in front of you today.
exp.23:3:
It says that Saul, while pursuing David, came to a sheepfold beside the road where there was a cave. He went in there to relieve himself, a delicate and old-fashioned way of saying so. David and his men were hidden deep inside that same cave, off to the sides, without Saul knowing it.

This is part of the account given by the narrator of 1 Samuel. Saul, king of Israel, was seeking to kill David with three thousand chosen soldiers. David, already anointed as the future king, was fleeing through the wilderness of Engedi. Without realizing it, Saul found himself defenseless, alone and close to David.

For today: sometimes God allows us the chance to take revenge or to gain something at someone else's expense. Before seizing it, it is worth stopping to ask whether doing so honors God. What looks like an open door may be a test of character.
exp.19:2:
Here David again swears to Jonathan that he is in real danger. He tells him that Saul, Jonathan's father, knows very well that Jonathan cares for David, and for that reason Saul will not tell him his plans, so as not to grieve him. "Grieved" means feeling sorrow or pain. "As the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth" is a solemn form of swearing. "There is but a step between me and death" means that death is very close.

David speaks with his friend Jonathan after fleeing from Naioth, in Ramah. Jonathan does not believe that his father Saul wants to kill David, because Saul usually tells him everything. David insists with an oath, since he knows that Saul is looking for him to take his life.

When someone close to us tells us that they are suffering or in danger, it is good to listen with humility, even when it is hard for us to believe. Listening patiently and helping in concrete ways, as Jonathan will do, is a way of truly loving.
exp.3:17:
This verse tells of the death of Eli. When the messenger mentioned the ark of God, Eli fell backward from his seat, beside the gate. He broke his neck and died, because he was an old man and heavy. It also says that he had judged Israel for forty years.

The one speaking is the narrator, who recounts what happened after the news of the defeat by the Philistines. The messenger brought four pieces of news: Israel fled, many had died, Eli's sons had died, and the ark had been taken. What struck Eli most deeply was the loss of the ark, which symbolized God's presence among his people.

For today: Eli was more shaken by the ark than by his sons, and this shows that the most precious thing is the presence of God. We can ask ourselves what matters most to us, and ask God to always hold first place in our hearts.
exp.24:35:
She came back to her house and found Nabal holding a great feast, like that of a king. He was in high spirits and completely drunk. So she told him nothing, less or more, until the morning light. The phrase "came to" means "went back to" or "arrived where he was."

It is part of the narrative. Abigail had just gone out to meet David, who was coming in anger because Nabal, her husband, had rejected his request for help. With food and wise words she prevented a massacre. Now she returns home, and the narrator shows the folly of Nabal, whose name means "fool."

For today: there are times to speak and times to wait. Abigail did not try to reason with someone drunk and unable to listen. She waited until he was sober. When a difficult conversation is necessary, it is wise to choose the moment carefully, so that what is said can really be heard.
exp.24:18:
She tells her servants to go on ahead with the gifts, and she will follow after them. The servants are the household's attendants. The verse says she did not tell her husband Nabal anything.

The narrator describes what Abigail did. Nabal had insulted David's men, and David was coming with armed men to take revenge. One of the young men warned Abigail about the danger. She acted quickly, without asking her husband's permission. Some think she did this because Nabal was very harsh and would not have listened to her. The Bible does not explain her reasons any further.

When a situation is urgent and dangerous, sometimes we must act with courage and wisdom to seek peace. Ask God for discernment, and act with humility and respect, not with pride or rebellion.
exp.14:20:
Saul says it was the people who kept the best of the plunder: sheep and oxen. He describes them as "the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed," meaning the best of what God had commanded to be completely destroyed. He says it was to offer them in sacrifice to the Lord in Gilgal.

Saul is speaking with Samuel, who confronts him for not having obeyed. God had ordered him to destroy everything belonging to the Amalekites, but Saul spared King Agag and the best of the livestock. Here he puts the blame on the people and presents his disobedience as something religious. Samuel will answer that obedience is worth more than sacrifice.

For today: we should not dress up disobedience in good religious intentions. God does not want us to offer him things to cover up what we refuse to obey. If he has already spoken to us, let us start by obeying, acknowledge our wrong without excuses, and ask his forgiveness with humility.
exp.29:15:
The passage tells how the Egyptian servant led David to the camp of the Amalekites. They were spread out over the whole area, eating, drinking and celebrating, because they had taken a great deal of plunder from the land of the Philistines and from Judah.

Earlier, the Amalekites had burned Ziklag and carried off the families of David and his men. David found an abandoned servant, helped him, and the servant promised to guide him if David did not kill him or hand him back to his master. The narrator shows that the enemies were confident and careless.

For today: pleasures gained through injustice may seem secure, but they do not last. And when we feel we have lost everything, God can open unexpected paths. Trust in Him, act with prudence, and seek his direction before taking the next step.
exp.14:24:
Saul asks Samuel to come back with him so that he can worship the Lord. The word "worship" here means that Saul wants to give honor to God. The request "turn again with me" is a plea that Samuel not leave him and that he come along.

Speaking is Saul, the first king of Israel. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but he did not fully obey and justified himself by saying he feared the people. Samuel has just told him that God has rejected him as king. Saul admits his sin, but he seems more concerned about looking good before the people than about a change of heart. Interpreters debate how sincere his repentance was.

For today: worshiping God does not replace obedience. Before seeking ceremonies or appearances, it is wise to honestly acknowledge our failures and turn to God with our whole heart.
exp.7:18:
The explanation says that the people of Israel refused to listen to Samuel. "Nevertheless" means "but," and "obey the voice" means to pay attention to what is said. They answered firmly: "Nay; but we will have a king over us." They rejected the warning without giving it much thought.

Samuel had just warned them, on God's behalf, what it would cost to have a king: the king would take their sons, their fields, and their flocks. The leaders had asked for a king so that they could be like all the other nations, and so that he would lead them in war. Samuel was distressed, and God told him that the people were rejecting Him as their King. Some see here a desire for political security; others, a lack of trust in God.

Today, before deciding something important, it is wise to listen to wise counsel, even when we do not like it. And we should ask ourselves whether we are looking for security in God or only in copying what others do.
exp.16:5:
This verse describes more of Goliath's battle gear. The greaves were protection for the shins. The word that here says "shield" is uncertain: many modern translations say "javelin" or "short spear" that he carried slung over his shoulder. And "bronze" was probably brass in the original.

The narrator of the book describes Goliath, the Philistine champion, just before he challenges Israel. He wants the reader to notice how imposing he was: his size, his armor and his weapons. This helps us understand why the whole army of Israel was afraid to face him.

Today, we sometimes face problems that seem enormous and well armed. This passage reminds us not to measure everything by appearances. David, later on, trusted in God and not in visible strength. When you feel fear, pray and remember that God is greater than your giant.
exp.16:55:
Abner swears: "I do not know, as your soul lives, O king." Then Saul orders him to find out whose son the young man is. The phrase "as your soul lives" is an old way of swearing, like saying "as you live." "Young man" is the word for a youth.

Saul and Abner have just watched David face Goliath. Saul asks about David's family, not necessarily about his name. Earlier David had played the harp for Saul, so many wonder why Saul does not recognize him. Several explanations have been proposed, such as Saul's troubled mind or his interest in the family of the victor because of the promised reward. The Bible does not make it clear.

For today: God can use people whom others do not notice or do not know well. Serve faithfully even when no one recognizes you yet.
exp.4:5:
The explanation says that God acted with force against the city of Ashdod. Speaking of "the hand of the Lord" is a way of speaking about God's power. The phrase about his hand being heavy means that his hand weighed more heavily on them. The reference to "emerods" most likely refers to painful tumors or sores; it is not known for certain what disease it was.

The narrator recounts what happened when the Philistines captured the ark of God and placed it in the temple of their god Dagon. Dagon was found fallen and broken before the ark. Then this plague came. The people of Ashdod understood that the ark could not remain with them, although they still did not fully acknowledge God.

For today: nothing and no one can take the place of God. We can examine the things in which we place our trust and surrender them to Him with humility, before they fall apart.
exp.9:23:
Samuel speaks to all the people and asks them to look at Saul, the man whom the Lord chose. He says there is no one like him among all Israel. The people answer with shouts of joy: "Long live the king!" Here the word "shouted" means calling out loudly, and "like" means alike or the same.

Samuel, the prophet and judge of Israel, has just cast lots to point out the first king. Saul was chosen, but he was hiding among the baggage. Samuel presents him as God's choice, not the people's idea. Also, Saul stood out for his height, and the people are excited because of it.

For today: God chooses and uses people who sometimes feel small or doubt themselves. We can trust his calling, and at the same time remember that looking only at outward appearance is not enough; what matters is obeying God.
exp.11:3:
Here the people of Israel answer Samuel and say that he never mistreated them or deceived them. The verse's wording "defrauded" means cheating or taking advantage of someone, "oppressed" means harming or treating someone unjustly, and "taken ought of any man's hand" means taking what belongs to others or accepting a bribe.

Samuel is now an old man and hands over leadership to the new king, Saul. Before he steps aside, he asks the people to examine him before God. He wants it to be clear that he served with honesty. Later he will remind them of God's faithfulness.

For today: live with integrity in small things and in large ones, so that others can witness to our honesty. If you have any responsibility, at work, in the family, or in the church, carry it out with clean hands, knowing that God also sees.
exp.9:10:
They say that those who had known Saul from way back saw him prophesying along with a group of prophets, and they were amazed. They asked one another, "What has happened to the son of Kish? Is Saul also among the prophets?" "Prophesying" here seems to describe a Spirit-filled expression, like praise or inspired speech. The phrase "from way back" is the same as "always."

The speakers are Saul's acquaintances and neighbors. God had just changed his heart, and Samuel had announced this sign to him after anointing him as the future king. People did not expect that change in an ordinary young man from a simple family. The saying became a popular proverb. Scholars understand it in several ways: as astonishment, as mockery, or as doubt.

For today: God can work in people whom others have already "filed away" and labeled. Let us avoid pigeonholing anyone, and if God calls us, let us not depend on what others think of us.
exp.19:34:
The explanation says that the next morning Jonathan went out into the field at the time he had agreed with David. A small boy, his servant, was with him. Where it explains the wording: the word for the boy means a young servant who attends someone, and the word for the time means the moment that had been set beforehand.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jonathan has just seen that his father, King Saul, wanted to kill David, and he left the table in great anger and sorrow. Now he carries out the plan he made with David: going out to shoot arrows, and by the way he would signal the boy, David would know whether he could return or had to flee. The boy does not know the real reason.

For today: when a painful truth shakes us, we can act faithfully to our word and to those we love, even when it costs us. Jonathan kept what he had promised despite the conflict with his own family.
exp.18:3:
Jonathan speaks up for David in front of his father, King Saul. He asks the king not to sin against David, who is his servant, because David has done him no wrong. On the contrary, everything David has done has been of great benefit to the king. The phrase "spake good" means that he defended David with kind and well-chosen words.

Jonathan is Saul's son and David's loyal friend. Saul, consumed by jealousy, had decided to kill David. Jonathan warned David to hide and promised to plead for him. Here he keeps his word, reminding Saul of the victories God gave through David. Saul listened and swore that he would not kill David, although afterward his attitude changed.

We can defend with courage and kind words someone who is treated unjustly, even when doing so makes us uncomfortable. A true friendship does not stay silent in the face of wrong; it seeks truth and peace with respect.
exp.21:8:
Doeg, an Edomite who was in charge of Saul's servants, speaks up. He says he saw David come to Nob, where the priest Ahimelech was. The phrase "son of Jesse" is not used here in the English verse; the reader's verse names David's father only as Jesse, so I will refer to David directly.

Saul is furious and suspicious. He believes everyone is plotting against him, and he complains that no one tells him what his son Jonathan is doing with David. Doeg seizes that moment and speaks. What he says is true, but he tells it without mentioning that Ahimelech did not know David was fleeing from the king. That missing information will lead to tragedy.

For today: before you speak, ask yourself why you are saying it. A truth spoken without love, out of ambition, or in order to harm can cause great damage. Let us speak to help, not to destroy.
exp.4:8:
It says that when the Philistines carried the ark to Gath, God acted against that city with a very great destruction. He struck everyone, from the least to the greatest, and they had painful swellings, which were probably tumors or sores.

The narrator tells what happened after the Philistines captured the ark. In Ashdod they had already suffered, and their leaders decided to move it to Gath, thinking that this way they would escape the problem. But the punishment followed them. Some scholars debate exactly what the disease was.

For today: we cannot treat God as an object that can be moved from place to place to avoid his consequences. When God confronts us, the best thing is to humble ourselves, acknowledge the truth, and seek him, instead of running away.
exp.12:9:
This verse tells us that Saul had just finished offering the burnt offering (a sacrifice that was burned completely on the altar) when Samuel arrived. Saul went out to meet him in order to greet him. The phrase "went out to meet" here means that he went to welcome him.

The narrator describes the moment with irony and tension. Saul waited seven days, just as Samuel had instructed, but the people were scattering out of fear of the Philistines. Saul decided to offer the sacrifice himself, something that was not his task, since that duty belonged to the priest or the prophet. Samuel arrived just after.

When pressure mounts, it is tempting to take shortcuts and justify ourselves. God values obedience and trust more than quick results. Waiting on Him, even when it is hard, is an act of faith.
exp.22:26:
A messenger came to Saul with urgent news: the Philistines had invaded the land. The phrase "Haste thee, and come" means "come quickly, right away." "An invasion" is a sudden, violent attack, a raid that comes by surprise.

Saul and his men had almost surrounded David in the wilderness of Maon. Just as they were about to catch him, this warning arrived, and Saul had to abandon the pursuit to defend his people. The messenger speaks out of the urgency of war. The place was called "Sela-hammah-lecoth," which is usually understood as "the rock of divisions" or "of escapes."

For today: when everything seems lost, God can change the situation in unexpected ways. Trust that He cares for you, even when you cannot see how the way out will come.
exp.19:5:
Here David explains to Jonathan what to say if Saul asks about his absence. He is to say that David asked permission to hurry to Bethlehem, his city, because his family was holding its yearly sacrifice there.

David speaks with Jonathan, Saul's son and his faithful friend. Saul was looking for him in order to kill him, and David wanted to test the king's intentions without exposing himself. So he proposes a believable family excuse. The Bible does not say in detail what that yearly sacrifice was like, but it shows that David used an explanation Saul could accept. It is a test, not a direct confrontation.

For today: when you face a conflict or a threat, seek the counsel of someone you trust and act with prudence. If you depend on God, you do not have to react impulsively. Ask for wisdom, lean on faithful friends, and move forward with patience.
exp.16:56:
This verse tells how David, after defeating Goliath, came back carrying the Philistine's head in his hand. Abner, the commander of the army, took him and brought him before King Saul.

The narrator of the book now speaks. Saul asks whose son David is, even though David had earlier played the harp for him (1 Samuel 16). Scholars explain this in several ways: perhaps Saul did not remember David well, or perhaps he was asking about the family that would receive the promised reward. The reason cannot be known for certain.

For today: God can use the one the world overlooks. David came to the palace without fame, but with faith. Be faithful in what God places in front of you, even when no one yet knows who you are.
exp.18:10:
Saul sent messengers to David's house to keep watch over it through the night and to kill him in the morning. But Michal, David's wife, found out and warned him: if he did not escape that very night, the next day he would be dead. Saul's men were set to watch, so that David would not get away.

It is a narrated scene, not a speech. Saul, filled with jealousy and fear, had already tried to pin David to the wall with his spear. Michal is Saul's daughter, yet she protects her husband. The text says that an evil spirit from the Lord was upon Saul, and scholars explain that phrase in several ways. What is clear is that Saul was acting with great violence.

For today: when God gives you a warning through someone sensible, do not put it off. Listen with humility and act with prudence, without neglecting your trust in God.
exp.11:20:
They say we should not go after "vanities," that is, empty, false, or worthless things such as idols. These things do not "profit" (they serve no purpose and bring no benefit) and do not "deliver" (they cannot rescue anyone in a moment of danger). The reason is simple: they are vanity, and they have no real power.

Samuel, the prophet and judge of Israel, is speaking. The people had just asked for a king, and they acknowledged that this was a mistake. Samuel does not frighten them but encourages them not to turn away from God. He reminds them that God does not abandon his people, and that he himself will continue to pray for them and teach them the good way.

Today we can ask ourselves where we place our trust: money, success, the approval of others. Those things may help a little, but they do not sustain us in a crisis. Even after failing, we can return to God with our whole heart.
exp.20:12:
He said that David changed his manner of speaking and of behaving before the men of Gath. He pretended to be mad: he scratched marks on the gate doors and let his spittle run down into his beard. The source's comment that "changed his speech" means he altered the way he spoke is not needed here, since the verse itself says he changed his behaviour; "the doors of the gate" are the leaves of the gate, and "in their hands" means that he did this while they had him under their control.

The narrator tells that David was fleeing from King Saul and came to Gath, a Philistine city, where the servants of Achish recognized him as the famous warrior. David was very much afraid that they would kill him, and for that reason he feigned madness. Psalm 34 and Psalm 56 are traditionally connected with this episode, although not all scholars agree on the details.

This passage shows that even a man of faith can feel fear and act with human awkwardness. When you are afraid, do not stay silent: cry out to God, as David did in his psalms, and trust that He can care for you even in your weakest moments.
exp.8:21:
Samuel took Saul by the hand and brought him and his servant into the dining hall where the meal was being served. He gave them the place of honor, at the head of the table, among about thirty guests.

Samuel is a prophet and judge of Israel. Saul had been searching for some lost donkeys, and God had already told Samuel that this young man would be the first king. Saul had just said that he came from a small tribe and a small family. Samuel answers by honoring him, though he does not yet tell him everything.

For today: God often honors people who are simple and humble, even when they do not see themselves as important. We can receive others with respect and trust that God knows what he is preparing for us, even when we do not yet understand it.
exp.29:16:
This verse tells that David and his men attacked the Amalekites from dawn until the evening of the next day. No one escaped, except four hundred young men who fled riding on camels.

This is part of the story, not a speech. The Amalekites had burned Ziklag and taken the families of David and his men. An Egyptian servant, sick and left behind by them, guided David to their camp. They found them celebrating the plunder, confident and unprepared. Some scholars also see here the judgment on a people who had long been an enemy of Israel.

For today: when you feel you have lost everything, first seek God and then act with courage and perseverance. David did not stay weeping; he moved forward, and God sustained him until he recovered what was his.
exp.1:6:
It says that God is the one who governs the changes in life. The words "poor" and "rich" speak of losing or receiving possessions. "Bringeth low" means to humble or bring down, and "lifteth up" means to raise up or give honor. The verse shows that God has the final word over wealth, position, and the destiny of people.

Hannah speaks, in a prayer of thanksgiving. She was barren and suffered mockery, but God gave her Samuel. Her song celebrates that God changes the circumstances of the weak and humbles the pride of the powerful. Scholars see in her prayer an announcement of the kingdom that would come in Israel.

For today: if you are in a time of scarcity or humiliation, you can entrust your situation to God with hope. And if things are going well for you, do not become proud, because you receive everything from Him. Be humble and generous.
exp.14:29:
Saul admits that he has sinned, but right away he asks Samuel to honour him before the elders of his people and before all Israel. He also asks Samuel to return with him so that he may worship the Lord his God. The request to "honour" him uses the verse's own wording, and "worship" is the same idea of paying reverence to God.

Saul speaks after Samuel has announced that God is taking the kingdom from him because he disobeyed in the war against the Amalekites. Saul says, "I have sinned," but his main concern seems to be his public standing. Some readers see in this an incomplete repentance; others see a real fear mixed with pride. The text does not explain his heart in detail. Samuel does return with him, and Saul worships.

Today we might ask ourselves whether, when we fail, we grieve more over offending God or over losing our reputation. Sincere repentance seeks first the truth and the forgiveness of God, and trusts that he cares for our name.
exp.8:10:
This verse tells how Saul and his servant were going up the slope toward the city when they came upon some young women coming out to draw water. They asked them whether the seer was there. "Young maidens" means young girls, and "seer" was the old name for the prophet, someone who received messages from God.

It is Saul and his servant who speak. They were searching for his father's lost donkeys, and the servant suggested consulting the man of God to learn which way to go. The young women answered promptly and gave them directions. Without knowing it, Saul was on his way to meet Samuel, who would anoint him as king.

For today: when you need direction, do not hesitate to ask and to seek wise counsel. God can use an ordinary search, such as one for lost donkeys, to lead you to an important encounter.
exp.6:6:
The verse tells that the Philistines learned that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah. Then their lords went up to attack Israel. When the Israelites heard it, they were afraid.

The narrator describes what happened after Israel had repented at Mizpah. Samuel had gathered them to pray, and they fasted and confessed their sin. Perhaps the Philistines saw the gathering as an opportunity to attack. What follows shows that the people, frightened, sought help from God through Samuel.

Turning back to God does not always remove problems right away; sometimes they arrive just after. But fear can lead us to cry out to God, as Israel did. When something frightens us, we can pray and turn to Him, without waiting to have everything resolved.
exp.16:24:
The soldiers of Israel are talking among themselves about Goliath, who comes out every day to challenge the army. "Taunt" here means to insult and dare. They say that King Saul offers a reward to whoever defeats him: great riches, his daughter's hand in marriage, and that the man's family will be exempt. The phrase about making the household free probably means exempting it from taxes or service to the king, although the text gives no further details.

The Israelites speak, and David listens. Everyone was afraid and fled from Goliath. That is why the king was offering rewards, hoping someone would dare. David, who had come to bring supplies to his brothers, begins to ask what is happening.

For today: when everyone looks at the size of the problem, we can look to God. David did not fix his attention on the prize, but on the fact that someone was insulting the living God.
exp.25:8:
Here David tells Abishai not to kill Saul. He asks firmly: "who can stretch forth his hand against the Lord's anointed, and be guiltless?" That is, no one who does that will go free from blame.

David speaks at night, inside Saul's camp, the camp of the man who had been pursuing him to kill him. Everyone is asleep, and Abishai sees an opportunity that seems sent by God. David, however, honors Saul because God had placed him as king. He prefers to wait for God to judge and act in his own time.

For today: an opportunity for revenge is not the same as God's permission to take it. When someone has done us harm, we can choose not to repay evil with evil, to trust God's justice, and to act with integrity even when no one sees us.
exp.18:9:
This verse tells how Saul tried to pin David to the wall with his spear. But David stepped aside, and the spear struck the wall. Then David fled and escaped that night.

The narrator describes how Saul, full of jealousy because David was winning battles and was admired, was taken over by an evil spirit from the LORD. People understand this phrase in different ways: some see it as God's permission as a judgment, others as a tormenting spiritual distress. David would play music to calm him, but Saul answered with violence.

For today: when someone treats us with hatred without reason, we do not have to answer with the same evil. We can step away with wisdom, seek protection, and trust that God cares for us.
exp.17:5:
This verse tells that, when David was returning after defeating Goliath, the women from all the towns of Israel came out to meet King Saul and the army. They did it with singing, dancing, and joy.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. It was customary to celebrate victories this way in Israel. David was already very beloved by the people and by Saul's servants. However, what seems like a festival soon becomes a cause of jealousy in Saul's heart, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: when others receive praise or success, we can choose to rejoice with them instead of comparing ourselves. If we feel envy, it is better to acknowledge it before God and ask Him for a grateful heart, before it grows and harms us.
exp.17:21:
Saul orders his servants to speak with David in private. They are to tell him that the king is pleased with him, that everyone at court thinks well of him, and that he should accept becoming the king's son-in-law. Saul's officials are his servants, and when the explanation says they hold David in affection, it means they regard him kindly.

Saul speaks, but he has a hidden purpose. The previous passage says he wanted to give his daughter Michal to David as a snare, that is, as a trap, so that the Philistines would kill him. That is why he uses messengers and flattery instead of speaking frankly himself.

For today: not all praise is sincere. We can be grateful for kind words, but it is wise to examine motives with prayer and discernment. And let us seek to speak honestly, without using pleasant words to manipulate others.
exp.5:20:
This verse tells how the people of Beth-shemesh sent messengers to the inhabitants of Kirjath-jearim. They told them that the Philistines had brought back the ark of the Lord, and they invited them to come down and take it away.

The people speaking here were the ones who had just suffered a terrible punishment for looking inside the ark. They were frightened and mourning, and they asked who is able to stand before such a holy God. That is why they wanted the ark to leave their town. The number of those who died (50,070) is much debated among scholars because of the way it is written in the Hebrew, and some think the original figure was smaller.

For today: God is to be approached with respect and humility, not with careless curiosity. His holiness is not meant to push us away, but so that we seek him with reverence and obedience.
exp.11:4:
Explanation of what it says: Samuel tells them that God is witness that they found no fault in him, and that the king, the one God has chosen, is also a witness. An anointed one is someone set apart by God for a task, anointed with oil. The phrase "found anything in my hand" means they did not find him guilty of theft or abuse. The people answer: "He is witness."

Context: Samuel is now an old man. Israel asked for a king, and Saul has just been confirmed. Before leaving leadership, Samuel asks the people to declare whether he treated them unjustly. They confirm his honesty, and so he can remind them with authority what God has done for them.

For today: Living with integrity gives us freedom and credibility. Try to act so that, if anyone examined your work, your money, and your dealings with others, there would be nothing to hide. And when you fail, admit it and repair the harm.
exp.1:12:
This verse describes how the priests in Shiloh treated the people who brought sacrifices. When someone offered a sacrifice, the priest's servant came while the meat was boiling. He carried a large fork with three prongs to take meat out of the pot.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He has just said that the sons of Eli did not know the LORD. For this reason he explains how they abused their position. What follows shows that they took the meat by force, with no respect for what belonged to God. This contrasts with the young Samuel, who served faithfully.

For today: if we serve in the church or in any responsibility, let us not use that place for our own benefit. Serving God calls for a humble heart and honesty with what belongs to Him and to others.
exp.17:25:
When Saul's servants told David the king's terms, David was pleased with the idea of becoming the king's son-in-law. The word translated "pleased" in the verse above is the one this explanation is referring to, and the "bride price" was the payment given for the bride. The "foreskins" were proof of having killed one hundred Philistines. The phrase "the days were not expired" indicates that David set out before the set time had run out.

Saul's servants were speaking on the king's orders. Saul was jealous of David and hoped the Philistines would kill him in the attempt. David did not know about this trap, or at least the text does not say so. He saw an opportunity to serve Israel and to become related to the king.

For today: sometimes the people around us have hidden motives, even when they speak to us kindly. It is wise to act with simplicity and integrity, and to trust that God cares for us, as he cared for David, even when we cannot see the whole picture.
exp.27:16:
It says that God carried out what he had already announced through Samuel. The kingdom was no longer in Saul's hands, because God had handed it over to David. Here, the word that is rendered as "neighbour" means someone close to Saul, a fellow member of his community. The phrase "rent … out of thine hand" means taken away in a definitive way.

Samuel speaks to Saul, or an apparition presenting itself as Samuel does. Saul, desperate before the Philistines and without any answer from God, sought out a medium in Endor. Some believe that Samuel truly appeared with God's permission; others think it was something else. The text presents the message as a word of judgment for Saul's disobedience.

For today: do not wait until you are in crisis to turn back to God. Obeying him in good time and with sincerity is better than seeking answers by mistaken paths when it is already too late.
exp.1:0:
Hannah begins her prayer with joy: her heart rejoices in God. The image of "my horn is exalted" is a picture of strength and dignity, like an animal that lifts its head with power. "My mouth is enlarged over my enemies" means that she can now speak with confidence in the face of those who looked down on her.

The one speaking is Hannah, the wife of Elkanah. For years she had no children and suffered the taunts of Peninnah, the other wife. She prayed in pain at the sanctuary, and God granted her Samuel. After giving him over to serve the Lord, Hannah lifts up this prayer of thanksgiving. Her joy is centered on God, not only on the gift she received.

When God helps you through a difficulty, do not stop at relief. Take some time to thank Him aloud or in writing, and acknowledge that He was your strength and your refuge.
exp.1:20:
It says that God "visited" Hannah, that is, he showed her kindness and granted her desire to be a mother. She had three sons and two daughters more. "Bare" means gave birth. Meanwhile, the young Samuel, whom she had dedicated to God, kept growing in the sanctuary, "before the Lord," that is, under his care and in his presence.

The narrator tells this after Eli blessed Elkanah and Hannah for having given Samuel over. Hannah had made a request and a vow to God. Now it is shown that God answers with generosity. The account contrasts Samuel, who grows faithfully, with the sons of Eli, who behave badly, as becomes clear soon after.

For today: God cares for what we entrust to him in faith. We can dedicate to him our children, our time, and our plans, and trust that he is faithful, even though he does not always respond in the same way.
exp.15:13:
What it says: The Spirit of the Lord left Saul, that is, He no longer guided him or gave him strength to reign. In his place, an evil spirit troubled him. The word "tormented" in the source means that it distressed him and took away his peace. That it came "from the Lord" indicates that God allowed it or used it as judgment; the text does not explain how, and scholars understand it in several ways.

Context: The narrator of the book recounts this right after Samuel anointed David. Saul had disobeyed God before, and for that reason he lost God's favor. While the Spirit passes to David, Saul is troubled. His servants notice and suggest he seek a musician who can play the harp to soothe him.

For today: Obeying God guards the heart. If we have failed, let us not harden our soul; let us seek God's forgiveness and guidance quickly. And, like Saul's servants, let us help with love those who are suffering.
exp.16:25:
Here David asks the soldiers what will be given to the man who defeats the Philistine and takes away the reproach from Israel. Then he says that this man is uncircumcised, meaning he does not belong to the covenant people of God, and yet he dares to defy the armies of the living God.

David has just arrived at the camp, sent by his father to bring food to his brothers. He sees that everyone is running away from Goliath out of fear. David is not thinking only about the reward; he is angered that God is being insulted. His brother Eliab misreads his motives and rebukes him, but David presses on.

For today: when everyone freezes in fear, remember that God is real and present. See your problems from God's perspective, not only from their size, and be brave even when others discourage you.
exp.13:10:
This verse tells how Jonathan and his armor-bearer showed themselves to the Philistine outpost. The Philistines saw them and mocked, saying that the Hebrews were coming out of the holes where they had hidden themselves. "Garrison" in the verse means a group of soldiers standing guard over a place. "Armor-bearer" refers to the young man who carried the warrior's weapons.

Here the narrator speaks, and then the Philistines. Jonathan had proposed a sign: if the enemy invited them to come up, it would be a sign that God was giving them the victory. The Philistines, confident and proud, did not realize they were walking into that very sign.

For today: sometimes others look down on us or underestimate us. Instead of being discouraged, we can take steps of faith and obedience, trusting that God can act even when we seem few or weak.
exp.2:11:
God says he will carry out against Eli everything he had already announced about his family. "I will bring it about" means to set in motion, to make it happen. The phrase "when I begin, I will also end" means that God will both start and finish: he will not leave his word half done.

The LORD speaks, calling the young Samuel at night in the sanctuary at Shiloh. Earlier, a man of God had already warned Eli (1 Samuel 2:27-36). Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, abused their priestly office, and Eli did not correct them firmly. Now God confirms the judgment through Samuel.

For today: God takes correction and responsibility seriously, especially for those who lead others. If something in your home, church, or work needs to be corrected, do not put it off. And if God speaks to you through his Word, respond with Samuel's attitude: "Speak, for your servant is listening."
exp.29:7:
David asks God whether he should pursue the band that carried off the families of his people. "Consulted" means he asked for direction. "Troop" is a group of raiders, "overtake" means catching up with them to fight, and "recover" means he would rescue what had been taken. God answers clearly: pursue, you will overtake them, and you will recover everything.

David speaks after the Amalekites burned Ziklag and carried off the women and children as captives. His men, filled with grief, were talking about stoning him. He strengthened himself in the Lord and asked the priest Abiathar for the ephod, which was a means of seeking God's guidance.

When you are distressed or under pressure, do not act on impulse alone. Seek God first in prayer and in His Word, and then take the steps He shows you with confidence.
exp.24:1:
This verse introduces a man from Maon who had his lands and livestock in Carmel. He was very wealthy: he had three thousand sheep and a thousand goats. "Possessions" here means his property and his livestock business. "Shearing" means cutting the wool from the sheep, and at that very moment he was doing it.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who introduces a new character. Samuel has just died, and David is running from Saul in the wilderness. This Carmel is a town in the south of Judah, not the mountain in the north. The next verse will reveal that this rich man is named Nabal. Sheep-shearing was usually a time of celebration and abundance.

For today: having wealth says nothing about a person's heart. What matters is how we use it. Let us ask God for a generous and humble heart, one that serves others instead of boasting.
exp.18:13:
This verse tells how Saul sent his messengers to arrest David, but Michal, David's wife, answered them that he was sick. She said this to buy time.

Michal is Saul's daughter and David's wife. Saul wanted to kill David out of jealousy. She had helped him escape through a window and put a statue in the bed to deceive the soldiers. That lie gave David an advantage to flee. The Bible only tells what happened; it does not say whether God approved of the deception. Some readers see courage here, others a questionable method.

For today: when loving and protecting someone costs us something, God calls us to have courage. But let us always seek to act with wisdom and truth, trusting that He cares for his own.
exp.29:11:
This verse tells of a hungry young Egyptian who was given a piece of fig cake and two clusters of raisins. When he ate, he regained his strength and was revived, because he had gone three days and three nights without eating or drinking. The "piece of a cake of figs" and the "two clusters of raisins" were food for the weary, and his being revived means that his strength came back to him.

This is a narrative account. David was pursuing the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families. On the way, his men found this servant abandoned because he was sick. David first cared for him, and afterward he himself gave them the clue to find the attackers.

For today: compassion is not a waste of time. Even in haste and grief, David stopped to help a needy stranger, and that kindness became a doorway to help. Let us care for those who suffer near us.
exp.24:38:
David says that when he heard Nabal was dead, he praised God. He recognized that the Lord had taken up his cause when Nabal insulted him, and had kept him from doing evil with his own hand. The word "reproach" in the verse means an insult or offense, and "returned" means paid back, and "wickedness" is the evil Nabal had done. Then David sent word asking Abigail to become his wife.

David is the one speaking. Nabal, a rich and hard man, refused him help and humiliated him. David was going to take revenge with violence, but Abigail calmed him with good sense. Ten days later Nabal died, and David saw in it the hand of God. The text tells the details of his marriage plainly, without giving further explanation.

For today: when someone wrongs you, do not take revenge. Leave your hurt in God's hands, for he is just, and trust that he cares for you and keeps you from doing something you would regret.
exp.24:21:
David makes a very strong oath: he asks that God punish his enemies, and even more, if he leaves alive by morning any male of Nabal's household. The crude expression of that time for "male" is rendered in the verse your reader sees as "any that pisseth against the wall," which is an old and blunt way of saying a male person. Many understand that "the enemies of David" is a way of not naming himself, though this is not entirely certain.

David speaks in anger. Nabal, a rich man, refused to give him provisions and insulted him, even though David and his men had protected his flocks. Because of this, David sets out with four hundred men to take revenge. Abigail, Nabal's wife, goes to meet him to stop him.

Today: when you are hurt or angry, do not make decisions or impulsive promises. Stop, seek wise counsel, and listen to the person God puts in your path, as David listened to Abigail. In this way you will avoid harm that you would later regret.
exp.0:19:
This verse tells us that Hannah became pregnant and, when the time had come, gave birth to a son. She named him Samuel and explained the reason: "Because I have asked him of the Lord." Where the old wording speaks of the time having come around, the verse says "when the time was come about."

Hannah had suffered for years from the sadness of having no children. At the temple in Shiloh, with a broken heart, she asked God for a son, and the priest Eli sent her away with a blessing. The text says that God "remembered her." Here it is the narrator who speaks, and he emphasizes that the child's name recalls the answered prayer. Some understand that the name sounds like the word for "heard," while scholars explain it in different ways.

Today we can do what Hannah did: bring our requests to God with sincerity, and when we receive an answer, remember it and give thanks for it in a concrete way.
exp.19:0:
David fled from Naioth in Ramah and came to find Jonathan. He asks him three questions in a row: what he has done, what his fault is, and what his sin is, since Jonathan's father is trying to kill him. The word "fault" here means a guilt or wrong, and the verse uses it in the same way the King James does.

David is speaking, and he has already been anointed as the future king. King Saul, out of jealousy, was pursuing him. Shortly before this, David had been with the prophet Samuel in Ramah. Jonathan, Saul's son, was his faithful friend. David feels confused and innocent, and he looks for someone he can trust.

Today, when someone attacks us without reason or we feel misunderstood, we are not alone. We can seek a wise and trustworthy friend to unburden ourselves and ask for counsel, and we can also bring our distress to God with sincerity, as David did.
exp.21:19:
Of all those who died at Nob, this verse says that only one of the sons of the priest Ahimelech survived. His name was Abiathar. He escaped the massacre and went to find David.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. King Saul, consumed by jealousy and suspicion, had ordered the priests killed because Ahimelech had helped David. Doeg the Edomite carried out that terrible command. Abiathar was left as the only survivor of that family, and he sought refuge with David, whom Saul was pursuing.

Even in the midst of the greatest injustice and grief, God can preserve someone. When everything seems lost, we can seek refuge with those who follow God, and we do not have to carry our sorrow alone.
exp.22:25:
This verse describes a very tense chase. Saul went along one side of the mountain and David with his men along the other. David hurried to escape from Saul. But Saul and his men were closing in around him, surrounding David and his men to catch them.

It is part of the narrative, not a speech. Saul, the king, was pursuing David out of jealousy, even though David had done him no wrong. David was in the wilderness of Maon, fleeing. Just when it seemed there was no way out, a messenger arrived with news of a Philistine attack, and Saul had to leave.

For today: sometimes we feel surrounded, with no way out. This passage reminds us that God can act in unexpected ways, at just the right moment. We can keep doing what is right and trust that He cares for us, even when we cannot see how.
exp.16:43:
Goliath tells David to come closer, because he is going to leave his dead body for the birds of the air and the beasts of the field to eat. It is a very harsh threat.

Goliath is the Philistine giant who defied the army of Israel. Seeing David, young, good-looking, and without weapons of war, he despised him and even cursed him in the name of his gods. He mocked because he trusted in his strength and his armor. David, in contrast, answers that he comes in the name of the Lord.

For today: do not let yourself be intimidated by words of mockery or threats that seem bigger than you. When you face something difficult, do what is right and trust in God, not only in your own strength or in what others think of you.
exp.3:20:
Here the wife of Phinehas, already dying after giving birth, names the boy Ichabod. She says: "The glory is departed from Israel." The reason she gives is that the ark of God was taken by the Philistines, and that her father-in-law Eli and her husband Phinehas had died.

She speaks in the midst of enormous grief. Israel had lost a battle, and the bad news reached her at the very moment of childbirth. The name Ichabod is commonly understood to mean "where is the glory?" For her, the capture of the ark meant that the presence of God was departing.

For today: the presence of God is not reduced to objects or rituals. Let us seek God with a sincere heart, and not only with religious customs, and remember that He remains faithful even in our darkest hours.
exp.0:7:
Elkanah notices that his wife Hannah is weeping and will not eat. He asks her four questions: why she is weeping, why she is not eating, why her heart is grieved, and whether he himself is not worth more to her than ten sons. "Barren" means she could not have children; "rival" is the other wife, Peninnah.

The speaker is Elkanah, Hannah's husband, during the yearly trip to Shiloh to worship. Peninnah, who did have children, provoked Hannah and made her suffer. Elkanah wants to comfort her with love, though he does not fully grasp the depth of her pain. His question shows affection, but also its limits.

For today: when someone suffers, listening patiently is worth more than giving quick answers. And if you are in pain, as Hannah was, you can bring your honest distress to God, who understands what others cannot see.
exp.20:14:
King Achish speaks here with anger and sarcasm. He asks whether he is short of madmen in his house, that they had to bring him one more. The phrase "lack of" in the sense of "do I need" is what he means, and "play the mad man" refers to acting out madness. With this he rejects the idea that David should come into his house.

David was fleeing from King Saul and arrived at Gath, a Philistine city, where they recognized that he was the famous Israelite warrior. Fearing for his life, he pretended to be mad. Achish, convinced, rebukes his servants and sends David away. Psalm 34 is connected to this episode according to its title, and there David gives thanks to God for rescuing him.

For today: God can take care of us even when we act out of fear and with very human means. We do not have to depend on our own cleverness. We can ask him for help with sincerity, thank him for his deliverance, and keep trusting that he sustains us.
exp.23:5:
This verse says that David felt a strong sense of remorse. The phrase "his heart smote him" means that his conscience troubled him. The "skirt" is the edge of Saul's robe, which David secretly cut off.

David and his men were hiding in a cave, fleeing from Saul, who wanted to kill him. Saul went in there without knowing it. David's men urged him to take advantage of the opportunity and finish off his enemy. David only cut off a piece of the robe, but even that weighed on him, because Saul was the king anointed by God. Immediately David stopped his men.

For today: let us not ignore the voice of conscience, even in faults that seem small. And when someone wounds us, let us trust that God will do justice, without taking revenge with our own hands.
exp.14:12:
Samuel arrives where Saul is, and Saul greets him with a blessing: "Blessed be thou of the Lord." Right away he states with confidence: "I have performed the commandment of the Lord." That is, he says he fully obeyed what God commanded him. "Then came" means "arrived at that time."

Saul speaks here, the first king of Israel. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but Saul and the people kept the best of the livestock and their king. Samuel already knew that Saul had failed, since Saul had spent the night crying out to God. Saul comes forward with a declaration of obedience, and the next verse contradicts it with the bleating of the sheep.

For today: it is easy to tell ourselves, or to tell others, that we obey God while we keep excuses or things He did not ask for. It is wise to ask Him to examine our hearts and to obey Him completely, not only in what is convenient for us.
exp.24:39:
The explanation says that David's servants went to Abigail, who was at Carmel, and delivered their master's message: David wanted to marry her. The word for the servants here means the servants or messengers. The phrase about taking her as his wife means asking her to marry him.

Abigail had been the wife of Nabal, a foolish man who insulted David and treated him with contempt. She stepped in with wisdom and kept David from shedding blood. Now Nabal has died, and David, who recognizes that God brought about justice, proposes marriage to her. In that period it was common for leaders to have several wives; the Bible records this, but does not necessarily approve of it.

For today: God sees those who act with prudence and humility in the midst of unjust situations. Trust that He cares for you and can open new doors, even after difficult times.
exp.12:13:
Samuel tells Saul that his kingdom will not last. God has already sought out a man after his own heart, meaning someone who seeks Him and remains faithful to Him, and has chosen him to be the leader of his people. The reason is that Saul did not keep what God commanded him. The word "But" in this verse is what links this statement to what came before, and "shall not continue" means that his family line would not go on ruling.

Samuel speaks in Gilgal. Saul, frightened by the Philistines and seeing that Samuel was delayed, offered the burnt offering himself, something that was not his place to do. Samuel rebukes him for acting out of fear and not obeying. Many believe this refers to David, although the verse does not name him here.

For today: when we feel pressure or fear, it is tempting to take shortcuts and justify ourselves. God values an obedient and trusting heart more than hurried solutions. We can wait on Him and obey Him even when it costs us.
exp.14:26:
As Samuel turned to leave, someone caught hold of the hem of his robe, and it tore. The hem is the edge of the garment, and the robe is the cloak. The text does not say who grabbed it, but most readers understand that it was Saul, trying to stop Samuel.

Samuel had just told Saul that God had rejected him as king because he did not obey God's word. Saul was begging Samuel to come back with him. Right away, Samuel uses the torn robe as a sign: in the same way, God was tearing the kingdom out of Saul's hands.

For today: it is not enough to grieve once we already see the consequences. It is better to obey God in time and with sincerity. If we have failed, let us come to Him with humility and without excuses, not only out of fear of losing something.
exp.26:2:
David went to live with Achish, king of Gath, one of the Philistine rulers. He did not go alone: he took his men, each one with his household, and also his two wives, Ahinoam of Jezreel and Abigail, Nabal's widow, from Carmel.

The narrator is describing what happened after David came to believe that Saul would eventually kill him. That is why he chose to take refuge in Philistine territory, where Saul would stop pursuing him. Some see here a prudent decision, and others a lack of trust in God. The text does not make this clear.

When fear presses on us, it is easy to look for quick ways out. We can ask God for wisdom before we decide, and remember that He also cares for our families in uncertain times.
exp.13:40:
Saul asks God to show the truth, and the lot falls on him and his son Jonathan, while the people are set free. "Give a perfect lot" is a difficult phrase: the Hebrew can be understood as "show what is right" or "give a clear answer." Other translations add that Saul was asking God to answer with exactness.

Saul had made a hasty oath: no one was to eat that day, on pain of death. God did not answer, and Saul wanted to discover who had failed. Jonathan, not knowing about the oath, had tasted a little honey. Scholars debate how this lot was carried out, and the text does not explain it.

For today: before making promises or declaring strong decisions, let us think calmly. A vow spoken in haste can hurt those we love most.
exp.29:8:
This verse tells that David set out at once, together with his six hundred men, to pursue the Amalekites who had burned Ziklag and carried off their families. They came to the brook Besor, a stream that can carry a great deal of water, and there some of the men stayed behind. The word "went" in the verse means "departed" or "set out."

The narrator describes what happened just after God answered David through the ephod, the priestly garment used to inquire of the Lord. David was distressed, for even his own people were speaking of stoning him. God promised him that he would overtake the enemies. The text does not say why some stayed behind, but the next verse makes clear that they were too exhausted.

For today: when God gives us clear guidance, it is good to obey without delay. We should also treat with understanding those who, because of weariness, cannot keep the same pace.
exp.24:0:
This verse tells us that Samuel died. All of Israel gathered together, mourned him, and buried him at his house in Ramah, his hometown. After that, David got up and went down to the wilderness of Paran. The sentence explaining the old word is removed, since the reader's verse does not contain it.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Samuel had been a prophet and a judge, and he was the one who anointed David as the future king. His death marks the end of an era. David was still running from King Saul, which is why he sought refuge in the wilderness. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact location of Paran, but it was an arid region in the south.

For today: when someone who guided us dies, it is natural to grieve. But life goes on and God keeps working. We can honor that person and, even in sadness, take the next step with faith.
exp.5:15:
This verse says that the five lords of the Philistines saw what happened at Beth-shemesh: the cart with the ark, the sacrifice of the cows, and the offering. After they saw it, they returned to Ekron that same day. "Lords" means the rulers or chiefs of the Philistine cities. "Whole burnt offering" was an offering burned completely for God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark and suffered plagues, so they decided to return it with an offering of gold. The lords followed the cart to Beth-shemesh to see what would happen. The text does not explain what they thought when they went back, so it is best not to invent their motives. It does show that they witnessed the ark arrive at its place.

For today: when we recognize that we have acted wrongly toward God or toward others, feeling fear or unease is not enough. It is good to take concrete steps to make things right, to return what is owed, and to approach God with reverence.
exp.13:8:
Jonathan tells his armor-bearer how they will recognize what God wants them to do. If the Philistines call out to them, "Wait until we come to you," then they will stand still in their place and will not go up to them.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, is speaking during the war against the Philistines. He and his armor-bearer approach the enemy outpost alone. Jonathan does not want to act on impulse but proposes a sign: the Philistines' reaction would show whether God is giving them the victory. If the enemies come down, they will wait; if they invite them to come up, they will go.

For today: before taking an important step, we can pray and calmly look for clear signs of God's guidance, without rushing ahead. It is also wise to know how to wait when doors do not open.
exp.27:11:
It says that when the woman saw Samuel, she cried out with a loud voice. Then she spoke to Saul and addressed him. "She cried with a loud voice" means she shouted out strongly, out of fright or surprise.

Saul, king of Israel, was afraid before the Philistine army. God was no longer answering him, so he went in disguise to look for a woman who consulted the dead, something the law of God forbade. She was frightened because the appearance was different from what she expected. Scholars disagree about whether it was truly Samuel or something else, but the text presents it as Samuel.

For today: when we feel fear and it seems that God is silent, let us not look for answers in forbidden paths. Rather, let us return to Him with humility, pray, and listen to His Word, even when the answer is slow in coming.
exp.15:22:
It says that when the evil spirit sent by God came upon Saul, David would take the harp and play it with his hand. Then Saul would calm down, feel better, and the evil spirit would depart from him. The word "played" is the verb used for making music on an instrument.

It is the narrator who tells this. Shortly before, the Spirit of the Lord had departed from Saul, and an evil spirit troubled him. His servants suggested finding a skilled musician, and so David came to him, the one who would later become king. How the evil spirit could be understood as coming "from God" is explained in several ways; the text gives no further detail.

For today: music and humble service can bring relief to someone who is suffering. Think of someone who is distressed and offer them your company, a song, or a simple prayer. Sometimes God uses small acts to bring rest.
exp.5:7:
The explanation says that the Philistines were to place the ark of the Lord on a new cart. Beside it, in a box, they would put the "jewels of gold," that is, gold objects, as a trespass offering, meaning a payment to make up for the offense. Then they were to let the cart go on its own.

The Philistine priests and diviners speak here. The ark had been among them for seven months and had brought them plagues. They wanted to return it and find out whether those troubles came from God or were just chance. The cows, which had never worn a yoke and had calves, would go against their nature if they went toward Israel. It was a pagan test, not a method that God had commanded.

Today we can learn that when we recognize we have offended God, gifts or rituals are not enough. God looks for a humble heart that surrenders and obeys, not an attempt to fix things on our own.
exp.29:17:
The explanation says that David rescued everything the Amalekites had taken, including his two wives, Ahinoam and Abigail.

The verse itself says David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away, and rescued his two wives. Because the reader sees that wording, the sentence about the two words and what they mean is removed, since "rescued" and "recovered" already appear in the verse above.

The narrator then tells what happened at Ziklag. The Amalekites burned the city and carried off the families of David and his men. David was deeply distressed, since his own men were talking about stoning him. Even so, he strengthened himself in the Lord, asked God what to do, and set out after the enemy. God assured him that he would recover everything.

For today: when everything seems lost, do not freeze or give in to despair. Seek God first in prayer, ask for direction, and then take the steps He shows you. He can restore what seemed to be lost.
exp.29:28:
He says David sent part of the spoil to the people of Rachal, to the cities of the Jerahmeelites, and to the cities of the Kenites. The word "Á" is the old way of writing "a." These names are peoples and regions in the south of Judah, and they are part of a longer list of places that received gifts.

The author of the book tells what David did after defeating the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families. David recovered everything and received a great deal of spoil. Some of his men did not want to share it, but David said it should be divided among everyone. Then he sent gifts to the friends who had helped him while he was fleeing from Saul. We do not know exactly where Rachal was.

Today we can learn to be thankful and generous. When God gives us something good, it is not only for us. We can remember those who supported us in hard times and share with them.
exp.24:16:
A servant tells Abigail that a great danger is coming. He asks her to think carefully and decide what to do, because a punishment has already been determined against Nabal and all his household. The phrase "evil is determined against our master" means that the disaster has already been decided and is on its way. And "a man cannot speak to him" means that Nabal is so stubborn and so ill-tempered that no one can reason with him.

It is one of Nabal's young servants who speaks. Nabal had insulted David's men, who earlier had protected his flocks. David, angry, was coming with armed men. The servant does not dare to speak to Nabal, so he goes to Abigail, known for her good judgment.

For today: when you see a serious problem, do not stay silent or wait for it to change on its own. Humbly seek out the wise person who can act with calm, and do what is within your power to prevent the harm.
exp.29:2:
It says that David and his men returned to Ziklag and found the city burned. Their wives, their sons and their daughters were no longer there: they had been taken away as prisoners. The old spellings with accents are not needed here. Where the explanation refers to the phrase meaning the city had been burned with fire, that is the same as saying it was set on fire.

This is the narrator of the book speaking. David was living among the Philistines, and while he and his men were away, the Amalekites attacked Ziklag. The text makes clear that they killed no one, but carried off the people. David arrived on the third day and found this total loss, at a moment that was already very hard for him.

For today: when a loss seems total, it is natural to weep and to feel the blow. But one should not remain alone in the grief. In verse 6 of this same chapter, David strengthens himself in the Lord. He seeks God before deciding what to do.
exp.19:21:
It says that Jonathan will use a signal with arrows. If he calls out to the young man, "The arrows are beyond you," it will mean that David must leave, because the Lord is sending him away. The word "arrows" refers to the weapons shot from a bow, and "young man" means a young servant. "Beyond" means farther away, ahead.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, is speaking to his friend David. Saul wanted to kill David, and Jonathan had promised to find out his father's intentions. Since they could not speak openly, they agreed on a secret signal during the feast of the new moon. Jonathan recognizes that, if David must flee, that escape is under God's direction.

For today: sometimes God calls us to leave a place that is no longer safe, even when it hurts. We can accept such changes in faith, trusting that He cares for us, and lean on faithful friends who tell us the truth with love.
exp.15:21:
Here Saul sends a message to Jesse, David's father. He politely asks that David be allowed to stay in his service. He says David has "found favor in my sight," meaning that he likes him and holds him in high regard. The phrase "sent to Jesse" simply means that he sent a message.

Here King Saul is speaking. His spirit was tormented by an evil spirit, and his servants had recommended David to play the harp. David arrived with a gift from his father, and Saul valued him greatly. It is striking that God had already anointed David in secret, and now he enters the palace through a humble door: serving.

For today: God often prepares people in small places and through service. Do with a good attitude what is at hand today, for there God may be shaping your character.
exp.2:9:
It says that God came and stood beside Samuel and called him by name twice, as before. The word "stood" in the verse is the same as "stood up" in the explanation. This time Samuel answered as Eli had taught him: "Speak, for your servant hears." That is, he was ready to listen and obey.

Samuel was a boy who served in the sanctuary under the priest Eli. In those days, the word of God was rare. Samuel did not yet know the voice of the Lord, so Eli, already old, understood that it was God and gave him the right instruction. Later God would give him a hard message about Eli's house.

For today: before asking God for anything, learn to be quiet and to listen. Open the Bible with a willing heart and say: "Speak, Lord, for your servant hears."
exp.24:7:
Nabal can ask his own servants, and they will confirm that David and his men behaved well. For this reason David asks that his messengers be welcomed. The phrase "we come in a good day" refers to a day of feasting. He asks that Nabal give whatever comes to his hand, meaning whatever he has available. David calls himself Nabal's son out of courtesy.

David speaks through his young messengers. He and his men had been living in the wilderness, and they had protected Nabal's shepherds. Now it was time for sheep-shearing, a season of plenty, and David asked for a sign of gratitude. Nabal answers with contempt, as will soon be seen.

For today: when you have done good, ask with respect and without demanding. And when someone asks you humbly, remember what you have received and respond with gratitude and generosity, not with pride.
exp.7:15:
Here the text says that the king will take for himself the workers and servants of the people, their best young men, and their donkeys, to use in the king's labor. The people who worked in the households are the ones it describes as servants, and the strong young men are the ones it calls the young men. Donkeys were very valuable beasts of burden.

Samuel speaks to the people of Israel, who had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. God told him to warn them plainly about what it would cost. Samuel describes how a human king, with so much power, would demand much from them. Many understand this as a serious warning and not as a simple list of rules.

For today: before we trust someone or something to give us security, let us think about what it will ask of us in return. Let us place our trust first in God, who serves his people with love.
exp.23:17:
Saul says to David: "You are more righteous than I." He recognizes that David treated him well, while he had treated David badly. The word "paid" here means "returned" or "dealt with." And "á" is an old way of writing "a."
