Wait: the instructions say to delete or rewrite comments about archaic words for words that appear in the verse above. The verse contains "shewed," "dealt well," "thine hand," and "killedst." The sentence about "paid" and "á" should be rewritten or removed. Here is the corrected translation:

King Saul speaks. For a long time he had been pursuing David in order to kill him. In a cave, David had the chance to kill him, but he only cut off a piece of his robe and spared his life. When David shows it to him and speaks to him with respect, Saul weeps and admits his wrong. Even so, the Bible later shows that his heart did not change completely.

Today we can learn to respond well when someone treats us badly, leaving God to be the judge. It also invites us to humbly acknowledge our faults, without excuses, and to seek a true change, not just words or tears of the moment.
exp.18:6:
Jonathan called David and told him all that he had said to Saul. Then Jonathan himself brought David to Saul, and David was back in the king's service as before. "Shewed" means "told," and "brought" means that he took him there in person.

Saul had wanted to kill David out of jealousy. Jonathan, Saul's son and David's loyal friend, spoke up for David before his father and reminded him that David had risked his life against the Philistine. Saul promised with an oath that he would not kill him. This verse shows the result of that mediation. As we see later, the peace did not last, and Saul again tried to harm him.

Today we can learn from Jonathan to be peacemakers. When there is conflict between people, God sometimes calls us to speak with truth and respect, without taking sides out of resentment. Even so, we do not control the hearts of others, so we do what is right and trust God.
exp.22:27:
This verse tells how Saul stopped pursuing David and went to fight against the Philistines. For this reason, the place was given the name Sela-hammahlekoth. That name is usually translated as "Rock of Separation" or "Rock of Division," although some understand it in another way.

The one who narrates is the author of the book. Saul had David nearly surrounded in the wilderness of Maon, but a messenger called him away because the Philistines were raiding the land. David was saved just in time. The text does not say that David planned this; the reader understands that God watched over him in the midst of danger.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, remember that God can act at exactly the right moment and by unexpected means. Trust Him, faithfully do what is yours to do, and thank Him when He delivers you.
exp.13:9:
Jonathan tells his young armor-bearer that if the Philistines say, "Come up to us," then they will go up. They will take this as the sign that the Lord has handed them over to Israel, that is, that God will give them the victory. In the verse, "come up" is the word for "go up," and "delivered" means "given into our hand."

Jonathan, son of King Saul, speaks with his young assistant in front of a Philistine outpost. Israel was at a disadvantage and afraid. Jonathan does not act recklessly: he asks for a clear sign before taking the step. He trusts that God can save by few or by many, as he says in the verse just before this passage.

For today: before making a difficult decision, pray and place your trust in God. Seek his direction humbly, and then take the step with courage when you see the door open.
exp.1:29:
God says he had promised that Eli's family would serve before him as priests forever. But now he takes that promise back, saying, "Be it far from me." The principle is clear: God honors those who honor him, and those who despise him will be lightly esteemed.

A prophet, sent by God, speaks to Eli the priest. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing the offerings, and Eli did not correct them firmly. So God announces judgment on his house. The promise was real, but it depended on faithfulness.

For today: honoring God is not only saying so, but obeying him in everyday life. We can ask ourselves whether in some things we are putting people, or our own comfort, above him.
exp.13:36:
Saul asks God whether he should pursue the Philistines and whether God will hand them over to Israel. But God does not answer him that day. "Asked counsel" means that he sought direction, and "did not answer him" refers to the silence that followed.

Saul speaks after a great victory, when the army was hungry and exhausted. Earlier, he had made a hasty vow that no one should eat until evening. Jonathan, his son, did not know of it and ate some honey. The text suggests that God's silence led Saul to look for what had gone wrong. The passage does not explain everything in detail, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

When God is silent, it is wise to pause and examine our decisions, words, and promises with humility. Sometimes silence is an invitation to set something right, though we will not always know the reason.
exp.10:1:
Nahash, king of the Ammonites, tells the men of Jabesh that he will make a treaty with them only if each one agrees to have his right eye gouged out. He says that this will bring a public shame, a humiliation, upon all of Israel.

The people of Jabesh Gilead were surrounded by the Ammonite army, and they offered to surrender and serve him. Nahash was not seeking peace, but cruelly intended to humiliate the whole people of Israel. For this reason the elders ask for seven days to look for help. This happens before Saul rescues them.

For today: there are people who offer agreements that in reality aim to harm and humiliate. Before accepting any deal, it is wise to examine their intentions and to seek help from others, as the elders of Jabesh did. God invites us to seek counsel and support within the community.
exp.27:2:
This verse reminds us that Samuel, the prophet and judge of Israel, had already died. All the people mourned him, and they buried him in Ramah, his city. It also says that Saul had driven out of the land those who called up the dead, and those who claimed to know the future by forbidden means.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Before he tells us that Saul, frightened by the Philistine army, would seek out a woman who consults spirits, he makes two things clear: Samuel was no longer there to guide him, and Saul himself had banned these practices, which God's law condemned. This shows a contradiction in his heart.

For today: when fear comes, it is easy to set aside what we say we believe. Let us seek God in prayer and in his Word, and not take shortcuts that he has forbidden.
exp.6:7:
The Israelites ask Samuel to keep praying to the LORD for them, so that God will rescue them from the power of the Philistines. "Cease not to cry" means "do not stop asking earnestly," and the word "save" in the verse means "protect" or "rescue."

The people have gathered at Mizpah. They have just confessed their sin through fasting and by pouring out water before God (its exact meaning is not explained in the text). When they learned that the Philistines were coming to attack them, they were afraid and turned to Samuel as their intercessor. God then answered with a thunder that threw the enemy into confusion.

For today: when you are afraid, begin by returning to God with humility and sincerity. Ask Him for help, and also let other believers pray with you and for you.
exp.5:8:
It says the Philistines would make a test. If the cows carried the ark along the road toward Beth-shemesh, which was Israelite territory, then the God of Israel had caused them that great disaster. If they did not head that way, they would know that it was not God's hand that punished them, but a chance event, a mere coincidence.

The speakers are the priests and diviners of the Philistines. They had captured the ark and were suffering plagues. They wanted to know whether the evil came from the God of Israel. They chose cows with calves, which would naturally want to return to their young. If even so the cows turned away from them and kept straight on, it would be a clear sign.

Today we can learn not to attribute everything to luck. Even those who doubt can be led to recognize God. Let us ask him for open eyes to see his hand, and for humility to answer him.
exp.8:0:
This verse introduces Kish, a man from the tribe of Benjamin. He is called "a mighty man of power," a phrase that can mean brave, but also influential or of good standing. His ancestors are named back to Abiel, Zeror, Bechorath and Aphiah, as was customary to show a person's lineage.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. After the story of Samuel and the people's request for a king, the Bible begins to introduce the man who will become Israel's first king. It does not yet speak of Saul, but of his father and his family. This prepares the account that follows.

God often begins important things in humble places, within an ordinary family, without anyone noticing. Today we can remember that our home and our daily life also matter to God, even when they seem small.
exp.30:8:
This verse tells what the Philistines did with Saul after his death. They cut off his head and took his armor. Then they sent messengers throughout their territory to announce the news in the temples of their idols and among the people.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the events without commenting on them. Israel had just lost the battle on Mount Gilboa, and Saul and his sons had died. The Philistines wanted to celebrate their victory and credit it to their gods. The verses that follow show that the armor was placed in the temple of Ashtoreth and that the body was hung on a wall.

For today: when the world celebrates a defeat or mocks something we love, let us remember that the story does not end there. God is still at work, and it is better to live faithfully than to meet an end like Saul's.
exp.17:10:
He says that Saul threw his spear at David, thinking to himself that he would pin him to the wall. But David stepped aside, and this happened twice. The verse's word for the spear hitting its mark is not used here; the spear is simply thrown.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. David was playing the harp to soothe Saul, who was tormented by a harmful spirit that came from God. Scholars explain this phrase in several ways, and the text gives no further detail. Saul was already jealous of David because the people praised him. Then the account says that Saul was afraid of him, because God was with David.

For today: unaddressed jealousy can grow until it turns into violence. If you feel envy, bring it to God quickly in prayer and rejoice in the success of others, before it harms you and those around you.
exp.16:0:
The Philistines gathered their troops to fight against Israel. They came together at Shochoh, a town that belonged to the tribe of Judah, and camped between Shochoh and Azekah, in a place called Ephes-dammim. The phrase "pitched their camp" means they set up their military encampment.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, setting the scene before the famous story of David and Goliath. The Philistines were an enemy people of Israel, and they had moved into the territory of Judah. The next verse shows that Saul and his army went out to face them, and that the two sides ended up facing each other, separated by a valley.

For today: big problems sometimes arrive all at once and settle in close to us. Before we look at the size of the conflict, we can remember that God remains faithful and can give us courage to face it, as he will do with David.
exp.27:24:
She set the food before Saul and his servants, and after they ate, they got up and left that very night. "Servants" here means attendants or companions, and "as soon as" can be read as "right after."

The narrator describes the end of a very dark night. Saul, king of Israel, was afraid of the Philistines, and God did not answer him. So he sought out a medium, something God's law forbade. She told him of his defeat, and Saul collapsed, weak and without having eaten all day. The woman served him a meal with kindness, and then he set out toward his fate.

When we turn away from God, we can end up looking for answers in the wrong places, and those answers do not bring peace. Today we can come to God with sincerity, in prayer and in his Word, before the night of despair arrives.
exp.13:47:
This verse says that Saul gathered an army, defeated the Amalekites, and rescued Israel from those who plundered them. The word "smote" means that he defeated them in battle. The word "delivered" means that he saved or rescued them. "Them that spoiled them" refers to the enemy peoples who attacked and plundered Israel.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. He summarizes Saul's military victories at the beginning of his reign, before introducing his family and his general Abner. He shows that God used Saul to give protection to the people. Later, the story reveals that Saul failed to obey God, and so this success does not tell the whole of his story.

For today: achievements and strength do not replace obedience. We can thank God for what He allows us to accomplish, but it is wise to keep asking ourselves whether we do it with a heart that is faithful to Him.
exp.16:31:
David tells King Saul that no one should lose heart because of the giant Goliath. The phrase "let no man's heart fail" means that no one should lose courage or nerve. David offers himself as the king's "thy servant," that is, as his attendant, and says that he himself will go and fight against this Philistine.

David speaks after hearing that Goliath was defying the army of Israel and that everyone was afraid. He had asked several soldiers and was brought before Saul. David was young, and he had come to the camp to visit his brothers. His courage comes from the fact that Goliath was defying the people of the living God.

Today, when others are paralyzed by fear before a great problem, we can take a step of faith. It is not a matter of trusting our own strength, but of trusting that God is with us. Your courage can encourage others.
exp.19:39:
Jonathan hands his equipment (bow, arrows, and what he was carrying) to his young attendant. He tells him to go and carry them back to the city. The word "lad" here means a young servant, and "artillery" refers to his archery gear.

Jonathan and David had agreed on a signal with the arrows to learn whether Saul meant to kill David. He had already given it, and only the two of them understood its meaning. Jonathan sends the lad away so that he can say farewell to his friend in private, without witnesses. What follows is a very emotional farewell, with tears and a covenant before God.

There are moments when love and loyalty call for privacy and courage. Jonathan cared for his friend with prudence: he protected the secret and gave him time to truly say goodbye. Today we can do the same: guard the trust of someone who is suffering, and be present in difficult moments.
exp.19:18:
Jonathan tells David to stay hidden for three days. After that, David must go down and return to the place where he hid before, at the time of the matter in hand, that is, the earlier occasion when this business took place. There he will wait beside the stone Ezel. Going down means leaving his hiding place. Some scholars debate the exact meaning of "the time of the matter in hand," so it is wise to read it with caution.

Jonathan speaks with David, whom he loves as his own soul. Saul, Jonathan's father, seeks to kill David. The feast of the new moon is near, and Jonathan will watch how his father reacts. For this reason he arranges a secret signal with arrows to warn David if there is danger.

For today: when you face an uncertain situation, do not act on impulse. Seek counsel from someone faithful, make a careful plan, and wait patiently, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.29:0:
This verse tells that David and his men returned to Ziklag after three days of travel. They found that the Amalekites had invaded the south and burned the city with fire.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David had been living in Ziklag, a city that the Philistine king Achish had given him while he was fleeing from Saul. David's men had gone off with the Philistine army, and the city was left without defense. The following verses explain that the women and children were taken captive, and that no one was killed.

For today: sometimes we come home and find that we have lost everything all at once. In those moments we are not alone. The chapter shows that David, though deeply distressed, ended up seeking strength in God. When loss comes, bring it to Him before deciding what to do.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that the Spirit of God would come upon Saul with power, that he would prophesy together with a group of prophets, and that he would be turned into another man. The word "come upon" here means to come on someone with force. "Prophesy" probably refers to praising or speaking under the inspiration of God. "Turned" means changed.

Samuel is speaking to Saul after anointing him as the first king of Israel. He gives him several signs to confirm that God had chosen him. This is one of them. Saul was going to need an inner change to take on such a great responsibility, and God himself was promising it. It is not known exactly what that change was like, but the text shows that it came from God.

For today: when God calls us to something that feels bigger than us, it does not depend only on our own strength. We can ask him for his Spirit, who gives us courage, character, and direction to carry it out.
exp.14:2:
Here God, through the prophet Samuel, orders Saul to attack the Amalekites and destroy everything they have, sparing no one: people and animals alike. Words like "smite" mean to strike down or attack; "spare" means to hold back from harming; and the phrase about infants and sucklings refers to the youngest children, who are still nursing.

Samuel speaks in God's name. The reason given is that Amalek attacked Israel when it came out of Egypt, a tired and defenseless people (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). It is a very harsh text. Scholars understand it in several ways: as God's judgment on a hostile people, or as exaggerated language typical of ancient warfare. Even so, it remains difficult, and it is fair to acknowledge that.

For today: do not use this passage to justify violence. Instead, learn to obey God fully, without leaving things half done, and trust that He is just even when we do not understand everything.
exp.22:6:
It was reported to Saul that David had arrived at Keilah. Saul thought God himself had handed David over to him, because David was shut in by entering a city with gates and bars (the bars being the wooden beams that lock the gates).

The speaker is Saul, the king, who pursues David out of jealousy. David had just rescued Keilah from the Philistines. Saul reads the situation in his own favor and credits God with his own desire to do harm. But the account does not say that God did this; soon David, by inquiring of God, discovers Saul's plan.

Today, we must be careful not to call something "God's will" when it only suits our desires. An open door or a good opportunity is not always a sign from God. It is wise to pray, to compare it with the Word of God, and to ask for a humble and clean heart.
exp.0:16:
Eli tells Ana to go in peace, and that the God of Israel will grant her what she has asked for. The words "grant" and "petition" in the verse above are the ones this explanation is referring to, so the sentence about the meaning of an old word is rewritten here to fit that: "grant" means to give or allow something to happen.

The speaker is Eli, the priest. A moment before, he had thought Ana was drunk, because she was praying silently and only her lips were moving. Ana explained to him that she was suffering greatly and was pouring out her heart before God. Eli then changes his attitude and blesses her. The text does not say that Eli knew what her request was, only that he wishes God would grant it.

For today: when you are weighed down by pain, pray sincerely, as Ana did, without pretending to be strong. And when someone tells you of their sorrow, listen before you judge, and bless them. Notice that Ana left that place in peace, even before she saw the answer.
exp.15:6:
It says that God spoke to Samuel and asked him not to look at Eliab's appearance or his great height, because God had rejected him. People look at what can be seen on the outside, but God looks at the heart.

Samuel had been sent to Bethlehem to anoint a new king, because God had rejected Saul. Seeing Eliab, tall and impressive in appearance, Samuel thought he was the chosen one. God corrects him. Then Jesse presents other sons, and God does not choose any of them either.

Today we can remember that we should not judge people, or ourselves, only by appearance, success, or what others think. Let us ask God for a sincere and humble heart, and learn to value others for who they are on the inside.
exp.8:6:
Saul agrees with his servant's idea of going to see the man of God, but something practical troubles him: they have nothing to bring him. The bread in their bags is gone, and those were the travel bags. The word "man" in the verse above simply means "man." Saul asks, "What have we?"

Saul and his servant have been looking for their father Kish's lost donkeys for days. They no longer know where else to search. It was customary to bring a gift to the one you consulted, as a sign of respect. The servant suggests going to the man of God, who is Samuel, and finds a solution: he has a little silver.

For today: when we seek direction, it is good to acknowledge our need and ask for help from someone wise. And sometimes God uses ordinary people, like this servant, to give us a good idea.
exp.17:14:
This verse says that Saul saw how wisely and successfully David acted, and for that reason he was afraid of him. The phrase "behaved himself very wisely" means acting with good sense and sound judgment.

The narrator tells us that Saul had appointed David as commander of a thousand soldiers. David carried out his duties well, and the text says that the Lord was with him. Saul already knew that the Lord had departed from him, so David's good conduct troubled him instead of gladdening him. His fear would lead him to plot against David.

For today: when you see that someone else is doing well, do not let envy or fear take control of you. Ask God for a thankful and humble heart, and seek to live with wisdom and honesty in whatever task is yours.
exp.16:47:
The explanation says that when Goliath rose up and began to advance to attack David, David did not stay waiting or pull back. He hurried and ran toward the enemy. The phrase "hurried" in the verse is the same word the verse uses for David's haste, so no further explanation is needed here. Goliath is the Philistine warrior, the champion of the Philistine people.

The narrator tells this moment just after David told Goliath that God would give the victory, not the sword or the spear. David was a young shepherd, without armor for war, and he trusted that the battle belonged to God. That is why his words now show up in action: he advances with courage.

For today: when we trust God, sometimes it is time to take a step forward with courage instead of being frozen by fear. Praying and trusting do not rule out acting. We can face with faith that conversation, decision, or problem we have been avoiding for so long.
exp.22:24:
Saul went out with his men to look for David, but someone warned David. So he went down into the rock and stayed in the wilderness of Maon. When Saul heard this, he pursued David into that wilderness.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Saul, the king, was chasing David out of jealousy and fear, even though David had done him no harm. The people of Ziph had offered to help Saul find him. David, for his part, kept moving from one place to another to save his life. Shortly afterward, a message about the Philistines interrupts the pursuit.

When we feel hunted or in danger, God can use warnings, people, or circumstances to care for us. It is wise to act with prudence, without despairing, and to trust that God continues to work even in times of uncertainty.
exp.13:25:
The explanation says that Israel's army came to a forest where honey was dripping onto the ground, but no one dared to taste it. "Put the hand to the mouth" means to eat. They were hungry and the food was right there, yet they respected Saul's oath. "Fear" here means taking a curse seriously.

The narrator tells us that Israel was fighting against the Philistines. Saul, without anyone asking him to, had forbidden eating until evening. Many understand that it was a hasty order, one that left the people weak and exhausted. The Bible does not say that God asked for it.

Today we can learn to take care with our words and promises. A commitment made in haste or pride can burden others unnecessarily. Before demanding something from others, it is wise to pray and to think about whether it truly serves God and helps people.
exp.0:9:
This verse tells us that Hannah, with her soul full of bitterness, prayed to the Lord and wept greatly. "Bitterness of soul" means a deep grief inside. "Abundantly" means she wept without holding back. Some old words here are "Jehová," which is the name of God, and "á," which we would write today as "a."

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who shows us Hannah at Shiloh, beside the temple. She had no children and suffered because of it. Her husband Elkanah tried to comfort her, but her pain went deeper. So she stopped speaking to people and went to speak with God, and there she made her request.

For today: when pain weighs on you, you do not have to pretend or polish your words. You can bring your tears to God and tell him honestly what you feel. He does not tire of listening to you, and praying with honesty is a good first step.
exp.0:20:
Elkanah, Hannah's husband, went up with his whole household to Shiloh to offer to God the sacrifice they made every year. He also fulfilled his vow, that is, a promise he had made to God. The word "man" in the verse simply means a man, and the sacrifice is described as the yearly one, the one they made as a regular custom.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, who describes how family life continued after Samuel was born. Hannah stayed at home with the small child, because she wanted to take him to the sanctuary once he was weaned. Elkanah respected her decision. We do not know for certain what Elkanah's vow was; the text does not explain it.

For today: God values constant faithfulness, even in everyday life. Keeping what we have promised, and respecting with love the decisions of those we care about, strengthens faith and family.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that, when David had finished speaking with Saul, the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David. Jonathan loved him as his own soul.

Here there is no character speaking; it is the narrator of the book. David had just spoken with Saul after defeating Goliath. Jonathan, the king's son, listened and felt a deep bond with him. Afterward they made a covenant, that is, a pact of loyalty. The text does not explain all the reasons, but it shows a sincere friendship.

For today: value and care for loyal friendships. A good friendship shows itself in affection, faithfulness, and support, even when there is envy or difficulty around.
exp.22:17:
The explanation says that David and Jonathan made a solemn promise, a covenant, with God as witness. Afterward they parted: David stayed in the wood, and Jonathan went back home. The words "the two of them" are the same as "both of them," and a covenant is a binding promise or commitment.

The narrator tells this moment while Saul is pursuing David in order to kill him. Jonathan, Saul's son, risks his own safety to encourage his friend. He tells him that God will protect him and that he will be king. This was his last recorded meeting with David in the Bible. Right after this, the people of Ziph betray David to Saul.

For today: a faithful friendship encourages the other person to trust God, even when everything seems difficult. Look for someone who is going through a hard time, encourage them with sincere words, and remind them that God is still with them. And keep the promises you make.
exp.20:10:
The servants of Achish, king of Gath, recognize David and wonder whether he is not the famous warrior of Israel. They call him "the king of the land," and they remember the song that the women sang in dances: Saul has slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands. The word "dances" refers to groups of people dancing in a circle.

David was fleeing from Saul and had come to Gath, the city of Goliath, the giant he himself had defeated. It is the Philistine officials who speak, and they see in David a dangerous enemy. They may call him "king" because of his fame, not because he already was one. This frightens David, as the next verse shows.

When fear leads us to look for a way out on our own, we can end up in dangerous places. David was strong, yet here he appears weak. This reminds us that we should bring our fears to God honestly. Later, Psalm 34 is traditionally connected with this episode and speaks of God who delivers the one who seeks him.
exp.19:27:
Jonathan answers his father Saul that David earnestly asked him for leave to go to Bethlehem. "Earnestly" means with great insistence, with all his eagerness. Jonathan repeats the excuse that he and David had agreed on to explain David's absence from the king's table.

Saul noticed that David's place was empty at the feast of the new moon. Jonathan speaks to protect his friend, while he finds out whether Saul really intends to kill David. His answer provokes Saul's anger, and so Jonathan confirms that the danger is real. Some think his answer is only an agreed-upon excuse, not a malicious lie; the text does not judge this directly.

For today: loyalty to a friend sometimes costs dearly. Jonathan risked his relationship with his father to do what was right. Let us ask God for wisdom and courage to defend others with truth and love, even when it brings us discomfort.
exp.8:8:
This verse is an explanatory note within the story. It says that long ago in Israel, anyone who wanted to consult God would say, "Let us go to the one who sees." Over time, that person came to be called a "prophet." The word "seer" means someone to whom God gave the ability to see or know things others did not.

The narrator of the book explains this change in wording for readers of his own time. Saul and his servant are looking for some lost donkeys. When they cannot find them, the servant suggests they go to the man of God so that he can give them direction. That man is Samuel. Scholars do not know for certain when this note was written, but it shows that the language changed over the years.

For today: when we do not know which way to take, let us seek God in prayer and also the counsel of wise and faithful people. Asking for direction is not weakness; it is humility.
exp.22:12:
This verse tells that David left Keilah together with his men, about six hundred of them. They kept moving from place to place, never staying fixed in any one spot. When Saul learned that David had escaped, he gave up going out after him to Keilah. The word "news" in the source is the message that reached Saul, and the phrase about him giving up going out means that he called off his journey.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book. Before this, David had asked God whether Saul would come and whether the people of Keilah would hand him over, even though he had rescued them from the Philistines. God told him yes. David obeyed that warning and left in time.

For today: when God warns us of a danger, whether through his Word, through prayer, or through good counsel, it is wise to act with prudence and not simply wait for things to resolve on their own.
exp.13:32:
Here the people are told to Saul that they are sinning against the Lord by eating meat with the blood. The word "transgressed" in the verse means they broke or disobeyed a known law. Saul tells them to roll a large stone to him, so that it can later be used as the place where the animals are slaughtered.

The Israelite soldiers were exhausted after chasing the Philistines. They threw themselves on the spoil and killed animals on the ground, without letting the blood drain out. The law of Moses forbade eating blood (Leviticus 17:10-14), because the life is in it. Those speaking are some of the people, who report, and Saul, who reacts and corrects. Interpreters do not agree on how much genuine zeal there was in Saul.

For today: even in the middle of tiredness or haste, let us not allow need to make us neglect what God says. And when someone points out a mistake to us, let us correct it promptly.
exp.3:8:
The Philistines urge one another to be brave. "Be strong" means to take courage and resolve. "Quit yourselves like men" means to act with valor. "That ye be not servants" means that they should not become slaves to the Hebrews, as the Hebrews had once been to them.

The speakers are Philistine leaders or soldiers. They had heard that the ark had come into the camp of Israel, and they felt terror, remembering the plagues of Egypt. Even with that fear, they decide to fight. The following text shows that they won, and the ark was taken. Israel had treated the ark as a good-luck charm, not in obedience to God.

For today: fear does not have to paralyze us, but we must not use what is sacred as an object of luck. Let us seek God with an obedient heart, and face challenges with courage and responsibility.
exp.16:13:
The explanation says that David was the youngest son of Jesse, and that his three older brothers had gone with King Saul to war. The word "youngest" means the smallest in age. "Followed Saul" means they joined his army.

Here the narrator of the book introduces David's family while Israel faces the Philistines. The brothers are on the battle front, and David, being the youngest, stays behind to tend his father's sheep. So the account sets the scene in which Goliath challenges Israel and David appears.

For today: God can use the one others overlook. If you are given a simple, little-noticed task today, do it faithfully. That is where the character is formed that God can later use in important moments.
exp.11:0:
Samuel speaks to all the people of Israel. He reminds them that he listened to them and granted what they asked for: a king. "I have listened to your voice" means "I listened to you." The phrase "I have made a king over you" indicates that Samuel did what they asked him to do, although the appointment came from God.

Samuel was a prophet and judge of Israel. The people had asked for a king so they could be like the other nations, and this grieved Samuel. Now, with Saul already acknowledged as king, Samuel prepares to step away from leadership and to defend the integrity of his service, as the following verses show.

For today: when we serve others, let us strive to live so that we can look everyone in the eye, with clean and honest conduct. And when God gives us a path different from the one we expected, let us keep trusting in Him.
exp.29:18:
It says that David recovered absolutely everything the Amalekites had taken. Nothing was missing, neither the small nor the great, neither the sons nor the daughters, nor the other possessions. "Spoil" here means the plunder, and "recovered" means that he got it back into his hands.

The narrator tells this after the Amalekites burned Ziklag and carried off the families of David and his men. David was distressed, since his people even spoke of stoning him. Even so, he strengthened himself in the Lord, asked him what to do, and God told him to pursue them with the assurance that he would recover everything (verse 8). This verse shows that the promise was fulfilled completely.

When everything seems lost, we can do what David did: seek God before we act. We will not always recover what was lost in the same way, but God remains faithful and knows how to guide us step by step. Ask him for direction today.
exp.12:0:
The verse says that Saul had already been king for a year, and that after he had reigned two years over Israel, what follows happened. The phrasing looks odd in the text, and with reason: in the Hebrew the numbers seem incomplete or damaged. For that reason modern translations present it in different ways, and scholars do not agree on how many years Saul reigned at this point.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book. He wants to place us in time before telling of Saul's first great war against the Philistines, enemies who dominated the region.

For today: power and success are not permanent, and they are not measured only by years. What matters is how we live each stage. Let us ask God for obedience and humility from the beginning, because Saul's early days show us how fragile a good start can be.
exp.17:13:
This verse says that David acted with wisdom and good judgment in everything he did, and that God was with him. The phrase "behaved himself wisely" means that he conducted himself with care and skill. "Business" here means his tasks, his affairs, and the way he carried out his responsibilities. "The Lord was with him" means that God accompanied him and supported him.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks. Saul, the king, was afraid of David because he saw that God favored David and had departed from Saul. For that reason he moved him away from his side and made him commander over a thousand soldiers. Even so, David continued to prosper, and this increased Saul's fear, while the people loved him.

For today: do your work and your responsibilities with honesty and care, even when others treat you unjustly. Ask God for wisdom and trust that He is with you, without depending on the applause of people.
exp.9:24:
Samuel explained to the people "the manner of the kingdom," that is, the rules and the duties of the king and of the people. Then he wrote it in a book and laid it up "before the Lord," probably in a sacred place, near the sanctuary.

Israel had just asked for a king, and Saul was presented publicly. Samuel, prophet and judge, speaks so that the new reign would not be a power without limits. Scholars do not know exactly what that writing said, but it shows that the king too was under God's authority.

Today it reminds us that all authority, in the home, the church or the workplace, must submit to God and to clear principles. If you have any leadership, exercise it with humility and accountability.
exp.0:11:
This verse tells us that Hannah was praying at length before God, and that the priest Eli was watching her. The phrase "watching her mouth" means that Eli was paying attention to how her lips were moving. The word "it came to pass" is an older way of saying "it happened," and "as she continued praying" means that she kept on praying without hurry, for quite a while.

The narrator of the book places us at the sanctuary in Shiloh. Hannah had no children and was deeply distressed. She had just made a vow: if God gave her a son, she would dedicate him to God. Eli, who was observing closely, saw her lips moving without hearing any voice, and so he mistakenly thought she was drunk.

For today: God hears sincere prayers, even silent ones that others do not understand. Speak with Him honestly about your pain. And when you see someone weeping or acting strangely, do not rush to judge them; ask gently and listen first.
exp.8:16:
When Samuel saw Saul, God confirmed to him: "Behold the man whom I spake to thee of." The word "shall reign" is an older way of saying that he will rule or hold authority over the people.

God had told Samuel a day earlier that He would send him a man from the tribe of Benjamin to anoint as prince. Samuel was a prophet and a judge. Saul was looking for his father's lost donkeys and did not know what God was preparing. The text says that God had heard the cry of his people, who were oppressed by the Philistines.

For today: God can work in the middle of ordinary life, even when we do not notice it. Trust that He hears your cry and directs your steps, even in common tasks, and stay attentive to what He may want to show you.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that the boy Samuel served God in the sanctuary, wearing a linen ephod. "Ministered" means that he served or helped with the tasks of worship. The linen ephod was a simple garment, something like an apron or vest, worn by those who served in the presence of God.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Earlier, the sons of Eli were mentioned, who despised the offerings and abused their office. With that contrast, the text shows Samuel, a boy who served with reverence. Afterward it is told that his mother, Hannah, made him a small robe each year and brought it to him.

For today: even if you are young, or are in a setting where others do not take holy things seriously, you can serve God with simplicity and faithfulness in the small things that fall to you to do.
exp.17:29:
Here it says that whenever the leaders of the Philistines went out to fight, David acted with more wisdom and success than all of Saul's other officers. For this reason his name was very respected and well known. The phrase about acting with good judgment and success is simply about David's conduct and results. The word about being highly honored and recognized is simply about how well regarded he was.

This is the closing part of chapter 18, and it is told by the narrator. Saul already felt jealousy and fear, because he saw that God was with David. Even so, David kept carrying out his military duties with good results. The text shows that his reputation grew because of how he conducted himself, and that Saul's envy had no just reason behind it.

For today: do your work and your responsibilities well, even when someone envies you or treats you badly. Consistent good conduct, with God's help, speaks for itself. You do not need to defend yourself with pride; serve with honesty and trust that God watches over your path.
exp.25:6:
So David and Abishai went to the camp at night. They found the king asleep inside the trench, which was probably the ring of chariots or baggage that surrounded the camp. His spear was stuck in the ground beside his head. Abner, his commander, and all the soldiers were sleeping around him.

Saul had been chasing David for a long time, trying to kill him, even though David had done him no wrong. Here the narrator describes the scene to show how close David was to Saul and how easy revenge seemed. In the verses that follow, Abishai sees an opportunity that God seems to be giving them, but David refuses to kill the Lord's anointed.

For today: not every chance to take revenge is a door that God opens. When someone wounds us, we can trust that God will do justice and choose to act with respect and self-control.
exp.11:19:
Samuel tells the people not to be afraid. He acknowledges that they did wrong, but he asks them not to turn away from God. Instead of running from Him out of shame, they should serve Him with all their heart. The phrase "do not turn aside from following the Lord" means not stopping in your following of the Lord.

Samuel speaks after God sent thunder and rain as a sign. The people were frightened, because they had asked for a king like the other nations, and that showed little trust in God. Samuel does not downplay their sin, but neither does he condemn them without hope. He invites them to return to God.

When we fail, guilt can pull us away from God. This verse encourages us to do the opposite: to admit our mistake, draw near to Him, and keep serving Him today with sincerity.
exp.1:32:
God says he will not completely remove all of Eli's descendants from service at the altar. But great sorrow awaits Eli: his eyes will grow dim with grief, and his heart will be filled with sorrow. Many of his descendants will die young, in the prime of their adult lives.

A man of God speaks to Eli, the priest. God rebukes him because he allowed his sons to treat the offerings with contempt, and because he honored them more than God. Many believe the survivor who is announced refers to Abiathar, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: God is merciful, but he also takes obedience seriously. If you have authority at home or in the church, do not ignore what is wrong in order to avoid conflict. Correct with love, and put God first.
exp.16:53:
David took the head of the Philistine Goliath and brought it to Jerusalem. The giant's weapons, on the other hand, he kept in his own tent. The word that translates as "brought" is a plain word meaning he carried it there, and the word for his tent is his own tent or dwelling.

This is part of the account of David's victory over Goliath. The narrator summarizes what happened after the battle. There is one difficult detail: at that time Jerusalem did not yet belong to Israel, since David conquered it years later. Some think the author names the place as it would be known later, or that the head was taken there afterward. It is not known for certain.

For today: David did not boast about his victory, but kept the trophy simply. When God gives you a triumph, thank him and do not fill up with pride.
exp.16:12:
This verse says that the three eldest sons of Jesse, a man of Bethlehem, had gone with King Saul to the war. Their names were Eliab (the firstborn), Abinadab, and Shammah. "Followed Saul" means joining his army.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. After describing Israel's fear before the Philistine giant, he introduces David's family. The names of his brothers prepare what follows: David, the youngest, went back and forth between the camp and his father's sheep. Later, Eliab will be the one who rebukes him (17:28).

For today: God often works through people who seem small or little noticed, like David among his brothers. Do not look down on your own place or the place of others. Be faithful in everyday things, because God can use them for something great.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that the ark of the Lord, the sacred chest that represented God's presence among Israel, remained for seven months in Philistine territory. The word "was" means that it stayed there. The Philistines had captured it in battle.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. During those months, the ark brought trouble and sickness to the Philistine cities where it was kept. That is why, in the verses that follow, their priests and diviners look for a way to return it. They suggest sending it back with a guilt offering, to acknowledge that they had wronged the God of Israel.

For today: God cannot be treated as an object that we control or use as it suits us. The Philistines learned by force that he had to be acknowledged. We can do this willingly: come near to God with humility and admit our wrongs, before the consequences force us to.
exp.5:17:
This verse says that the Philistines also sent golden mice, as many as the cities they had under their five lords, both the fortified cities and the villages without walls. It also mentions the great stone where they set down the ark of the Lord, and that this stone was still there to this day, in the field of Joshua, a man of Beth-shemesh.

The one telling the story is the author of the book, and he writes after the events took place. The Philistines had captured the ark and suffered plagues. Their priests advised them to return it with a guilt offering of repayment, in the form of tumors and golden mice. The stone served as a sign that all of this really happened.

For today: when we recognize that we have failed, fear alone is not enough. God wants us to take it seriously, to honor Him with humility, and to seek to be reconciled to Him, who is holy and also merciful.
exp.24:2:
This passage introduces two very different people. Nabal was a wealthy man, but he was harsh and wicked in his dealings, stubborn and rough to deal with. His wife Abigail was intelligent and wise, and she was gracious and pleasant in her manner. The text also says that Nabal was of the house of Caleb, that is, a descendant of a respected family. Some scholars note that his name means "fool," but not all of them interpret it the same way.

Here the narrator is setting the stage for the story. Samuel has just died, and David is living in the wilderness. In describing Nabal and Abigail, the text foreshadows the conflict that comes when David asks for help and Nabal treats him badly.

For today: having a good family, money, or position does not guarantee a good character. Let us ask God for wisdom and a kind heart, and treat others with respect, as Abigail did.
exp.13:18:
This verse tells us that Saul was still speaking with the priest when the noise and confusion in the Philistine camp kept growing louder. Then Saul said to him, "Withdraw thine hand." That is, "stop what you are doing." The phrase "armor-bearer" refers to the young man who carried the weapons of Jonathan.

Saul had noticed that Jonathan and his armor-bearer were missing. He asked for the ark of God so that he could seek the Lord through the priest. But when he saw the enemy's chaos increasing, he cut off the inquiry and went into battle. Scholars understand this in different ways: as a practical urgency, or as Saul's impatience. The text does not make it clear.

For today: seeking God should not be a formality that we drop when we are in a hurry. Pray calmly, listen, and act in obedience, without letting haste or fear pull you away from Him.
exp.13:1:
This verse tells where King Saul was while his son Jonathan went out to attack. Saul was on the outskirts of Gibeah, resting under a pomegranate tree, close to a place called Migron. With him were about six hundred men, a very small army.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He wants us to see the contrast: Saul, the king, is still and without a plan, while Jonathan, without telling him, takes a risk in faith. Some scholars think the pomegranate tree shows Saul's passivity, although the text does not say this clearly.

For today: sometimes we expect others to take the first step. God can use the one who trusts in Him and acts with courage and humility. Ask Him for wisdom to know when to leave comfort behind and obey Him.
exp.13:12:
This verse tells how Jonathan climbed up a steep slope, using both his hands and his feet, and his armorbearer, the young man who carried his weapons, followed closely behind him. Jonathan struck down the enemies he met at the front, and the young man coming behind finished them off. The armorbearer is the helper or attendant who serves a soldier.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan and his armorbearer had come near a Philistine outpost, and the Philistines challenged them to come up. Jonathan took this as a sign and said that the LORD had delivered the enemies into the hands of Israel. They were only two men against a garrison, but Jonathan trusted in God.

For today: when you feel God calling you to take a difficult step, do not expect it to be easy. Move forward with faith, effort, and companionship, as Jonathan did, who climbed up and was not alone.
exp.19:19:
Jonathan explains a secret plan. He says that he will shoot three arrows to one side, as though he were shooting at a target. In reality, it will be a signal. The word "target" here is the mark that is aimed at.

Jonathan is speaking to David. Saul, the king, seeks to kill David, and Jonathan, his son, is David's loyal friend. He wants to find out his father's intentions without putting them both in danger. David will hide near the stone of Ezel, and the warning will come through the servant and the place where the arrows fall. The following verses explain each signal.

For today: true friendship is loyal and sometimes requires prudence and courage. Ask yourself whom you can protect or encourage this week, and do it wisely, without seeking your own advantage.
exp.15:10:
Samuel asks Jesse whether he has any more sons ("are here all thy children?"). Jesse answers that the youngest is still left, the one who looks after the sheep. Samuel tells him to send for him, and says they will not sit down to eat until he arrives.

Samuel, the prophet, had been sent by God to the house of Jesse in Bethlehem to anoint a new king, since Saul had been rejected. God had already set aside the seven sons who were presented. Jesse had not even thought of David for this moment, and the text does not explain why; we only see that he left him out in the field.

For today: God does not look as people do, and sometimes he calls the one whom everyone overlooks. Do not belittle yourself or underestimate others; be faithful in small things, as David was with his sheep.
exp.7:9:
This verse says that Samuel told the people everything the Lord had commanded him to say. The name of God in the source appears here as "the Lord," and the phrase about the people who asked Samuel for a king refers to the people who demanded a king from him.

Samuel speaks as a prophet and judge of Israel. The people wanted a king like the other nations, and this grieved Samuel. God told him to listen to their request, but first to warn them clearly. God explains that they had rejected his guidance, as they had done before with other gods. For this reason, Samuel does not soften the message: he shows them what it would cost to have a king.

For today: before insisting on something, it is good to ask ourselves what it will cost and whether we are beginning to stop trusting God. He warns us out of love, even when he allows us to choose our own path.
exp.14:31:
Samuel orders that Agag, the king of the Amalekites, be brought to him. Saul had spared him. Agag comes "delicately," that is, calmly or confidently, and says: "Surely the bitterness of death is past." In other words, he believes the danger is over. Some translators take his words as a question or as a confident statement, and it is not entirely certain what the exact meaning is.

Samuel speaks as a prophet of God. God had commanded that the Amalekites be destroyed, but Saul spared the king and kept the best of the spoil. Samuel corrects that disobedience and does what Saul should have done. It is a hard passage, tied to a particular judgment in the history of Israel.

For today: do not feel secure when you think a problem is over, and do not leave unfinished what God asks of you. Partial obedience is a form of disobedience, and God invites us to obey him completely.
exp.2:6:
This verse explains why Samuel did not recognize the voice calling him. "Did not yet know the Lord" does not mean that he did not believe in God, but that he had not yet had a personal experience of God speaking to him. "Neither was the word of the Lord yet revealed unto him" means that God had not yet made his message known to him.

The narrator is the author of the book. Samuel was a boy who served Eli at the sanctuary in Shiloh. It was a time when the word of God was scarce. The narrator makes clear that Samuel mistook God's voice for Eli's, and that this moment was new to him.

For today: knowing about God and knowing him personally are different things. We can grow in faith by listening with humility, asking help from mature believers, and praying: "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening."
exp.5:18:
God punished the people of Beth-shemesh because they looked into the ark of the Lord, that is, they opened it or looked into it without proper respect. Many died, and the people mourned (they lamented) over that great blow.

The narrator tells what happened when the Philistines sent the ark back, the ark that represented God's holy presence. The people of Beth-shemesh treated it lightly. The figure of 50,070 is difficult: some scholars believe there was a copying error and that far fewer died. This cannot be stated with certainty. Even so, the central message is clear: God is holy.

Today we can approach God with confidence, but also with reverence. Before praying or reading the Bible, pause and remember who God is.
exp.22:5:
This verse tells how Abiathar, the son of Ahimelech, escaped and came to David at Keilah. He brought with him the ephod, a sacred garment of the priest, used to seek God's guidance.

The one telling the story is the author of the book. Abiathar was the only priest who survived when Saul ordered the priests of Nob to be killed (chapter 22). By joining David, he gave David a way to ask God what to do. That is why, in the verses that follow, David can inquire of the Lord before he acts, while Saul only relies on his own fortune.

For today: God knows how to give us help just when we need it. Before deciding something important, let us seek his direction in prayer and in his Word, and let us value the people who walk beside us in faith during difficult times.
exp.11:23:
It says that the people should revere and honor God, and serve him sincerely and with all their heart. The reason is that they should remember the great things he has done for them. "Fear" here means to reverence with respect and trust, not to live in dread. Serving him truly means serving him honestly, without pretense.

Samuel, now old, speaks in his farewell address. Israel had just asked for a king, and Samuel reminds them that God will not abandon them. He calls them not to turn away from him, and then warns them of the consequences if they insist on doing evil.

For today: when you feel tempted to serve God out of habit or just to fulfill an obligation, stop and call to mind what he has done in your life. Giving thanks for what you have received awakens a sincere desire to obey him and serve him with joy, not out of duty.
exp.5:19:
The people of Beth-shemesh, frightened by the death of so many men, ask two questions. The first: "Who is able to stand before this holy Lord God?" That is, who can come into the presence of so pure a God without being punished? The second: "To whom shall he go up from us?" In other words, to whom shall we send it so that the ark will leave here?

The people of Beth-shemesh are the ones speaking. The Philistines had returned the ark, and the inhabitants received it with joy, but some looked into it with irreverence and God struck them down. The figure of 50,070 is much debated: some scholars think the original text or its copy may have varied in the number. For that reason the people, in mourning and fear, decide to send the ark to Kiriath-jearim.

God is holy, and drawing near to Him calls for respect, not carelessness. Today we can approach Him with confidence thanks to Christ, but always with humility and sincere reverence.
exp.16:32:
Saul tells David that he cannot go out to fight the Philistine Goliath. He gives two reasons: David is a "youth," that is, a young boy, and Goliath is "a man of war from his youth," a soldier who has been experienced in battle since he was a child. The word "able" means "capable."

King Saul is speaking. The whole army of Israel was afraid of Goliath, who challenged them every day. David offers to fight, and Saul calls him, but he hesitates, because by human measure the difference seems enormous. His concern is understandable. What Saul does not yet see is David's trust in God, which appears in the following verse.

For today: sometimes others will tell us that something is too big for us, and they may be right if they measure only our own strength. Before you give up, remember how God has sustained you before, and ask him for courage and wisdom for the challenge you face.
exp.29:1:
The passage says that the Amalekites took the women of Ziklag prisoner, from the youngest to the oldest. They killed no one; they only carried them off and went on their way. "Captives" means prisoners, and "went on their way" means they went on their way.

No one is speaking here; it is the narrator of the book who tells what happened. David and his men returned home after being away and found the city burned and their families gone. It was a terrible blow, and the Bible says they wept until they had no strength left. The text does not explain why God allowed this, and it is not right to invent a reason.

For today: when a loss leaves you without strength, you do not have to pretend to be strong. Weeping is honest. But do not stay there: the story goes on, and David ended up seeking strength in God. Bring your pain to Him in prayer.
exp.1:23:
Eli tells his sons to stop this behavior. He explains that what people are saying about them is not good news, because through their conduct they are leading God's people into sin.

The speaker is Eli, an elderly priest and the father of Hophni and Phinehas. These sons were abusing their position at the tabernacle, and all of Israel was talking about it. Eli rebukes them, but his tone seems gentle, and they did not listen to him. The text says that God had already decided to judge them.

For today: our example influences others, especially if we carry some responsibility. Let us be careful how we live and, if we correct someone, let us do it with clarity and firmness, without putting it off.
exp.24:15:
They were like a wall around Nabal's shepherds, protecting them day and night while they tended the sheep in the field.

The one speaking is a servant of Nabal, who tells Abigail what happened. David had sent greetings to Nabal and asked him for some provisions, but Nabal treated them with scorn. The servant defends David's men and warns of the danger, because he knows the situation could end very badly. Abigail is seen as a wise woman who can act.

For today: it is worth recognizing and thanking those who have looked after us without asking for anything, and not repaying their kindness with contempt. Also, when we see danger, it is wise to warn honestly the person who can help resolve it.
exp.8:11:
The young women answer Saul that yes, the seer is right there in front of them. They tell him to hurry, because the man came to the city today, and the people have a sacrifice today at the high place.

These young women were going out to draw water from the well. Saul and his servant had been looking for his father's donkeys that had been lost, and they had come to ask about Samuel, who was called the seer. The women give them precise and urgent information, since Samuel was about to go up and bless the meal of the sacrifice. Without knowing it, Saul is about to meet the one whom God will use to anoint him as king.

For today: God often guides our steps through simple things, like an ordinary conversation with someone on the way. Pay attention to the opportunities that come your way and act with diligence, trusting that God works even in the everyday.
exp.19:32:
Saul, in a fit of rage, threw a spear at his own son Jonathan with the intention of striking him. With this, Jonathan understood that his father was set on killing David.

Jonathan had just defended David at a new moon feast. Saul saw David as a threat to his family's throne. When Jonathan asked, "What has he done?", Saul gave no reasons, only violence. In this way it became clear that there was no room for dialogue.

For today: there are moments when anger shuts the ears and reason no longer gets in. If you defend what is right, do it with courage but also with prudence, and do not rest in the illusion that everything will work itself out. Ask God for wisdom to see the reality clearly and to act with love and firmness.
exp.19:9:
Here David asks Jonathan: "Who will tell me if your father answers you harshly?" The word "roughly" means with anger and in a bad manner. David fears that there is no sure way to find out what King Saul is thinking.

David speaks with his friend Jonathan, Saul's son. David suspects that Saul wants to kill him, but Jonathan does not yet believe it. They had already made a covenant before the LORD. David asks for help, and Jonathan promises to warn him. So they immediately go out into the field to talk in private and make a plan.

For today: when you are afraid or in an uncertain situation, do not hide it. Speak with a faithful friend, ask for help with humility, and seek together a sensible plan, trusting that God cares for you in the midst of uncertainty.
exp.25:21:
David answers Saul and shows him that the king's spear is there, in his possession. He asks that one of his servants (his helpers or attendants) be sent to cross over and pick it up. It is a way of returning it without Saul having to come near him.

David speaks from the other side of the valley, after he entered Saul's camp at night while everyone was sleeping. He could have killed the king, but he did not, because Saul was the anointed one of the LORD, that is, the one chosen by God. He took the spear as proof that he had respected him. Saul acknowledges his wrong, although the Bible shows that his change did not last.

When you have the chance to take revenge, trust that God is just. Do what is right, even if others do not do so toward you, and leave it to God to judge and to defend.
exp.5:14:
The Levites, who were in charge of the sacred service, lifted the ark of the Lord down from the cart. They also took down the chest that held the golden jewels, and placed them on the great stone. The men of Beth-shemesh offered burnt offerings, which were sacrifices burned up completely, and other sacrifices to the Lord that same day.

This is historical narrative. The Philistines had returned the ark with a gift of gold to make up for their offense. The cows had carried the cart as far as Beth-shemesh, and the people, who were harvesting wheat, rejoiced when they saw it. They respond with worship, and the Levites care for the ark as the law required.

For today: when God gives us back something good or gives us joy, our first response can be to thank him and worship him. We can set aside a moment to thank him before going on with our tasks.
exp.19:41:
Jonathan sends David away with the words "Go in peace." He reminds him that the two of them swore an oath in the name of the Lord: that God would be a witness between them and between their descendants, the seed, forever. David got up and left, and Jonathan went back into the city.

Jonathan speaks after warning David, by a sign with arrows, that his father, King Saul, wanted to kill him. It was a farewell full of tears. They had already made a covenant of friendship and loyalty, and now David had to flee. Jonathan trusted that God would uphold that commitment.

For today: when you have to part from someone you love, or when a promise is hard to keep, place God at the center of the relationship. Keep your word faithfully, pray for that person, and trust that God cares for them even when you are not near.
exp.17:28:
Saul was still more afraid of David, and from then on he regarded him as his enemy for as long as he lived. The word that the verse renders as "afraid" simply means he was afraid. The phrase "continually" means that this hostility did not end but remained steady.

No one speaks in this passage; the narrator is explaining what was going on in Saul's heart. Saul had hoped the Philistines would kill David, but David returned successful and married Michal, the king's daughter. Saul saw that God was with David and that his daughter loved him. That did not lead him to peace, but to more fear and jealousy.

When fear and envy rule the heart, we see as a threat the one whom God is blessing. Today we can ask God to deliver us from envy and teach us to rejoice in the good of others.
exp.27:17:
The explanation says that Saul is living with the consequences of not obeying God. The judgment God ordered against Amalek is what the verse refers to, and the words "furor" and "hoy" are older wording for "a" and "today" in the text. Saul did not carry out that command fully, and for this reason God allows what is now happening.

Samuel, or someone presenting himself as Samuel, speaks to Saul. Saul, distressed by the Philistine army and without an answer from God, had sought a medium in Endor. Many understand that God allowed Samuel to appear; others think it was something else. The text does not fully clarify this. The message repeats what Samuel had already said earlier about the kingdom.

For today: partial obedience is not obedience. If we know what God asks of us, we should do it honestly and without excuses. And when we fail, it is wise to return to Him soon with humility, rather than looking for ways out through other paths.
exp.1:14:
This verse tells how, before the fat of the animal was burned, which belonged to God, the servant of the priest came and demanded raw meat to roast. He would not accept boiled meat. He wanted the best, and he wanted it first, without waiting.

The one speaking is the servant of Eli's sons, who were priests in Shiloh. The law stated that the fat was burned for God and that the priest received a set portion. But these men used their position to take more than they were due, and by force. The text says that in this way they despised the offerings of the LORD.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use spiritual things for our own benefit. Whoever serves God or others should do so with humility, giving God first place and never taking advantage of the trust of others.
exp.0:13:
Eli asks Anna how much longer she is going to stay drunk, and tells her to let her wine go, that is, to let the drunkenness wear off. Here "put away" means to get rid of it, so that she becomes sober again.

Eli, the priest, was watching Anna's mouth in the sanctuary. She was praying in silence, only moving her lips, and he judged her wrongly. Anna was deeply distressed because she had no children, and that is why she prayed with such pain. Afterward she explains to him that she has not drunk anything and that she was only pouring out her soul before God.

Today we can learn not to judge by appearances. Before drawing conclusions about someone who is suffering, it is wise to approach them with respect and to listen. And if you are anguished, you can pray with sincerity, even when others do not understand you.
exp.0:21:
In this verse, Hannah decides not to go up with her husband to Shiloh on that journey. She explains that she will wait until the child is weaned, that is, until he stops drinking his mother's milk. Then she herself will take him to present him before the Lord, and the boy will stay there forever. "But" means "however," and "to take him" means "to take him myself."

Hannah speaks with her husband Elkanah. Before having children, she had prayed in anguish and had promised God to give her son back to Him if He gave her one. Now she wants to keep that promise at the right time. Elkanah supports her and lets her decide what seems best to her.

For today: keeping what we have promised to God, even when it costs us, and doing so with patience and good order. We can also entrust to God what we love most, trusting that He cares for it.
exp.30:12:
The men of Jabesh gathered the bones of Saul and of his sons, buried them under a tree, and went without eating for seven days. "They buried them" is the same as "they buried them." The reading of the verse here is that they spent those days without eating, as a sign of mourning.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after Saul died in battle. The Philistines had dishonored his body. The brave men of Jabesh risked their lives to recover it. Many think they did this out of gratitude, since Saul had rescued them years earlier (1 Samuel 11), although the text does not state this directly.

For today: gratitude and respect are shown through deeds. Think of someone who helped you in the past, even if they are no longer at their best, and look for a concrete way today to honor or accompany them.
exp.12:5:
This verse tells us that the Israelites realized they were in great danger. Seeing the enemy so numerous, the people became frightened and looked for places to hide: in caves, holes, cliffs, rocks, and cisterns (pits used to store water).

The narrator of the book speaks here. Saul, the first king of Israel, had attacked a Philistine garrison, and the Philistines responded with an enormous army. The Israelites gathered at Gilgal, but fear took over them, and some fled across the Jordan. Samuel had not yet arrived.

For today: when fear closes in on us, we are tempted to hide or to act on impulse. It is better to stop, pray, and trust God, waiting patiently for his direction.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that this happened year after year. Each time the family went up to the house of the Lord at Shiloh, Peninnah, Elkanah's other wife, would provoke Hannah. The word that here means to provoke, irritate, or make suffer is what the verse conveys by "provoked," so Hannah wept and had no desire to eat.

The narrator describes Hannah's pain, since she could not have children. Peninnah, her rival, humiliated her precisely on the yearly journey to worship. It is striking that the place of worship was where the hurt cut deepest. Elkanah loved her, but he could not take away that sorrow. The text does not say that God was punishing her; it only states that the Lord had closed her womb, and it does not explain his reasons.

When someone wounds us, it is natural to weep and to feel drained of strength. Hannah teaches us not to stay alone with that pain. In the verses that follow she brings her anguish to God. We can do the same: pray honestly and seek support.
exp.23:14:
Here David asks Saul some questions to make him think: whom is the king of Israel pursuing? He compares himself to a dead dog and to a flea, something of no worth and no danger. The phrase about whom he has come out after is rendered as "whom he is chasing."

David speaks from a distance, after he was able to kill Saul in the cave and did not do it. Saul, the king, was pursuing him with soldiers because he saw him as an enemy. David humbles himself to show that he is no threat, and he trusts that God will be the judge between the two of them.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not take revenge with your own hands. Speak with truth, with humility and respect, and leave your cause in the hands of God, who judges with justice.
exp.24:10:
Nabal answers David's request with contempt. He says he will not take his bread, his water, and the meat (the "victim" is the animal prepared for the feast) that he has kept for those who shear his sheep, and give it to men he knows nothing about, that is, strangers to him. "Shearers" are the workers who cut the wool.

Nabal, a rich man from Maon, speaks during the sheep-shearing feast. David, who was fleeing from Saul, had protected his flocks in the wilderness and asked for some food respectfully. Nabal despises him and does not even acknowledge what David had done for him. This kindles David's anger.

For today: generosity and gratitude guard us against pride. Before refusing help or answering harshly, let us think about the good we have received and treat others with humility.
exp.13:51:
He says that throughout Saul's reign there was fierce war against the Philistines. He also says that whenever Saul saw a strong or valiant man, he took him to be with him.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of the book, who closes his summary of Saul's reign after naming his family and his general Abner. It shows that Israel lived under constant military pressure and that Saul sought to strengthen his army. The text does not say whether this was wise or not; it only describes it. Later, David would be one of those valiant men who came to his court.

For today: surrounding ourselves with capable and committed people helps us face struggles. But, more than strength, we need to seek God's guidance and companions who draw us closer to Him.
exp.24:24:
Here Abigail asks David not to take Nabal, her husband, seriously. The word "man of Belial" translates a term meaning a wicked or worthless person. "Nabal" means "fool" or "senseless." She acknowledges that the name fits him. She also makes clear that she did not see the young men David sent. The "servants" in this passage are the young men who worked for someone.

Abigail speaks with David, who was coming with four hundred men intent on taking revenge. Nabal had despised his request for help and had insulted him. Abigail goes out to meet him with provisions, humbles herself, and seeks to prevent bloodshed. Some think she blames herself to calm David.

When someone offends us, we do not always have to respond with anger. We can pause, listen with humility, and seek peace before we act. A calm word can prevent harm that we would later regret.
exp.22:18:
The people of Ziph went up to Saul at Gibeah to betray David. They told him that David was hiding in their territory, among the rocks in the forest, on the hill of Hachilah, to the south of the desert. The word "hill" here means a small hill or rise of land, and "on the right hand" means to the south.

The Ziphites speak to Saul, who was pursuing David out of jealousy. Just before this, Jonathan had encouraged David, and the two of them had made a covenant before God. Now neighbors from the same tribe of Judah betray David, perhaps out of fear of Saul or to win his favor. The Bible does not explain their motives with certainty.

For today: when someone fails us or betrays us, let us remember that God remains faithful. Let us seek friends like Jonathan who strengthen us, and let us take care not to use our words to harm others.
exp.10:3:
The messengers from Jabesh came to Gibeah, the city of Saul, and told the people about Nahash's threat. Everyone wept aloud, with great grief. The phrase in the verse, "lifted up their voices," means crying out loud, without holding back.

The men of Jabesh-gilead were under siege by Nahash, king of Ammon, who wanted to gouge out their right eyes as a humiliation. They asked for seven days to look for help in Israel. The messengers spoke in Gibeah, and the people responded with weeping. But the weeping was not yet action. God would later move Saul to act.

When someone suffers, we should not be content with tears or lamentation alone. Weeping with the one who suffers is good, but we can also ask God to show us how to help, through prayer, time, words, or resources.
exp.17:8:
From that day forward, the explanation says, Saul began to look at David with suspicion and jealousy, after the women sang that song. The phrase "eyed David" here is an old way of saying he looked at him sideways, with distrust or anger, and not straight on or with goodwill.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Saul had just come back from a battle, and the women were celebrating the victories with a song that put David above him. Saul, already turned away from God, felt threatened, and his anger turned into a watchful stare. The verses that follow show where that leads: he tries to kill David.

For today: jealousy usually starts small, with a look or a thought. If someone else receives praise and that bothers you, bring it to God early and rejoice with that person before resentment grows.
exp.18:16:
Saul confronts his daughter Michal: "Why have you deceived me like this, and let my enemy escape?" She answers that David told her, "Let me go; otherwise I will kill you." The word "deceived" means that Saul felt tricked, and "enemy" is how he saw David.

Saul wanted to kill David, but Michal, David's wife and Saul's daughter, helped him escape and put a statue in the bed to buy time. Now, before her father, she gives an excuse.
