The Bible does not say whether that threat was real or whether Michal made it up to protect herself. Many believe it was an excuse, but this is not certain.

For today: When we must choose between obeying an unjust authority and protecting a life, let us ask God for wisdom and courage. And when we stand up for what is right, let us take care that our words are honest, for the truth honors God.
exp.3:15:
This verse shows the moment a man runs in to bring news to Eli. He says he has come from the battle and has barely managed to escape with his life. Eli, already old and nearly blind, asks him gently: "What has happened, my son?" The word "quickly" in the old wording means swiftly, and "news" is the same as tidings.

The man who speaks first is a messenger from the tribe of Benjamin, who had come from the battlefield against the Philistines. Eli was waiting in anguish, because the ark of God had been taken into the battle. Eli was ninety-eight years old and could not see, so he depended on what others told him. Soon he would receive the worst news of his life.

For today: when someone is waiting for difficult news, they need patience and closeness. We can be people who listen with calm and compassion, and also learn to hand our fears over to God before we know what is coming.
exp.2:16:
Eli asks Samuel to tell him everything the Lord said to him in the night. The words "I pray thee" mean "please," and the phrase about God doing so and more also was a strong form of oath, calling on God to punish anyone who does not keep what he promises. Eli wants Samuel to hide nothing, not even a single word.

Eli speaks as the aged priest. Samuel was a young man serving in the sanctuary, and God had given him a hard message of judgment against the house of Eli. Samuel was afraid to tell it. Eli, with the authority of a father and teacher, insists that he tell the whole truth.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, it is wise to receive it in full, even when it is uncomfortable. And if we must speak a hard truth to someone, let us do it with respect, adding nothing and leaving nothing out.
exp.16:34:
He says that David would go out after the animal that carried off a sheep, strike it, and rescue the lamb from its mouth. If the beast turned on him, he would seize it by the jaw (the lower jaw) and strike it until it died.

David speaks with King Saul. Saul doubted that a young man without experience could face Goliath, a seasoned warrior. David does not boast of his own strength; he tells how he cared for his father's sheep with courage and faithfulness. Then he says that the LORD, who delivered him from the lion and the bear, would deliver him from the Philistine as well.

For today: God often prepares our trust through small and hidden tasks. Be faithful in everyday matters, and remember how God has helped you before; that strengthens faith for the great challenges.
exp.14:11:
This verse tells how Samuel got up very early to go and meet Saul. Someone brought him word that Saul had come to Carmel, that he had set up a monument there to his own victory, and that afterward he had moved on to Gilgal. The verse says Samuel rose early in the morning, and the word "told" shows that he was given the news.

God had just told Samuel that he regretted making Saul king, because Saul had not obeyed. Samuel spent the whole night crying out to God, deeply troubled. Now he is going to confront the king. While Samuel prays, Saul is busy setting up a monument for himself. Some understand this as a sign of pride; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when we fail, God asks us for obedience and humility, not applause. It is worth asking ourselves whether we seek to honor God or to be recognized ourselves.
exp.19:10:
Jonathan proposes to David, "Come, let us go out into the field," and the two of them go out together. The word "field" refers to an open place outside the city. It is a simple gesture, but it marks a change: they are going to talk in private.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, is the one speaking. David has just asked him who would warn him if Saul answered harshly. Jonathan wants to give him reassurance, but he needs a private place, far from curious ears, to make a covenant and plan how to find out his father's intentions. The Bible does not explain why he chose the field, but it fits the need for discretion.

For today: when someone is afraid or confused, sometimes the best thing is to step aside with them to a quiet place. Listening calmly, speaking the truth, and offering concrete support can be a real way of showing love.
exp.13:41:
Saul asks that lots be cast between him and his son Jonathan, and the lot points to Jonathan. "Cast lots" means throwing or using a means by which God would show who was guilty. "Was taken" means he was singled out as the guilty one.

Saul had made a hasty oath: no one was to eat until evening while they fought against the Philistines. Jonathan did not know about it and tasted a little honey. Since God was not answering Saul, he looked for who had failed. We do not know exactly how the lot worked; it is understood as a way of seeking God's answer.

Today we learn that words spoken in haste can hurt those we love. Before promising something great, it is wise to pray, think, and ask God for wisdom.
exp.16:4:
He says that Goliath wore a helmet of bronze or strong metal on his head and a suit of armor made of plates or scales. That body armor weighed five thousand shekels, which according to many scholars would be about 57 kilograms, although the exact calculation may vary. The helmet is the covering for the head, and the armor is what covered the chest and body.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book. He describes Goliath so that the reader feels how imposing he was. Israel and the Philistines stand face to face, and this giant appears as a threat that paralyzes everyone. The story sets up the contrast with David.

For today: sometimes problems look enormous and well protected, and they frighten us. This description reminds us not to measure everything by what we see. We can pray and face our fears trusting in God, not in our own strength.
exp.10:0:
This verse tells that Nahash, king of the Ammonites, came up with his army and pitched his camp against Jabesh-gilead, an Israelite town. Afraid, the people of the town asked him to make a peace agreement with them, and they offered to serve him, that is, to put themselves under his rule.

Here the men of Jabesh are speaking. They were in a weak position and were seeking to save their lives. This happens at the beginning of Saul's reign, at a time when Israel had no leader who could defend it clearly. What follows shows that Nahash's offer was cruel and humiliating.

For today: when we feel fear, it is easy to accept quick solutions that cost us our dignity or our faith. Before giving in, it is wise to stop, ask God for help, and seek the counsel of other believers.
exp.26:7:
David and his men would go out on raids, meaning surprise attacks, against the Geshurites, the Gezrites, and the Amalekites. These peoples had lived for a long time in the area stretching from Shur to Egypt, south of Canaan.

The narrator tells what David was doing while he lived in Ziklag, the town that the Philistine king Achish had given him. The Amalekites were enemies of Israel and had been condemned by God before. But the account that follows shows that David was deceiving Achish about whom he was attacking. The text describes these events, and it does not say that everything David did was right.

Today we can learn that God can carry out his plans even in the midst of our weaknesses, but that does not justify deception. Let us strive to live with truthfulness and without a double life, trusting that God cares for us without our having to pretend.
exp.7:4:
The elders of Israel tell Samuel that he is now old and that his sons do not follow his example. So they ask him to appoint a king to rule over them, just like the other nations.

The leaders of the people speak, gathered in Ramah, where Samuel lived. His sons, who were judges, took bribes and twisted justice. Their complaint had some merit, but the desire to be like all the other nations showed that they wanted to stop depending on God as their king. God Himself made this clear to Samuel shortly afterward.

For today: when we face real problems, such as injustice or the failures of leaders, let us first seek God's guidance in prayer, and not thoughtlessly copy the world's solutions.
exp.6:16:
This verse says that Samuel would return to Ramah, his home, after traveling to other places. There he also attended to the people's cases and built an altar to the Lord. The source's comment on the old wording is about two words that do not appear in the King James text, so that sentence is removed, and the name of God is rendered as it appears in the verse.

This passage is the narrator of the book speaking. It describes what Samuel's life was like after Israel turned back to God and defeated the Philistines. Samuel made a yearly circuit through Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah to guide the people, and then he ended up at his house. It is noteworthy that, even in his own home, he kept worship of God going.

For today: make your home a place where God is honored. Even if you work or serve away from home, set aside time each day in your household to pray, read the Bible and give thanks to him.
exp.16:52:
This verse tells that the Israelites, after chasing the fleeing Philistines, came back and plundered the enemy camp. The sentence that explains the word meaning "returning" and the word meaning "spoiled" has been left out, since those words are not in the verse your reader sees. What is clear from the verse is that they carried off what was there: supplies, weapons and other goods.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book who relates what happened. Goliath had just fallen at the hands of David, and the Philistine army had fled. Now Israel, which had trembled with fear before, gathers the fruits of a victory that began when a young man trusted in God. The account shows that the courage of one man encouraged the whole people.

For today: when someone takes a step of faith, they can encourage others to follow. And after a victory, it is good to remember that it was God who gave it, and to use what has been received with gratitude.
exp.24:22:
This verse tells how Abigail, when she saw David, quickly got down from her donkey and bowed low to the ground with her face toward the earth. The phrase about getting down quickly means she dismounted right away from her animal. The actions of falling forward and bowing down show a gesture of deep respect and humility.

David was coming in anger with his men to kill Nabal, because Nabal had refused him help and had treated him with contempt, even though David had protected Nabal's shepherds. Abigail, Nabal's wife, learned what had happened from a servant and went out in great haste with provisions to stop the disaster. Here the narrative shows her acting with wisdom and courage.

For today: when a conflict is about to break out, humility and quickness to seek peace can prevent a great deal of harm. Sometimes it is wise to set aside pride and speak calmly before anger makes the decision for us.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that there is none holy like the Lord, that there is no other God beside him, and that there is no refuge as secure as our God. "Holy" means set apart, pure, unique in his goodness. The word translated here as "rock" in the Hebrew is an image of firm and steady protection.

Speaking is Hannah, who for years could not have children and had asked God for a son. Now she has left her son Samuel in the service of the Lord at the sanctuary. Her prayer is one of gratitude. She praises God because he sustained her in the face of those who despised her, and she sets this against the human arrogance she mentions next.

When you face a difficult situation, do not place your security only in your own strength, your money, or other people. Go to God in prayer, as Hannah did, and rest in the fact that he is a firm rock who does not fail.
exp.11:2:
Samuel stands before all the people and invites them to accuse him, if they can, of any wrong. He asks whether he has taken anyone's ox or donkey, whether he has cheated or oppressed anyone, or whether he has accepted a bribe to look the other way. A bribe is what is meant by the bribe he asks about, and to look the other way is to let an injustice pass in exchange for money. If there were anything like that, he promises to make it right.

Samuel speaks at the end of his time as judge. Israel had just asked for a king, and he now presents them to the new king, Saul. Now elderly, he wants to make it clear that he exercised his authority with honesty. The anointed one here refers to the king. All the people acknowledge that Samuel was upright.

For today: live in such a way that we can be held accountable without fear. Let us take care with the small decisions about money, work, and how we treat others, so that our conscience and our witness are clean before God and before people.
exp.4:3:
They say that the Philistines got up another morning and found Dagon, their god, fallen face down before the ark of the Lord. This time the idol was broken: its head and the palms of its hands had been cut off on the threshold, and only the trunk was left. The phrase "rising again" means "getting up once more," and the threshold is the entrance of the doorway.

The narrator tells what happened after the Philistines captured Israel's ark and placed it in the temple of Dagon, as a sign of victory over the God of Israel. Dagon was a deity greatly honored by them. The text shows that the Lord is not just one god among others, and that he is not defeated even when his ark is in enemy hands.

Today we can remember that nothing and no one takes the place of God. If something in my life competes with Him, it is better to surrender it to Him, because only God stands firm.
exp.1:26:
A prophet, whom the Bible calls "man of God," comes to the priest Eli with a message from the Lord. God reminds him that he made himself known to the family of Eli's ancestor, who would be Aaron, back when they were still slaves in Egypt. The words "did I plainly appear" mean that God had shown himself clearly to them.

Eli was both priest and judge of Israel, but his sons, Hophni and Phinehas, abused their office and despised the offerings. Eli did not correct them firmly. Through this messenger, God begins by reminding him of his past kindness, to show that the sin of that family was even more serious, since they had received so much.

For today: God has given us much, beginning with rescuing us and calling us. Before asking him for anything, let us remember what he has already done for us. This helps us live with gratitude and not put anything, not even our family, above him.
exp.10:7:
It says that Saul counted the army in a place called Bezek. There were three hundred thousand men of Israel and thirty thousand of Judah. Some scholars think the numbers are literal, and others believe the word for "thousand" could have meant groups or military units. It is not known for certain.

The narrator tells how Saul gathered the people to rescue Jabesh-gilead, a city threatened by Nahash the Ammonite. Saul sent the pieces of the oxen as an urgent call. God moved the people's hearts, and everyone came out united. This count shows that they responded in great numbers, including Judah, the southern tribe.

For today: when someone suffers injustice or serious need, we should not just stand by and watch. Let us ask God for courage and unity, and help together, each with what we have.
exp.4:9:
The explanation says that the Philistines sent the ark of God to Ekron, another of their cities. When it arrived, the people cried out in fear: "They have brought the ark of the God of Israel to us, to slay us and our people!"

The one speaking is the people of Ekron. They had already seen that the ark had caused great harm in Ashdod and Gath, so they were afraid before anything happened to them. The Philistines had captured the ark in battle, but they did not know what to do with it. They wanted to move it away from their cities, not to obey God.

For today: it is possible to recognize that God is powerful and still try to keep Him at a distance. Today we can stop running from God and come near to Him with humility, trusting in His mercy.
exp.13:42:
Saul asks Jonathan to tell him what he has done. Jonathan answers honestly: he tasted a little honey with the end of the rod he was carrying in his hand. Then he asks, with grief and amazement, whether for that he has to die.

Saul had made a rash vow: no one was to eat that day while they pursued the enemy. Jonathan did not know about it, because he was not there when it was made. Since Saul received no answer from God, he cast lots to find the guilty one, and the lot fell on his own son. Here Saul questions him, and Jonathan answers without hiding anything.

Jonathan teaches us to tell the truth even when it costs us. The scene also reminds us to think carefully before promising something so forcefully, because hasty decisions can hurt the people we love.
exp.15:4:
Samuel answers the elders of Bethlehem that he has come in peace, to offer a sacrifice to the Lord. He asks them to sanctify themselves, that is, to prepare and cleanse themselves to present themselves before God. He himself sanctifies Jesse and his sons, and invites them to the sacrifice.

The prophet Samuel is speaking. The elders were afraid, perhaps because Saul was king and Samuel was coming with a delicate errand. God had commanded him to anoint a new king among the sons of Jesse. The text does not explain why Samuel does not state his whole purpose; God himself had shown him how to proceed.

For today: before we draw near to God, it is good to prepare the heart with humility and sincerity. We can set aside a few minutes to pray, confess what weighs on us, and listen, knowing that God looks at what is within us.
exp.16:3:
The verse presents Goliath, a Philistine warrior from the city of Gath, who comes out into the space between the two armies. The word "champion" in the King James Version is the word used for this kind of warrior, and "camp" refers to the army's encampment. His height was six cubits and a span, roughly three meters by the most common calculation. Some ancient manuscripts say four cubits and a span, so the exact figure is debated.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel and the Philistines stand facing each other, each on its own hill, with the valley between them. The author introduces Goliath to show the enormous threat that had paralyzed Israel and to prepare for David's arrival.

For today: problems can seem like giants and leave us paralyzed. Before giving up, let us remember that God is greater than any threat, and ask him for the courage to take the next step.
exp.1:24:
When one person wrongs another, there are judges who can settle the matter. But if someone sins directly against God, who will be able to plead for him? Elí's sons did not listen to their father, and the explanation says that God had already decided to put them to death. The word "intreat" here means to plead or intercede on behalf of another.

Elí, an elderly priest, is rebuking his sons Hofni and Finehas. They abused their position at the sanctuary and led the people into sin. The closing words of the verse do not say that God took away their freedom; they show that, because of their persistent stubbornness, judgment was already coming. Some scholars see it as hardening that came from their own folly.

For today: do not take sin lightly or the calls to correct you. If someone warns you with love, listen to them, and come before God today with humility.
exp.22:20:
Saul responds to the people of Ziph with a blessing: "May the Lord bless you, for you have had compassion on me."

Saul, the king of Israel, pursues David with the intention of killing him. The Ziphites inform him where David is hiding, and Saul thanks them. But there is a sad irony here: he calls on the name of the Lord while he chases an innocent man whom God had chosen. His "compassion" is in fact help for his own obsession.

Today we can learn to examine our motives. It is easy to use spiritual words to justify actions that do not please God. Before we say "God bless you" or look for support, let us ask whether what we are doing is truly aligned with his will and with justice.
exp.8:22:
Samuel asks the cook to bring the portion of meat that he had given him and told him to set aside. The cook was the one who prepared the food for the feast. The verse says "I gave thee" and "Set it by thee."

Samuel is speaking at a feast at the high place, with about thirty guests. Saul had just said that he came from the smallest tribe. Samuel receives him with honor and gives him the best place. That separate portion shows that God had already prepared Saul for that day. Some believe the portion had a special value, but the text does not explain its meaning in detail.

God sees and prepares things for us long before we notice. When you feel small or unimportant, remember that God knows you and can have a place prepared for you. Trust in Him with humility.
exp.14:1:
Here God, called "the Lord of hosts," says that he remembers what Amalek did to Israel. The explanation of the other wording is removed here, since the reader's verse says "how he laid wait for him in the way," which needs no gloss. The attack is in the way that Israel came up from Egypt toward the promised land.

Samuel speaks to Saul, the first king of Israel, and passes on an order from God. That attack by Amalek is recounted in Exodus 17, and Deuteronomy 25 recalls that it was against the weak who were lagging behind. The verses that follow command that Amalek be destroyed, which is hard to read. Scholars explain it in different ways, and it is wise to read it with humility.

For today: God sees and remembers the unjust treatment that his people suffer. We can trust that justice is in his hands, and so we do not need to take revenge. We are also called to listen to and obey his voice attentively.
exp.13:19:
This verse tells how Saul gathered the soldiers who were with him and went to the place of the battle. There they saw that the Philistines, confused, were fighting among themselves: each one used his sword against his companion, and there was a very great slaughter. Saul's men were the ones who came together to face them.

Earlier, Jonathan and his armor-bearer had attacked a Philistine outpost, and God sent great fear and trembling over the enemy camp. Saul, noticing the uproar, stopped consulting the priest and went out to fight. The text presents this victory as the work of God, not only of men. Afterward, even Israelites who had been hiding decided to join in.

Today we can learn that God can change situations that seem impossible. When a person takes a step of faith, as Jonathan did, God can do more than we imagine. Trust, act in faith, and do not forget to give the glory to Him.
exp.21:13:
Ahimelech, the priest, answers King Saul with courage. He asks who among all the king's servants is as faithful as David. He reminds Saul that David is the king's son-in-law, that he carries out his orders, and that he is highly respected in the king's house. Honourable here means worthy of respect and good standing.

Saul accuses Ahimelech of conspiring with David, who is fleeing from him. Ahimelech did help David with bread and a sword, but he did so without knowing that David was being hunted. To him, David was a loyal servant of the king. His defense is sincere, though Saul, ruled by jealousy and suspicion, does not accept it.

For today: Ahimelech told the truth even while afraid. We can speak with honesty and respect when something is unjust, and trust God, even when others do not believe us.
exp.23:8:
David came out of the cave after Saul and called out to him from behind: "My lord the king!" When Saul turned around, David bowed with his face to the ground and paid him reverence, that is, a gesture of respect and humility. Saying that David "called out" means that he spoke in a loud voice.

David was hiding from Saul, who was pursuing him to kill him. Saul had gone into the cave without knowing that David and his men were inside. David could have killed him, but he did not want to, because Saul was the anointed of the LORD, the king set in place by God. Now he speaks to him with respect to show him that he is not his enemy.

For today: even when someone treats us unjustly, we can respond with respect and self-control, without seeking revenge. Leaving justice in God's hands keeps us from acting out of bitterness.
exp.14:15:
What it says: Samuel interrupts Saul's excuses and asks permission to tell him what God spoke to him during the night. Saul agrees and replies: "Say on."

Context: Samuel, the prophet, confronts Saul, the king. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites, but Saul and the people kept the best of the livestock. Saul says it was to offer as a sacrifice. Samuel stops him because before responding to the excuse, he wants Saul to hear what God actually said.

For today: Before justifying our decisions, it is wise to be quiet and listen to what God says in His Word. A humble attitude, like Saul's "Say on," helps us see our mistakes in time and correct our course.
exp.25:23:
This verse is a prayer and a statement from David. It says that just as he valued and protected Saul's life that day, he wants God to value and protect his life. "Much set by" means held in great value. "Tribulation" means distress, trouble or danger. David asks the Lord to deliver him from all of that.

David is speaking to Saul, the king who was pursuing him to kill him. That night David went into the camp and could have killed Saul while he slept, but he did not, because Saul was the Lord's anointed. Now he shows Saul the spear as proof of his innocence and entrusts his future to God.

For today: when someone treats you badly, do not take revenge. Do what is right, treat others with respect, and leave your defense in God's hands, trusting that He cares for you.
exp.30:11:
The explanation says that the valiant men of Jabesh-gilead walked all night to Beth-shan. There they took down from the wall the bodies of Saul and his sons, which the Philistines had hung up. Then they carried them to Jabesh and burned them. "Took" means they took the bodies down from the wall, and "burnt them" is the act of burning them.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Saul had died in battle, and the Philistines displayed his body to humiliate him. Years earlier, Saul had rescued Jabesh-gilead (1 Samuel 11), and for that reason they showed him gratitude and loyalty. Some wonder why they burned the bodies, since this was not the common practice in Israel. The Bible does not explain it, and perhaps it was done to protect them from further insult.

Today we can remember with gratitude those who helped us, even when they can no longer repay us. A brave act of respect and care, done at a cost to oneself, honors God and comforts others.
exp.26:1:
It says that David arose and went with his six hundred men to live with Achish, the son of Maoch, king of Gath, a Philistine city. The word "passed over" means that he crossed over into Philistine territory. Gath was the city of Goliath, the giant whom David had defeated.

The narrator tells us what David decided after thinking in his heart that Saul would one day kill him. He had been pursued many times and was tired of running. Escaping among Israel's enemies seemed to him the way out. The Bible does not say here that God had commanded him to do this, and many readers see in this a moment of fear rather than of faith.

When fear weighs heavily on us, we may make decisions only to get out of the problem. Before acting, it is wise to pray, to seek counsel, and to remember God's promises, since He had already anointed David as the future king.
exp.23:20:
Saul says that he now understands, with complete clarity, that David is going to be king. He adds that the kingdom of Israel will be "firm and secure in your hand," that is, well established and safe under his rule. It is a statement that prepares the request in the next verse.

King Saul is speaking. David has just spared his life in a cave, when he could have killed him. Saul, moved, publicly acknowledges that God is with David. Since he knows David will reign, he asks him not to destroy his family when that day comes. Some think his repentance was sincere but temporary, since he afterward continued pursuing David.

For today: when God shows you something clearly, do not stop at feeling it. Respond with steady obedience. And if someone admits their wrong, try to respond with the same peace and kindness David showed.
exp.13:0:
One day, the verse says, Jonathan, the son of King Saul, spoke to the young man who carried his armor: "Come, let us go over to the Philistines' outpost, which is on the other side." An outpost is a group of enemy soldiers stationed in one place. Jonathan did not tell his father.

The narrator of the book speaks here and introduces Jonathan. Israel was at war with the Philistines, and Saul's army was small, about six hundred men. The verses that follow show Saul sitting still under a pomegranate tree while Jonathan acts. The Bible does not explain why he did not tell his father; some think he wanted to avoid a "no," but that is an interpretation.

For today: when you see something that God places on your heart to do, take a step of faith, but with humility and prayer. Doing something brave is not the same as acting in secret; seek wise counsel before you decide.
exp.22:21:
Saul asks the men of Ziph to go back and check carefully. They must find out the exact place where David hides and who has seen him there. The word "prepare" here means getting ready and making sure everything is in order, and "subtle" means very skillful at avoiding being caught. Saul says he has been told that David is very cunning.

King Saul, who pursues David out of jealousy and fear, is the one speaking. The Ziphites, people of that region of Judah, have just offered to hand David over to him. Saul blesses them in the name of the LORD, though he is seeking something unjust. He wants certainty before he acts, because he knows David has already slipped away from him.

Today we can notice how much effort is spent when the heart is full of envy. Saul calls on God, yet he pursues his own desire. It is worth asking ourselves whether what we do truly pleases God, or whether we only decorate it with pious words.
exp.1:28:
God reproaches Eli: why have you trampled on my sacrifices and offerings that I commanded to be brought to the tabernacle? Moreover, Eli has placed his sons above God, for they have grown fat on the best of the people's offerings. The "offerings" are the gifts brought to God, and "honour" here means giving them the first place.

A "man of God" speaks, a prophet whose name is not given, sent to Eli the priest. God reminds him that his family was chosen to serve. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing the offerings (1 Samuel 2:12-17), and Eli did not restrain them firmly. That is why judgment is coming.

For today: examine whom you give first place. Sometimes, out of affection or to avoid conflict, we let pass what offends God. Truly loving someone includes correcting them gently and putting God first.
exp.8:24:
This verse tells that Samuel and Saul came down from the high place, a raised spot where sacrifices and meals were held, into the city. There Samuel talked with Saul upon the top of the house, that is, the flat roof of the house, a quiet and secluded place.

The narrator now relates what followed the feast. Samuel already knew, because God had shown him, that Saul would be the first king of Israel. The text does not say what they talked about that night; some think Samuel was preparing him for what was coming, but that is a guess.

For today: before major decisions or callings, God often uses moments of calm and conversation. Look for quiet spaces to listen, and surround yourself with wise people who speak to you with patience.
exp.16:27:
Eliab, David's eldest brother, overhears him speaking with the soldiers and becomes very angry. He confronts him with harsh questions: why he came down, and with whom he left the few sheep. He accuses him of pride, meaning arrogance, and of having a wicked heart, that is, bad intentions. He says David came down only to watch the battle.

Eliab speaks in the camp of Israel, where the army is afraid of Goliath. David, who had arrived sent by his father with supplies, asks what reward there will be for the one who defeats the Philistine. Eliab may have felt embarrassed or annoyed, but the text does not state his exact reasons. What we do see is that he judges David without knowing his heart.

For today: when someone criticizes you harshly, do not respond with the same anger. David answered with calm and went on with what God placed on his heart. And we too must be careful not to judge the intentions of others.
exp.9:3:
He says that when Saul meets three men going up to Bethel, they will greet him and give him two loaves of bread, and he will receive them from their hands. "As soon as they have greeted you" means "as soon as they greet you." The loaves were part of the offering they were carrying to worship God.

The speaker is the prophet Samuel, who had just anointed Saul as the future king of Israel. He gives him a series of concrete signs to confirm that God was with him. It is interesting that Saul, being the chosen one, was to receive the bread with humility, and not ask for it or demand it. Scholars do not agree on the exact meaning of the gesture, but it is clear that God cared for every detail of the journey.

Today we can learn to receive with gratitude the help God sends us through other people, even in simple things like a loaf of bread, and to recognize his care in the small details of each day.
exp.15:18:
Saul sent messengers to Jesse, David's father, asking him to send his son. He described David as "the one who is with the sheep," meaning the one who looks after the flock.

Here King Saul is speaking. He was troubled by an evil spirit, and his servants suggested he look for someone who could play music. One of them recommended David. Saul did not know that God had already chosen David in secret to be the future king. It is striking that David was out in the field, doing simple work, when he was sent for.

For today: God often prepares people through ordinary and little-seen everyday tasks. Be faithful in what you have been given to do today, even when no one notices; that way you will be ready when God opens a door.
exp.25:9:
David says that God himself will decide Saul's fate. Where the explanation mentions "Vive Jehová," that is a way of swearing an oath, so the phrase is rendered as: "as surely as the Lord lives." David names three possibilities: that the Lord will strike Saul, that Saul's natural day to die will come, or that he will die in battle. In every case the decision rests in God's hands, not David's.

David speaks with his nephew Abishai in Saul's camp at night. Saul had been pursuing David to kill him, and Abishai saw an opportunity to end the threat. David refused, because Saul was the Lord's anointed, the king chosen by God, and David would not take justice into his own hands.

When someone wounds us or treats us unjustly, we can resist the temptation to take revenge. Trusting that God is the righteous judge frees us to act with integrity and to wait on him.
exp.1:10:
Elkanah returns to his home in Ramah (the Ramatha of that older version), and leaves his young son, Samuel, behind in Shiloh. "Ministered" means that he served or helped with the tasks of worship. He did this "before Eli the priest," that is, under his supervision.

Hannah, the mother, had just prayed with gratitude, and Elkanah had been with her. She had promised to give to God the son she was given, and here that promise is fulfilled. The verse works as a bridge: after Hannah's song, which speaks of a God who cares for his own, we see a child serving, and immediately it is set in contrast with the sons of Eli, who were corrupt.

For today: serving God does not require being great or perfect. Samuel was a child in an environment with bad examples, and yet he served faithfully. We can do the same with whatever simple things we have at hand, even when others around us do not give a good witness.
exp.18:7:
It says that war broke out again with the Philistines, and that David went out to fight against them. He defeated them with a great slaughter, and the enemies fled before him. The phrase about war starting again simply means that the fighting began once more.

This account comes from the narrator of 1 Samuel. It follows directly after Jonathan succeeded in reconciling his father Saul with David. Saul had sworn not to kill him. David went back to serving him and kept bringing victories to Israel. But the next verse shows that jealousy and an evil spirit took hold of Saul again, so the peace did not last long.

For today: do your work well even when someone looks at you with envy or distrust. David stayed faithful and useful, without seeking revenge. That does not always prevent problems, but it keeps your conscience clear and leaves the outcome in God's hands.
exp.4:7:
This verse tells how the Philistine rulers came together to decide what to do with the ark of God. The phrase "sent and gathered" means they had everyone called together. The "lords" were the rulers of the five Philistine cities. They decided to move the ark to Gath, another Philistine city.

The Philistines had taken the ark in battle. In Ashdod, the people suffered a plague, and their god Dagon fell before the ark. The leaders speak with fear, but they do not repent. They only move the ark from place to place, as if the problem were a matter of location. The following text shows that the plague followed them.

For today: when God confronts us, it is tempting to change our place or our excuse instead of surrendering our heart. God does not evade us; let us ask him for humility to listen to him and obey him.
exp.6:13:
This verse says that Israel got back the cities the Philistines had taken from them, from Ekron to Gath, along with the land around them. "Restored" means given back. The "coasts" are the surrounding land and boundaries of each city. The Amorites were the Canaanite peoples of the region. There was also peace between Israel and them.

Here the narrator of the book summarizes what happened after the people put away their idols and turned back to God under Samuel's leadership. God gave them victory over the Philistines, and Samuel set up the stone Ebenezer, saying, "Hitherto hath the LORD helped us." This verse shows the result of that help.

For today: when we return to God with our whole heart, He can restore what was lost. It will not always be the same or immediate, but we can remember His past help and trust that He will remain with us.
exp.13:37:
Saul calls the leaders of the people to come forward. He asks them to investigate and find out who committed a sin that day. The phrase "Draw ye near hither" in the verse above is the same as "come closer here," and "the chief of the people" means the leaders or those with the most authority.

Saul speaks after God did not answer his inquiry about pursuing the Philistines. He takes that silence as a sign that there is a hidden sin. Without knowing it, Jonathan had eaten honey, breaking an oath that Saul had imposed on the army. Some think Saul acts with sincere zeal, but his hasty oath was also a mistake.

When God seems silent, it is worth examining our hearts with humility. But let us be careful not to rush to judge others, and let us first acknowledge our own hasty decisions.
exp.24:30:
Abigail tells David that, when God makes him king, he will have no burden on his conscience. A "stumbling block" is something that makes a person fall, and "trouble of heart" is an inner unrest. She asks him not to shed blood without cause or take revenge with his own hand. "Take heed" means "be careful." In the end, she asks him to remember her when God blesses him.

Abigail, the wife of Nabal, speaks. Nabal was a foolish man who treated David and his men badly. David was armed and set out to kill Nabal and his household. Abigail goes out to meet him with provisions and stops him with humility, trusting that God will care for David and bring about justice.

When someone wrongs us, anger pushes us to respond at once. This passage invites us to pause, listen to wise counsel, and leave justice in God's hands, so that we do not carry regret afterward.
exp.30:9:
The Philistines put Saul's weapons in the temple of Ashtaroth, a goddess they worshiped. They also hung the king's body on the wall of Beth-shan, a nearby town. The word "hung" simply means they displayed it publicly, as a sign of victory and mockery.

The narrator of the book tells this without speaking in the first person. He describes the tragic end of Saul, who died on Mount Gilboa. The Philistines believed their victory came from their gods, and that is why they displayed the spoils. Afterward, the men of Jabesh-gilead rescued the bodies, grateful for what Saul had done for them earlier.

For today: Saul's life reminds us that disobedience to God has painful consequences. Today we can ask him for a humble and obedient heart. We can also honor with gratitude those who have helped us, as the people of Jabesh did.
exp.29:27:
This verse is part of a list of places. David sends gifts from the plunder to the people who lived in Aroer, in Siphmoth, and in Eshtemoa. Plunder means goods taken in war. "Siphmoth" and "Eshtemoa" are old names of towns in the south of Judah. Today they would be written Siphmoth and Eshtemoa.

The narrator of the book speaks here, telling what David did. He had recovered everything the Amalekites had taken at Ziklag. Instead of keeping the riches for himself, he shared them with the leaders of Judah who had supported or helped him while he was fleeing from Saul. Some details about these places are uncertain, since not all of them are known for sure.

For today: David saw the victory as a blessing from God, not only as something of his own. We can ask ourselves whom I can bless with what God has given me, and give thanks to those who have supported us in difficult times.
exp.1:9:
Verse 10 says that those who oppose God will be broken before Him, and that God will make His power heard like thunder from heaven. He will judge the whole earth, even to its farthest places. He will also give strength to His King and lift up the horn of His anointed one; the horn was a sign of power and victory, and "anointed" means one who has been set apart with oil.

Hannah speaks in her prayer of thanksgiving, after giving her son Samuel to serve God. She celebrates that God lifts up the humble and brings down the proud. There is not yet a king in Israel, so many see here a look forward: to anointed kings and, for Christians, to Jesus.

Today we can trust that God does justice, even when we do not see it right away. If you feel small or unfairly treated, bring your situation to God in prayer, without depending only on your own strength.
exp.11:6:
Samuel asks the people to stand still and listen. The word translated "stand still" in the verse above means to wait or to hold your position. The phrase about presenting a case against them is rendered in the verse above as "reason with you," which means he is going to lay out the matter before them. The "righteous acts" refers to the faithful and just deeds of God, that is, what He did to save and care for Israel, both for them and for their ancestors.

Samuel is already an old man, and the people have asked for a king. He first defends his own honest conduct and then, as in a trial, goes over the history of God's faithfulness. He wants to show them that asking for a king was a way of distrusting the Lord, who had always rescued them.

For today: before we worry about the future, let us remember how God has sustained us in the past. Remembering His works strengthens trust and helps us not to seek security in other things.
exp.8:19:
Samuel tells Saul not to worry anymore about his father's donkeys, because they have been found. Then he asks him a question: for whom is all the desire of Israel? And he answers: for Saul and his family. "Don't worry" is the same as "do not be concerned," and "three days ago" means "three days back."

Saul was looking for the lost donkeys and came to Samuel, the seer, or prophet. God had already told Samuel that Saul would be the first king. That is why Samuel speaks this way. Some understand "the desire of Israel" as the people's longing to have a king. Saul, surprised, answers with humility.

God can use ordinary things, even a search for lost animals, to lead us toward his purpose. Perhaps today something small worries you, or you feel that you are not worth much. Trust that God sees further than you do, and is attentive to your path.
exp.23:0:
He says that David left where he was and settled in hard-to-reach places, at En-gedi. Strongholds are places protected by nature, such as caves, cliffs, or natural fortresses. En-gedi lies by the Dead Sea, in a desert area with rocks and springs.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who tells the story. David was fleeing from King Saul, who pursued him out of jealousy and fear of losing the throne, even though David had already been anointed as the future king. Shortly before, David had spared Saul's life on another occasion, and now he had to look for refuge again. The verses that follow show that Saul came after him with three thousand men.

For today: in times of pressure or injustice, seeking a safe place is not a lack of faith. We can protect ourselves with prudence, rest in God, and keep trusting that He keeps His promises, without responding with revenge.
exp.7:16:
It says the king would take a tenth of the people's sheep and goats. "Will take a tenth" means taking one out of every ten. In the end, the people would no longer be free and would live as servants of the king, working for him.

Samuel is the one speaking. The people had asked for a king so that they would be like the other nations, and Samuel was saddened. God told him to warn them clearly about how a king would rule. Even so, the people did not want to listen and kept demanding a king. Some see here a rejection of God being their King.

For today: before we insist on getting something, let us think about what it will cost us. What we desire can end up controlling us. Let us ask God for wisdom and trust that He cares for us better than any human power.
exp.22:22:
Saúl asks the men of Ziph to investigate carefully. They must examine all of David's hiding places, make sure of where he is, and return with solid information. "Certainty" means assurance, something proven. "The thousands of Judah" refers to the clans or large groups within the tribe of Judah. Saúl promises to go with them and search for him throughout the whole territory.

King Saúl is speaking, pursuing David out of jealousy and fear of losing the throne. The Ziphites offered to help him, and Saúl blesses them in the name of Jehová, although his goal is unjust. Meanwhile, David remains protected and receives warning in time.

We can use religious words without our hearts being aligned with God. Saúl speaks of blessing while he pursues an innocent man. Today it is worth asking ourselves whether our plans truly please God, or whether we merely cover them with spiritual language.
exp.27:14:
Samuel asks Saul why he has troubled him by bringing him up. Saul answers that he is in great distress: the Philistines are attacking him, God has departed from him, and he no longer answers him, neither by prophets nor by dreams. That is why he called Samuel, so that he could tell him what to do.

Saul, the first king of Israel, had disobeyed God, and now he faced a war without divine guidance. In his desperation, he sought out a medium, something the Law forbade. The text presents the appearance as Samuel, though scholars debate how it should be understood. What is clear is that Samuel's answer confirms the judgment already announced.

When we are distressed, it is better to return to God with humility and repentance than to seek answers by forbidden or desperate means. He continues to listen to those who come to him sincerely.
exp.19:23:
It says that David went to hide himself in the field, just as he and Jonathan had agreed. When the new moon came, which was a monthly festival, King Saul sat down to eat. The word meaning "went" appears with an older spelling, and "new" here refers to the new moon, the beginning of the month. "Eat bread" means to take a meal, a feast.

This is part of the account in which Saul seeks to kill David. Jonathan, Saul's son and David's faithful friend, had made a plan to discover his father's intentions. David was to be absent from the king's table, and Jonathan would watch Saul's reaction. The narrator describes the scene before the empty seat is noticed.

For today: when we face threats or injustice, we can act with prudence, seek the counsel of loyal friends, and trust in God, as David and Jonathan did, without seeking revenge or acting in haste.
exp.6:14:
This verse says that Samuel was judge over Israel for all the days of his life. The word "judged" does not refer only to handing down sentences in a court. In that time, a judge also guided, corrected and defended the people. "All the days of his life" means that Samuel served until the end of his days.

The narrator of the book tells this, summarizing Samuel's leadership. It comes after Israel returned to God and the Philistines were defeated. The verses that follow explain how he worked: each year he traveled through Bethel, Gilgal and Mizpah, and then returned to Ramah, where he built an altar to the LORD.

For today: serving God and others with steadiness, not only in special moments. A faithful life, day after day, leaves a lasting mark.
exp.23:6:
David told his men that God would keep him from harming Saul. He calls Saul "my lord" and "the anointed of the LORD," that is, the king whom God had set apart with oil to rule. To "stretch out my hand" means to attack or do violence to someone. "His own" refers to his companions.

David and his men were hiding from Saul, who was pursuing him to kill him. Saul went into a cave without knowing that David was inside. The men saw in this a sign from God, but David only cut off the edge of Saul's robe, and afterward his conscience troubled him. Even though Saul was his enemy, David respected the place God had given him.

For today: even when we have the chance to take revenge, we can choose to trust God and not repay evil with evil. Sometimes the right thing is not the easiest thing, nor what others advise us to do.
exp.0:15:
Anna asks Eli not to think of her as a wicked woman or as someone without reverence for God. Her words mean she is not an evil person and does not lack the fear of God. She explains that she has been praying for so long because her sorrow was overwhelming.

It is Anna speaking, a woman who could not have children and suffered greatly because of it. She was praying silently in the sanctuary, moving her lips without her voice being heard. The priest Eli thought she was drunk and rebuked her. She answers him with humility and sincerity, and he blesses her.

For today: when you are deeply troubled, you can tell God everything you feel, even when others do not understand you or judge you wrongly. Anna poured out her soul before God, and afterward she left in peace. Do the same with your burdens.
exp.22:28:
The text of verse 29 seems to have come through empty. The verse reads: "And David went up from thence, and dwelt in strong holds at En–gedi."

It says David left that place and went to live at En-gedi, an area of caves and rocks, with springs, beside the Dead Sea. "Strong holds" refers to places that are hard to attack, like natural fortresses.

The narrator tells what happened after David escaped from Saul, thanks to the Philistines distracting Saul. David was still on the run, for Saul was pursuing him unjustly. En-gedi gave him shelter and time to catch his breath. There the episode will later take place in which David spares Saul's life.

For today: when a lull comes in the middle of a trial, do not waste it. Rest, seek refuge in God, and prepare for what comes next. He often gives us safe places along the way.
exp.11:22:
Samuel says it would be a sin against God for him to stop praying for the people. "Far be it from me" means "I will never do that." "Ceasing" means stopping or giving up, and the verse uses that idea of stopping prayer. He also promises to keep teaching them "the good and the right way," that is, the correct and honest way of living before God.

Samuel speaks in his farewell address, when Israel already has a king. The people had asked for a king and admitted that this was a mistake. Samuel does not reject them or become bitter. He reminds them that God will not abandon them, and that he himself will continue serving them through prayer and teaching.

For today: praying for others is not optional. Even when someone has failed us or does not listen to us, we can keep interceding for that person and teaching them with patience and good example.
exp.2:18:
It says that Samuel grew up and that God was with him. It also says that God did not let any of his words "fall to the ground." That expression means that nothing Samuel announced went unfulfilled. Samuel's words proved to be true.

The narrator is the author of the book. Samuel was a young man who served at Shiloh, alongside the priest Eli. God had given him a hard message of judgment against Eli's house, and Samuel delivered it honestly. This verse shows the result: God backed Samuel, and soon all Israel recognized him as a faithful prophet.

For today: God values those who speak the truth with humility, even when it costs them. Ask Him to be with you, and be honest in what you say, trusting that He cares for your witness over time.
exp.27:10:
Here the woman asks Saul whom he wants her to call up. Saul asks her to bring up Samuel, the prophet who had already died. "Bring me up" means "call him for me."

Saul, in disguise, and a woman who consulted the dead at Endor are speaking. Saul was frightened by the Philistine army, and God was no longer answering him. He himself had driven out the mediums, yet now he was doing exactly what he had forbidden. The Bible does not fully explain what happened next, and interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: when you feel fear and see no answer, do not look for forbidden shortcuts. Return to God with humility, even when you are in silence, because He remains the only safe refuge.
exp.12:15:
Saul, his son Jonathan, and the soldiers who were with them stayed in Gibeah, a place in the territory of Benjamin. Meanwhile, the Philistines, Israel's enemies, had set up their camp at Michmash. The word "present" here refers to the people who were gathered with them. There were two armies facing each other, not far from one another.

Here it is not a character speaking, but the narrator of the book. Shortly before, Samuel had told Saul that his kingdom would not last, because he did not obey God. Samuel leaves, and Saul tells his people: only about six hundred men remain. The account shows a weakened king, with a small army and a huge threat in front of him.

For today: when you feel small before a big problem, do not act out of fear alone. Stop, pray, and seek to obey God in what you already know He has asked of you. His guidance is worth more than any hasty plan.
exp.14:13:
Samuel asks Saul a question that sounds simple: where is the noise of sheep and oxen coming from that I can hear? The "bleating" is the sound the sheep make, and the "lowing" is the deep sound the oxen make. A monument is a memorial that Saul set up to his own glory.

Samuel speaks with Saul after the war against the Amalekites. God had commanded that everything be destroyed, but Saul said, "I have carried out the word of the LORD." The living animals showed the opposite. Samuel does not accuse him right away; he lets the evidence speak and lets Saul explain himself.

For today: saying "I already obeyed" is easy, but the facts show the truth. Let us ask God to make us honest enough to recognize where we have obeyed only halfway, without excuses or cover-ups.
exp.30:6:
The explanation says that the Israelites who lived on the other side of the valley (probably the Valley of Jezreel) and on the other side of the Jordan learned that the army had fled and that Saul and his sons had died. So they abandoned their cities and ran away. The Philistines came and settled in those cities.

No one is speaking here; it is the narrator of the book, who recounts the consequences of the defeat on Mount Gilboa. The king's death left the people without protection or direction, and the Philistines gained territory. The text does not explain more; it only shows how serious the fall was.

For today: when firm guidance is missing, fear can make us let go of what God had entrusted to us. Let us seek strength in God and live united, so that we do not flee at the first defeat.
exp.30:7:
The explanation says that on the day after the battle, the Philistines went out to the field to take the valuable things from the dead soldiers. There they found the bodies of Saul and his three sons lying on mount Gilboa. Stripping the fallen means taking their weapons, clothing and belongings, and the bodies lying there means they had been left on the ground.

It is part of the account of the end of Saul's reign, the first king of Israel. The narrator tells with simplicity how the defeat ended. Earlier, Saul had turned away from God, and here we see the sad end of his life. At the same time, the story prepares the way for David to become king.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and power or reputation do not last forever. Today you can choose to obey God and trust in Him, instead of relying only on your position or your own strength.
exp.15:19:
Here the account tells us that Jesse, David's father, prepared a gift: a donkey loaded with bread, a bottle of wine, and a young goat. He sent it all to Saul with David. The words "sent them" are the wording of the verse itself, and the phrase "by David his son" means that David carried the gift himself.

The account describes what happened after Saul asked for David to be brought to him, because a servant had recommended him as a brave and prudent musician. It was customary to bring a gift when appearing before a king. Jesse acts with respect and humility. The text does not explain his motives any further.

For today: God often begins great things with simple gestures. David came before the king with bread, wine, and a young goat, not with pride. Serve with humility in small things, and let God open the doors.
exp.1:34:
God promises to raise up a faithful priest, someone who will act according to what is in his heart and in his mind, that is, according to his desires and his will. To that priest he will give a sure house, meaning a lasting line of descendants, and he will walk before God's anointed one forever. The word "raise" here is the same as "raise up."

A man of God speaks to the priest Eli. His sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were abusing their office, and Eli did not correct them. Because of this, God announces judgment on that house. Many believe the faithful priest points first to Samuel or to Zadok, though some also see in him a shadow of Christ. Interpreters do not fully agree.

For today: even when others fail, God still looks for faithful people. Ask him to give you a heart that seeks to please him more than to gain something for yourself.
exp.5:5:
This verse is a question that serves as a warning. The speakers are telling the Philistine people: do not be stubborn like the Egyptians and Pharaoh. "Harden the heart" means refusing to obey or to acknowledge God. When God punished them, the Egyptians in the end let the Israelites go.

The speakers are the Philistine priests and diviners. They had captured the ark of the LORD, and since then they had suffered plagues. Now they advise returning it with an offering, so as not to repeat Egypt's stubbornness. Interpreters debate whether they truly believed or only acted out of fear, but they knew the story of the exodus.

For today: when God corrects us, it is better to listen quickly and change course than to resist until we suffer more. A humble heart saves much pain.
exp.19:8:
Jonathan answers David firmly: "Far be it from you!" He promises that if he were to learn that his father had firmly decided to harm him, he would tell him without fail. "Malice" here means ill intent, and "determined" means decided or already settled.

David speaks to Jonathan because he fears that King Saul wants to kill him. He asks him to find out Saul's attitude during the New Moon feast. Jonathan, Saul's son, is David's loyal friend, and the two made a covenant before God. That is why David trusts him, and Jonathan does not hesitate to promise his help, even though it puts him in tension with his own father.

Today it teaches us the value of sincere loyalty. A good friend tells the truth, even when it is difficult, and protects the other person. Think of someone who trusts you and look for a concrete way to support them honestly this week.
exp.9:12:
He says that Saul stopped prophesying and then went up to the high place, an elevated site where people would often worship and offer sacrifices. Prophesying here means speaking or praising under the impulse of God's Spirit, not only foretelling future events.

The narrator tells what happened when Samuel had already anointed Saul as the future king. God gave him a sign: the Spirit came upon him and he joined a group of prophets. The people were amazed, and the saying "Is Saul also among the prophets?" arose. Some think it was an expression of surprise, others that it was mockery; the text does not make this clear. Then Saul arrived at the high place, and his uncle asked him what had happened.

For today: a strong spiritual experience is not enough; what counts is steady obedience. Let us ask God to make us faithful in daily life as well.
exp.12:21:
It tells us that when the day of battle came, the soldiers of Israel had no swords or spears. Only Saul and his son Jonathan had them.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Earlier, it is explained that the Philistines did not allow any blacksmiths to remain in Israel, so that the Israelites could not make weapons. The people depended on them even to sharpen their farming tools. In this way the text shows how weak and subjugated the nation was.

For today: sometimes we feel without resources in the face of a big problem. This verse reminds us that a lack of means is not the end of the story. God can work even when we see ourselves as small, so we can pray, trust, and take the next step with humility, without relying only on what we have.
exp.27:19:
This verse says that Saul fell suddenly to the ground, stretched out full length on his body. He was filled with fear because of what Samuel had told him, and he was left without strength. Moreover, he had eaten nothing all day or all night.

Saul, the king of Israel, was desperate because the Philistines were coming to attack him and God no longer answered him. So he sought out a woman who consulted the dead, something God's law forbade. What appeared to him announced his defeat and his death. Scholars debate how to understand this scene, but the message is clear: Saul had disobeyed God.

For today: when we are in trouble, let us seek God with humility and obedience, not forbidden shortcuts. And let us remember that fear, fasting and exhaustion weaken us; caring for the body matters too.
exp.26:5:
This verse says that King Achish gave David the city of Ziklag that same day. From then on, Ziklag belonged to the kings of Judah, and the text adds that it has remained so "unto this day." That phrase was written by someone telling the story long after it happened.

David had fled from Saul and sought refuge among the Philistines, Israel's enemies. He asked Achish for a place of his own to live, rather than staying in the royal city, where he would be watched. In this way he kept some distance, although the Bible does not explain all of his reasons, and scholars interpret them in different ways.

For today: God can care for us even in confusing or difficult times. Even when we do not understand the whole path, we can ask him for wisdom to decide well and trust that he is still at work.
exp.27:9:
Saul makes an oath to the woman. He invokes the name of the Lord, "As the Lord liveth," a solemn form of swearing. He promises that no harm will come to her ("there shall no punishment happen to thee") for practicing divination.

Saul is in disguise and speaks at night with a medium in Endor. He himself had driven the diviners out of the land, in keeping with God's law. The woman fears a trap that could cost her life. God no longer answered Saul, and in desperation he seeks what he had earlier forbidden. It is striking that he swears by God to ask for something God condemns.

For today: when we are desperate, it is easy to look for shortcuts and even to use holy words to justify them. Better to return to God with sincerity, for He receives the one who repents.
exp.15:2:
God tells Samuel to invite Jesse to the sacrifice. There God will show him what to do. The word "call" means "invite." The phrase "thou shalt anoint unto me" means that Samuel will pour oil on the person God points out. Samuel does not yet know who it will be; he only has to wait for God's direction.

God speaks to Samuel, who was grieving over Saul, the rejected king. God has already chosen a new king from among the sons of Jesse. Samuel fears that Saul will kill him, so God gives him a plan: go with a young cow and offer a sacrifice. The sacrifice was real, and it served as an occasion to gather Jesse's family.

For today: God often shows us only the next step, not the whole road. We can obey what we already know and trust that He will guide us afterward, even when we feel afraid or do not understand the full plan.
exp.17:20:
Saul says he will give his daughter Michal to David, but with a bad purpose: that she will be a "snare," that is, a trap, and that the Philistines will attack him. A "son-in-law" is the husband of one's daughter. "In the one of the twain" is understood as the second chance, since the first daughter, Merab, had already been given to another man.

The king Saul speaks. He was jealous of David because of his success and feared losing the throne. Since Michal loved David, Saul saw an opportunity: to use that marriage to expose David to death in battle, without getting his own hands dirty.

For today: jealousy can lead us to disguise as favor what is really harm. Let us ask God to heal our hearts from envy, and sincerely rejoice in the success of others, instead of seeing them as a threat.
exp.26:0:
He says that David thought to himself: "One day Saul is going to kill me. The best thing I can do is flee to the land of the Philistines." In this way Saul would stop searching for him throughout Israel, and David would escape from his hands. The explanation of the word "flee" and the other unusual word has been removed here, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

David is the one speaking, but he is speaking to himself. Saul, the king, was pursuing him out of jealousy, even though God had already anointed David. Tired of running, David takes refuge with Achish, king of Gath, an enemy of Israel. The Bible does not say here that God told him to do this, and he did not consult the Lord. Some see wisdom in his decision; others see a lack of faith.

When fear and weariness weigh on us, we can reach conclusions without praying. Before making a major decision, stop and ask God. Remember also his promises, even when the road is long.
exp.8:3:
This verse tells of the journey of Saul and his servant searching for his father's lost female donkeys. They passed through the hill country of Ephraim, through the land of Shalisha, through Shalim, and through the land of Benjamin, and they did not find them. The words "female donkeys" mean she-donkeys, and the word "found" means came upon or located. It was a long and tiring search that brought no result.

Context: the account is narrated by the author of the book, not by a character. Kish, Saul's father, had sent his son to look for the lost animals. Kingship is not yet mentioned here. Later, in this same search, Saul will meet the prophet Samuel. The exact locations are not known with certainty, but all of them lie in the central region of Israel.

For today: sometimes our efforts do not bear fruit, and we feel discouraged. This passage reminds us that God can use ordinary tasks, even those that seem like failures, to lead us to what He has prepared. Keep faithfully doing what is your responsibility and trust in God.
exp.25:10:
David says he will not lay a hand on Saul, because Saul is the one "anointed of the Lord," that is, the king whom God himself set apart for that office. Instead, he asks Abishai to take the spear that is by Saul's head and the water jug, and then the two of them should leave.

David speaks with Abishai, his companion, during the night, in Saul's camp. Saul was pursuing him to kill him, and Abishai saw the perfect opportunity to end the matter. David refuses: he prefers to wait for God to settle the matter in his own way and in his own time. Taking the spear and the jug would serve as proof that he could have harmed Saul and did not.

For today: when someone treats us unjustly and the opportunity for revenge presents itself, we can choose to trust God and not take justice into our own hands.
exp.7:2:
It says that Samuel's sons, Joel and Abijah, did not follow their father's good example. They let themselves be carried away by the love of money, accepted bribes, and twisted justice, that is, they judged without integrity. The sons turned aside from the right path.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel was already old and had appointed his sons as judges in Beersheba, in the south of Israel. Their wrongdoing led the elders of the people to ask for a king. This is how the shift toward the monarchy in Israel begins.

For today: faith is not passed down automatically, and positions of responsibility must not be used for personal gain. If we have authority, whether at home, at work, or in the church, let us ask God for integrity and reject all unjust profit.
exp.12:22:
It says that a group of Philistine soldiers, a garrison or military post, advanced to the pass of Michmash. A "pass" is a narrow road between mountains. The phrase "went out to" means they moved to occupy or guard that place.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. Israel was at a disadvantage: it had almost no weapons, because the Philistines controlled the work of iron. This verse prepares the story that follows, where Jonathan, son of Saul, confronts that enemy post. What follows in the account (chapter 14) shows how he acted.

For today: sometimes we feel few and poorly equipped in the face of a great problem. This verse reminds us that God does not depend on our resources. We can take the next step with faith and trust that he can act even when everything seems against us.
exp.14:0:
Samuel reminds Saul that God sent him to anoint him as king over Israel, the people of God. Therefore he asks him to listen carefully to what God is about to say. Old words: "anoint" means to set someone apart for a task with oil, and "hearken" means "listen."

Samuel speaks as the prophet and judge of Israel. Before giving a hard command from God, he reminds Saul that his reign depends on God. Saul is king because God allowed it, and so he must obey. The orders that follow about the Amalekites are harsh, and scholars understand them in different ways. Here the emphasis is on listening and obeying.

For today: before deciding something important, ask yourself whether you are truly listening to God or only looking to confirm what you already want to do. Read his Word with humility and obey what you understand.
exp.16:16:
Jesse asks his son David to take his brothers an ephah of this parched grain and these ten loaves. An ephah was a measure of capacity for grain, about twenty liters, although estimates vary.

Jesse is a father who cares about his three oldest sons, who were serving in Saul's army. Meanwhile, the Philistine Goliath had been challenging Israel for forty days. Jesse does not know that this journey will change David's story. He only wants to know whether his sons are well.

God often uses small, everyday tasks to lead us to great things. Today we can faithfully do what is asked of us, such as caring for our family, without despising it, because we never know what door God may open through it.
exp.19:17:
Jonathan tells David that tomorrow is the feast of the new moon, and that his absence will be noticed, because his place at the table will be empty. "Missed" means that someone will notice that a person is gone. "Seat" refers to the place David used to occupy at the king's table.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, is speaking. David is fleeing because Saul wants to kill him. Jonathan, who loves him as himself, makes a plan to learn his father's true intentions. David's absence at the feast will be the signal. Scholars give no further detail about how that celebration was held, but it was an important gathering where the king's close companions were expected to be present.

For today: a true friend notices when someone is missing and cares about them. Think about who has stopped coming to your church, your family, or your group, and reach out to them with kindness this week.
exp.17:12:
This verse says that Saul moved David away from his side and put him in charge of a thousand soldiers. The word "removed" in the verse above means "moved away," and "captain over a thousand" referred to a commander over a thousand men. The phrase "he went out and came in before the people" describes David leading the people in their daily activities and in war, in full view of everyone.

The narrator is the author of the book, not Saul. Saul had already thrown his spear at David and was afraid of him, because he saw that God was with David and had turned away from Saul. Many think this promotion was a way of moving him away from the palace, and perhaps of putting him in danger. The text does not say this clearly.

For today: sometimes others treat us badly or push us away out of envy. Even so, God can use that place to shape us. Serve faithfully where you are, and trust that God cares for you.
exp.19:22:
Jonathan reminds David of the covenant the two of them made. He says that the Lord himself is the witness and guarantor of what they promised each other, and that he will be so forever. The phrase "as touching" means "as for" or "concerning," and the words "the Lord be between thee and me" mean that God stands as judge and guardian of his promise.

Jonathan speaks with David in the field. Saul, his father, wants to kill David. Jonathan promises to warn him with a signal of arrows if the king is angry with him. Since there could be danger for both of them, Jonathan calls God to witness their friendship and their loyalty, even in difficult times.

Today, when you make a promise, whether in friendship, in family, or at work, take it seriously, as if God were a witness. And when life becomes hard, keep your word faithfully, and not only when it suits you.
exp.2:7:
God called Samuel a third time. Once more the boy got up, went to Eli, and said, "Here I am; you called me." This time Eli understood that it was God who was calling the boy. The phrase "here I am" is simply the answer "I am here," and "boy" refers to a young lad, perhaps quite small.

Samuel served in the sanctuary under the care of Eli, the aging priest. In those days the word of God was rare. Samuel did not yet know the Lord through his own experience, so he did not recognize his voice. Eli, though it took him a while, finally understood what was happening and was able to guide Samuel.

For today: God can speak to us, and sometimes we do not recognize him right away. We need to look for his voice in the Bible and also accept the help of mature believers, who can help us discern and respond to him with a willing heart.
exp.15:15:
Saul's servants offer him a simple solution: that the king command them to seek out someone who knows how to play the harp. Then, when the evil spirit from God troubles him, that man will play with his hand, and Saul will find relief.

The ones speaking are Saul's attendants. God had already withdrawn his Spirit from Saul because of his disobedience, and the king was suffering torment. How to understand the "evil spirit from God" is debated: some see a spiritual being that God allowed, others an inner torment. The Bible does not explain it in more detail. This advice prepares the way for David's arrival.

For today: when someone is suffering, God can use simple means, such as music, companionship or good advice. Receive the help of others with humility, and offer yours with kindness.
exp.30:3:
Saul, wounded and surrounded by the enemy, asks his armor-bearer, the soldier who carried his weapons, to kill him with his sword. He fears that the Philistines, whom he calls "uncircumcised" (people who did not belong to Israel's covenant), will kill him and mock him. The armor-bearer refused out of great fear, so Saul himself fell upon the sword.

Saul, the first king of Israel, speaks in his last battle on Mount Gilboa. His sons had already died, and the archers had struck him. His life ended in despair, after years of turning away from God. The Bible only records the event and does not present it as an example to follow.

When everything seems lost, do not face your distress alone or let fear or pride decide for you. Seek God and people you trust. If you are having thoughts of harming yourself, ask for help today.
exp.21:18:
This verse tells that Nob, the city where the priests lived, was destroyed by the sword. Men, women, children, infants and also the animals were killed. The phrase "put to the sword" means that they were killed with the sword, and "nursing infants" refers to the babies who were still drinking milk.

The one who gives the order is King Saul, angry and filled with jealousy against David. He thought the priests had helped David escape. His own soldiers refused to kill the priests of the LORD, but Doeg the Edomite obeyed. Here the text narrates what happened without approving of it. This cruelty was not a command from God, but the fruit of Saul's heart.

For today: jealousy and pride, if they are not confronted, can lead us to do terrible harm. Let us ask God for a humble heart and the courage to refuse to obey what is unjust, as the soldiers did.
exp.6:11:
Samuel took a stone and set it between Mizpah and Shen. He gave it the name Ebenezer, which means "stone of help." He said, "Hitherto hath the Lord helped us."
