The narrator tells what Samuel did. Samuel was the prophet and judge of Israel. The people had turned away from their idols and gathered at Mizpah. When the Philistines attacked, God thundered and confused them, and Israel won. Samuel raised the stone as a reminder that the victory came from God, not from Israel's weapons.

For today: make your own "stone of help." Write down or remember the times God has sustained you. Looking back with gratitude strengthens confidence to face what comes next.
exp.12:14:
Samuel rose and went up from Gilgal to Gibeah, a town in the territory of Benjamin. There Saul counted the men who were still with him, and they were about six hundred. Here "people" means soldiers.

This is the narrator's account. Samuel had just rebuked Saul for offering the sacrifice without waiting, which disobeyed God's command. Samuel goes away, and Saul is left with a very small army facing the Philistines. Earlier he had about three thousand men (13:2), so many had left. The text does not explain all the reasons, but the fear and weakness are evident.

For today: obedience to God matters more than the results we can see or the pressure of the moment. Saul counted his soldiers, but he did not stop to correct his heart. When we fail, it is good to acknowledge it with humility and to trust God again, not only our own resources.
exp.29:21:
This verse shows that some of the men who went with David, whom the text calls "wicked and worthless," were unwilling to share the plunder with the two hundred companions who stayed behind. They were only willing to give back their wives and children, so that they could take them and leave. The "spoil" is the plunder taken in war, and the word translated "band" in the next verse means a company or crowd.

The ones speaking are men from David's group. They had recovered everything the Amalekites had taken from them at Ziklag. Two hundred companions had been left at the brook Besor because they were too exhausted to go on. The selfish men reasoned that, since these had not fought, they did not deserve any of the spoil.

For today: what we receive comes from God's grace, not only from our own effort. For that reason we should value and treat generously those who support quietly or cannot give more.
exp.13:27:
A man from the people warns Jonathan that his father, King Saul, had made everyone swear that no one would eat that day, and that whoever ate would be cursed. "Charged with an oath" means made to swear under the threat of punishment. "Food" is anything a person eats. "Faint" means worn out and without strength.

The soldier speaks after Jonathan, not knowing about the oath, had tasted some honey and felt refreshed. Israel was chasing the Philistines in the middle of the battle. Saul perhaps wanted to focus the army on victory, but his order left the troops weak. Jonathan himself says it was a harmful decision.

For today: before demanding something very firmly, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it truly helps or only looks very spiritual. Seeking God's help is good, but the rules we set should care for people, not burden them further.
exp.29:3:
This verse tells how David and all his men wept aloud, without holding back, until they were worn out. They no longer had the strength to keep weeping. The phrase about raising their voice means they wept loudly, and the word for the men refers to his soldiers.

No one speaks here; the narrator describes the scene. David and his men returned to Ziklag and found it burned. The Amalekites had taken captive their wives, sons, and daughters. They did not know whether they were still alive. The grief was enormous, and soon it turned into tension, because the men spoke of stoning David. Even so, the text says that David strengthened himself in the Lord his God.

Weeping is not a lack of faith. The Bible shows that even a man of faith can be left without strength in the face of a loss. First we can unburden ourselves honestly before God, and then seek encouragement in Him to take the next step.
exp.18:2:
Jonathan tells David that he will go out and stand beside his father Saul, in the field where David is hiding. There he will speak well of David in front of Saul. Afterward he will tell David whatever he manages to see or hear.

Jonathan, Saul's son, is the one speaking. Saul had ordered David killed out of jealousy, but Jonathan loved David as a loyal friend. That is why he warns him of the danger and proposes a plan: to find out the king's intentions and to plead for David. What happened next is seen in the verses that follow.

Today we can learn from Jonathan's brave loyalty. He risked his relationship with his father to defend an innocent man. When someone is treated unjustly, we can speak up for them with respect and sincerity, and help them with prudence, without gossip or violence.
exp.7:14:
It says the king would take the tenth of the harvests and of the vineyards of the people, to pay his officials and servants. "Seed" here refers to sown fields, that is, the grain.

Samuel speaks to the people of Israel. They asked for a king so as to be like the other nations. Samuel was grieved, and God told him to warn them how a king would act. These words describe the cost of that decision: taxes, labor, and loss of freedom.

For today: before we insist on getting something, let us think about what it will cost. We often look for security in human persons or systems and forget that only God is our true King and protector. Let us ask Him for wisdom before we decide.
exp.30:2:
This verse says the battle turned very hard against King Saul. The archers, that is, the Philistine soldiers who shot bows, reached him, probably wounding him. Seeing himself in that state, Saul felt great fear. The word "sore" in the verse means the situation became harder and more dangerous.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book, who tells of the end of Saul's reign. The Philistines had already killed his sons, among them Jonathan. Earlier, Saul had turned away from God and disobeyed, and God no longer answered him (1 Samuel 28:6). Some interpreters see in this the result of that path. The Bible tells of his death without hiding his grief.

Today, this passage invites us not to put off turning back to God. If we walk alone, fear takes control when troubles come. Let us seek God with humility today, and He will sustain us.
exp.28:1:
The explanation describes how the lords of the Philistines reviewed their troops, arranged in companies of a hundred and of a thousand men. David and his men marched at the rear of the line, alongside Achish, the Philistine king of Gath. The "lords" were the rulers or chiefs of the Philistine cities.

The narrator describes how the Philistines were preparing to fight against Israel. David was living among them because he was fleeing from Saul, and Achish trusted him. The other chiefs did not trust him, and that is why the account goes on to their protest. The text does not explain what David was thinking at that moment, so it is not wise to assume it.

For today: sometimes we find ourselves in situations where we do not know how to get out without compromising what we believe. This passage reminds us that God can open a way out that we did not expect. In the meantime, it is good to pray, to act with prudence, and not to give up hope.
exp.20:9:
This verse says that David got up that same day and fled from Saul. He came as far as Achish, king of Gath, a Philistine city. The word "fled" in the verse means he went away and kept his distance from the place where Saul could reach him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. David was running away because Saul wanted to kill him. He had just passed through Nob, where the priest Ahimelech gave him bread and the sword of Goliath. Then he went to Gath, land of the Philistines, the same city Goliath came from. The text does not explain why he went there, so one can think he was looking for shelter, although his decision proved risky, as the fear he felt afterward shows.

For today: when fear presses on us, we can make decisions without consulting God. Before we run, let us ask God for direction in prayer.
exp.25:24:
Saul blesses David and tells him that he will surely do great things and come out victorious. Then each of them goes his own way.

Some older words: "shalt do great things" means you will carry out great deeds, and "prevail" means you will get ahead or win.

Saul was pursuing David in order to kill him. David had the opportunity to strike Saul while he slept, but he did not do it, because he respected the king anointed by God. Saul acknowledges his wrong, although the Bible does not show a lasting change in him. David, for his part, does not return to Saul, perhaps out of prudence, since he had earlier regretted trusting his promises.

We can act with integrity even when others treat us badly, leaving justice in God's hands. We also learn to be prudent: forgiving does not always mean putting ourselves back in the same danger.
exp.7:8:
In this verse God tells Samuel to listen to the people and give them a king. But first he must warn them with seriousness, and explain to them the rights the king would claim over them, which here means the customs and demands a king would place on them.

God speaks to Samuel. The Israelites asked for a king like the other nations. God explains that they are rejecting not only Samuel, but Him as their King. Even so, He allows them to choose, but He wants them to know what it will cost them, for the king would take their sons, their goods, and their labor.

God respects our freedom, but He does not hide the consequences from us. Before asking for something that seems like a good idea, it is wise to pray and ask ourselves what it will cost us and whether we are putting God in second place.
exp.19:1:
Jonathan answers David: "Certainly not! You will not die." He says that his father, Saul, never does anything, great or small, without telling him. So why would he hide it from him? Jonathan believes this cannot be true. Here "reveal" means to tell or make known, and "conceal" means to keep hidden.

David has just fled from Naioth, in Ramah, because Saul is searching for him to kill him. He comes before his friend Jonathan and asks what wrong he has done. Jonathan speaks from what he knows of his father, but he is mistaken: Saul was in fact keeping his plan from him, as will be seen later.

For today: even when we trust someone deeply, we sometimes do not see everything that is going on. Listening humbly to someone who warns us, and not dismissing their fears at once, can save us from mistakes and help us care for those who are suffering.
exp.9:0:
Samuel takes a small flask of oil and pours it on Saul's head. Then he kisses him and asks whether it is not the Lord who has anointed him as leader over his people.

Samuel speaks as a prophet and judge of Israel. Israel had asked for a king, and God allowed Saul to be the first. Samuel anoints him privately, and the kiss was probably a sign of respect and affection. Afterward he gives him signs to confirm that God was with him. Scholars debate how to understand that first anointing, but the text stresses that the calling comes from God.

God can call us to a task without our seeking it. If we receive a responsibility, let us remember that it is not ours: we serve in what belongs to God, and we should do so with humility and depending on Him.
exp.6:0:
The men of Kiriath-jearim went and took the ark of the Lord and placed it in the house of Abinadab, which stood on a hill. There they set apart his son Eleazar to take care of the ark.

The account is told by the book's narrator, who does not name himself. The Philistines had sent the ark back, and the people of Beth-shemesh could no longer keep it (chapter 6). That is why it was brought to Kiriath-jearim. The text does not say that Eleazar was a Levite, so we cannot claim it.

Today, when God entrusts us with something sacred, we care for it with reverence and responsibility. We might ask ourselves what room we give God in our home and our daily routine.
exp.25:5:
Here David asks for a volunteer to go with him to Saul's camp. He addresses Ahimelech the Hittite and Abishai, son of Zeruiah and brother of Joab. The word "asked" in the verse means that he questioned them or spoke to them directly. Abishai answers at once: "I will go down with thee."

David speaks this way because Saul was pursuing him with three thousand soldiers to kill him. David already knew from his spies where Saul was, and he wanted to enter the camp while the men were asleep. Only Abishai offers himself, and the text does not say that Ahimelech responded. Later, Abishai will want to kill Saul, but David will refuse.

For today: when we face risky or confusing situations, it is wise not to go alone and to seek companions who are willing. But we must also test their advice by the Word of God, because a loyal friend may propose a mistaken path.
exp.7:17:
It says the people will cry out in pain because of the king they chose for themselves. And on that day the Lord will not listen to them. Samuel is the one speaking. Israel asked for a king to be like the other nations, and Samuel warns them what it would cost: the king would take their sons, servants, animals and part of their possessions. Samuel speaks this way because God told him to warn them. Many understand that God's silence would speak of the consequences of their decision, not of a total rejection of them.

Before making an important decision, ask yourself what it might cost you and whether you are seeking God's guidance or just copying what others do. God loves us, but decisions have consequences.
exp.16:15:
This verse says that the Philistine, Goliath, came out toward the battlefield every morning and every evening. He did this for forty days in a row. The phrase "presented himself" means that he showed himself in front of Israel's army to challenge them.

The narrator describes how things stood before David arrived. Israel's soldiers lived under constant threat. Meanwhile, David was going back and forth between his father's sheep and the camp. The text does not say what each soldier was thinking, but it does show that fear became a habit over so many days.

For today: the voices that frighten us often repeat themselves every day and can wear us down. Don't let them set your mood. Begin and end your day listening to God's Word and speaking with Him in prayer.
exp.8:17:
Saul meets Samuel at the entrance of the city, at the gate, and politely asks him to tell him where the seer lives. "Seer" was another name for the prophet, someone to whom God showed things. Saul does not know that he is already speaking with the very person he is looking for.

Saul, a young man from Benjamin, is searching for his father's lost donkeys. God had already told Samuel that on that day the man who would be prince over Israel would arrive. Saul comes without knowing any of this, but God is guiding him in the middle of an ordinary task.

God can work in our everyday days, even in small problems, to lead us toward something greater. It is wise to faithfully do what is before us and to trust that He directs our steps, even when we cannot yet see all of his plan.
exp.29:10:
It tells that some of David's men found an Egyptian in the field and brought him before David. They gave him bread to eat and water to drink. The words "found" and "gave" in the source wording are rendered here as the plain English words you see in the verse above.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book. David and his men were pursuing the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and taken away their families. Tired and hungry, this young man was a slave of an Amalekite, and his master had left him behind when he became sick. Later, he will guide David to the enemy camp. The Bible does not explain everything, but it shows that God works even in an unexpected encounter.

For today: even in the midst of your own urgency, do not walk past a person in need. A simple act of compassion, like giving food or water, can open doors you never imagined.
exp.14:3:
Saul gathered the people together and counted them in Telaim. The word "counted" here means that he reviewed them and took stock of their numbers. There were two hundred thousand foot soldiers, and ten thousand men of Judah, counted separately.

Samuel had passed on to Saul a command from God against the Amalekites, because they had opposed Israel when it came out of Egypt. It is a hard passage, which must be understood within that time and that special commandment. Telaim was probably in the south, but its exact location is uncertain. Saul gathers the army to carry out what God asked.

Having resources and organization is good, but what matters most is obeying God completely. Before we trust in our numbers, plans, or strength, let us ask ourselves whether we are truly listening and sincerely following what He is actually telling us.
exp.11:1:
Samuel tells the Israelites that they now have a king to lead them. He himself is old and gray-headed, and his sons are among the people. He has lived before them from his youth until this day.

Samuel speaks at an assembly in Gilgal, after Saul had been made king. The people had asked for a king, and Samuel lays down his role as judge. Before he steps aside, he reminds them of his conduct over his whole life, so that they can examine it. The verses that follow show that he submits himself to their testimony.

For today: live in such a way that your conduct over the years can speak for you. Integrity is built day by day, and whoever has been honest can give an account with calm and humility.
exp.9:2:
Samuel goes on telling Saul what will happen to him on his way home. When he reaches the plain of Tabor, he will meet three men going up to God at Bethel. One will be carrying three young goats, another three loaves of bread, and the third a bottle of wine. "Going up to God" means they are heading to a place of worship, probably to offer sacrifices.

Samuel has just anointed Saul with oil, a sign that God chose him to lead Israel. These specific signs, which would happen one after another, would confirm that Saul was not acting on his own impulse but that God was guiding him. The exact location of this plain of Tabor is not known with certainty.

God often gives us small, concrete signs to encourage us when He calls us to something great. We can pay attention to those everyday details and remember that He watches over our steps, even in the ordinary parts of the road.
exp.7:6:
God tells Samuel to listen to what the people say and give them what they ask for. But he makes clear that they have not rejected Samuel; they have rejected God himself, because they do not want him to be their King.

The Lord speaks with Samuel, the prophet and judge. Samuel was already old, and his sons did not follow God's ways. Israel's leaders asked for a king "like all the nations," that is, like the neighboring peoples. Samuel was hurt by this, and he prayed. God answers him that the root problem was a lack of trust in him, something that had been building for a long time.

For today: sometimes we want to copy what everyone else does, instead of trusting God's guidance. Before asking for something, it is wise to ask ourselves whether, deep down, we are ceasing to trust him.
exp.21:7:
Saul accuses his servants of having all conspired against him. He complains that no one told him in private that his son Jonathan had made a covenant with David, "the son of Jesse." He says that no one felt sorry for him. The phrase "tell me privately" means the same as "let me know in secret," and "lie in wait" means to watch in order to attack; the "commanders" and "captains" mentioned in the source were military leaders.

King Saul speaks in Gibeah, spear in hand, surrounded by his officers from the tribe of Benjamin. David has fled, and Saul, filled with jealousy and suspicion, sees traitors everywhere. His accusation seems to come more from fear than from proven fact, and his words reveal self-pity.

For today: when fear and envy take hold of us, we begin to see enemies where there are none. It is wise to bring those fears to God and to wise people before we accuse others.
exp.19:3:
Jonathan asks David what he really wants or needs. The old-fashioned phrasing used in some versions, which asks what one's soul is thinking, is simply another way of asking "What do you think?" or "What do you want me to do?" Jonathan offers to help without attaching any conditions.

David is running away from King Saul, who wants to kill him. Jonathan, Saul's son, does not believe his father is as determined as David fears, but he sees David's fear and hears how serious his words are. Because of their friendship, Jonathan decides to listen to him and act.

Today we can imitate Jonathan: before offering quick advice, we can kindly ask what the other person needs. Really listening and offering concrete help is a practical way of showing love.
exp.29:29:
This verse is part of a list of places. It says that David sent gifts to the people of Hormah, of Chorashan (other versions write it "Cor-ashan") and of Athach. These were towns in the south of Judah.

After defeating the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families, David recovered everything. With the spoils he had won, he wanted to share gifts among the leaders and the towns that had helped him or welcomed him during his time of flight from Saul. The narrator tells this to show David's generosity. The exact location of some of these places is not known.

God blesses us and also invites us to remember those who helped us in difficult times. Today you can show your gratitude with a message, a visit, or a concrete gesture to someone who supported you when you needed it most.
exp.27:20:
The woman says she came to Saul and saw that he was deeply troubled. She reminded him that she had obeyed him and risked her life, and that she had listened to what he asked of her. The sentences that explained the old words "handmaid" and "sore troubled" are removed, since those words appear in the verse above and their meanings are clear from context: a handmaid is a female servant, and sore troubled means very anxious.

The speaker is the woman whom Saul sought out to consult Samuel, even though he himself had banned mediums from the land. She was in danger if she were found out. Saul had just heard his condemnation, and he was weak because he had not eaten all day. She speaks to him with compassion and offers him food. The Bible does not fully explain how Samuel appeared, and it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: do not wait until you are in despair to seek God. Turn to Him and to His Word early. And when someone suffers, help them with simple, kind gestures.
exp.16:40:
This verse says that Goliath, the Philistine, kept coming forward toward David, drawing closer little by little. In front of him went his shield-bearer, that is, the helper who carried his shield.

The narrator describes the moment just before the battle. David had just turned down Saul's armor because he was not used to it, and he went out with his staff, five stones, and his sling. The contrast is strong: a giant protected by a helper and his weapons, facing a young shepherd with simple tools. Later David will say that he trusts in the name of the Lord.

For today: you do not need to look strong or have the resources of others to face your giants. Use faithfully what God has already given you, and trust in Him.
exp.3:5:
The Philistines heard a great shout of joy coming from the camp of Israel. Puzzled, they asked what all that noise meant. Soon they learned that the ark of the Lord, the sacred chest of the covenant, had arrived in the camp. The shout here is the loud cry of the Israelites, and it reveals how intense their rejoicing was.

The Philistines were Israel's enemies and were in the middle of a war. Israel had just lost a battle and, instead of seeking God with humility, they sent for the ark, as though it were a charm that would guarantee them victory. The Philistines speak here, and their reaction shows that they knew the reputation of Israel's God, though they understood him in their own way.

For today: we should not confuse religious symbols with the presence of God. He is not to be handled like an object of luck; he seeks a repentant and obedient heart, not merely emotion or ritual.
exp.1:35:
It says that whoever survives from Eli's family will have to come and humble himself before the faithful priest whom God will raise up. He will come to ask him for a piece of silver and a morsel of bread. He will beg to be put into one of the priests' offices, only so that he may have something to eat.

The one speaking is a prophet, a man of God sent to Eli. His message announces God's judgment on his house, because his sons Hophni and Phinehas dishonored the service of God and Eli did not correct them. Many believe the faithful priest is fulfilled first in Samuel or in Zadok, though interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: serving God is a privilege, not a business. Examine your motives and ask him to give you a faithful heart, one that honors him even when it is hard to correct what is wrong.
exp.14:30:
It says that Samuel went back and followed Saul, and that Saul bowed down to worship the Lord. Here "worshipped" means that he fell prostrate as a sign of reverence. The word "turned again" means "went back" or "followed behind him."

Samuel, the prophet, had just told Saul that God had rejected him as king for disobeying the command to destroy the Amalekites. Saul acknowledged his sin, but asked to be honored before the people. Samuel agreed to go back with him. There are different opinions on whether Saul's worship was sincere or whether he was more concerned with protecting his image. The text does not make this clear.

For today: worshipping God is good, but it does not replace obedience and heartfelt repentance. Before we worry about what others think of us, let us ask God for a humble heart willing to obey him.
exp.2:4:
Samuel heard a voice in the night and thought it was the priest Eli. So he ran to him and said, "Here I am; you called me." Eli answered that he had not called him and told him to go back to bed. Samuel obeyed.

Samuel was a boy who served Eli in the sanctuary. The one calling him was God, but the text makes clear that Samuel did not yet know the Lord or had received his word. That is why he did not recognize the voice. His willingness to get up and run shows a helpful heart.

God sometimes speaks to us in ways we do not know how to recognize at first. It is wise to stay alert, to be willing, and to seek the guidance of mature people of faith, like Eli, who help us discern.
exp.0:26:
Hannah tells the priest Eli that this child is the answer to her prayer. She prayed earnestly, and God granted what she asked for. The word "gave" appears here in its usual modern form.

Hannah, a woman who could not have children, speaks. Years earlier, at the sanctuary in Shiloh, she had prayed with tears and promised to dedicate her son to God. Eli had seen her praying and at first thought she was drunk. Now she returns with Samuel, already weaned, to fulfill her promise and remind Eli of that moment.

When God answers a prayer, it is worth remembering it and giving thanks. Hannah did not only receive; she also gave back, with gratitude, what God had given her. We may ask ourselves: how can I use what God has given me to serve Him and others?
exp.24:27:
Abigail asks David to forgive what she calls "this offense," that is, the foolish behavior of her husband Nabal. She assures him that God will make David a sure house, meaning a lasting line of descendants and a stable kingdom. She says that David fights the Lord's battles and that no wrongdoing has been found in him all his days.

Abigail, Nabal's wife, is the one speaking. Nabal had scorned David and his men, and David was marching out armed to kill her household. Abigail goes out to meet him with provisions and tries to calm his anger. With tact and humility, she reminds him of God's calling on his life so that he will not stain his future with revenge.

For today: when someone wrongs you, before you act in anger, remember what God wants to do in your life. Leaving vengeance in God's hands protects you from carrying guilt that you would later regret.
exp.26:10:
He says that David would leave alive no man or woman who could reach Gath, so that no one would tell what he was really doing. This was his custom for as long as he lived among the Philistines.

The narrator tells how David, fleeing from Saul, lived in Ziklag under King Achish of Gath. David raided enemy peoples of the south, but he led Achish to believe he was attacking Judah. The text only reports what happened; it does not approve of either the violence or the deception. No direction from God about these actions is mentioned here.

For today: fear and pressure can lead us to lie, and to cover our steps with more lies. David was a man of faith, but here we see his frailty. We can ask God for the courage to live in truth, without depending on deception to protect ourselves.
exp.14:23:
Saul admits that he sinned. He says that he disobeyed the commandment of the Lord and Samuel's words. He explains that he was afraid of the people and listened to their voice. Then he asks for forgiveness. The phrase "having broken the word" means he did not carry out what God had commanded, and "I obeyed their voice" means he gave in to what the people were asking for.

Samuel has just rebuked Saul. God had told him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but Saul and the people kept the best of the spoil. Saul had made excuses before. Now he acknowledges his wrong, although in the verses that follow he seems more concerned with how he looks before the people than with any real change. Some think his repentance was only partly sincere; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Obeying God can cost us the approval of others. If you feel pressure from your group today, ask God for the courage to obey him first, and when you fail, admit it honestly, without excuses.
exp.25:12:
This verse tells that David crossed to the other side of the valley and climbed to the top of a hill. He was "turned aside," that is, set apart, far from Saul's camp. Between him and them there was a great distance, so he was safe.

The narrator describes what happened after David and Abishai entered the camp while everyone was asleep. David did not want to kill Saul, because he was the Lord's anointed, and he took only his spear and his water jug. Now David moves away so that he can speak to them without danger. He does this to show that he could have killed Saul and did not.

Today, David teaches us to act with wisdom and respect. We can defend the truth without seeking revenge, and keep a prudent distance when there is danger, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.2:17:
Samuel told Eli everything that God had said to him, hiding nothing from him. Eli answered, "It is the Lord; let him do what seems good to him."

Note: the quoted-word sentence about "encubrir" and "manifestar" is deleted, since neither word appears in the verse the reader sees, and the reader's verse uses "hid" and "told" instead.

God had spoken to Samuel, a young man who served in the sanctuary, to announce judgment on Eli's household for not restraining his sons. Eli, now an old man, insisted that Samuel not hold anything back. Samuel, though he was afraid, was honest. Eli acknowledged that God has the authority to act.

Today we can learn from both of them. Like Samuel, we should speak the truth with respect, even when it is hard. Like Eli, we can accept correction with humility, trusting that God is just, without becoming defensive or looking for excuses.
exp.22:9:
Here David prays to God and tells him what he has heard: that Saul is preparing to go to Keilah and destroy the city because of David. "Hath certainly heard" means "has found out." "Seeketh" means "seeks" or "plans." "Thy servant" is the humble way David refers to himself.

David speaks with God after asking the priest Abiathar for the ephod, a priestly garment used to seek God's guidance. Saul was pursuing him, and David had just rescued Keilah from the Philistines. Now he fears that the city will suffer for protecting him, and he wants to know what to do before he acts.

Before making a difficult decision, we can bring God our concerns honestly and in detail. David did not act on fear alone or on what he himself thought. He asked first. Today we too can pray, seek wise counsel, and wait for direction before we move.
exp.9:6:
It says that when Saul sees the signs that Samuel told him about come true, he should act with confidence and do what lies within his reach, "what occasion serves," that is, whatever presents itself before him. The reason is that God is with him, meaning God accompanies him.

Samuel speaks with Saul shortly after anointing him in private as the future king of Israel. He gives him several signs to confirm that God has chosen him, among them meeting a group of prophets. Saul doubted himself, so Samuel encourages him. Some understand that "do what occasion serves" means to act according to the circumstance; others take it to mean that Saul should wait for God's guidance, as verse 8 indicates.

For today: when God shows you that He goes with you, do not be paralyzed by fear. Take the step that lies before you, with humility and prayer, and trust that He guides you.
exp.21:15:
Here King Saul pronounces a sentence of death against Ahimelech, the priest, and against his whole family. The phrase "thou shalt surely die" is a strong expression, meaning that he is certain to die. Ahimelech had already defended himself by saying that he knew nothing of the conflict between Saul and David.

Saul speaks full of jealousy and suspicion. David was fleeing from him, and Ahimelech had given him bread and the sword of Goliath, without knowing that David was escaping. Doeg, a servant of Saul, had accused him. Saul did not want to hear the priest's explanation.

For today: when fear and pride rule the heart, they shut our ears to the truth, and we can hurt innocent people. Let us ask God for humility to listen before we judge.
exp.10:6:
Saul takes a yoke of oxen, cuts them into pieces, and sends the pieces with messengers throughout all of Israel. The message is clear: whoever does not come out after Saul and Samuel, the same will be done to his oxen. The explanation of "cut them up" and "sent them" is simply what the verse says: he took the oxen, hewed them in pieces, and sent them out. Then the fear of the Lord fell on the people: a strong fear, placed by God, and everyone came out "with one consent," that is, united.

Saul speaks after hearing that Jabesh-gilead was threatened and that the people were weeping. The Spirit of God came upon him, and he burned with anger at the injustice. He uses a harsh sign, which in that culture was understood as an urgent call and a warning. The oxen were valuable working tools.

Today, when someone suffers an injustice, do not look the other way. Ask God for courage and seek to unite others to help, in concrete ways and with humility.
exp.13:45:
This verse tells us that Saul stopped chasing the Philistines, and that they returned to their own land. The word "following" here means pursuing. The battle that day ended without Israel completely destroying them.

The narrator is the author of the book, and he writes right after a serious conflict. Saul had made a rash oath, and because of it he wanted to kill his son Jonathan, who had broken it without knowing. The people defended Jonathan, since God had given the victory through him. After that episode, Saul calls off the pursuit. The text does not fully explain his reasons, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: impulsive decisions and inner conflicts can halt what God is doing. Before speaking or promising something in haste, it is wise to pray, think calmly, and listen to wise people.
exp.4:10:
The people of Ekron, frightened, sent for all the lords of the Philistines. They asked that the ark of the God of Israel be sent away and returned to its own place, so that it would not kill them or their people. The word "deadly destruction" in the verse refers to a blow that brought death, and the phrase "the hand of God was very heavy" means that the punishment was becoming more severe.

The Philistines had captured the ark in battle and had carried it to Ashdod and then to Gath. In each city, suffering followed. Now in Ekron, the people speak with fear. They believed the ark was the cause, and the text presents these events as the hand of God at work.

For today: we cannot treat God as an object we use for our own convenience. With humility, let us acknowledge his holiness and, instead of resisting him, seek his forgiveness and his guidance.
exp.1:19:
It says that Eli, the priest, blessed Elkanah and his wife Hannah. He asked the Lord to give them more children through this woman, in place of the son she had given over to the Lord. The word "seed" means children or descendants. "Loan" refers to Samuel, whom Hannah had asked of God and then dedicated to his service. After that, the family went back to their home.

The narrator speaks, and within the account, Eli speaks. Each year Elkanah and Hannah went up to the sanctuary to offer sacrifice and visited Samuel, who served there. Eli expresses gratitude and a wish for good for them. The text that follows shows that God gave them three more sons and two daughters.

For today: when we give something to God sincerely, we can trust that He cares for us. We can also bless with words those who serve at a cost to themselves, encouraging them and praying for them.
exp.24:6:
Here David, through his messengers, tells Nabal that he has heard that he is shearing his sheep, a season of feasting and abundance. He reminds him that his shepherds stayed near David's men and were never mistreated or robbed. The phrase about "doing violence" means abusing or pressing someone with force. The word translated as "lately" here refers to something that happened a short time ago.

David was living as a fugitive in the wilderness with his men. They had looked after Nabal's shepherds, and now David asks, courteously, for some provision. We do not know exactly what that protection looked like, but the text takes it for granted, and the servants can confirm it.

For today: when we have done good, it is right to ask with respect and humility, without demanding. And when someone has helped us, gratitude is a form of justice that honors God.
exp.24:23:
Abigail throws herself at David's feet and says, "Upon me, my lord, upon me let this iniquity be." She asks him to let her speak and to listen to the words of her, his servant. The sentences that explain the old and unusual wording are removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Abigail, the wife of Nabal, a rich and foolish man, is the one speaking. Nabal had insulted David's men and refused them help. David, furious, was on his way with four hundred men to take revenge. Abigail goes out to meet him to stop the violence. By offering to bear the blame, she tries to calm David and win his attention.

For today: when there is a conflict, humility and wise words can stop greater harm. Sometimes it is worth taking the first step toward reconciliation, even if the mistake was not ours, and asking God for wisdom before reacting in anger.
exp.14:27:
Samuel tells Saul that God has taken the kingdom from him, as one tears a piece of cloth. "Torn away" means ripped off forcefully. "Neighbour" here means another person close by, someone from his own people. That other person is "better than thou," meaning more faithful to God. The text does not give his name here.

Samuel, the prophet, speaks after Saul disobeyed a clear command from God. Saul grabbed Samuel's robe to stop him, and it tore. Samuel uses that moment as a sign: in this way Saul's kingdom is broken. Many understand that he is referring to David, although this verse does not say so.

For today: obedience to God matters more than titles or appearances. If God corrects us, it is best to respond with humble and sincere repentance, not with excuses.
exp.8:26:
Samuel and Saul were walking down to the edge of the town. Then Samuel asked Saul to tell the young servant to go on ahead. The servant went on ahead, and Samuel asked Saul to stay behind for a moment so he could tell him a word from God.

Samuel speaks here as the prophet and judge of Israel. Saul had come looking for his father's lost donkeys, and God had already told Samuel that this man would lead the people. Samuel wants a private moment, with no one else present, to give him the message. Soon he will anoint him, as the next chapter describes.

For today: sometimes God speaks best when we stop. Pause, turn off the noise, and stop rushing, even for a few minutes, so you can listen to his Word calmly, without hurry or distraction.
exp.19:14:
Jonathan asks David never to stop showing kindness and loyalty to his family. That promise was meant to hold even when God destroyed every one of David's enemies. The second sentence is difficult and is translated in several different ways. It seems to be a solemn formula: if David failed to keep this promise, Jonathan would be cut off from David's house.

Jonathan, the son of King Saul, is speaking. Saul wanted to kill David, but Jonathan was his faithful friend. He sensed that David would be the future king, and so he asks for protection for his descendants. In this way they make a covenant of friendship before God.

For today: keep your promises, especially the ones you make to those you love. Show steady kindness, not only when it suits you, and think also about the well-being of your friends' children and family.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the young assistants at the sanctuary were committing a very serious sin before God. The young helpers of the priests are the ones described here. The verse's word for how they treated the offerings the people brought to worship God is rendered in the King James Version as "abhorred": they regarded those offerings with contempt.

The narrator explains the conduct of Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, and of their servants. According to the law, the fat was burned for God first. They demanded the meat before that and took it by force, turning worship into abuse. By contrast, the account goes on to the young Samuel, who served faithfully.

For today: God notices how we treat what is holy and how we treat those who come to worship. If we serve in the church, let us examine whether we seek to honor God or to take advantage of our position.
exp.3:19:
This verse tells of the last moments of Phinehas's wife. As she was dying after giving birth, the women attending her said to her, "Fear not, for you have borne a son." But she did not answer, nor did she take any notice of it, which means she paid no attention to their words and gave them no importance.

The women who assisted her in childbirth speak, and they try to comfort her with what was normally a great joy. But she had just learned that the Philistines had captured the ark of God and that her father-in-law Eli and her husband had died. Her grief over the loss of the ark weighed more heavily than the news of the son. That is why she named him Ichabod, a name explained in the following verse.

Today, we sometimes offer comfort with good intentions, but without understanding the person's deeper pain. Let us learn to accompany others with patience, by listening and simply being present. And let us remember that the most valuable thing in life is the presence of God.
exp.13:11:
The Philistine soldiers of the garrison, that is, the outpost, call out to Jonathan and his armourbearer (the one who carried his weapons) and say, "Come up to us, and we will shew you a thing." It was a mocking challenge. Jonathan tells his armourbearer to climb up after him, because the Lord has already given the Philistines into the hand of Israel.

Jonathan and his armourbearer had agreed on a sign: if the Philistines invited them to come up, they would take it as a sign that God was giving them the victory. Israel was weak and afraid, and Jonathan acted in faith, not knowing how everything would turn out.

For today: faith can take a concrete step when we see an open door, and trust that God is at work, even when we feel few or weak.
exp.13:50:
This verse gives family information. It says that Kish, the father of Saul, and Ner, the father of Abner, were sons of Abiel. In other words, Saul and Abner were close relatives. The previous verse already said that Abner was Saul's uncle, although some understand the word to mean a close relative in general. Also, other passages (such as 1 Chronicles 8:33 and 9:36-39) present the names of this family somewhat differently, and scholars explain this in several ways.

The narrator of the book, whose author is unknown, pauses the story to introduce the family of King Saul and his military commander. In this way he makes clear who the most important men of the kingdom were at its beginning.

For today: God works through royal families, with names and roots. Value your family and pray for it, knowing that God can use those who are close to you.
exp.19:11:
Jonathan makes a solemn vow before God. He promises that when he finds out, tomorrow or the day after, what his father thinks, if Saul is well disposed toward David, he will let David know. The source's explanation of the old word meaning "appear favorable" and the word meaning "reveal" and the phrase meaning "send a message" are omitted here, since those words are not in the verse your readers see.

David fears that Saul wants to kill him and asks who will warn him if the king answers harshly. Jonathan, Saul's son and David's loyal friend, takes him out into the field so they can speak in private. There he calls God as witness to his commitment. His loyalty to David is great, even though he is the king's son.

For today: when you promise something to someone, keep your word sincerely and openly, even when it is difficult. True friendship tells the truth and protects the other person, even when it costs something.
exp.22:10:
David asks God two questions: will the people of Keilah hand him over to Saul, and will Saul really come down, as David has heard? He asks respectfully: "tell me, please," that is, "let me know." God answers, "Yes, he will come down," meaning, "yes, he will go down."

David speaks with God through the ephod, which the priest Abiathar carried in order to inquire of the Lord. Scholars do not agree on exactly how it worked. David had just saved Keilah from the Philistines, but Saul was pursuing him and wanted to catch him there. David needed to know what to do.

For today: before deciding something difficult, do not follow only your fears or assumptions. Bring your questions to God with honesty, seek his direction in prayer and in his Word, and act wisely when he shows you the way.
exp.5:11:
The verse tells that the two cows, which had been yoked to the cart carrying the ark, went straight toward Beth-shemesh. They were lowing, that is, mooing, and they did not turn aside to the right or to the left. The Philistine lords followed them at a distance as far as the border of the town.

The narrator recounts what happened after the Philistines, punished with plagues for having taken the ark, decided to return it. To test whether the punishment came from God, they placed the ark on a cart pulled by cows that had just given birth, which would normally have stayed with their calves. That they went straight into Israelite territory was taken as a sign. The text does not explain how this happened; it presents it simply as the work of God.

Today we can remember that God guides us even when circumstances seem against us. Let us trust in Him and move forward with firmness, without turning aside.
exp.21:12:
Saul accuses the priest Ahimelech of having joined forces with David against him. He charges that Ahimelech gave David bread and a sword, and that he inquired of God on David's behalf. To "conspire" means to make secret plans against someone. To "lie in wait" means to hide and wait in order to attack. Saul believes David is lying in wait to harm him.

King Saul speaks here, full of jealousy and distrust toward David. Ahimelech, in Nob, had helped David without knowing that David was fleeing from Saul (1 Samuel 21). The accusation had no evidence behind it, and Ahimelech's answer in the next passage shows that he acted in good faith.

Jealousy and fear can make us see enemies where there are none. Before accusing someone, it is wise to stop, ask questions with humility, and look for the facts. Let us ask God for a heart free from unjust suspicion.
exp.2:13:
God says he has made a solemn oath concerning Eli's family: the sin of that house will not be forgiven through sacrifices or offerings. "Purged" means covered over or wiped away through a payment or sacrifice. "Offering" refers to the gifts brought to God. "Iniquity" means wickedness or sin.

God speaks at night to the young Samuel. Eli's sons, who were priests, treated the holy things with contempt, and Eli, although he knew it, did not correct them firmly. Some scholars point out that this judgment refers to an attitude of rebellion without repentance, and not to God rejecting everyone who repents. The Bible does not explain this in more detail.

For today: it is not enough to carry out religious rituals if the heart keeps disobeying. If you have responsibility over others, as a parent, leader, or teacher, correct them with love and truth, without looking the other way.
exp.28:3:
The Philistine lords were angry with Achish and demanded that he send David back to the place he had given him (Ziklag). They did not want him to go with them to war, because he could turn against them in the middle of the battle. They said David could make peace with Saul, his master, by handing over the heads of the Philistine soldiers. "Lords" here means leaders or rulers.

The Philistine leaders speak, distrustful of David and his men, who had taken refuge with Achish while fleeing from Saul. Achish trusted David, but the others saw the risk. Without knowing it, they spared David from having to fight against his own people. The Bible does not say that David planned this; it shows that God was at work in that situation.

For today: sometimes a door closes and it hurts or seems unfair. Even so, God may be protecting us from a worse path. Trust Him, and thank Him for the closed doors too.
exp.4:1:
The Philistines, who had captured the ark of God in battle, brought it into the temple of their god Dagon and placed it beside him. The wording in the verse is plain: the ark was brought in and set down by the idol.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel lost the ark to the Philistines. They thought their god had defeated the God of Israel, so they put the ark on display as a trophy of war. Dagon was a deity highly honored in the region, although scholars debate the details of his origin. The verses that follow show that God needs no one to defend him.

Today we can remember that God shares his place with nothing. When we place something beside him, such as money, success, or pride, sooner or later it becomes clear that they are not equals. Let us ask him to occupy first place.
exp.5:4:
It says the Philistines were to make golden figures of their tumors (the "emerods" were painful sores or swellings) and of the mice that were ruining their fields. In this way they would give honor to the God of Israel. They said "peradventure," hoping that God would lift his heavy hand from them, from their gods, and from their land.

The priests and diviners of the Philistines are speaking. They had captured the ark of God, and since then they had suffered a plague. They wanted to return it with a guilt offering. We do not know for certain what the sores were exactly; some think of tumors or of a disease linked to the mice, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: when we recognize that God is greater than whatever we worship or trust in, the first step is to humble ourselves and honor him. We do not have to pay to be forgiven, but we can come to him with sincerity and not with pride.
exp.22:14:
This verse says that David saw, or knew, that Saul had come out to seek his life, that is, to take his life. That is why David stayed hidden in the wood, in the wilderness of Ziph. "Wood" here may refer to an area of hills or bushes; the name of the place is Ziph.

It is part of the narrative, not a speech. David was fleeing from Saul, who was pursuing him out of jealousy and fear of losing the throne. David had just left Keilah with about six hundred men. Although Saul sought him every day, the text makes clear that God did not hand him over into his hands.

For today: when you feel persecuted, pressured, or afraid, you are not alone. David was afraid and hid himself, but he kept trusting in God. God can also use people like Jonathan, who comes right after this, to encourage you. Seek that support and rest in God's care.
exp.28:9:
Here Achish, the Philistine king of Gath, tells David to rise up early in the morning, together with his men, and go. The men of David are described as servants of Achish's lord, meaning they were regarded as serving Achish. The verse's command to get going is clear: leave as soon as it is light in the morning.

Achish speaks this way because the Philistine lords distrusted David and did not want him to fight alongside them against Israel. Although Achish trusted him, he had to send him away. Some think this protected David from having to fight against his own people, though the text does not directly explain it that way.

For today: sometimes a door closes without our understanding why. We can obey calmly and trust that God watches over our path, even when He saves us from situations we did not know were dangerous.
exp.22:13:
David stayed hidden in the wilderness, in strongholds and rocky places, and lived on a mountain in the wilderness of Ziph. Saul searched for him every day, but God did not let him be caught.

The narrator of the book is speaking here. David was running away because Saul, out of jealousy, wanted to kill him. Shortly before this, David had left Keilah because God warned him that its people would hand him over. With about six hundred men, he kept moving from one place to another. Later, Jonathan would come to encourage him in God.

For today: even when you go through times of pressure or danger, God keeps caring for you, often in ways you cannot see. Do what you can with wisdom, listen to his guidance, and trust that he sustains your life.
exp.13:3:
This verse describes the place where Jonathan wanted to cross over toward the Philistine camp. In the pass there were two sharp rocks, one on each side. They were called Bozez and Seneh. The word "guard post" refers to a military station with soldiers. "Sought" means he was looking for a way or trying.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator's account. Jonathan, the son of King Saul, went out in secret, and neither his father nor the people knew about it. Saul had only about six hundred men. The author describes the terrain to show how difficult and risky the plan was. Shortly afterward, Jonathan says that God can save by many or by few.

For today: sometimes the path God sets before us is narrow and seems dangerous. Jonathan did not wait to have the advantage; he took a step of faith, trusting that God could act. Let us ask God for wisdom and courage to obey Him, without depending only on our own strength.
exp.28:0:
The verse tells how the Philistines gathered all their armies at Aphek, a place where they were getting ready to fight. Meanwhile, Israel camped by the fountain that is in Jezreel. Here "armies" is the word for the forces themselves, and "Jezreel" is a well-known valley in the region.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The two peoples are preparing for a great battle, and Saul is the king of Israel. David is living among the Philistines, because he had been fleeing from Saul, and now he finds himself in a difficult situation: it seems he will have to march with the enemies of his own people. The verses that follow show how God delivers him from that conflict.

For today: at times we find ourselves in situations with no clear way out, through our own decisions or because of circumstances. We can trust that God cares for us and can open paths we never imagined. Let us pray for wisdom.
exp.14:19:
Saul answers Samuel that he did obey God. He says he went on the mission the Lord gave him, that he brought back Agag, king of Amalek, and that he utterly destroyed the Amalekites.

Samuel has just rebuked Saul for not obeying fully. God had commanded him to wipe out Amalek, but Saul let King Agag live, and the people kept the best of the livestock. Here Saul defends himself and presents his obedience as complete, even though Samuel had already pointed out the opposite. The verses that follow show that he blames the people.

For today: when God or his Word correct us, it is easy to justify ourselves by saying "I did almost everything right." Let us pray for a humble heart that acknowledges its failures and obeys completely, without excuses.
exp.16:7:
Goliath stands up in front of Israel's army and shouts at them. The explanation's word for "stood" and the phrase "cried out" are covered by the verse itself: he stood and cried unto the armies of Israel. The rows of soldiers are the army ranks that he faces.

He mocks them: he asks why they have come out to set their battle in array, and he calls himself the Philistine, while they are only servants to Saul. He demands that they choose a man to fight with him.

The one speaking is Goliath, the Philistine champion, who is in the valley of Elah. Israel and the Philistines are face to face. His proposal was to settle the war with a single combat between two men. With his words he sought to intimidate and shame God's people, and he succeeded: later the text says that Saul and all of them were filled with fear.

For today: many times our problems shout at us that we are small and incapable. Before listening to those voices, let us remember who our God is. We can ask Him for courage and trust that He is with us.
exp.19:6:
It says that King Saul's reaction will serve as a sign. If Saul answers calmly, "It is well," David will be safe. But if he becomes angry, that will be evidence that he has already decided to harm him. "Evil is determined by him" means that his ill intent is completely settled. "Thy servant" here is David speaking with humility.

David speaks with Jonathan, Saul's son and his faithful friend. David is fleeing because Saul wants to kill him, but he is not sure how serious the situation is. So he proposes a test: not to attend the New Moon feast and to see how the king reacts to his absence. Jonathan doubted that his father would go so far, and for that reason they agree to this plan.

Today it teaches us not to act only out of fear or naivety. When a situation is difficult, we can wisely look for clear signs, ask advice from a trustworthy friend, and pray so that we decide with prudence.
exp.15:1:
Samuel tells God that he is afraid: if King Saul finds out what he is about to do, Saul will kill him. God answers that he should take a heifer (a young cow) from the herd and say, "I am come to sacrifice to the Lord." The quoted phrase "I am come to sacrifice to the Lord" appears in the verse above, so no explanation of old wording is needed here.

Samuel speaks with God after Saul has been rejected as king. God sends him to Bethlehem to anoint secretly one of Jesse's sons as the new king. The sacrifice was real, and Samuel truly was going to offer it. God gives him a prudent way, without any lie, to protect his life and carry out his plan. Many scholars read it this way, though some debate the matter.

For today: you can speak to God about your fears with honesty, as Samuel did. He does not scold you; he gives you the next step, with wisdom and patience.
exp.2:19:
This verse says that the people, from north to south, came to recognize that Samuel was a true prophet of God. The word "knew" in the verse means "recognized" or "understood." "Dan" and "Beersheba" were the cities at the two ends of the land, so the phrase means "all Israel." Being "faithful" here describes someone who can be trusted, whose words came true.

It is the narrator who speaks. Earlier, God had given Samuel, while he was still young, a hard message for the priest Eli, and Samuel told it to him without hiding anything. Because God fulfilled what Samuel said, the people began to trust him. This happens at a time when the word of God was rare in Israel.

For today: faithfulness is recognized over time. Try to speak the truth with humility, even when it costs you, and live in such a way that your words and your actions deserve trust.
exp.25:19:
David asks Saul not to kill him, so that his blood will not fall to the ground far from the presence of God. He says that the king of Israel has come out to search for "una pulga," that is, something very small and insignificant. He also compares himself to someone who chases a partridge through the mountains, a bird that tires itself out from so much running away.

David speaks to Saul in the wilderness of Ziph. He had just spared Saul's life once again, although he could have killed him while he slept. Saul pursued him out of envy and fear. David presents himself humbly, but he also defends his innocence and trusts that God is the judge between them.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, do not respond with revenge. Speak with truth and humility, and leave the matter in God's hands. He sees everything and knows how to do justice in his own time.
exp.7:11:
It says the king will appoint some of the people's sons as commanders over thousands and commanders over fifties, that is, officers of the army. Others he will force to plow his fields and reap his harvests (the wheat or barley crops). They will also have to make weapons of war and the equipment for his chariots, that is, the gear and parts for the battle chariots.

Samuel, the prophet and judge, is speaking. The people had asked for a king so that they could be like the other nations. God told Samuel to warn them clearly what the king's demands on them would be. It was a warning, not a command.

For today: before we place our trust in any leader, system, or human security, let us consider the cost. Only God deserves our complete trust, and He never charges us too much.
exp.5:1:
The Philistines call for their priests and diviners, that is, their religious guides, and ask them what they should do with the ark of the Lord. They want to know how to send it back to its place.

The rulers and the people of the Philistines are speaking. They had captured the ark in battle, but for seven months they suffered plagues and troubles wherever they kept it. Now they understand that they cannot keep it without consequences. Since they do not know the Lord well, they turn to their own religious experts. Some scholars see here a sincere fear; others see only an attempt to appease a powerful god.

When something troubles our conscience, we can look for advice everywhere except to God. Today, instead of running away or making excuses, it is wise to acknowledge his authority, seek his direction in the Bible, and correct what is wrong.
exp.7:3:
This verse tells us that all the leaders of the people of Israel, called "elders," gathered together and went to find Samuel in Ramah, which was their town. The words "gathered together" and "came" are older forms that we would today say as "assembled" and "arrived." It is the beginning of an important conversation.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samuel was already old, and his sons Joel and Abijah, whom he had appointed as judges, were accepting bribes and bending justice. The elders come to Samuel with a real complaint and with a request that, as the account goes on, displeased Samuel and ended up leading him to pray.

For today: when we see injustice or problems in our church, family, or community, we can speak with those who have responsibility. But before asking for a solution, it is wise to pray and to ask ourselves whether what we are asking pleases God, not only whether it seems practical to us.
exp.6:4:
Samuel asks that all the people gather at Mizpah, and he promises to pray to God for them.

Samuel is a prophet and judge of Israel. The people had spent years suffering under the Philistines and worshiping idols such as the Baals and Ashtaroth. Samuel called them to turn back to God with all their heart, and they removed their idols. Now he summons them to a time of prayer and repentance, where they acknowledge: "We have sinned against the Lord."

Turning back to God is not only leaving what is wrong; it also means coming near to Him with humility. It is also a great help to have brothers and sisters who pray for us and with us. Today you can ask someone you trust to pray for you and pray for others.
exp.20:7:
Here David asks the priest Ahimelech whether there is a spear or a sword on hand. He explains that he left without his sword or his other weapons, because the king's business required haste, a matter that allowed no time for anything.

David is fleeing from Saul, who wants to kill him. He speaks with Ahimelech, the priest at Nob, and gives him an excuse to hide the fact that he is running away. That explanation was not entirely true, and later Doeg, who was present, reported it to Saul, with terrible consequences for the priests. The Bible records what David said, but it does not approve of his deception for that reason.

For today: when you are afraid, it is tempting to hide the truth to protect yourself. Remember that God can care for you without your having to lie, and that your words can affect other people.
exp.13:43:
Saul responds with a very strong oath. The words "God do so and more also" were a way of saying: "May God punish me if I do not carry this out." And what he vows is that Jonathan will die without fail. "Thou shalt surely die" means "you are certain to die."

Speaking is King Saul, in the middle of the war against the Philistines. Earlier he had made a hasty oath: no one was to eat until evening. Jonathan had not heard it and tasted a little honey. Saul, bound to his word, wants to keep it even though it means acting against his own son. The people step in and rescue him.

For today: let us think before we speak or make promises. Words spoken in haste or pride can wound those we love. Let us seek God's guidance and also the humility to correct ourselves.
exp.18:21:
Saul, tired of sending messengers who never come back, goes himself to Ramah. He arrives at the great well that is in Sechu, and asks where Samuel and David are. Someone tells him they are at Naioth, in Ramah.

The narrator is the author of the book, not a character in the story. Saul wants to catch David, who had fled to Samuel. Three groups of messengers were touched by the Spirit of God and ended up prophesying. Now Saul himself goes, and he too will be stopped by God. Some think God is protecting David in this way.

When someone insists on going against God's purpose, they can be stopped in surprising ways. Today we can ask God to make us let go of plans driven by pride or resentment, and trust that He cares for His own.
exp.23:18:
Saul tells David that today he has shown that he did him good. David could have killed him, because God himself had put him into his hands, but he chose not to do it. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "delivered thee into mine hand" means "allowed me to overcome him."

It is King Saul speaking, the man who was hunting David to kill him. Saul had entered a cave without knowing David was hiding there. David cut off a piece of his robe, but he spared his life and then showed it to him. Seeing this, Saul wept and admitted that David was more righteous than he was. Some see here a sincere repentance, although afterward Saul went back to pursuing David.

Today we can answer evil with good. When someone wounds us and we have the chance to take revenge, we can choose to forgive and trust that God will do justice. That path can also move the heart of the person who wronged us.
exp.19:30:
Saul tells his son Jonathan that as long as David is alive, Jonathan will not be secure as the future king, and neither will his kingdom. Then he orders: "Send and fetch him," that is, send for David, "for he shall surely die," meaning he deserves death. "Established" means settled and secure.

Saul speaks in fury against Jonathan, because David did not come to the king's table and Jonathan defended him. Saul already knew that God had taken his kingdom away from him, and out of jealousy and fear he wants to kill David. Some think he also tries to pressure Jonathan through his ambition, but the text only shows that Saul is not thinking clearly.

For today: jealousy and fear can make us unjust and cruel. When you feel envy toward someone, stop, pray, and ask God for a humble heart. Like Jonathan, choose to do what is right, even when it costs you.
exp.18:5:
Saul listened to the words of his son Jonathan and made a solemn oath. He swore "as the Lord lives" that he would not kill David. In today's English: "As surely as God lives, David will not die."

Jonathan, David's faithful friend, spoke with his father the king. Saul was jealous of David and had wanted to kill him. Jonathan reminded him that David had done him no wrong, that he had risked his life against the Philistine (Goliath), and that God had given Israel a great victory. Saul was moved and promised not to harm him. Later on, however, his jealousy returned, so his change of heart did not last.

Today we can learn to be peacemakers: speaking well of someone who is unjustly attacked and defending the truth with respect. But we must also guard the heart, because good intentions without a true change can fade away.
exp.16:45:
David is confident that God will deliver Goliath into his hands that very day. He says he will defeat him and cut off his head. He also says the bodies of the Philistines will be left for the birds of the air and the wild beasts of the earth. In the end, the purpose is that all the earth may know there is a God in Israel. "I will take thine head from thee" means cutting off his head. "Defeat" here means overcoming him.

David, a young shepherd, speaks in front of Goliath, the Philistine giant who mocked Israel's army and its God. Goliath had just threatened to leave David's body to the birds and the beasts, and David returns those very words. He does not trust in weapons, but in the name of the Lord.

For today: when you face a problem that seems enormous, do not rely only on your own resources. Place it in God's hands, act with courage, and seek to do what honors his name, not your own.
exp.13:7:
Jonathan tells his young helper that they are going to cross over toward where the Philistines are and let themselves be seen by them. "We will pass over unto these men" means they will go up close to the enemy. "We will discover ourselves unto them" means they will let themselves be seen, without hiding.

Jonathan, son of King Saul, speaks with his armor-bearer, the young man who carried his weapons. Israel was in a difficult situation in the face of the Philistine garrison. Jonathan trusts that for the LORD it is no hard thing to save by many or by few. So he proposes a sign: if the enemies invite them to come up, he will take that as a sign that God will give them the victory.

For today: when you feel you are taking a step of faith, do not act recklessly, but with confidence and attention to God. Take the step that lies before you, ask for direction, and stay willing to accept his guidance, whether he opens the door or closes it.
exp.24:5:
The explanation says that David's messengers are to greet Nabal with a wish for well-being. Saying "Peace be both to thee" is much like saying "may you have life and health." The word "peace" means far more than the absence of quarrels: it is complete well-being. That wish reaches Nabal, his household, and everything he owns.

David is fleeing from Saul and living in the wilderness with his men. Meanwhile, his men have looked after Nabal's flocks, for Nabal is a rich man. It is now sheep-shearing time, a season of feasting and abundance. David sends ten young men to ask him for help with courtesy. With this greeting he opens his request in a respectful way. Later in the story, we see that Nabal responds with contempt.

For today: before asking for something or raising a difficult matter, begin by sincerely wishing the other person well. A kind approach does not guarantee a good answer, as we see here, but it helps us act with dignity and peace.
exp.16:49:
This verse sums up the battle: David defeated the Philistine Goliath using only a sling and a stone. He struck him and killed him, though he had no sword in his hand.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks here, summarizing how the encounter ended. The verses that follow clarify one detail: David then took the giant's sword to cut off his head. Before the battle, David had said that the fight belonged to the Lord and that God would give the victory without the need for sword or spear (v. 47).

For today: God can work through what seems small or even ridiculous in the face of great problems. Do with faith what you have at hand, however simple it may be, and trust that the outcome is in God's hands.
exp.26:4:
Here David asks King Achish to give him his own place to live, in one of the towns in the countryside. He uses courteous words: "if I have now found grace in thine eyes" means "if I am pleasing to you" or "if you think well of me." He asks why he, being only a servant, should have to live beside the king in the royal city, that is, the city where the king had his court.

David speaks while fleeing from Saul, who was pursuing him to kill him. He was already in Philistine territory with his men and their families. When Saul learned that David was in Gath, he stopped searching for him. The Bible does not explain all of David's reasons; some think he wanted more freedom and less supervision, and others think he sought to avoid friction with the Philistines.

For today: sometimes the Lord places us in difficult situations, and we should ask with humility and think with wisdom, never forgetting that God cares for his people even in confusing times.
exp.16:33:
David answers King Saul by telling about his experience: he was looking after his father's sheep, and when a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock, he did not stand still.

The words "your servant" are a respectful way of speaking to the king. Here "flock" refers to the sheep being kept together.

David speaks before Saul, who doubted him because he was young, while the giant Goliath was defying Israel. David does not boast of his strength; he is building his argument. The verses that follow show that he trusted God had protected him in private and would protect him now.

For today: God often prepares our character through small and unseen tasks. Be faithful in everyday things, without waiting for applause, and trust that God uses those experiences to prepare us for greater challenges.
exp.21:1:
This verse tells us that everyone who was in trouble gathered around David: those who were distressed, those who were in debt, and those who were bitter of soul. David became their leader, and about four hundred men followed him.

David was fleeing from King Saul, who wanted to kill him, and he hid in the cave of Adullam. The text is a narrative; it is not David speaking. It shows that David, though still without a throne and pursued, drew in people who had no one to turn to. The Bible does not detail why each one came, or what their lives had been like before.

Today we can remember that God often builds community among wounded and needy people. If you are going through a difficult time, do not isolate yourself: seek healthy companionship. And if you are standing firm, open your heart to accompany someone who is suffering.
exp.13:16:
Saul tells his men to take a count to find out who had gone missing from the camp. "Number now" in the verse means to call the roll, to check who is present. The "armourbearer" was the young man who carried a soldier's weapons. When they counted, they found that Jonathan and his armourbearer were missing.

Saul speaks as king and commander of the army. The Philistines were in great confusion and panic, and Saul's watchmen noticed the disorder in the enemy camp. Saul wanted to understand what was happening, and in this way he realized that Jonathan had attacked on his own. Afterward, Saul asks for the ark and speaks with the priest, but then he stops him, because the commotion was growing.

For today: when something strange happens, it is good to pause and calmly find out what took place, but without forgetting to seek God before acting. Many times He works through ordinary, faithful people who take a step of faith.
exp.5:12:
The people of Beth-shemesh were reaping their wheat harvest in the valley. When they lifted up their eyes, they saw the ark of the LORD coming toward them, and they were filled with great joy. The explanation of the two words from the source is removed here: "reaping" means cutting the wheat, and the sentence about "rejoiced" is deleted since that word is not in the verse above.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistines had captured the ark, but they suffered plagues and decided to return it. They placed it on a cart pulled by two cows, and the cows went straight toward Beth-shemesh, an Israelite town. For the Israelites, the ark represented the presence of God, so seeing it returning was a cause for great joy.

For today: sometimes God surprises us in the middle of our daily work. These men were only harvesting when they saw something extraordinary. Let us live attentively, lifting our eyes to recognize the hand of God in the ordinary, and respond with joy and gratitude.
exp.1:27:
God says he chose the family of Levi, the family Eli came from, to serve him as priests. He gave them important duties: to offer sacrifices on his altar, to burn incense, and to wear the ephod, a priestly garment used for seeking God's guidance. He also gave them a share of the people's offerings for their support.

A prophet, described as a man of God, speaks to Eli on behalf of the LORD. Eli was a priest, but his sons were abusing their office and taking the best of the offerings. God reminds him of everything he had given them before rebuking him for honoring his sons more than him.

All service to God is a privilege received, not a right to be used for our own gain. If we have any responsibility in the church or in the family, let us ask God to help us serve with humility and always put him first.
exp.13:13:
This verse tells of the first blow against the Philistines. Jonathan and his armor-bearer, just the two of them, killed about twenty men. This happened on a small piece of ground, what the older text calls a "half acre," a measure used for fields that roughly equals what a yoke of oxen could plow in half a day.
