The narrator then tells what happened after Jonathan climbed up to the Philistine outpost. He had said that the LORD was giving them into Israel's hands. Israel was at a disadvantage, short of weapons, and Jonathan acted in faith, without telling his father Saul. This first blow set off the panic described next.

For today: sometimes God uses a small, brave step to open the way to something much greater. We do not need to have every resource; we need to trust God and take the step within our reach, with humility and good counsel.
exp.20:1:
Here David speaks with the priest Ahimelech at Nob. He tells him that King Saul had given him a secret task and that no one was to know what it was about. He also says that he had already told his servants, that is, his young helpers, where to meet him.

David is fleeing from Saul, who wants to kill him. He arrives alone, hungry and without weapons, and Ahimelech is alarmed to see him in that state. David then gives an explanation that is not true: Saul had not sent him. The Bible only reports what he said, without approving it. Later there were serious consequences (1 Samuel 22).

For today: fear can lead us to bend the truth, even when we are believers. Instead of trusting in a lie to save ourselves, we can pray and ask God for wisdom and courage to act honestly.
exp.21:6:
Saul speaks to his servants who are standing around him, and he calls them "ye Benjamites", that is, men of his own tribe. He asks them with irony whether the son of Jesse will give them fields and vineyards, and make them all captains of thousands and captains of hundreds.

Saul is in Gibeah, with his spear in his hand, surrounded by his people. He feels betrayed because David has fled and has followers. He suspects that everyone is conspiring against him. For this reason he appeals to self-interest and to tribal loyalty. He does not even say David's name, only "the son of Jesse", as a sign of contempt. Afterward Doeg the Edomite will accuse him before everyone.

For today: when fear and jealousy dominate us, we begin to see enemies where there are none. Let us ask God for humility and a trusting heart, so that we may listen calmly before we accuse.
exp.13:21:
This verse tells us that other Israelites, who had been hiding in the hill country of Ephraim out of fear of the Philistines, heard that the enemy was running away. Then they came out of their hiding places and joined in the pursuit. The words about "reaching" and "chasing" describe going after the enemy as it flees.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jonathan had bravely attacked the Philistine camp, and God caused confusion among them, so that they began to strike one another. Seeing this change, even the Hebrews who had been with the Philistines switched sides to join Israel. The text then says that it was the LORD who saved Israel that day.

For today: sometimes fear keeps us hidden, and we only move forward when we see that God is already at work. Let us ask him for the courage to take the step and join others in what he is already doing, without waiting for everything to be perfect.
exp.20:8:
Here the priest Ahimelech tells David that the only sword available is that of Goliath, the Philistine giant whom David defeated in the valley of the terebinth (or of Elah). It was kept wrapped in a cloth, behind the ephod, which was a priestly garment. David replies that there is none like it and asks that it be given to him.

David was fleeing from Saul, who wanted to kill him. He arrived without weapons and told Ahimelech that he was on an urgent mission for the king, which was not true. Nearby was Doeg, a servant of Saul, and his presence signals that this will have serious consequences for the priests.

For today: when you are in trouble, remember how God helped you before. That sword reminded David of the victory God had given him. Even so, his fear led him to lie, and that teaches us to trust God without resorting to deception.
exp.27:0:
These verses tell how the Philistines gathered their armies to attack Israel. Achish, the Philistine king, tells David that he must go out with him to war, along with his men.

Here the one speaking is Achish, king of Gath, where David had taken refuge while fleeing from Saul. Achish trusted David and believed that David was hated by his own people. David finds himself in a difficult bind: appearing loyal to the Philistines could lead him to fight against Israel. The Bible does not resolve this tension right away; David's response is ambiguous.

For today: when our past decisions lead us into difficult situations, it is wise to stop and ask God for wisdom and a way out, instead of pressing on without thinking. God can guide us even in our tangles.
exp.24:29:
Abigail tells David that when God fulfills all the good things He promised him, and appoints him ruler over Israel, something is going to happen. The sentence is left open and continues in the next verse.

Abigail speaks with David, who was coming with his men to kill Nabal, her husband, because Nabal had treated them with contempt. She goes out to meet him and asks him not to act out of revenge. She reminds him that God will call him to be king, and that it is not good for him to carry the guilt of bloodshed without need.

For today: when you feel that you have been wronged, think about what God wants to do with you over the long run. Do not let the anger of a moment rob you of peace or damage your future. Trust that God can bring about justice better than you can.
exp.29:4:
This verse says that David's two wives were also taken prisoner. One was Ahinoam, from the town of Jezreel, and the other was Abigail, who had previously been the wife of Nabal, the man from Carmel. The word "captives" means that they were seized and carried away by force.

The narrator tells what happened in Ziklag, the town where David and his men lived. While they were away, the Amalekites burned it and carried off all the families. David lost his wives and his loved ones too, and his own men, overcome with grief, spoke of stoning him.

When everything seems lost, we do not have to pretend to be strong. David wept until he had no strength left, but afterward he sought God and found strength in Him. We can weep honestly and then turn to God in prayer, asking Him for direction.
exp.11:10:
God answered the cry of his people and sent them deliverers: Jerubbaal, Bedan, Jephthah, and Samuel. Through them he rescued them from the enemies all around, and they lived in safety. "Jerubbaal" is another name for Gideon. About Bedan we are not certain: some think it is a copying error or a little-known name for one of the judges.

In his farewell speech to Israel, Samuel reminds them that every time they turned back to God, he saved them. He says this because they are now asking for a king, as if God were not enough to protect them.

For today: when you feel threatened, remember how God has helped you before. Before looking for security in other things, return to him sincerely and trust that he is still faithful.
exp.19:13:
Jonathan makes a request of David: "While I am still alive, show me the kindness of the Lord; and if I die, do not stop doing so with my family." The word "kindness" here means loyal love, a goodness that stays faithful to a covenant. The phrase "that I die not" means "if I die." The sentence is left unfinished and continues into the following verse.

Jonathan speaks with David, his friend, whom his father, King Saul, wants to kill. Jonathan suspects that David will be the next king, and so he asks him to look after his family. They had already made a covenant of friendship before God.

For today: when we promise loyalty to someone, that promise should not depend on circumstances. We can care for the family of a friend who is no longer with us, or faithfully keep the commitments we have made, thereby reflecting the faithfulness with which God treats us.
exp.17:17:
Here David answers Saul with humility, when Saul offers him his daughter Merab. He asks, "Who am I?", meaning that he does not feel worthy. "What is my life" refers to his origin or station, and "my father's family" to his humble household.

David speaks with King Saul, who offers to give him his daughter in marriage, but on one condition: that he fight the wars of the LORD. The text says that Saul, in reality, hoped the Philistines would kill David. David does not know that intention and answers with simplicity. Afterward, Merab is given to another man.

When you receive an honor or an opportunity, receive it with humility, without boasting. And if someone treats you with deceit, trust that God cares for you, as He cared for David.
exp.13:30:
This verse says that Israel defeated the Philistines that day, chasing them from Michmash to Aijalon, a long distance. But the people were left very exhausted. The word "smote" means they struck them down in battle, and "faint" speaks of extreme weariness from not having eaten.

The narrator recounts what happened after Saul made a hasty oath: no one could eat until evening. Jonathan, who did not know of it, tasted honey and his strength returned. He criticizes his father's command, saying the people would have fought better had they eaten. Here we see the cost of that command: victory, but with a worn-out people.

For today: before demanding something of others, let us consider whether it truly helps or only weighs them down. Seeking God with zeal is good, but it should be done with wisdom and compassion.
exp.20:2:
David asks the priest Ahimelech for something to eat: five loaves of bread, or whatever he has on hand. "What is under your hand" means "what is within your reach," that is, whatever is available. The phrase "whatever is present" means "whatever may be found."

David, who is fleeing from King Saul, speaks here. He arrives at Nob, where the priest was, alone and hungry. He tells Ahimelech that he comes on a secret mission from the king, but this was not true: David was hiding the fact that he was escaping from Saul. The text does not justify that lie, and later it brought serious consequences for the priests (1 Samuel 22).

For today: when we are in need, it is good to ask for help with humility and simplicity. But we do not need to resort to deceit to get it. God is the one who cares for us, and honesty also protects those who help us.
exp.22:0:
This verse tells that someone brought word to David that the Philistines were attacking the city of Keilah and robbing the threshingfloors. A threshingfloor was a flat place where wheat and barley were beaten to separate the grain from the straw. To rob the threshingfloors was to take away people's harvest, their food for the whole year.

The verse does not say who brought the news, only that they told David. David was running from King Saul and living with a small band of followers. Keilah was a town in Judah, and its people could not defend themselves alone. The news reaches David as a plea for help, and he responds by first asking God what to do.

For today: when you learn of a need, do not act only on impulse or fear. First pray and ask God for direction; then obey, even when others doubt.
exp.19:28:
Here Jonathan repeats to Saul the excuse that David had asked him to use: that David had to go to Bethlehem for his family's yearly sacrifice, and that his brother had ordered him to be there. The verse quoted above says "our family hath a sacrifice in the city" and "let me get away." So the explanation's comments on "clan" and "a short trip" are rewritten here to match the verse: "family" appears in the verse, and "get away" means to slip off for a short while. The phrase about finding favor in someone's eyes is a polite way of saying "if you think well of me," which matches the verse's "if I have found favour in thine eyes."

Jonathan is speaking and quoting David. Saul had noticed that David was absent from the table at the New Moon feast. David and Jonathan had agreed on this explanation in order to test whether Saul wanted to kill David. Some think the excuse was partly true and others that it was a cover story; the text does not make this clear. Saul's furious reaction confirms his intentions.

For today: when the truth is dangerous, it is not enough to look after our own safety; we must also look after our integrity. Let us ask God for wisdom to be honest and to protect the innocent, while continuing to trust Him.
exp.16:1:
Saul and the men of Israel were also gathered together, the text says. They set up their camp in the valley of the Oak (other versions call it the valley of Elah) and lined up in formation to fight against the Philistines. The phrase "were gathered together, and pitched... and set the battle in array" means that they took their positions in rows, ready for combat.

The narrator of the book tells how the Philistines, Israel's enemies, had invaded territory belonging to Judah. Israel responds, and both armies end up facing each other, separated by a valley. This is the setting where Goliath will appear and, afterward, David. The verse prepares the scene of a great conflict that seems to have no way out.

For today: we often face big problems that leave us paralyzed, as if we were standing in a valley waiting. This verse reminds us that God works in the middle of those situations of waiting and tension. While you carry out your part responsibly, trust that He can intervene in ways you do not expect.
exp.0:14:
Hannah answers Eli the priest respectfully: "No, my lord." She explains to him that she is not drunk, but a woman of a sorrowful spirit, that is, with a heavy and aching soul. She says that she has drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but has poured out her soul before the Lord, that is, she opened her whole heart to God in prayer.

Hannah had no children and suffered greatly because of it. She had gone to pray at the sanctuary in Shiloh. She prayed silently, only moving her lips, and Eli, seeing her like that, thought she was drunk. She corrects the misunderstanding with humility and sincerity, without taking offense.

For today: God does not ask for perfect or well-arranged prayers. You can tell him your pain just as it is, even though others do not understand it or misjudge it. And if someone judges you wrongly, you can answer with calmness and gentleness, as Hannah did.
exp.16:23:
This verse says that all the men of Israel, when they saw Goliath, ran away to get away from him, and felt great fear. The word "men" in the verse simply means men, and "fled from him" means that they moved away from where he was standing.

The narrator describes what was happening in the camp of Israel. Goliath had been challenging the army for days, and no one dared to face him. David had just arrived to visit his brothers and heard the challenge for the first time. His reaction, in the verses that follow, contrasts with the fear of the others, because he focuses on the fact that Goliath is defying the living God.

Today we too can become paralyzed when we look only at the size of a problem. This passage invites us to remember who God is before deciding how to respond. When you feel afraid, pray and fix your eyes on Him, not only on the difficulty.
exp.16:50:
The explanation says that David ran toward the fallen Philistine and stood over him. He drew the giant's sword from its sheath, finished him off, and cut off his head with it. When the Philistines saw that their champion was dead, they fled.

This is part of the account where the narrator describes the duel between David, a young shepherd, and Goliath. David had turned down Saul's armor and trusted in God, not in weapons. He had already won with the stone from his sling; this final act secured the victory. For the Philistines, the defeat of their champion meant the defeat of their whole army, which is why they fled.

When God places you before an enormous problem, take the step in faith and do not freeze. Use what you have, persist until the end, and trust that God is the one who gives the victory.
exp.20:6:
This verse introduces a new man into the scene: Doeg, an Edomite who served Saul as chief of his herdsmen. He was held back before the Lord that day, that is, kept or set apart at the sanctuary. The text does not say with certainty why. Some think he was fulfilling a vow, a purification, or some matter of religious duty.

The narrator speaks here, not David. He interrupts the scene between David and the priest Ahimelech to tell us that someone saw them. David was fleeing from Saul and had asked for bread and a sword. What follows, in chapter 22, shows that Doeg reported to Saul, and this brought terrible consequences upon the priests.

For today: even when we believe no one sees us, our words and decisions have witnesses and consequences. Let us act with wisdom and truth, and trust that God cares for us.
exp.14:22:
It says that rebelling against God is as serious as divination, which looked for guidance apart from God. And that stubbornness, or deliberately disobeying, is as serious as idolatry, which is putting something else in the place of God. Because Saul rejected the word of the Lord, God rejected him as king.

The prophet Samuel speaks to Saul. God had commanded him to destroy the Amalekites completely, but Saul and the people kept the best of the spoils. Saul said it was to sacrifice to God. Samuel explains to him that God cares more about obedience than about religious offerings.

For today: we cannot replace obedience with religious acts or good intentions. Today you can ask yourself in what area you know what God asks of you, and give him your sincere yes, even when it costs you.
exp.11:8:
It says that the people of Israel forgot the Lord their God. Because of this, God "sold them," meaning he allowed them to fall under the power of their enemies: Sisera, captain of the army of Hazor, the Philistines, and the king of Moab. Those peoples waged war against them.

Samuel, now an old man, is speaking at the ceremony where Saul is confirmed as king. Samuel wants the people to remember the story: God was always faithful, but they kept turning away again and again. He shows them that their troubles did not come because God failed, but because they left him.

For today: when life becomes complicated, it is worth asking ourselves whether we have drifted away from God. If so, we can return as Israel did, with humility, because God is still willing to forgive and to rescue.
exp.17:27:
This verse says that Saul watched closely what was happening and reached a conclusion: God was with David, and also his own daughter Michal loved David. The phrase "that the Lord was with David" means that God was accompanying him and blessing him. "Considering" means thinking carefully about it.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book. Saul had set a trap for David: he asked for a hundred foreskins of Philistines, hoping they would kill him. But David came back with twice that number. Saul could no longer deny that God backed David. What follows shows that this did not lead him to surrender to God, but to fear him more.

For today: one can clearly see the hand of God and still resist it. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that recognizes his work in others without envy and that responds with confidence, not fear.
exp.9:11:
A man from the same place answered with another question: "But who is their father?" That is why people repeated the saying: "Is Saul also among the prophets?" "Became a proverb" means it turned into a popular saying.

Saul had just been anointed by Samuel, and the Spirit of God came upon him. Those who knew him were astonished to see him prophesying. The man's words are hard to interpret. Perhaps he meant that the gift of prophecy does not depend on family, neither on the fathers of the prophets nor on Saul's. Others understand it as mockery or amazement. The text does not make it clear.

God does not work according to appearances or people's background. Avoid pigeonholing others by their past or their family. And if God calls you, do not let other people's opinions hold you back.
exp.23:9:
David asks Saul why he listens to those who tell him that David wants to harm him. It is a direct and respectful question.

David is speaking to King Saul, who had been pursuing him in order to kill him. He had just had the chance to finish off Saul in the cave, and his men urged him to do it. But David held back, cut off only a piece of the robe, and now comes out to show Saul that he is not his enemy. His question points to the rumors that had poisoned Saul's heart.

Today we can learn not to believe everything we are told about others, and not to let gossip fill us with anger. When people accuse us unfairly, we can answer with calm, with respect, and with facts, without repaying evil for evil.
exp.2:3:
The explanation says that God called Samuel, a young man who was sleeping in the sanctuary, and that he answered right away: "Here am I." Note that Samuel believed it was Eli who was calling him, as the following verses show.

The narrator tells this moment at a time when Eli, the priest, was already old and nearly blind. Samuel served him in the sanctuary at Shiloh, near the ark. Later the text says that Samuel did not yet know the Lord's voice well. God calls him to give a message and to begin his work as a prophet.

For today: God can speak to us in ways we do not recognize at first. We can have a willing heart like Samuel's, read the Bible, pray, and ask advice from mature people in the faith, as Eli helped Samuel understand what was happening.
exp.16:20:
This verse describes the scene of the battle. Israelites and Philistines had lined up for combat, in battle formation. "Army against army" means that each force had its ranks drawn up facing each other, ready to fight.

The narrator places us in the Valley of the Terebinth (or of Elah). David has just arrived with supplies for his brothers, sent by his father Jesse. Everything seems about to become a battle, but the text shows a standoff: the armies looked at each other without charging. This sets up the appearance of Goliath and the challenge that will change the story.

For today: sometimes we live through long tensions, with fear and no progress. David came to do something simple, carry food, and there God put him in the right place. Be faithful in small things; God can use them in great ways.
exp.22:2:
David's men said that they were already afraid while in Judah, so they were far more afraid of going to Keilah to face the Philistine army. The phrase "driven their livestock ahead of them" describes how they moved their herds along in front of them, and the threshing floors are the places where grain was beaten out.

Here the speakers are David's followers, who were fleeing from King Saul and living as fugitives. God had already told David to go and rescue Keilah. Even so, his men hesitated, because they felt weak and vulnerable. David consulted God again, and God confirmed the command and promised victory.

For today: being afraid is normal, and it is not sin. When we are afraid, we can do what David did: pray again, seek God's direction once more, and move forward with confidence in his promise, even when the task seems larger than our strength.
exp.9:14:
Here the uncle of Saul asks his nephew to tell him what Samuel said to them. The phrase in the original wording is an old way of saying "Please, tell me," and the uncle is curious, because Saul and his servant had gone to see the prophet.

The uncle speaks because he sees them come back after searching for some lost donkeys. Saul had just been secretly anointed by Samuel as the future king, and he had prophesied. That is why the people were amazed. In the next verse, Saul tells about the donkeys, but he keeps silent about the kingdom. Some see in this humility or prudence; others, fear. The text does not explain the reason.

For today: not everything God entrusts to us has to be told right away. Ask Him for wisdom to know when to speak and when to wait with humility.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that when the Israelites needed to repair or sharpen their tools, they had to go down to the Philistines. The word "mattocks" refers to the points of the plow, the "coulters" are the blades that cut the soil ahead of the plow, the "forks" are tools used to turn over straw or grain, and the "goads" were a pointed stick used to guide the oxen. In other words, even the simplest parts of daily work depended on the enemy.

The narrator describes Israel's situation under Saul. The Philistines controlled the working of iron so that the Israelites could not make weapons. In this way they kept them weak and dependent. That is why, on the day of battle, almost no one had a sword or a spear.

For today: when we depend completely on something that dominates us, we lose our freedom. It is wise to ask God for wisdom so that we are not tied to anything that weakens us, and to remember that He can work even when we lack resources.
exp.26:9:
This verse tells how King Achish asked David, "Where have you made a raid today?" David answered that they had raided the south of Judah, the south of the Jerahmeelites, or the south of the Kenites. The word "south" is used here for the direction, and "raid" refers to armed attacks.

David was living among the Philistines, fleeing from Saul. Achish had given him the city of Ziklag. In reality, David was attacking peoples who were enemies of Israel, but he led Achish to believe that he was attacking his own people. So Achish trusted him. The text recounts this without approving or condemning the deception; the reader should notice it carefully.

For today: the Bible sometimes shows the failings of its heroes. Let us be honest and seek God with integrity, rather than holding onto the truth with half-measures or deceit.
exp.10:8:
This verse tells how the men of Israel answered the messengers of Jabesh-gilead by saying that the next day, when the sun grew hot, they would be rescued. "When the sun grew hot" means when the sun was already strong, around mid-morning. The men of Jabesh were overjoyed to hear it.

The ones speaking are the Israelites gathered by Saul and Samuel. Jabesh was surrounded by the Ammonites, and its people had asked for help urgently. Saul had called the people to join together, and the fear of the LORD moved them to set out united. This answer brings hope to a distressed city.

For today: when someone is in trouble, a word of encouragement and a real commitment to help can restore their joy. We can be people who stand with others, keep an honest promise, and then act together with courage.
exp.21:11:
Saul calls the priest Ahimelech and tells him to listen. "Hear now" is a direct command from a king to his subject. "Son of Ahitub" is the way of naming Ahimelech by his father. He answers, "Here I am, my lord," which means "I am here, at your service." It is a response of respect and readiness.

Saul is furious because Ahimelech helped David, who was fleeing from the king. He summoned all the priests of Nob and accuses them of conspiring. Ahimelech answers calmly and without fear, since he did not know that David was being pursued. Here an unjust trial begins, and the Bible does not present it as right.

Today we can learn from Ahimelech: when someone accuses us unjustly, it is wise to respond with truth and calm. We should also be careful not to let jealousy or fear lead us to judge and hurt the innocent.
exp.5:6:
It says that the Philistines were to build a new cart and hitch to it two cows that had just given birth, which had never pulled a yoke. The calves, that is, the young, would be separated from them and taken home. The verse's word for "hitch" means to put a yoke on, and "return" means to go back or come home.

The speakers are the Philistine priests and diviners. They had taken the ark of God, and a plague had fallen on them. They wanted to send it back and to know whether the punishment came from the God of Israel or was mere chance. The cows, which would naturally want to return with their calves, would be a test: if they went toward Beth-shemesh, it would be a sign that God was guiding them.

For today: when we recognize that we have done wrong, fear alone is not enough. It is good to humble ourselves, make right what we did, and seek God sincerely, without hardening our hearts.
exp.14:16:
Samuel reminds Saul of something important: although he once saw himself as small, God made him leader of all the tribes of Israel. The word "head" means chief or leader, and "anointed" means that he was set apart by God to be king, with oil as the sign.

Samuel speaks after Saul did not obey the command to destroy the Amalekites completely. Saul excused himself by saying the people kept the best of the flock to sacrifice to God. Samuel confronts him with firm affection, reminding him where God took him from and why He put him there.

For today: when God gives us responsibility, blessing, or influence, let us not use it to do whatever seems right to us. Let us remember that everything we have comes from Him, and respond with humble and complete obedience, without excuses.
exp.16:2:
This verse describes how the two armies were positioned. The Philistines occupied one mountain, Israel occupied the mountain across from it, and a valley lay between them. Some older wording is explained here: "one side" and "the other side" are the phrases the verse uses to show which army stood where.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting the events without giving an opinion. The Philistines, enemies of Israel, had gathered to fight, and Saul with his men went out to face them. The verse sets the scene where Goliath will appear. The valley separates the two sides and shows that the battle has come to a standstill, with both armies looking at each other.

For today: sometimes we feel stuck in front of a "valley" of fear or waiting, looking at a large problem. While the solution has not yet come, we can ask God for calm and trust, instead of letting ourselves be paralyzed by what we see.
exp.2:0:
The explanation says that the young Samuel served God under the guidance of the priest Eli. In those days the word of the Lord was rare, that is, scarce and uncommon, and for that reason very precious. There was also no open vision, meaning that it was not common for God to communicate clearly and openly.

This is the beginning of the story of Samuel's calling. The narrator is the author of the book, who is not named. He describes a spiritually difficult time in Israel, when Eli's priesthood was weakened by the sin of his sons. Some scholars understand that God spoke little as a consequence of that condition of the people, although the text only says that it was rare.

Even when God seems silent, we can keep serving him faithfully in what is simple, as Samuel did. Keep your ear attentive to his Word, which we have within our reach today, and do not stop seeking him with humility.
exp.3:3:
The explanation says that the people of Israel sent men to Shiloh and brought from there the ark of the covenant of the Lord of hosts, which is described as dwelling between the cherubim (figures of angels on the lid of the ark). The two sons of the priest Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, came with the ark. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "of hosts" speaks of his power over all things.

The narrator tells what happened after Israel lost to the Philistines. The elders wondered why God had struck them, but they did not seek to repent. They thought the ark would save them like a charm. The sons of Eli were corrupt priests, according to chapter 2, so their presence already signals trouble.

For today: let us not treat religious objects as if they were a guarantee of God's help. When something goes wrong, let us first draw near to Him with humility and sincerity, not only with symbols or customs.
exp.14:28:
The verse says that God, called here "the Victor of Israel" (other versions say "the Glory" or "the Strength of Israel"), does not lie or change his mind the way a person does. "To repent" here means to back away from a decision. God is firm and faithful to what he says.

Samuel speaks with King Saul, who had disobeyed a clear command from God. Samuel announces to him that the kingdom will be taken from him. Saul tears Samuel's robe, and Samuel uses this as a sign that the kingdom would also be torn away. Some note that God does indeed "repent" of having made Saul king (vv. 11, 35), but here the point is that his judgment is not arbitrary and does not change because of human pressure.

For today: you can trust that God keeps his word, both in his promises and in his warnings. That invites you to obey him with seriousness and to rest in his faithfulness.
exp.22:23:
The verse says that the men of Ziph went up to their town ahead of Saul, to keep watch on David. Meanwhile, David and his men were in the wilderness of Maon, in the plain to the south of the desert.

The men of Ziph had betrayed David to Saul. Saul praised them and asked them to find out for certain where David was hiding, because he considered him very cunning. They went to investigate, and David was nearby, pursued although he had done nothing wrong.

For today: even when we sometimes feel cornered or wrongly judged, we can keep trusting that God sees our situation. And like David, we can act with prudence, without seeking revenge, trusting that God will care for us.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that Eli was ninety-eight years old and could no longer see anything. The phrase "his eyes were dim" means that his eyes had grown dark, as when night falls. He was a blind old man, sitting by the side of the road.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. It explains why Eli could not see the messenger and had to hear everything. Eli was waiting for news of the battle against the Philistines, and his heart trembled for the ark of God. Soon he would be told that his sons had died and that the ark had been captured.

For today: even though we cannot see what is coming, we can care more about what belongs to God than about what belongs to us. And while we wait, it is good to ask God for strength to receive bad news with faith and not only with fear.
exp.19:31:
Jonathan answers his father Saul with two questions: "Why shall he be slain? What hath he done?" These are words of defense. Jonathan asks Saul for a just reason to kill David.

Jonathan speaks at a new moon meal, at the king's table. David was absent, and Jonathan had to find out whether Saul meant to kill him. Saul grew angry, insulted his son, and ordered that David be brought. Jonathan, even knowing his father was furious, defended an innocent friend. Afterward Saul hurled a spear at him, and so Jonathan understood the truth.

Today we can learn to defend with respect someone who is treated unjustly. Sometimes it costs dearly, but speaking the truth and asking "What hath he done?" helps to halt accusations that have no basis.
exp.19:37:
Jonathan called out again to his young helper, telling him to hurry, not to delay, and to make haste. The boy gathered up the arrows and came back to his master.

Jonathan was speaking with a signal agreed on beforehand with David, who was hiding because Saul wanted to kill him. If Jonathan said the arrows were beyond the boy, it meant David had to flee. The boy did not understand anything; he only obeyed. The shouts seemed like an ordinary command, but they were a secret message.

For today: sometimes truly loving someone means acting with prudence and faithfulness, even when others do not understand what we are doing. Jonathan risked his own position for his friend. Ask yourself today whom you can protect or support with loyalty, without seeking recognition.
exp.21:4:
The explanation says that the prophet Gad told David to leave the stronghold and go back to the land of Judah. David obeyed and went into the forest of Hareth.

Here Gad speaks, a prophet who was with David while he was fleeing from King Saul. David had left his parents with the king of Moab and was hiding in a stronghold, probably a place of concealment. It is not known with certainty which one it was. Gad's message led him out of a safe refuge into a more exposed place, within his own people. Later Saul learned where David was.

For today: sometimes God asks us to leave a comfortable and secure place in order to follow his way. Listening to wise counsel and obeying, even when it costs us, is a sign of trust in him.
exp.16:37:
Saul, the explanation says, put his own war clothing on David. He placed on his head a strong metal helmet, and he fitted him with a breastplate, a protective covering for the chest. Saul wanted David to be well armed.

David had just told Saul that he trusted God to defeat Goliath, just as God had delivered him from the lion and the bear while he was caring for sheep. Saul gave him his blessing, but then wanted to help him in his own way, with the armor that Saul knew. Because Saul was king, his equipment was the safest that could be offered. Afterward David took it off, because he was not used to wearing it.

We can receive the help of others with gratitude, but what works for them does not always suit us. God has guided us through our own story, and we should trust Him by humbly using what we really know how to do.
exp.5:9:
The Philistines did what their priests and diviners had told them. They took two cows that had just given birth and were still nursing, hitched them to the cart, and shut their calves up at home. The verse says the men did so, took two milch cows, and tied them to the cart while shutting up their calves at home.

The Philistines had captured the ark of God and suffered plagues. They wanted to know whether the suffering came from the God of Israel or was just a coincidence. The cows, by instinct, would return to their calves; if instead they went toward Beth-shemesh, it would be a clear sign that God was at work. This test was their idea, not a command from God.

God can speak to us even when we do not seek him in the right way. But we do not need to ask for strange signs: today we have his Word. When you are in doubt, look for him in it and in prayer, and obey what he has already shown you.
exp.2:12:
It says that God will judge Eli's house once and for all. The reason is "the wickedness he knows about": Eli knew of his sons' sin. The phrase "made themselves vile" means they behaved in a shameful and contemptible way. The word "restrained" means to stop or correct. Eli did not stop them.

The speaker is the LORD, and He says this to the young Samuel during the night, in the sanctuary at Shiloh. Eli's sons, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests and abused their office (1 Samuel 2:12-17, 22). Eli rebuked them with words, but he did not remove them from service. God counts this as a responsibility that Eli failed to fulfill.

For today: if we have authority or influence, whether as parents, leaders, or teachers, God calls us to correct with love and firmness, without looking away out of comfort or fear of conflict.
exp.23:13:
David tells Saul there is an old saying: wickedness comes from wicked people. By this he means that if he were a wicked man, he would already have harmed Saul. Since he is not, he will not raise his hand against him.

David speaks in a cave, after Saul, who was pursuing him to kill him, entered there without knowing David was inside. David cut off only the edge of Saul's robe and did him no harm. Now he shows it to Saul as proof that he is not his enemy, and he leaves God to be the judge between the two of them.

For today: when someone treats us unfairly, we do not have to answer with the same wickedness. We can act with integrity, speak the truth with respect, and trust that God will do justice in his time.
exp.17:9:
The verse tells us that the next day an evil spirit, sent or allowed by God, came upon Saul. Inside his house he acted as if in a trance, prophesying and behaving in an agitated, wild manner. Meanwhile David played the harp as usual, and Saul had a spear in his hand.

The narrator relates this after the women sang that David had defeated his tens of thousands and Saul his thousands. Saul was filled with jealousy and anger. Scholars explain in several ways how an evil spirit could come from God; the text does not make this clear, but it shows that God had already withdrawn his favor from Saul.

Unchecked jealousy can become something that dominates us and leads us to harm others. When we feel envy at another's success, let us bring it to God in prayer and celebrate what he is doing in others before it grows.
exp.29:14:
Here David asks the young Egyptian whether he will lead him down to the band of raiders that burned Ziklag. The young man agrees, but asks for an oath sworn in God's name: that David will not kill him or hand him back to his master. The word "young man" here is the servant's term, and "master" is the owner whom he had served as a slave.

David had just returned to Ziklag and found it burned, with his people carried off captive. The young man was an abandoned slave, sick, left behind by the Amalekites. David had found him and given him food. Now the young man, knowing his life was worth nothing to his master, seeks protection. David accepts the arrangement, and the young man leads him to the enemy camp.

For today: God can use people who seem insignificant or cast aside to show us the way. Treat everyone with kindness and respect, even those you do not see as important. Your compassion may open a door you did not expect.
exp.14:17:
God sent Saul on a mission with a clear command: to destroy the sinners the Amalekites and to fight against them until they are consumed. The explanation of the old word for "sent" is removed here, since "sent" is already in the verse, and the word for "mission" is likewise not needed because the verse says "journey," which means the same thing in this context: a mission or expedition. The phrase meaning "utterly destroy" is simply the verse's own wording.

Samuel speaks in God's name and reminds Saul of what he was commanded. Before that, he reminds him that God made him king when he felt small. Later Saul did not fully obey: he spared Agag and the best of the plunder. This passage is difficult, and many Christians understand it as God's judgment on a nation with a long history of wickedness, not as a model for us.

For today: partial obedience is not obedience. If God shows us something clearly, such as leaving a bad habit or forgiving someone, we should do it with humility and without excuses.
exp.12:4:
The Philistines gathered together to fight against Israel: thirty thousand chariots, six thousand horsemen, and soldiers as numerous as the sand on the seashore. They came up and set up camp at Michmash, east of Beth-aven. The sand of the seashore is a comparison meaning an uncountable crowd.

The narrator is the author of the book, who tells what happened after Jonathan attacked a Philistine garrison. Saul blew the trumpets to call Israel together, and the Philistines responded with great force. Some scholars think the number of chariots is very large, or that the text may have been copied differently, but the point is that Israel was greatly outmatched.

When we face problems that seem bigger than we are, fear can paralyze us, as it did Israel. Today we can bring that fear to God in prayer before we act, and trust that he continues to care for us.
exp.29:19:
It says that David also took the sheep and the larger cattle, that is, cows and oxen. His men would drive them out in front of everyone, and the people would say, "This is David's spoil." "Spoil" means plunder, what is gained by defeating the enemy.

David and his men had just pursued the Amalekites, who had raided Ziklag and taken captive their families. God gave them the victory, and they recovered everything. This livestock seems to be extra plunder from the Amalekites. The text does not make clear who was saying it, but it was probably David's men, who acknowledged him as their leader. Right away a dispute arises over how to divide it.

For today: when God gives you a victory or a blessing, do not see it as yours alone. Recognize that it is a gift and share it generously, especially with those who could not help you.
exp.25:0:
This verse tells how some people from Ziph went to Saul at Gibeah and let him know where David was hiding. The old form of their name, which the explanation mentions, is simply the people of Ziph, and the reader can take it as the Ziphites named in the verse. The word meaning hill or ridge is the hill of Hachilah, and the phrase meaning in front of the wilderness refers to the hill lying before the desert area, or in view of it.

The Ziphites were people from the land of Judah, and they spoke to King Saul. Saul had been pursuing David for some time out of jealousy and fear. Earlier, in 1 Samuel 23, the Ziphites had given him similar information. Here they betray David again, and this leads Saul to set out with three thousand men to search for him.

For today: we should be careful about what we say about others. A word spoken out of convenience or fear can put an innocent person in danger. Let us ask God for the courage to speak the truth and not feed injustice.
exp.13:22:
It was the Lord who gave Israel the victory that day. The explanation says he rescued them from the enemy. The pursuit of the fleeing Philistines reached as far as Beth-aven, a place west of the hill country of Michmash. Its exact location is not known for certain.

The narrator is the one speaking. Jonathan had attacked a Philistine outpost with his armor-bearer, and God sent panic into the enemy army. When the Israelites who had been hiding or scattered joined together, the battle turned. The narrator makes clear that the victory came from God, not only from human effort or from Saul's leadership.

For today: when you see progress in your life, give thanks to God and recognize his hand. He can use small, brave actions to open the way, and he also reminds us not to trust only in our own strength.
exp.29:25:
It says that when David came back to Ziklag, he sent some of the spoil to the elders of Judah, who were his friends. He sent the gift with these words: "a blessing for you," taken from what was taken from the enemies of the Lord. "Spoil" means plunder taken in war. "Blessing" here means a gift.

David had defeated the Amalekites, who had burned Ziklag and carried off the families. After recovering everything, he decided that the spoil should be shared equally between those who fought and those who guarded the baggage. Then he also shared with several towns of Judah, probably in gratitude for their support while he was fleeing from Saul. The text presents it as a victory given by the Lord.

For today: what God gives us is not only for ourselves. We can share with generosity and gratitude, remembering those who supported us in difficult times.

sum.29:
When David and his men came back to Ziklag, they found the city burned and their wives, sons, and daughters taken captive. David strengthened himself in the LORD his God, inquired of the LORD, pursued the Amalekites, and recovered everything that had been taken.

Afterward he insisted that the plunder be divided equally, even with the men who had stayed behind exhausted, and he sent a share to the elders of Judah.
sum.2: God calls Samuel at night, and the young man, not recognizing the voice, runs three times to Eli, until Eli teaches him to answer: "Speak, Lord, for your servant is listening." God announces judgment on Eli's house, and Samuel tells him about it honestly. God was with him, and all Israel knew he was a faithful prophet.
sum.28: The Philistines gather at Aphek to fight against Israel, and David goes along with King Achish. But the Philistine commanders distrust David and insist that he leave, out of fear that he might turn against them in the battle. Achish praises David, but he sends him away, and David returns early to Philistine territory.
sum.8: Saul sets out with a servant to look for his father's lost donkeys, and when they cannot find them, they go to consult the prophet Samuel. God had already told Samuel that this young man from the tribe of Benjamin would be the leader of his people. Samuel honors him at the feast and sets him apart to give him a message from God.
sum.26: David feared that Saul would someday kill him, so he fled with his six hundred men into Philistine territory, and King Achish gave him the city of Ziklag. From there he raided neighboring peoples, but he deceived Achish by telling him that he was attacking Judah, and Achish believed him. The text shows David's fear and his questionable decisions, without either approving or condemning them.
sum.10: Nahash the Ammonite threatened Jabesh Gilead with a cruel condition, and Saul, moved by the Spirit of God, gathered all Israel and delivered them. After the victory, Saul pardoned his critics and acknowledged that the Lord had given the salvation. Then the people confirmed him as king at Gilgal with joy.
sum.1: Hannah prayed and praised God because he brings down the proud, lifts up the poor, and watches over those who are faithful to him. While the boy Samuel grows up serving God, the sons of Eli abuse the offerings and the people, and God announces judgment on Eli's family and promises to raise up a faithful priest.
sum.23: David had Saul in his hands inside a cave and, instead of killing him, only cut off the edge of his robe, because he respected the anointed one of God. He then showed Saul that he was not his enemy and left the judgment in God's hands. Saul wept, admitted that David was more righteous, and asked him to look after his family.
sum.15: God sends Samuel to Bethlehem to anoint a new king from among the sons of Jesse, and he teaches that God does not look at outward appearance but at the heart. He chooses David, the youngest, who tends the sheep, and the Spirit of the LORD comes upon him. Meanwhile, Saul is tormented, and David soothes him by playing the harp.
sum.9: Samuel anointed Saul in private and told him of signs that would take place that very day. The Spirit of God came upon him, changing him, and he prophesied among the prophets. Afterward, at Mizpah, Samuel rebuked the people for asking for a king, and God pointed to Saul, who had hidden himself. Some cheered for him, but others looked down on him, and he kept silent.
sum.18: Saul wants to kill David, but Jonathan defends him, and then Michal helps him escape at night. David flees to Samuel in Ramah, and when Saul pursues him, the Spirit of God stops him among the prophets. In this way, God protects David against the king's threat.
sum.13: Jonathan and his armor-bearer, trusting that for the LORD it is no hard thing to save by many or by few, attack the Philistines, and God sends panic and victory to Israel. But Saul's hasty oath wears the people out and almost costs Jonathan his life, and the people rescue him.
sum.24: David asks Nabal, a rich but harsh man, for help, and Nabal insults him, so David sets out with his men intending to take revenge. Abigail, his wise wife, brings food and begs David not to shed blood without cause, and he listens to her. Afterward God strikes Nabal down, and David takes Abigail as his wife.
sum.3: Israel lost a battle to the Philistines and brought the ark of the covenant out to the fighting as if it were a good-luck charm, but they were defeated again. Thirty thousand men died, Eli's sons were killed, and the ark was captured. When Eli heard the news, he died. His daughter-in-law gave birth, and she named the boy Ichabod, saying, "The glory has departed from Israel."
sum.22: David consults God, rescues the city of Keilah from the Philistines, and then learns that Saul is coming to trap him, so he flees with his six hundred men. Jonathan encourages him and renews his covenant with him. Saul almost catches up with David, but a Philistine attack forces him to turn back, showing God's care over David.
sum.17: Jonathan loved David as he loved himself and made a covenant with him, while David succeeded in everything he did and all the people loved him. Saul, filled with jealousy and fear because the LORD was with David, tried to kill him with a spear and then sent him to fight against the Philistines. But David came through successfully and married Michal.
sum.0: Hannah, a woman without children and with a wounded heart, prayed with tears at Shiloh and promised to dedicate to God the son she might be given. God heard her prayer, and Samuel was born. When the boy was weaned, Hannah kept her promise and gave him over to God at the house of the LORD.
sum.16: The Philistines challenge Israel with the giant Goliath, and everyone is afraid. David, a young shepherd, trusts in the living God and faces him with a sling and a stone, without armor. In this way he defeats the giant and teaches that victory comes from the LORD, not from the sword or the spear.
sum.14: God commands Saul to completely destroy the Amalekites, but he and the people spare King Agag and the best of the livestock. Samuel teaches him that obeying God is worth more than sacrifices, and he announces that the kingdom will be taken away from him. Saul confesses his sin, but Samuel never sees him again and mourns for him.
sum.11: Samuel, now an old man, takes his leave before the people and shows that he has always acted with integrity. He reminds them how God rescued them again and again, and that asking for a king was a mistake. God sends thunder and rain, the people repent, and Samuel encourages them not to be afraid but to serve God with all their heart.
sum.5: After seven months of plagues, the Philistines send the ark back to Israel with gifts of gold, and two cows carry it on their own all the way to Beth Shemesh, showing that the LORD was at work. But some of the people there looked inside the ark and died, and the people understood that God is holy and must be treated with reverence. The figure of 50,070 is widely debated.
sum.27: When the Philistines attacked, Saul was gripped by fear, and since God did not answer him, he went looking for a medium in Endor, even though he himself had banned such practices. Samuel appears and tells him that he will lose the kingdom and die, along with his sons, because of his disobedience. Saul is devastated, but the woman takes care of him and gives him a meal.
sum.20: David flees from Saul and comes to Nob, where he lies to the priest Ahimelech in order to receive holy bread and the sword of Goliath. Doeg, a servant of Saul, sees all of this. Then David escapes to Gath, feels fear, and pretends to be insane so that King Achish will let him go. The Bible here shows his fear and his human decisions.
sum.4: The Philistines carried the ark of God into the temple of their god Dagon, but the statue fell and was smashed to pieces in front of the ark. Then a plague struck Ashdod, Gath, and Ekron, and the people asked for the ark to be sent away. The chapter teaches that God cannot be compared with idols.
sum.30: The Philistines defeat Israel on Mount Gilboa, and Saul and his three sons die. Saul takes his own life so that he will not fall into the hands of the enemy. The Philistines display his body, but the brave men of Jabesh-gilead rescue it, bury it with honor, and fast for seven days.
sum.7: As Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons as judges over Israel, but they were corrupt. They took bribes and twisted justice. So the elders of Israel came to Samuel and asked him for a king to rule over them, like all the other nations. Samuel was displeased by their request, but the LORD told him that the people had not rejected Samuel, but had rejected God as their king. Samuel warned the people about how much a king would cost them. Still, they refused to listen and insisted that they wanted a king. In the end, God allowed them to have one.
sum.19: David flees from Saul and asks his friend Jonathan for help. Jonathan promises to warn him if his father plans to kill him. At the New Moon feast, Saul becomes furious, tries to kill Jonathan with a spear, and makes clear his hatred for David. Jonathan warns David by means of arrows, and the two friends say goodbye in tears, faithful to their covenant before God.
sum.6: After twenty years of sorrow, Israel repents: they put away their idols, fast at Mizpah, and confess their sin. When the Philistines attack, Samuel offers a sacrifice and cries out to God, and the LORD defeats them with thunder. Samuel sets up a stone called Ebenezer, which means "Thus far the LORD has helped us."
sum.25: The Ziphites betray David, and Saul searches for him with three thousand men. At night, David and Abishai enter the camp and find Saul asleep, but David refuses to kill the Lord's anointed. He takes only Saul's spear and water jug. Saul admits his wrongdoing, and David trusts that God will deliver him.
sum.21: David flees to the cave of Adullam, where his family joins him along with about four hundred men who were in distress, and he leaves his parents in the care of the king of Moab. Saul, consumed by suspicion, has the priests of Nob killed through Doeg, and only Abiathar escapes. David feels responsible and offers him protection.
sum.12: Saul faces the Philistines, and when he sees the people growing frightened and deserting him, he offers the burnt offering without waiting for Samuel. Samuel rebukes him for not obeying the LORD and tells him that his kingdom will not last. Israel is left weak and without weapons, and obedience to God matters more than acting in a hurry.
